News.title: Body found in River Tyne during search for missing Gateshead man
News.content:
Body found in River Tyne during search for missing Gateshead man

The 20-year-old man, named only as 'John' by police, vanished on September 2 after he was last seen asking for directions in Gateshead near Newcastle

View Image A body has been found in the River Tyne (Image: Craig Connor/ChronicleLive)

A body has been found during a search for a young man who vanished after asking for directions near Newcastle.

‌



The 20-year-old, named as 'John' by police, from Gateshead, was reported missing on September 2 after he was last seen in Newcastle in the early hours of the morning.

‌



Northumbria Police conducted extensive enquiries to locate John, including a review of local CCTV and public appeals.

‌



Two people who were seen on CCTV speaking to John on Tower Street in Newcastle City Centre approached police to assist with their enquiries.

The individuals confirmed that at around 3am on September 2, John had asked them for directions before heading towards City Road.

‌



Sadly, a body matching the description of John was pulled from the River Tyne near Newcastle Quayside shortly after 11am on Wednesday, September 9.

Formal identification is yet to take place but John's next of kin have been notified. They are being supported by officers, reports Chronicle Live.

Detective Inspector Nick Went, of the Force's Missing Investigation Team, said: "This is an extremely sad development, and our thoughts are with John's family and friends.

Article continues below

"I would like to thank all of the officers involved in our investigation to locate John, along with everyone who shared our appeals and contacted us with information. It is much appreciated.

"We would continue to ask that people respect the family's privacy at this tragic time. As is standard practice, a report into John's death will now be prepared for the coroner."

News.title: Labour mayors in England vow to cap tourist tax at 5%
News.content:
Labour's regional mayors in England have pledged to cap a new fee on visitors' overnight stays at 5%, after hospitality bosses warned it could put jobs at risk.

Local leaders are set to gain new powers to charge an uncapped levy, dubbed a "tourist tax", as a percentage of the cost of hotels, bed and breakfasts and other types of accommodation.

But the Labour mayors in 10 city regions said they would voluntarily limit the charge if they do apply it, adding that they had listened to concerns over costs.

Reform UK's two regional mayors and the two Conservative ones are likely to oppose any levy given criticism from their national parties of the policy.

In a letter to Chancellor John Healey and Local Government Secretary Angela Rayner, the Labour metro mayors said 5% represented a "reasonable ceiling" on the tax.

"It provides a balance of ensuring that local levies are not excessive, or vary significantly between regions, while also leaving room for local variation as appropriate," they added.

They added this would still allow for "meaningful investment" in local areas, whilst stressing any future levies in their areas would be "subject to local consultation".

The letter was signed by Labour mayors in London, Greater Manchester, Liverpool City Region, West Midlands, North East, West of England, West Yorkshire, South Yorkshire, East Midlands and York and North Yorkshire.

The government had earlier pledged to protect budget holidays "by making sure low-cost accommodation always pays lowest levy" and said the extra cash could be invested in high streets and local transport.

While Labour mayors have backed the new levy, others have expressed caution or signalled they will not bring it in.

Local leaders, including heads of Foundation Strategic Authorities where there is no mayor, will need to clarify by early 2028 how the revenue raised should be reinvested.

They will also be allowed to offer exemptions, such as for campsites.

However, mayors will not be allowed to exempt whole localities within their regions from the tax, to avoid creating confusion for visitors and businesses.

The government said it would introduce a bill to Parliament "in due course" to bring in the levy, which would apply to both Britons and people visiting from abroad.

News.title: Oil, gas and borrowing costs surge as fears over Middle East escalate
News.content:
The price of oil has jumped to $105 a barrel amid signs the conflict in the Middle East will not be resolved quickly, fuelling fears that inflation could accelerate.

With the conflict between the US and Iran in the Gulf intensifying in recent days, the cost of both crude oil and gas has been rising sharply. Brent crude went back above $100 a barrel on Wednesday and has continued to climb.

The war has led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, preventing supplies of oil and gas from the Gulf from reaching global markets.

US and UK long-term borrowing costs also surged to their highest level in decades.

Speaking at a Republican Party convention in Texas on Wednesday, President Trump said he did not think the fighting would end until after the US mid-term elections in November.

Analysts said the combination of rising energy costs and higher borrowing costs was adding pressure on financial markets.

Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at trading platform IG, said investors were becoming increasingly concerned about the economic impact of higher oil prices.

"It feels like investors worldwide are now waking up to the crisis in oil markets," Beauchamp said. He warned that the surge in energy prices could weigh heavily on the global economy if it continues.

Concerns have also grown after Iran-aligned Houthi forces were reported to have seized Yemen's port of Mokha, a key Red Sea port.

The move could elevate fears of further shipping disruptions.

The price of natural gas has also been soaring on wholesale markets. In the UK, it rose above 200p a therm for the first time since the end of 2022.

Storage levels in Europe are much lower than normal for the time of year, and the need to fill reserves ahead of the winter has helped to push up prices.

News.title: Use all powers necessary on anti-migrant protests, home secretary tells police
News.content:
"These scenes have caused disruption for people and, given that people are dressed in black wearing balaclavas, there is a fear factor and obvious malign intent being communicated to our residents," the Home Secretary said.

"This makes it different from other protests, so we need to make sure we are learning lessons."

The BBC understands that police chiefs are now actively considering using recently-granted powers to completely ban face coverings in specific areas, in light of that demonstration.

Saturday's protest was followed 24 hours later with another in which men blocked the only road out of Langstone Harbour, near Portsmouth, after the RNLI had brought ashore 120 migrants.

It's unclear at this stage whether further such protests will go ahead - but in some areas of England local groups that have associated themselves with the Patriot Platform umbrella group have called for more demonstrations.

The meeting discussed the emergence of Patriot Platform with ministers believing the group aims to intimidate communities.

Mahmood is said to have told police chiefs to make better use of intelligence to make sure they had better plans in place ahead of this weekend.

That call came after Kent Police had earlier admitted it had been made aware of a potential demonstration in Dover but had not "fully assessed" the warning before the town's nationally critical port road was brought to a standstill.

During the meeting, Mahmood is said to have made clear the government expected police to make full use of powers and to deal robustly with any criminal offences.

Speaking after the meeting, Deputy Chief Constable Andy Mariner, the National Police Chiefs Council lead for public order, said forces were "continually assessing and preparing for protests and any potential impact on public safety".

This includes working closely with "local forces, specialist teams, communities and partners" to ensure support is available when needed.

He added: "Our priority is to keep people safe, maintain public order and support the right to peaceful and lawful protest. While people are entitled to express their views, anyone committing criminal offences can and should expect police action."

Major changes to protest law in the last three years mean officers can now intervene more quickly to end demonstrations that block critical national infrastructure, such as roads to ports.

They can also designate an entire area a face mask-free zone for the duration of a protest.

It's that second power that police chiefs are now considering using.

Police chiefs also say they have initiated an "enhanced and co-ordinated" approach to gathering as much intelligence as possible in the days ahead.

News.title: Watch: Is the Bayeux Tapestry exhibition worth the hype?
News.content:
Visitors flocked to the British Museum in London on Thursday as the Bayeux Tapestry exhibition opened its doors to the general public.

The Bayeux Tapestry is an embroidery almost 70m (230ft) in length and nearly 1,000 years old. It tells the story of the Norman conquest of England and the Battle of Hastings in 1066.

Adult tickets to see the tapestry are priced at Â£33 during peak times and Â£27 at off-peak times, with an additional Â£3.50 donation.

The BBC's Katie Razzall asked the first visitors if it was worth the price.

News.title: Four hurt and seven arrested in London stabbing
News.content:
Seven people have been arrested after four men were stabbed in south-east London, the Metropolitan Police has said.

One of the men remains in a critical condition in hospital, while the other three are being treated for injuries that are not believed to be life-threatening.

Paramedics and the London Air Ambulance were called at about 14:20 BST to Bromley High Street, where one eyewitness reported seeing a man wielding a machete.

A KFC spokesperson confirmed a "serious incident" had taken place at its Bromley High Street restaurant and an altercation had begun there. The company said it was assisting police and "supporting our team members and customers at this difficult time".

News.title: Drone display recreates the Twin Towers over New York City
News.content: According to organisers, 2,977 drones recreated the Twin Towers at full scale with each light representing a victim of the 9/11 attacks. The artwork, titled "2,977 Lights Over New York Harbor", is a commemorative public art installation in collaboration with artists, producers, and members of the 9/11 community, including victims' families, survivors, and first responders.

News.title: Esther Rantzen says she is too fragile to travel to Switzerland to end life
News.content:
Dame Esther Rantzen has said she is now "too physically fragile" to travel to Switzerland to end her life at an assisted suicide clinic.

The veteran broadcaster, 86, said she would have to fly to the country, where the practice is legal, alone, which she could only have done before her life became "unbearable" and before she was ready to end her life.

The Childline founder, who is terminally ill with cancer, first revealed in December 2023 that she had joined the Dignitas clinic.

Dame Esther used her statement on Thursday to reiterate a plea for MPs to vote in favour of legalising assisted dying in England and Wales when proposed legislation is revisited by Parliament on Friday.

She announced she had joined Dignitas about a year after being diagnosed with stage four lung cancer.

"Unfortunately, when I was strong enough to make the flight and go to Dignitas, my life was not unbearably painful, indeed I was able to relax in my beloved cottage in the New Forest," she said.

"And by the time life did become unbearable, I was too physically fragile to make the journey and go through the Dignitas process.

"So even though I had spent the money and made the plans, I was not ready to end my life back then, and did not realise that would be my last chance."

Dame Esther added that "everything I didn't want to happen I'm having to go through now", with loved ones either unable to visit her or "see me suffering pain or indignity" when they do.

The prominent assisted dying campaigner said the law - which she described as "messy and cruel" - must "change and change quickly".

Helping someone end their life is currently considered a criminal offence across England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Jersey legalised assisted dying for terminally ill adults earlier this year.

MPs are considering a draft law that, if passed, would make it legal in England and Wales under specific circumstances for people who are terminally ill with less than six months to live.

While Dame Esther, who is best known for presenting the BBC programme That's Life! for 21 years, is among several leading figures in favour of the bill, there are also campaigners against it, including Paralympian Baroness Grey-Thompson

They fear that a change in the law could mean that disabled and other vulnerable people could be pressured to end their lives, while also criticising the wording of the proposed legislation as not providing strong enough safeguards.

The bill has been through several drafts and has been scrutinised by several Parliamentary committees and the House of Lords, which submitted 1,200 amendments.

The bill was previously introduced in 2024, but the last session of Parliament ran out of time before it was passed.

It was reintroduced in this Parliament and a second vote will be held on Friday afternoon. If it passes the House of Commons, rarely invoked powers could be used, meaning it would not need the assent of the Lords to become law this time.

Proponents of the bill have indicated they would try to bring legislation again as soon as possible were it to be voted down on Friday.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he would not be voting on the issue and has suggested that palliative and social care should be better funded before legalising assisted suicide is considered.

Assisted dying is legal in a number of countries - including Canada, Australia and Belgium - as well as in Switzerland, though the circumstances under which it is legal differ between those nations.

News.title: Police and army attend funeral for officer killed in wrong-way A66 crash
News.content:
Police officers and army veterans gathered for the funeral of the second officer killed in a head-on crash.

PC Tom Clough, 38, died on the A66 in South Bank, near Middlesbrough, in the early hours of 22 August with his colleague PC Matthew Blades when a Volkswagen Passat hit their marked police car. Five young men in the Passat also died.

Members of the public also gathered for the funeral at Kirkleatham Walled Gardens, in Redcar, along with family, friends and former colleagues from British Transport Police and the Civil Nuclear Constabulary in Sellafield, Cumbria.

Cleveland Police Federation chair Lauren Somerville said PC Clough's partner said public support "brought them so much strength".

The ceremonial procession made its way along Plantation Road towards the Walled Gardens, accompanied by the music of a lone piper.

The road was lined on both sides with standard bearers who had lowered their flags before the cortege went past.

At its head was a mounted police unit of four horses.

Immediately behind them came the hearse carrying PC Clough's coffin, draped with the Union Flag and topped with his custodian helmet.

The hearse was flanked by officers in ceremonial dress escorting the coffin to the service.

News.title: Bayeux Tapestry unveiled to UK public for first time at British Museum
News.content:
Cecilia and Fabio Zanini were completely wowed by the scale of the Bayeux Tapestry.

"I was amazed by the vibrancy of the colours. The detail of the characters," Cecilia said. "It gave both of us goosebumps."

Fabio said he was constantly looking left and right to see all the action and he was surprised by the scale of the tapestry, particularly the number of Norman boats and cavalry.

"It feels like you're in the battlefield," he added, praising the "real sense of movement" in the embroidery.

"It really allowed you to go back to 1066."

But others told the BBC the event was "out of reach" because of its cost and London location.

Angie in Leeds said the "historic event" was "out of reach for many, many families in the north" when you factor in the cost of train tickets and food costs on top of the museum tickets themselves.

"London-only cultural events alienate many families north of Watford," she added.

Another man spoke of the "extreme queuing" required to view the exhibit. Hadyn Blakeston said he felt like he was on a "conveyor belt" while moving along the tapestry.

"It's one long queue," he said. "I know we're supposed to love queuing, but it was extreme queuing."

News.title: Teacher sexually abused pupils at multiple schools
News.content:
A teacher has been found guilty of sexually abusing a 16-year-old boy after previously admitting offences against two teenage girls.

Former PE teacher Bronwen James, 30, of Chippenham, Wiltshire, admitted nine sexual offences against two teenage girls - one a pupil at Bitterne Park School in Southampton and the other at Hardenhuish School in Chippenham.

She was convicted earlier at Winchester Crown Court of three counts of sexual activity with a 16-year-old boy who also attended Bitterne Park School.

During the trial the prosecution said James "craved" attention and "abused the trust put in her" as a teacher.

The jury found James guilty of the three counts of sexual activity with a child by a person in a position of trust by a majority of 11 to one and acquitted her of a fourth charge.

Due to legal restrictions covering the trial, media had been unable to report James' guilty pleas against two girls - which she made in January - and the jury were not told about them until after they had passed their verdict.

News.title: Theatregoer who throttled woman at show is jailed
News.content:
A 75-year-old man who strangled a woman after she started to sing along at a West End show has been jailed for two years.

Malcolm Potier was sitting near victim Kirsty O'Donnell in the audience at We Will Rock You at the London Coliseum in June 2023.

He said he had no recollection of being at the show, or of attacking O'Donnell, but was sentenced at Southwark Crown Court on Thursday after being found guilty of non-fatal strangulation by jurors.

Potier, a businessman and surveyor of Sarratt near Watford, was already jailed in Australia two decades ago having twice tried to arrange the murder of a former partner following a dispute over their child.

He is also the former laird - a Scottish term for someone owning a large long-established estate - of the Hebridean island of Gigha.

Judge Dafna Spiro said his behaviour was "extreme and horrific".

"It is an unusual offence," she said. "It's not a situation I have ever come across before."

She said there was a "thread" of "dominance, control and lack of accountability" in Potier's behaviour.

News.title: Father of A66 teen charged with funeral assault
News.content:
The father of one of the five men who were killed in a wrong-way crash with a police car has been charged with assaulting someone at his son's funeral.

Gye Worthy, 39, was arrested at Teesside Crematorium in Middlesbrough following a disturbance during the service on Wednesday.

His son Cole Worthy, 17, died when the Volkswagon Passat he and four others were in collided with a marked armed police car on the A66 in South Bank in the early hours of 22 August.

Cleveland Police said Gye Worthy has been charged with common assault and obstructing police and is due to appear at Teesside Magistrates' Court in October.

Cole Worthy's funeral was held on the same day as that of PC Matthew Blades, 37, who was one of the officers killed in the crash.

PC Blades had been travelling along the A66 with his colleague PC Tom Clough when their car was struck head-on by the Passat travelling in the wrong direction.

The pair were in a vehicle looking for the Passat after its cloned registration plates triggered a camera, although they were not involved in the pursuit which preceded the crash, according to the Independent Office for Police Conduct.

News.title: Ex-Tory campaign chief pleads guilty over election bet
News.content:
The Conservatives' former director of campaigning and his wife have pleaded guilty to cheating at gambling by placing bets on the date of the 2024 general election.

Anthony Lee stood to win approximately Â£15,000 after placing more than 60 successful bets totalling Â£1,549, the Gambling Commission said.

He passed confidential information to his wife about when former Prime Minister Rishi Sunak was planning to call the general election.

Laura Lee, who was a parliamentary candidate at the time, placed eight successful bets on the election date totalling Â£535 and would have profited by around Â£5,000.

On Thursday at Southwark Crown Court, Anthony Lee pleaded guilty to two offences and Laura Lee pleaded guilty to one offence.

They will be sentenced in October.

The trials of 10 other defendants will take place in September 2027 and January 2028.

Former MP Craig Williams, who was Sunak's closest parliamentary aide at the time, pleaded guilty in June and will be sentenced at a later date.

In Williams' case, the prosecution said he bet Â£250, Â£100, and Â£22.50 on the date of the 2024 election, telling the court he "used highly sensitive and confidential information".

When details of the scandal first emerged in June 2024, Williams admitted making a "huge error of judgment".

Sunak's decision to call the poll was a surprise to many, including many Conservative MPs, who were expecting an autumn date.

The Conservative Party has been approached for comment.

News.title: Catherine joins William as he says sport can save lives from suicide
News.content:
It was important that sports stars admitted their own vulnerability, said Olympic cyclist Dame Laura Kenny.

She spoke movingly of how a family member had tried to take their life and how she felt "almost ashamed to admit that this could happen in my family because it's not a subject that is easily spoken about".

The cyclist also described the darkness of her feelings after the loss of two babies, through a miscarriage and an ectopic pregnancy, "which ultimately ended up in an emergency situation".

On Your Side aims to use the reach of sport to raise awareness about suicide and to show people the help available in a crisis, with the Football Association, Premier League and Team GB providing support.

The level of suicide is disproportionately higher among men than women - it is the biggest cause of death for men under the age of 50 in the UK - and sport is seen as an effective way of communicating that help is available.

"My hope is that every sporting organisation in the country will look at what is being launched today and ask a question: 'What more can we do?' Because the opportunity before us is enormous," Prince William said.

The royal couple saw a bench at the ground dedicated in memory of Gary Speed, a footballer who once played at the club, and who died by suicide in 2011.

The bench, unveiled last year, is intended to give people a space to speak openly about their anxieties and the royal couple met Speed's mother there.

Shearer was a friend of Speed and is backing the call for people to try to support people they have worries about.

"You don't have to be an expert. You don't have to have all the answers," said Shearer. "But we can all be better at asking, listening, and helping someone find the right support."

News.title: Two arrested in London on suspicion of assisting Iran's intelligence service
News.content:
Two people have been arrested in London on suspicion of assisting Iran's intelligence service, the Metropolitan Police has said.

A 60-year-old man and 42-year-old woman were arrested at properties in London on Wednesday as part of an investigation into suspected National Security Act (NSA) offences.

The suspects, who were both held on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service, have been released on bail under strict conditions until late October, the Met said.

Police said the arrests were not "connected to any of the incidents or attacks" linked to Jewish and Iranian communities across London earlier this year.

The arrests took place following two searches carried out at properties in north and north-west London in June, the Met added.

Commander Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said she knows "news of these arrests will come as a concern to some members of the public" but stressed she does "not believe there to be any imminent threat to the wider public".

She added: "We've seen a marked increase in the tempo of our work linked to national security and state threats over the past year and this investigation is a continuation of that.

"As we've shown here, if we suspect any activity could threaten the safety of the UK or the public, then we will not hesitate to take action."

She added the UK's terror threat level was severe and called for people to be vigilant.

News.title: Michael Sheen says he was snubbed by first minister over toxic pollution claims
News.content:
Michael Sheen says an offer to meet Wales' first minister over claims people have been poisoned by decades of exposure to toxic waste dumps "was not taken up".

The Welsh actor contacted Rhun ap Iorwerth ahead of a BBC documentary which looked into claims of widespread chemical contamination in Wales.

In Parliament on Thursday, Sheen urged MPs to back a national testing programme for historic toxic dumps to make sure sites were safe, after high levels of cancer-causing chemicals - known as PCBs - were found in soil samples and in the blood of people living near sites linked to chemical giant Monsanto.

Eastman Chemical Company, which is responsible for its legacy production, was asked to comment.

The Welsh government said addressing the issue of contaminated land was "a key priority".

One MP at the UK Parliament committee hearing later suggested to the BBC that there was confusion about whether it was the Welsh or UK government that would be responsible for any testing.

Lawmakers from New Mexico have urged Apple and Google not to rename the state on their mapping apps after President Donald Trump suggested restyling it as “New America.”

On Thursday, the state’s congressional delegation — five Democrats — sent letters to the executives of both tech companies, asking them to “publicly commit” to keeping New Mexico on Apple Maps and Google Maps.

“Let us be clear: the President has no legal authority to rename New Mexico,” the lawmakers wrote. “Our state’s name belongs to the people of New Mexico and is rooted in our history and our Constitution, which clearly states that ‘the name of this state is New Mexico.’”

Trump, who over the weekend posted at least seven maps labeling New Mexico as “New America,” has demonstrated that his renaming push is more than just a trolling attempt.

Last month, amid his trade war with Canada, he signed an executive order directing federal agencies to refer to Lake Ontario as “Lake America.” Last January, he signed a similar order rebranding the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America.”

open image in gallery Lawmakers from New Mexico urged Apple and Google not to rename their state on their map services, following President Donald Trump's weekend posting spree indicating he would like the state to be called 'New America' ( @RealDonaldTrump, Truth Social )

While the president can direct how the federal government refers to geographic features, he cannot compel foreign nations, private entities or even U.S. states to follow his lead.

Yet, both Google and Apple have updated their maps so that users in the U.S. see the new Trump-given names for both the Gulf of Mexico and Lake Ontario.

“These updates follow our long-standing policy for bodies of water with names that vary from country to country, and are starting to roll out now,” Google said in a blog post.

The New Mexico lawmakers described these changes as “disappointing but unsurprising,” pointing out that both companies “have significant business interests before the federal government.”

open image in gallery Senator Ben Ray Luján was one of five New Mexico Democrats to sign the letters sent to Apple and Google executives ( Getty Images )

Since Trump’s return to office, the two companies have seemingly moved to cozy up with the administration. Both donated to Trump’s planned White House ballroom project, and executives from each attended his second inauguration last January. In a separate gesture last year, then-Apple CEO Tim Cook presented Trump with a 24-karat gold statue.

“Because of this history, we ask each of you to publicly commit that Apple Maps and Google Maps will continue to identify the State of New Mexico as New Mexico, regardless of what the President posts on social media, what executive order he attempts to issue, or what pressure he puts on your companies,” the lawmakers wrote.

The state’s delegation includes Senators Ben Ray Luján and Martin Heinrich, and Representatives Teresa Leger Fernández, Melanie Stansbury and Gabe Vasquez.

The Independent has contacted Google and Apple for comment.

Diesel prices in California are so high that some gas stations can't show the correct price on their pumps.

Patrick De Haan, the head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, found that five California gas stations have hit $9.999 per gallon — the maximum price that gas stations can show on their digital displays, which typically only display four digits.

The report is based on GasBuddy's data. The cities and specific stations were not identified in De Haan's post, but he showed a screenshot of the reported prices. GasBuddy is known for tracking gas prices as stations across the nation.

As of September 9, California's average diesel price was $7.76 per gallon, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. The increase comes as the U.S. war in Iran wears on and the world faces a limited supply after the Strait of Hormuz was closed.

That price was a 55-cent increase from a week prior, and up $2.81 from this time last year.

A man fills his car with gas at a New York gas station. Some gas stations in California has reportedly maxed out their displays, showing diesel prices on September 10 at $9.999 per gallon, according to a GasBuddy report ( Getty )

Diesel also hit a new high nationwide; the U.S. average for diesel hit a record $5.87 per gallon, topping the previous high of $5.81 that was set in June 2022.

The U.S. Energy Information Administration reports that national diesel prices were up 3.7 cents week over week and $1.97 year over year.

Reports of extremely high prices at individual gas stations have been plaguing California. At one station in Fenner, California, prices for regular gas were reportedly $9.69 per gallon, according to CBS 12 News.

In May, a Chevron station in downtown Los Angeles reportedly was charging $8.89 per gallon for diesel and $8.29 for regular gasoline.

Regulators in California have reportedly launched an investigation into extreme fuel pricing at individual stations in the San Bernardino and Los Angeles areas, though no alleged outliers have been proven.

President Donald Trump, whose war in Iran has been a major driver of high fuel prices, admitted that oil prices are not likely to fall until at least after the midterm elections.

"Right after the election, oil prices are going to be tumbling downward. They're going to be tumbling down, and we'll get them down. I think for gasoline we'll get them below $2 a gallon," Trump said Wednesday.

Trump has been insisting that gas prices will come down when the war ends since the early spring, just after he joined Israel in striking Iran. Then, he complained that prices weren't coming down fast enough in June.

"Customers are being 'gouged,'" Trump wrote in a Truth Social post at the time. "Gasoline prices better start going down a lot faster than what I'm seeing!"

They have remained high since his post, and show no signs of decreasing in the immediate future.

Trump has been desperate to try to force U.S. gas prices lower ahead of the midterms. He has even authorized the tapping of the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, which the U.S. maintains as an emergency stockpile of crude oil.

The president authorized the release of 172 million barrels of oil from the reserve earlier this year. Last week, the reserve fell by approximately 1.2 million barrels to 285.4 million barrels, according to Department of Energy data.

Pierce Brosnan has played down reports of friction on the set of MobLand involving his co-star Tom Hardy, saying the alleged disputes were a "storm in a teacup".

The Guy Ritchie crime drama, which also features Dame Helen Mirren, attracted media attention during the shooting of its second series following reports of conflict among the cast.

Hardy was rumoured to have delayed his fellow actors during filming and reportedly clashed with show co-creators Ronan Bennett and Jez Butterworth, raising questions over whether he would return for a third run.

Speaking at the series premiere in central London, Brosnan, 73, who reprised his role as the fierce head of a powerful mob family, Conrad Harrigan, said: “Oh my God, it was a storm in a teacup, really.

“I love the dude. I love Tom Hardy. I’m a massive fan of the man’s work. Truly.

“We are rock solid as a company, as a family.

Brosnan described the Moblans cast as a ‘family’ ( AP )

“Everyone shows up for work, and everybody’s just there on the spot. It moves very fast so it’s not like we go out and socialise and go to the pub or anything like that.

“Everyone goes home to their families and before you know it, you’ve done 10 episodes.”

The upcoming series will see the Harrigan family struggle to show a united front while confronted with increasing rivals – with “fixer” Harry Da Souza, played by Hardy, at the centre of the drama.

Hardy, 48, said it was a “privilege” to work with Brosnan and Dame Helen, and watch the actors continue “pushing the envelope”.

He said: “They’re awesome. In many aspects of course I look up to them. Coming up, these are actors that came before me.

“So to be able to work with them is a privilege, but also to be able to enjoy them, watching them spread their wings with their range now as well, and play against their type in some aspects, and really enjoy that is a beautiful thing to watch as a human being.

“These guys are really talented and they’re having a lot of fun. That’s beautiful.

“Taking it away as a person, just watching people enjoy themselves and watching a good team work together and having fun.

“That exists in the MobLand tribe, and Dame Helen and Pierce are of that family so in that respect, not only just to be a part of it, but to watch and observe them still enjoying themselves and pushing the envelope is brilliant.”

Dame Helen, 81, who portrays powerful matriarch Maeve Harrigan, said she hopes to have more scenes with Hardy in the third series, which was recently renewed.

She said: “The relationships are amazing. Obviously, Pierce and I have an extraordinary chemistry on-screen and off-screen. We’re very, very fond of each other. We respect each other enormously.”

She said she unfortunately did not have a lot of scenes with Hardy in the second series, however, she hopes to share the screen with him more in the next one.

MobLand series two will premiere globally on Paramount+ on September 18.

News.title: Lindsay Clancy’s attorney urges judge to acquit her to avoid a second trial
News.content:

Lindsay Clancy’s defense attorney has asked a judge to acquit her, arguing she shouldn’t be tried a second time for killing her three young children because prosecutors don’t have enough evidence.

Attorney Kevin Reddington is urging the court to rule that she’s not guilty by reason of insanity after 11 of 12 jurors were ready to clear Clancy of criminal responsibility last Friday. They were unable to come to a unanimous decision, forcing Judge William Sullivan to declare a mistrial.

Prosecutors have yet to say whether they'll seek to put the 36-year-old former labor and delivery nurse on trial again. Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz said on Friday that the decision would be announced at a later date.

Neither side disputed that Clancy strangled 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan Clancy in the family's home in 2023 before trying to end her own life. But her attorney said she was a loving mother in the grip of a rare condition called postpartum psychosis, while prosecutors argued she knew what she was doing.

open image in gallery Lindsay Clancy and her attorney, Kevin Reddington, at her murder trial ( Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger vía AP )

The trial generated intense interest for weeks, drawing attention to maternal mental health after childbirth.

Under Massachusetts law, prosecutors had to prove either that Clancy did not have a mental disease or defect or that, despite having one, she retained the substantial capacity to appreciate the wrongfulness of her actions or conform her conduct to the law.

Reddington argued in Thursday’s court filing that prosecutors proved neither, and asked Sullivan to consider the motion at a court conference scheduled for Sept. 29.

The defense attorney said none of the psychiatric experts, either called by the prosecution or defense, disputed that Clancy was suffering from a mental illness. “The testimony bears on which illness she had, not on whether she had one,” he wrote.

Prosecutors pointed to Clancy’s actions in the weeks, days and hours leading up to the killings — driving, planning a child’s birthday party, bringing her daughter to a doctor’s appointment — and her ability to perform other everyday tasks as evidence she was of sound mind when the killings took place.

open image in gallery Lindsay Clancy’s ex-husband, Patrick Clancy, with their three young children before their killings ( GoFundMe )

“Competence at routine tasks,” Reddington argued Thursday, “during a crisis which every witness agreed was acute, is not proof of criminal responsibility beyond a reasonable doubt.”

Reddington has also asked President Donald Trump to pardon her, saying on Tuesday, “Mr. President, I would hope that you would consider this young lady — the type of person she is, what she’s been through — and consider a pardon.”

The judge acknowledged during jury deliberations that the trial had been emotionally and physically exhausting for everyone. Much of the testimony was excruciating to hear, from the heartbreaking 911 call made by the children’s father who found their bodies, to the descriptions of how they died.

Clancy was brought to tears several times. At one point, the judge called a short break as Clancy’s loud sobs filled the courtroom while the children’s autopsy photos were shown.

She remains paralyzed from the waist down after jumping from the home's second story, and is expected to stay at a psychiatric hospital until her case is resolved.

If you are experiencing feelings of distress, or are struggling to cope, you can speak to the Samaritans, in confidence, on 116 123 (UK and ROI) or visit the Samaritans website to find details of your nearest branch.

If you are based in the USA, and you or someone you know needs mental health assistance right now, call or text 988, or visit 988lifeline.org to access online chat from the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. This is a free, confidential crisis hotline that is available to everyone 24 hours a day, seven days a week. If you are in another country, you can go to www.befrienders.org to find a helpline near you

News.title: Man United v Sabah LIVE: Lisandro Martinez extends lead for rampant home side on Champions League return
News.content:
Copa Independent | Why the Premier League's financial might still can't bully Europe's giants in the Champions League

Manchester United’s long-awaited Champions League return has been a happy one so far, with the Premier League side 4-0 up against Sabah.

United are back among the European elite for the first time since 2023, a spell of just over 1,000 days, after Michael Carrick’s transformative impact last season, with the manager now hoping to build on a slightly sluggish start domestically.

With a new-look midfield still bedding in, the United boss rotated slightly here, with a short turnaround to Sunday’s Manchester derby to come. Still, his team has had little trouble in pulling clear of Sabah – the champions of Azerbaijan and Champions League debutants here.

Matheus Cunha broke the deadlock just before the half-hour mark, and his close-range finish was followed by two goals in quick succession just before the break; Bruno Fernandes struck first, with Benjamin Sesko getting in on the act right after. Then, in the second half, Lisandro Martinez made it 4-0.

Follow all of the latest from the Champions League clash with our live blog below:

News.content:

A decision on stripping Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor of his Freedom of the City of London will be made as “a matter of urgency”, the City of London Corporation (CLC) said, as the corporation has approved a process to remove the honour from recipients itself.

CLC, the body which administers the ancient city centre, said on Thursday its court of common council, the organisation’s main decision-making body, had approved a process enabling the honour to be removed from individuals.

open image in gallery Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor (Jordan Pettitt/PA). ( PA Wire )

Elected members approved an act of common council, giving the court the power to remove a freedom.

The decision followed a legal review which concluded that there had been no effective lawful way to do so.

Under the new process, each case would be considered on its individual circumstances and in accordance with the law, CLC said, with the person concerned informed and given opportunities to make written representations before a final decision is made.

The new process will now begin for the disgraced former prince Andrew, after the corporation instructed officers to pursue steps to lawfully remove the honour.

open image in gallery Police stand guard at an entrance to Wood Farm on the royal family's Sandringham Estate in Norfolk, eastern England on February 21, 2026, after Britain's former prince Andrew was arrested on February 19 ( AFP/Getty )

In May, CLC criticised Andrew for failing to surrender his Freedom of the City of London “despite being asked to do so”.

The disgraced former prince inherited the freedom, one of his final remaining honours, in 2012 by patrimony, as the child of a freeman.

It is understood the proposal to strip Andrew of the honour will return to the court of common council for a decision in December.

CLC’s policy chairman, Chris Hayward, said: “Today, we have approved a lawful and effective process for considering whether the Freedom of the City of London should be removed from an individual.

“This ensures that future decisions are taken fairly, transparently, and in accordance with the law, with appropriate safeguards in place for all parties involved.

“The process will now be followed as a matter of urgency to ensure that a decision is made in relation to Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor’s Freedom.”

News.content:

Not a single federal judge has granted Donald Trump’s administration access to voter files in any of the 30 states where the Department of Justice is fighting a legal battle for sensitive data for millions of Americans.

After 23 straight losses in court, the Justice Department is now sending threatening letters to election officials, warning states that they are “currently under investigation” and subject to “ongoing litigation” for access to records related to the 2024 election.

That was news to Utah’s Republican Lt. Governor Deidre Henderson.

“Um, no, I was not aware, but I guess I am now,” she wrote on social media Wednesday, along with a copy of a letter from the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division. “It would be nice if the good folks at the DOJ would focus on actual problems instead of baselessly harassing election officials.”

Nevada’s Secretary of State Cisco Aguilar received a similar letter, which was in reference to the “Maintenance of All Election Records in Your Possession as Chief Election Officer During Pending Litigation.” He called the letter a “pretty direct threat.”

open image in gallery Democratic and Republican election officials in at least 30 states received letters from the Department of Justice threatening potential legal action as the Trump administration pushes states to retain sensitive voter files for opaque reasons ( Getty )

“They’re just using this as an opportunity to intimidate us, and I’m not going to fold in any way,” he told The Nevada Independent.

Similar letters were sent to more than two dozen other state election officials as the Trump administration wages a government-wide effort to assume federal control of the nation’s elections and restrict ballot access for tens of thousands of voters.

It’s unclear what, exactly, the Justice Department is investigating.

The letters don’t point to any criminal statutes or make any specific allegations of wrongdoing, but the pressure campaign follows the Trump administration’s efforts to identify alleged fraud in the nation’s elections, which the president baselessly insists are being manipulated by noncitizen voters and Democratic officials.

The Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division chief Harmeet Dhillon said her office sent the letters to “states that refused to comply with federal law” and have not provided her with voter registration lists.

“We sent the letter to ensure these states do not destroy election records related to our ongoing lawsuits,” she wrote Thursday. “This is standard litigation practice, not a ‘threat.’ We appreciate all states that cooperated with our data requests!”

open image in gallery Nevada Secretary of State Cisco Aguilar says the DOJ’s pressure campaign appears to be an attempt to ‘intimidate’ election officials ( AFP/Getty )

The letter says the Justice Department is enforcing election rules under the Civil Rights Act, but judges have repeatedly decided that the federal government does not have permission to vacuum up state data. The Justice Department has been seeking access to unredacted voter registration databases that contain sensitive information for virtually every voter in the U.S., including driver’s licenses and partial Social Security numbers.

The Civil Rights Act requires state election officials to preserve all voting records for 22 months after an election, which expired last week for the 2024 general election. But the Justice Department argues that the information must be retained while states are under litigation.

“Your failure to preserve relevant data may constitute spoliation of evidence, which may subject you to civil and criminal sanctions,” the letter says.

“It’s just one thing after another,” Henderson told The Salt Lake Tribune.

“Running elections is a lot of work, it’s very complicated, and it’s not something you can just pivot from all the time,” she said. “All of the things that have happened have been just way outside the scope of my imagination. Never expected to have the federal government insert themselves to this degree.”

open image in gallery The DOJ has lost 23 straight cases in its blitz of lawsuits for sensitive voter data, which federal judges across the ideological spectrum have uniformly shot down ( AFP/Getty )

If the Justice Department truly cared about election security, “you would not be threatening election officials with prison sentences, you would not be suing all of us, you would not be investigating all of us constantly,” Henderson added. “You would not be making it so that we’re not able to do our actual jobs.”

Election law expert David Becker with the Center for Election Innovation and Research said the letters appear to be "completely meaningless.”

“There’s only two reasons to send that letter: Either the lawyers who send it don’t understand litigation obligations, or they’re hoping that states will misinterpret it and retain more than they’re legally required,” he told The New York Times.

Despite losing every legal battle for voter data so far, the Justice Department continues to appeal orders against it.

The government announced Wednesday that it is appealing a West Virginia ruling after losing a case against the state’s Republican Secretary of State Kris Warner.

In his July order tossing the case, District Judge Thomas Johnson, who was appointed by George W. Bush, appeared frustrated by the wave of lawsuits filed by the government.

“Given the lack of an adequate basis or purpose, one is left to wonder what the real purpose was for the Justice Department to go to the trouble of filing civil actions like this one all around the nation,” he wrote. “Troubling though this question is, it is not before the Court at this time.”

News.title: Stephen Fleming learning nothing from rout of Pakistan
News.content:
Stephen Fleming arrives next week to start his job as England Test coach and his first task will be to apply his famously meticulous mind to assess a whitewash of Pakistan.

England are not quite there yet. Rain denied them a two-day win at Edgbaston, Pakistan finishing 52 for two, another 268 behind after England’s 453 all out.

But when the game does finish, and England complete a rout that started with Ollie Robinson taking a wicket with the first ball of the series, it will be time to look ahead to a proper challenge: a three-match series against Test champions South Africa over Christmas.

That series will give Fleming a much better guide to where his team stand in the lead-up to the Ashes summer. This one is less clearcut. Fleming has been in daily contact with Joe Root and will lean heavily on him and Marcus North. the national selector, for insight, but drawing definitive conclusions is impossible because of the lack of competitive cricket.

A quartet of quicks has emerged, led by Robinson, whose 21 wickets in the series at 6.6 look like a misprint. A double-wicket maiden to start Pakistan’s second innings would normally be headline-grabbing stuff. This time it felt almost predictable, even disappointing for those wanting to see some sort of contest.

News.title: West Nile virus hits Europe as temperatures climb
News.content:
“The future looks rosy for West Nile virus and other mosquito-borne viruses that follow it to the New World,” wrote the science writer Carl Zimmer in his 2011 book ‘Planet of Viruses’.

“That’s because the future is going to be warm and wet.”

More than a decade on, and after a record-setting hot summer, Mr Zimmer’s prediction has come to pass: the mosquito-borne disease, once confined mostly to the warmest parts of Africa, has become firmly entrenched in Europe, experts have warned.

At least 1,086 locally acquired cases of West Nile virus have been recorded across the continent over the last three months, as mosquitoes continue their slow march northwards.

The insects – which are cold-blooded – need warm weather to accelerate their life cycles and survive long enough to spread disease.

Across July and August, countries including Italy, Spain and France recorded West Nile cases in previously unaffected regions and cities, while others, including the Netherlands, recorded their first deaths from the virus this summer.

“I don’t think there are any more ‘tropical viruses’... the geographic barrier of these viruses no longer exists because of climate change,” said Dr Krishanthi Subramaniam, a microbiology lecturer at the University of Liverpool.

News.title: Britain pioneers new dried blood products for the modern battlefield
News.content:
A powdered blood product that can be mixed with water and used in minutes could help solve the challenges of treating severely wounded soldiers on hard-to-reach battlefields.

Britain is rethinking how to get blood to soldiers on the frontline, in the latest sign that the war in Ukraine has forced Western militaries to reconsider assumptions about modern combat medicine that had held since Iraq and Afghanistan.

The product, known as “spray-dried plasma”, is made by turning liquid plasma – the clotting-rich component of blood – into a stable powder that can be stored at room temperature for years before being rehydrated with water when needed.

“Plasma is vital for saving soldiers in war zones,” said Dr Ian Nesbitt, a former military anaesthetist and Faculty Lead for Anaesthesia at the David Nott Foundation, which trains doctors working in conflict zones.

“It helps blood clot when someone is injured. But in war zones, getting plasma to soldiers is incredibly complicated. It’s actually the logistics of it that are a real problem in maintaining a reliable supply of fresh frozen plasma for acutely injured patients.”

The NHS and the UK Ministry of Defence signed a strategic partnership this summer to jointly develop new blood products for frontline soldiers, focusing on dried plasma.

The agreement formalises work under way with a biotechnology company called Velico Medical. If successful, it will be used in future battlefields like the one in Ukraine.

“The war in Ukraine has woken up all countries, not just the UK,” Professor Renata Gomes, Chief Scientific Officer at NHS Blood and Transplant (NHSBT), told The Telegraph.

News.title: Mosquitoes are evolving to evade bed nets – but there may be a solution
News.content:
In Papua’s low-lying mangrove swamps and dense tropical rainforests, mosquitoes have always got to work early.

Here, the disease-ridden insects begin feeding in the early evening as people socialise and children play. It’s a characteristic that’s hampered malaria control efforts, because it has rendered bed nets less effective. People are bitten before they climb under the netting to sleep.

It’s also part of the reason that Indonesian Papua remains one of Asia’s most persistent malaria hotspots. Last year, cases across the country jumped by 30 per cent, to 706,000 new infections. The vast majority, roughly 90 per cent, were reported in Papua’s six provinces.

The same pattern is now emerging in parts of sub-Saharan Africa, where mosquitoes used to bite mostly at night and where the rollout of insecticide-treated bed nets is estimated to have averted 450 million malaria cases between 2000 and 2015, according to modelling in Nature journal.

A number of studies suggest mosquitoes in Africa are evolving in response to the mass rollout of bed nets, biting earlier in the evening, or later in the morning. In some cases, species which already did this have become more dominant, while others are adapting their habits.

“We’re battling evolution. And right now, we’re losing,” said Prof Neil Lobo, a research professor in the Eck Institute for Global Health at the University of Notre Dame.

“Mosquitoes are adapting. They’re biting outdoors, they’re biting earlier in the evening when people aren’t under their nets, and they’re becoming resistant to the insecticides we use. So we’re reaching the limits of what bed nets alone can do,” he told The Telegraph.

But there may be a solution.

News.title: Palmer and Rogers complete 12-minute rescue mission to save Chelsea
News.content:
Xabi Alonso needed the cavalry – and referee Jarred Gillett – to stop Chelsea making a quick exit from the Carabao Cup and, boy, did they come up trumps for him.

Chelsea had looked to be heading out of the competition shortly after half-time, but, in Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers, Alonso has a cheat code that is capable of masking even the worst defending.

Alonso’s side have shared 26 goals in the five games they have played this season. It has certainly been an entertaining start by Chelsea’s latest manager.

Palmer, Rogers and Pedro Neto stepped off the substitutes’ bench to complete a stunning rescue mission against Leeds United. Palmer scored twice, Neto once and Rogers helped himself to at least a hat-trick of assists. He claimed it was four, but the record books may say three.

When it was announced Palmer had been awarded the player of the match, Rogers responded by saying: “Mate, I got four assists. I can’t believe that! That’s mental. He scored a pen!”

News.title: Martin Odegaard bails out comically wasteful Arsenal
News.content:
In five matches this season, Odegaard has already scored four goals. That is three more than he managed in the whole of last season. The Arsenal captain is fit again and he is flowing. As ever, when Odegaard flows, Arsenal flow.

“That’s what we need, the players with that mindset to decide the game and play with that personality,” said Mikel Arteta. “He has got that edge. He’s getting into those positions much more in recent games.”

In the end it was a thoroughly deserved victory for the Premier League side, who were superior to Napoli in every department. Were it not for their comically bad finishing, they would have guaranteed the result long before Odegaard’s 75th-minute strike.

Their expected goals figure suggested they should have scored more than four goals, compared to Napoli’s 0.22. In total, they registered 26 shots – the most of any Arsenal team on record in a single Champions League match, and the most on record a Napoli team has ever faced.

“With the amount of chances we generated, the scoreline has to reflect a very different result,” said Arteta. “The number of players that got into this situation, the amount of situations that we generated in various ways was something that pleased me a lot.”

News.title: Mac Allister not so sad now after Liverpool comeback winner
News.content:
Do your talking on the pitch, as the old adage goes, and Alexis Mac Allister emphatically did just that as Liverpool came from behind to thrillingly win their first Champions League tie under new head coach Andoni Iraola in what was his debut at this level.

On the eve of this encounter, against a strong Atlético Madrid, one of the clubs who have recently tried to sign him, Mac Allister had spoken of his sadness. Sadness that, unlike fellow midfielders Dominik Szoboszlai – Liverpool’s other scorer here – and Ryan Gravenberch, he had not been offered and signed a new contract.

So, earn it. And many more goals – and overall performances like this – there is no doubt the Argentinian will have a deal placed in front of him. He scored with an arresting second-half shot, which proved to be the winner, and the smile across his face said it all. Not so sad now as he was later substituted to a standing ovation with Gravenberch taking his place.

The goal came early in the second half, with Iraola attributing that to adjusting his tactics after being flummoxed by Atlético’s back five and packed midfield in a first half when Liverpool were second best.

Mac Allister was heavily involved through the build-up, eventually picking out Rio Ngumoha on the left whose shot was blocked and pinballed around. It dropped to Mac Allister, 20 yards out, and he hit the kind of unerring drive that gives the goalkeeper no chance. And so it proved. Boom. And Anfield was bouncing.

Sports.title: Champions League manager RESIGNS with immediate effect in live press conference minutes after match
Sports.content:
FENERBAHCE boss Ismail Kartal resigned from his role in a press conference just minutes after his side’s draw with Roma.

The Turkish team had produced a 1-1 stalemate in their first Champions League league phase game before the abrupt announcement.

He said: “I thank my players tonight and I am resigning from my position. I have made this decision to pave the way for my club.



“I am resigning while there is still time. I am resigning with the understanding that I will never return.”



More to follow.

Sports.title: ‘World’s greatest stadium’ could start life in second tier with crisis club set to move into new 65,000-seater arena
Sports.content:
VALENCIA could open their new 70,000-capacity stadium in Spain’s second tier after their dismal start to the LaLiga season.

The Spanish outfit are rock bottom of the league after one draw and three defeats.



The crisis club were hammered 5-0 at home to Barcelona last time out and there are concerns they could be heading for the Segunda Division.

On top of that, there is discontent among fans towards owner Peter Lim, with protests outside the Mestalla after their thrashing by Barca.



The team’s severe injury crisis hasn’t helped either with key players like Sergi Canos, Diego Lopez, Justin de Haas and Mouctar Diakhaby all out.

Now there are fears their new stadium – which is expected to cost around £275million – could be hosting the team in Spain’s second tier.



The new ground is expected to be ready by the end of next summer following a lengthy delay.

Incredibly, construction begun nearly 20 years ago in 2007 before it was paused due to the club’s financial woes.

Construction eventually resumed in January 2025 after nearly 16 years of inactivity.

Some believe it will be one of the greatest stadiums of its kind in the world.

According to Stadium DB, the stadium’s construction is entering a “complex” stage as more than 100 hydraulic jacks are used to lift the 4,800-tonne roof.

Known as ‘The Big Lift’, it will be supported by 50 large steel pillars before work progresses to walkways and the stadium’s outer appearance.

Club CEO Ron Gourlay previously said the stadium was a symbol of Lim’s commitment to Valencia despite calls for him to sell.

He said: “ I don’t think the owner is going to leave the club, and the club is moving forward with Nou Mestalla, which is almost finished and will be very positive. The test will come then; there will be no excuses .



Gourlay added: “[The stadium] is our way of generating income and resources to comply with this regulation.

“It will create many opportunities commercially, in marketing, and opportunities at both a national and global level.”

There is already rising pressure on boss Carlos Corberan, who gave a bleak assessment of the club’s “difficult” situation last weekend.



He said: “It’s a situation that has affected us all, but it’s not one that has left us dejected.

“It’s a difficult situation that we will navigate together, that we will look at with great sincerity and honesty, and as a team we will seek solutions to turn this situation around.

Sports.title: Morocco claim they WILL host World Cup 2030 final reigniting blazing feud with Spain after Infantino claim
Sports.content:
THE head of the Moroccan FA claims the 2030 World Cup Final HAS been awarded to the North African country – to spark a renewed spat with co-hosts Spain.

In the latest apparent sign that Fifa chief Gianni Infantino is using the location of the Final venue as a prong in his attempt to stave off attempts to oust him, Fouzi Lekjaa said the game “will” be played at the Grand Hassan II Stadium in Casablanca.



The planned 115,000 capacity venue is not due to be completed until next year, while Spain has proposed Real Madrid’s Bernabeu or the Nou Camp in Barcelona.

Fifa have declined to confirm the schedule or approved host cities for the next World Cup, although more than half the currently-agreed 104 matches will be played in Spain.



But Lekjaa, who came out in support of Infantino despite his failed plan to sell off a £3bn stake in the World Cup to private investors, suggested the decision has already been made.

Speaking at a political rally ahead in Rabat of looming national elections, Lekjaa said: “The province of Bensliman in Casablanca will have the honour of hosting the 2030 World Cup final.



“Whoever wants to be in the next government has no other option than to develop the province.”

Lekjaa’s claim comes less than a week after his Spanish counterpart, Rafael Louzan, was adamant the Final “must” be played in his country because “it is the best football country today”.

Louzan conceded that the ultimate decision rests with Fifa but added: “It would not be understandable that Spain, which is the promoter of this World Cup along with Portugal, would not host the final.

“We have 55 per cent of the weight of organisation.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

“The 2030 tournament must be the best World Cup in history because it is the 100th anniversary of the first and there should be nothing that weakens this great candidacy.

“So we must all work together.

“This issue has been sufficiently debated and we will be waiting expectantly for the final decision that Fifa must make.

“There will be preliminary issues, since we have many cities to finalize with stadiums under construction and we await their confirmation to begin their work to carry out these major projects.”

Nevertheless, there are growing suspicions that Infantino is using the 2030 tournament as a part of his re-election campaign in the teeth of a global pushback against his leadership.



Leadership in Uefa, Asia and Concacaf are firmly opposed to Infantino being given a fourth term, while the African and South American confederations are in his corner.

But South American chiefs want to see a further extension to 64 teams from the 48 sides involved this summer.

Initially Conmebol was granted three matches – one each in Uruguay, Argentina and Paraguay – to mark the centenary of the inaugural event played solely in Montevideo in 1930.

But adding 16 more games – and 124 matches in total – would allow full opening groups to be played in each of the three South American countries.

Likewise, with Spain and Portugal strongly supporting Uefa’s stance against the Fifa leadership, awarding the Final to Morocco is seen as a tool to confirm support in Africa does not seep away.



Fifa have still to confirm when the full schedule and venues will be announced although it is likely to be at some point next year.

Sports.title: Liverpool goalkeeper Alisson learns punishment after booting fourth official’s board in fury against Nottingham Forest
Sports.content:
ALISSON was hit with an £8,000 fine for booting the fourth official’s board after Liverpool’s 2-2 Prem draw with Nottingham Forest.

The Reds goalkeeper conceded a penalty when he fouled Neco Williams and Morgan Gibbs-White slotted home the spot-kick to put Forest 2-1 up at Anfield.

Video footage emerged after the game that showed Alisson, 33, kicking the board — used to display substitutions and injury time — as he left the pitch.



Now the Brazilian has been disciplined by the FA for his actions near the tunnel last month.



The fourth official’s board had not worked during the fixture when Liverpool were trying to make substitutions with the score at 1-1.

The ball was out of play on three occasions but the Reds were unable to make a change.

Sports.title: Two Man Utd stars wearing DIFFERENT kit to team-mates in Champions League opener including Bryan Mbeumo
Sports.content:
A TRIO of Manchester United stars are wearing different kit to their team-mates tonight.

The Red Devils get their Champions League campaign underway against Azerbaijani side Sabah at Old Trafford.



And with the start of a new season comes a set of new Uefa rules.

One of them will see Champions League debutants wear a special patch on the sleeve of their kit.



The initiative is being rolled out in collaboration with sports merchandise company Fanatics.

Each patch, which is in the shape of a Champions League ball and features the word ‘DEBUT’, will be handed over to Fanatics’ trading card company, Topps, after matches before being turned into signed trading cards.

A handful of United players are wearing a debut patch tonight.

Bryan Mbeumo, Patrick Dorgu are sporting it on their sleeves having started the game, while Ayden Heaven will also have one if he makes it off the bench.

Former Troyes and Brentford forward Mbeumo, 27, has played every minute for United in the Premier League this term and started again tonight.

Dorgu, 21, was signed from Lecce last January, while United were in the Europa League, and they missed out on European football in his first full season.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

While Heaven, 19, started for the Red Devils in a Europa League knockout clash against Real Sociedad in March 2025, but is yet to make the step up to Europe’s premier club competition.

Karl Darlow, Harry Amass, Tyler Fletcher and Shea Lacey will also don a patch if they get any minutes against Sabah.

Meanwhile Carlos Baleba would have one too but is yet to make his debut after arriving from Brighton with an injury.

Sports.title: Former Arsenal star and England U21s all-time top scorer approached to switch international allegiance
Sports.content:
EDDIE NKETIAH has reportedly been approached to switch his international allegiance.

The Crystal Palace striker is the England U21s top scorer of all-time but has only ever played once for the senior side.



Nketiah, 27, made his full England debut in a friendly match against Australia in 2023.

The game ended 1-0 with the former Arsenal star coming off the bench in the 73rd-minute.



He could now make a change after reportedly being approached by the Ghana FA.

The Standard have claimed that the nation has previously attempted to get him to switch in the past.



It is now suggesting that it could make another approach to get Nketiah to represent the Black Stars.

Nketiah qualifies for Ghana through his parents despite being born in Lewisham, South London.

Nketiah played for the Three Lions at U18, U19, U20 and U21 levels.

He scored a staggering 35 goals across each age group, including 16 for the U21s.

His record for the U21s is the best ever, with Harvey Elliott in second place with 14 and Francis Jeffers in third with 12 goals.

Nketiah would still be allowed to make the allegiance swap as per Fifa rules.

It is stated that a player must have made more than three appearances for the senior team before their 21st birthday in order to be ineligible to switch.

This means that Nketiah could still represent Ghana and play alongside the likes of Man City star Antoine Semenyo and Tottenham’s Mohammed Kudus.

Nketiah has been a regular for Palace this season, having started all three Premier League games.



He is yet to score this season but has picked up one assist.

Sports.title: McIlroy four off Irish Open lead in tough conditions with Lowry near top
Sports.content:
Rory McIlroy battled on against testing blustery conditions at the Amgen Irish Open to sit four shots off the clubhouse lead following a one-under par opening round, with Ireland's Shane Lowry two off the top.

Gusts up to 35mph saw balls oscillating on greens with Frenchman Frederic Lacroix seeing his blown off the putting surface at the 13th, but he had fortunately already marked so was able to replace it.

All of which made for slow going at Trump International Golf Links and Hotel in Doonbeg during Thursday's first round.

As the day wore on, a course-record 65 from Chilean Joaquin Niemann looked increasingly good.

Having reached the turn at two under, Niemann had four successive birdies from the 14th to put him in contention for a $30,000 (£22,000) bonus for the lowest round of the week.

Austrian Maximilian Steinlechner and Renato Paratore appeared set to make a challenge for the top of the leaderboard at three under through 12 and 11 respectively, but could be thwarted by the fading light.

Home favourite Lowry, who won the event as a 22-year-old amateur in Baltray, kept himself in the mix, also in the clubhouse at three under.

Image: Ireland's Shane Lowry sits two shots off the lead following the opening round

Long waits on many tee boxes had been commonplace but McIlroy, who had won the event at the K Club last year, started with two birdies in his first four holes before getting to the turn in a two-under 34 - in three and a half hours.

After missing a four-foot birdie chance at the first he holed a 14-footer at the second, splashed out of a bunker to three feet at the par-five fourth for his second birdie, but missed from 10 feet at the seventh for a third.

McIlroy found the fairway bunker on the 13th, and a missed 10-foot putt saw him take a double-bogey hit before a fine approach to the 15th helped quickly pull a stroke back.

The world No 2, though, could not make the most of what proved limited opportunities over the closing run, narrowly missing a lengthy birdie attempt on the 18th, and will return on Friday morning hoping to improve along with the weather forecast.

McIlroy: A tough day to play in - I hung in there

"There was a couple of things that were tough today. Obviously the wind and the strength of the wind was one thing, and then the pace of play," McIlroy said.

"This course isn't conducive to sort of letting you get in a flow. Especially the first two days with so many people in the field, there is a lot of stopping and starting.

"It's hard when you are playing a round of golf and it takes six hours, it's hard to get into the rhythm of things, but felt like I did a good job.

"After making the double bogey on 13, I was just trying to get those two shots back by the end of the day. Didn't quite do that, but finishing under par for the day was a reasonable effort.

"I hung in there, shot under par, and at least don't feel like I'm out of the tournament. A good day tomorrow gets me right back in it."

Northern Ireland's Tom McKibbin - in a group with European team captain Luke Donald and Alex Fitzpatrick - finished at two under, having made a bogey on the final hole.

McIlroy was playing alongside Ryder Cup team-mate Robert MacIntyre, who finished at two over having followed a fine 37-foot birdie at 17 with a poor tee shot at the last into the deep rough before making a six.

Brooks Koepka, who received a tournament invite, endured a tough day, which started with a seven on the first and ended at five over.

Jon Rahm - linked with a return to the PGA Tour following doubts over the future of LIV Golf - was level par.

Sports.title: Root's lbw struggles and century drought - Nasser assesses post-Bazball batting
Sports.content:
Joe Root's susceptibility to lbw and England's failure to convert starts into centuries are the only blots on an improved post-Bazball batting display, according to Nasser Hussain.

England piled on 453 runs to establish a commanding first-innings lead of 320 in the third Test against Pakistan at Edgbaston.

The hosts were firmly in control and on course for a 3-0 series sweep, with Pakistan closing on 52-2, still 268 runs adrift, when rain curtailed play.

"I've liked the tempo of the batting in this series," former England captain Hussain said.

"We talked about it earlier in the Bazball era, England going too hard and not seizing opportunities.

"They've got the tempo right, especially through the middle order with Harry Brook, Jamie Smith, Dan Lawrence and Gus Atkinson.

"I know it's a poor Pakistan bowling attack, but even Josh Tongue and Jofra Archer have contributed with the bat.

"I like Emilio Gay's tempo at the top of the order. He bats time and knows when to absorb pressure. English cricket, and this side in particular, have been crying out for that."

'So obvious Root is struggling'

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player 21-year-old Razaullah gets the wicket of Joe Root on his Test debut.

Despite the overwhelming positives, Hussain highlighted two areas England have yet to address during the Pakistan series.

Root's four dismissals have all been lbw, with the world's second-highest Test run-scorer continuing to wrestle with that mode of dismissal.

"Obviously, there are two boxes they haven't ticked," Hussain explained.

"Their greatest player is struggling with one specific type of dismissal: lbw.

"It's so obvious he's struggling. He tried to address it in the first innings, made a technical adjustment and then got out lbw again."

'England need to convert starts to big scores'

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Stuart Broad and Nasser Hussain join Ian Ward to recap the second day of the third Test between England and Pakistan.

Meanwhile, England's wait for a hundred has reached historic levels.

Brook (75), Smith (69), Lawrence (65), Gay (60) and Ollie Robinson (50) have all reached fifty without kicking on to three figures.

A total of 14 half-centuries have been scored across the series without a single hundred, the first time that has happened in a Test series in England since the 1888 Ashes.

"The other one is getting hundreds," Hussain added.

"You can beat Pakistan with 40s, 50s and 60s. To beat Australia, or the New Zealand side we saw earlier in the summer, you need big hundreds and massive scores

"England just need to convert those starts into big scores."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Nasser Hussain labelled Pakistan’s selection of Saim Ayub as a ‘disrespect for Test Match cricket’ after they flew out the batsman for his first class game in 11 months, just 10 days after playing in the CPL.

'60 equal to a century this summer'

Reflecting on the absence of a century in the Test series, former England bowler Stuart Broad has called for a reassessment of what constitutes a good score after a scorching summer has made conditions favourable for bowlers.

Broad argued that some scores this summer have been every bit as valuable as centuries on flatter pitches.

"Top-order batting has been very difficult in this series," Broad said.

"Root, England's best-ever player, has struggled for runs in this series. If he's struggling, it's OK for everyone else to struggle.

"We can't praise the likes of Ollie Robinson, who is getting 20-odd wickets at an average of around 6.00, and also say, 'We should be getting more centuries.'

"To be honest, this summer I think a 60 has felt like a hundred.

"You've had to work as hard for a 60 on these pitches as you would for a hundred on a normal Test match surface."
