Sports.title: Russell: I have an answer to Antonelli's pace
Sports.content:
George Russell insists he does "have an answer" to Kimi Antonelli's pace but admits he will need good fortune to catch his Mercedes team-mate at the top of the Drivers' Championship.

​​​​​​Russell suffered a demoralising blow to his already faint title hopes at last weekend's Italian Grand Prix when he was beaten to victory by Antonelli despite the 20-year-old having started from 19th on the grid after receiving a penalty for exceeding his engine-part allowance.

The result saw Russell, who had started second in Monza, fall 66 points behind Antonelli with 10 rounds remaining, starting with this weekend's Spanish Grand Prix in Madrid.

Russell started the season as the clear title favourite but has won just two grands prix compared to Antonelli's seven, with the Italian being consistently quicker, especially in terms of race pace.

Asked about finding himself in situation where he doesn't have an answer to Antonelli's speed, Russell replied: "I do have an answer and I'm working on it, and it's been much improved.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch how Antonelli converted 19th to first to take a sensational victory at the Italian Grand Prix

"I'm very pleased with that sort of step I've taken because fundamentally changing the driving style is achievable for a lot of drivers, but then actually being fast with it is another topic."

Having reached a low point ahead of F1's summer break, Russell delivered solid weekends in the Netherlands and Italy, but was still unable to beat Antonelli on a Sunday.

"I feel my performance since the summer break has been... I've qualified ahead of him in the three qualifying sessions and my race pace has been on a par with him in these two races. And I couldn't say that pre-break. I'm definitely very pleased with that progression.

"We'll have to see where the rest of the season takes us."

Russell 'trying not to be delusional'

Russell has repeatedly insisted his focus is on improving his own performances rather than thinking about catching Antonelli, but ahead of F1's return to Madrid he admitted luck will be required if he is to claim his maiden drivers' title this year.

In addition to his deficit, Russell will also have to take a grid penalty for taking new engine parts between now and the end of the season, which will see him start a race from the back of the field.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Antonelli and Russell go wheel-to-wheel for the Italian Grand Prix lead in several epic team-mate battles

On his prospects of winning the title, Russell said: "I'm not trying to be delusional. The reality is my team-mate's done a better job than me this year.

"I've had some bad luck but he deserves to be leading and right now he deserves to be in the position he is.

"From my side, I'm just going race by race. I'm going to try and win as many as possible.

"If I want to win this championship, I'm going to need some luck and that's where we are. I'm sort of being quite realistic about the position we're in."

Antonelli: I want to avoid thinking about the championship

Antonelli's victory on a weekend where his rivals were expected to make ground on him has further cemented his status as an overwhelming favourite to close out the championship.

Behind Russell, Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton dropped 76 points behind Antonelli, while McLaren's Lando Norris trails by 96 points in fourth.

Despite the strength of his position, Antonelli claims it's "still early" to be thinking about the championship.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Antonelli: Championship not won until 'you cross final finish line'

He said: "I don't even know how many races are left. Ten? So, it's still a long way to go. It's still early.

"And I don't really want to drive thinking about championship. Monza was the proof that I wasn't driving thinking about or worrying about championship.

"I was just driving to win; to do my best and so that's the mindset.

"Of course, there might be occasions in the future where before taking a certain decision, I might think about the championship.

"But the thing I want to avoid is going on track for a free practice or a qualifying - or even a race - thinking about or worrying about the championship. That's the thing I want to avoid at all costs."

Sports.title: Joshua's driver in fatal car crash has trial adjourned
Sports.content:
Adeniyi Mobolaji Kayode was driving an SUV that struck a stationary truck on December 29 2025, injuring Anthony Joshua and killing two members of his team; He is facing a four-count charge

Anthony Joshua car crash: Trial of driver involved in fatal collision has hearing adjourned until November 17

Adeniyi Mobolaji Kayode (right) pictured arriving at court in January

The trial of Adeniyi Mobolaji Kayode, the driver involved in the crash that injured boxer Anthony Joshua and killed two members of his team, has been adjourned until November 17.

The case, which began in January at a magistrate court in Ogun State, was adjourned from September 10 as proceedings continued over charges arising from the fatal crash on the Lagos-Ibadan Expressway.

Joshua's personal trainer, Latif Ayodele, and strength and conditioning coach, Sina Ghami, were killed.

Kayode faces charges including dangerous driving causing death, reckless and negligent driving, driving without due care and attention, and operating a vehicle without a valid national driver's licence.

The 46-year-old Kayode denies the charges.

Prosecutors allege that Kayode was attempting to overtake another vehicle when the SUV carrying Joshua and his team crashed into a stationary truck.

Joshua, a two-time world heavyweight champion, survived injuries he sustained in the crash in December last year and was later discharged.

Image: ⁠Joshua was taken to hospital after suffering minor injures in the car accident that killed two

The crash occurred as the group was traveling to visit Joshua's father in Ogun State.

Police told the court in earlier proceedings that both vehicles had been removed from the scene before investigators arrived.

Sports.title: England closing in on emphatic series sweep of Pakistan
Sports.content:
England are closing in on the most emphatic of series sweeps of Pakistan after reducing the visitors to 52-2 - still 268 runs behind - before rain ended play early on day two of the third Test at Edgbaston.

Pakistan's score at stumps actually represented somewhat of a recovery after their prospects looked even gloomier than the darkening skies overhead when reduced to 0-2 in Ollie Robinson's first over.

Robinson (2-10) saw off Saim Ayub first ball - the opener, one of four players flown straight into the team after seven were axed from the touring squad, out for a pair - before Abdullah Shafique also nicked to the slips three deliveries later.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Ollie Robinson took two wickets for no runs in the opening over of Pakistan’s second innings

It means that Robinson now has 28 wickets across his four Test appearances this summer, taking them at a staggering 7.75 apiece. In this series that improves even further to 6.66.

Joe Root's grab at slip to send back Shafique moved him one clear of Australia's Steve Smith and onto 220 in their personal battle to claim the most catches by an outfielder in Test cricket.

The clatter of wickets didn't follow as it had in Pakistan's first innings, with Azan Awais (29no) and Shan Masood (21no) sharing a fifty stand before the rain arrived - albeit Masood was put down on 13 by Ben Duckett, his third spill of the Test, off the unfortunate Gus Atkinson.

Score summary - England vs Pakistan, third Test, Edgbaston Pakistan 133 all out in 33.5 overs in first innings (put in to bat): Saud Shakeel (43), Mohammad Abbas (21); Josh Tongue (4-42), Ollie Robinson (3-15), Jofra Archer (3-25) England 453 all out in 89 overs in first innings: Harry Brook (75), Jamie Smith (69), Dan Lawrence (65), Emilio Gay (60), Ollie Robinson (50); Razaullah (4-148) Pakistan 52-2 after 12.4 overs in second innings (trail by 268): Azan Awais (29no), Shan Masood (21no); Ollie Robinson (2-10)

Brook, Lawrence and Smith all miss out with Test tons looming

Earlier, England were bowled out for 452, earning a 320-run lead on first innings as Dan Lawrence (65), Jamie Smith (69) and Robinson (50) added half-centuries to those notched by Emilio Gay (60) and Harry Brook (75) on day one.

Brook added 23 to his overnight total before he was the first wicket to fall on the second morning, just at the point where he and Dan Lawrence - who had stormed through to a 47-ball fifty - had seemingly broken Pakistan's spirits with 73 scored off the opening 10 overs of the day.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Harry Brook spurned his chance of making a century as he ran himself out on 75 while England built a first-innings lead over Pakistan

The breakthrough was a gift, Brook practically running himself out as he called for a risky single to midwicket, where Masood did the honours with a direct hit.

The scoring didn't slow as Smith joined Lawrence at the crease, the pair putting on 64 together before Lawrence was left kicking himself as he chopped one from Mohammad Imran (2-47) back onto his stumps just before lunch.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Dan Lawrence couldn't hide his fury after knocking the ball onto his own stumps

Smith was the next through to fifty - off 54 balls - but failed to convert as, after Gus Atkinson (19) was bowled by a beauty from Imran, Smith chipped one back to the fired-up Razaullah (4-148).

While he was okay to bat, Smith would later be absent from the field - Jordan Cox subbing in at wicketkeeper - with the regular gloveman nursing an injured finger from the first day.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player A fiery Razaullah gave a strong celebration after he caught and bowled Jamie Smith

Robinson, hitting a second Test half-century, and Jofra Archer (32no) had some fun lower down the order, finding the boundary - or clearing it - with regularity as England pushed their total above 400 and lead beyond 300 before the innings was finally ended.

Pakistan carried their increasingly timid approach in the field over into the start of their second innings, and a two-day finish briefly looked a possibility after Robinson's double strike in the first over, before Azan and Masood showed some much-needed resilience and the rain intervened.

Lawrence 'gutted' to miss out on century

Lawrence was "gutted" at blowing the prospect of a first international century.

The 29-year-old, who made 51 at Headingley and 54 at Lord's in this series, said: "I'm obviously gutted that I didn't kick on and make a really big score, but I was pretty happy with how I did overall.

Image: Lawrence was one of five England players who amassed between 50 and 75 in their mammoth 453 all out

"I felt like I was playing really nicely and it was a really good surface to bat on against the tiring attack. I thought I was going to make a really big score to be honest, but it wasn't meant to be.

"I've missed out on two chances to make really big scores and really big contributions - at Headingley and here.

"But I'm quite happy with how I've played. I've got three fifties in four innings (in this series), which is pretty good. I think if I was offered 65 at the start of the day, I'd have taken it."

Meanwhile, seamer Robinson has been the star of the series with 21 wickets at a preposterous average of 6.66 - when he dismissed Shafique for the fifth time in six innings, it was 6.19 - and Lawrence, one of England's slip fielders, admitted the cordon have to be on red alert when the seamer is bowling.

Lawrence added: "When he's bowling, when he's putting it in the same spot pretty much every ball, you always feel in the game.

"The wickets have offered quite a lot to us as well and all the seamers. You certainly do feel in the game behind the stumps, especially when you've got someone pretty much at the peak of his powers."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Stuart Broad and Nasser Hussain join Ian Ward to recap the second day of the third Test between England and Pakistan.

Nasser: Ayub shouldn't be here

Sky Sports Cricket's Nasser Hussain:

"Saim Ayub, in particular, struggled. The truth is he shouldn't be here. He came from the CPL [Caribbean Premier League] and hasn't played first-class cricket in 11 months.

"I don't know who thinks it's the right thing to fly someone over from foreign conditions, and think they'll be fine in these conditions against a Duke's ball and Ollie Robinson's bowling attack? It's showing disrespect to Test match cricket.

"The players who are here, their friends and room-mates have been axed. People who have got five-fors have been axed.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Nasser Hussain labelled Pakistan’s selection of Saim Ayub as a ‘disrespect for Test Match cricket’ after they flew out the batsman for his first class game in 11 months, just 10 days after playing in the CPL

"How you treat players is so important. It's a two-way thing when players are presented with a Test cap. You're expected to meet the core values of representing Pakistan, but the team needs to look after the players in return.

"That goes the moment you send seven people home. People start looking after themselves. Why should I bother about a team that doesn't bother about me and has sent my team-mates home between Tests?

"This Pakistan side, not only are they in poor form, they look like a team that says, 'what will be, will be', and just looks after itself."

Sports.title: Overton, Leach help Somerset remain top with crushing win at Leicestershire
Sports.content:
Craig Overton and Jack Leach combined to inflict a 377-run thrashing on Leicestershire and keep Somerset top of the Rothesay County Championship with only two more rounds to go.

After title rivals Warwickshire claimed victory inside two days against Glamorgan, leaders Somerset responded with aplomb.

Henry Nicholls' unbeaten 100 helped the visitors declare on 316-5 to set Leicestershire an insurmountable victory target of 523.

The real question was whether Somerset could wrap up this latest triumph with a day to spare and Leicestershire only managed to bat out 45.1 overs, with Overton the pick of the bowlers - 4-33 - and England's forgotten man Leach taking 3-30 to dismiss the hosts for 145.

Ben Foakes made 54 to help Surrey to 294-7 against Sussex before bad light in Hove ensured they will trail by 99 runs ahead of Friday's final day.

In Division Two, Northamptonshire piled the pressure on promotion rivals Kent after they won by six wickets at Worcestershire, who were all out for 182 in their second innings, and George Bartlett's unbeaten 19 got his team over the line in pursuit of 94 at New Road.

Kent have dropped to third but will return to second if they can bat out day four at Derbyshire or chase down an unlikely total of 434. After the hosts declared on 352-8, visiting openers Zak Crawley and Ben Compton survived nine balls before the close.

Sports.title: Verstappen: New Madring circuit 'probably a car killer'
Sports.content:
Max Verstappen says the new Madring F1 circuit is "probably a car killer" with several drivers expecting a disruptive Spanish Grand Prix weekend.

The close proximity of the walls at the high-speed track, which includes a big banked corner in the middle sector, was the big talk of the paddock on Thursday.

It means Friday's practice sessions at 12.30pm and 4pm, live on Sky Sports F1, will be more important than usual so the drivers can get up to speed around the challenging circuit.

"It's a tough track. For me, what I feel while driving, it's a little bit the same kind of sensation that I get sometimes around Jeddah in places," said Verstappen.

"Of course, Jeddah is faster on average with the corners, but the walls are quite similar in how they are positioned.

"It's going to be tough. I think when F3 were testing here there were a lot of shunts, so it's not an easy track, easy to make a mistake also with the layout of the track. The kerbs that are there, we need to run over a few of them, and that's normally not the strong point of our car, but we will try to do the best we can."

Asked if it was a car killer, Verstappen added: "It probably is a car killer from what I've seen so far but you just need to try and stay out of the walls and try to get the best possible feeling in the car. When you're confident in the car on a street circuit it helps a lot."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Oracle Red Bull Racing swapped the asphalt for the underground, as the iconic RB8 took to the tracks of the Madrid Metro in a first-of-its-kind stunt

Last month, a two-day Formula 3 test took place at the Madring and there were 19 red flags, mostly for crashes at several areas of the track.

Williams' Carlos Sainz, who has given some input into the circuit design, says the track is "different to what we're used to".

"Realistically speaking, it's going to be now tomorrow in FP1 when we really know what this track is all about. And I'm going to say it looks different," he said.

"It looks that the track has character, that it's charismatic, with a lot of different kinds of corners."

Image: The Madring F1 track layout (Credit: F1)

Most risky circuit on the calendar?

Qualifying is expected to be pivotal due to the difficulty of overtaking as most corners only have one racing line, so the drivers will be keen to push the limits come Saturday afternoon, even if it means taking huge risks.

Last week's shock pole-sitter Pierre Gasly believes it will create "huge adrenaline" for the drivers.

"The track layout is something I've never seen before. You have these crazy corners, blind corners, a huge banking," said the Alpine driver.

"It took me a few laps in the sim to get my head around what's where. It's very challenging because everything is twisty. I'm excited. I expect a really hectic weekend with lots of disruption and mistakes and we will have to make sure we are on the right side of it."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player The F1 review the new Madring track!

It will be particularly important for the championship contenders to keep out of the barriers so they don't lose big points to their rivals.

After his spectacular Monza win, Kimi Antonelli leads George Russell by 66 points in the Drivers' Championship, Lewis Hamilton by 76 points and Lando Norris by 96 points.

"It's a crazy circuit. I would put it as arguably the most risky circuit of the whole calendar because you have real high-speed corners, sort of Jeddah-esque. The walls are very close, so there's no margin for error," said Russell.

"But then you have other corners that are quite like Baku, where you're coming from a high speed into a slow braking zone, you're braking and turning at the same time, so locking tyres is going to be easy. And if you lock up, you'll be straight in the wall."

Image: Despite its tightness, the Turn 5 chicane is one of the few overtaking spots at the Madring

Hamilton added: "There's probably some similarities with these kerbs compared to somewhere like Montreal where you saw obviously Mercedes was very quick, but there was a lot more straights there as well.

"It's a massively challenging circuit. Of all the new tracks that I've gone to, this one, maybe Saudi, are the two closest in terms of how difficult it was to get on top of the car and find the right lines etc."

Sports.title: Manchester United v Sabah: Champions League – live
Sports.content:
1m ago 16.02 EDT I’m returning to the same issues: United haven’t yet worked out how to control a game while playing at pace, sustaining attacks and boxing opponents while being hard to get at – something their 98-99 and 06-08 iteration did brilliantly. But structurally, they’re improving, and once Baleba is fit, they should get better at recovering high and defending channels. Share

12m ago 15.52 EDT Scores from elsewhere: Our early games finished Fenerbahce 1-1 Roma and PSV 1-1 Shakhtar; our other 8pms are Bayern 0-0 Bodo/Glimt, Slavia Praha 0-0 Lens and Como 2-0 Leipzig. United will play Roma, Bayern, Como and Leipzig. Share

14m ago 15.50 EDT HALF-TIME: Manchester United 3-0 Sabah It took United a while to get going, and Sabah have done a good job, but the gap in class is as chasmic as expected. Share

14m ago 15.49 EDT GOAL! Manchester United 3-0 Sabah (Sesko 45) Mainoo into Bruno and over to Mbeumo, who plays into the space for Sesko, lanking between the centre-backs. He opts to go around the keeper – a finish we see too rarely these days and doesn’t go down when touched though, if he does, it’s a red card. But he stays on his feet, slides into the empty net, and this, as a contest, is did. View image in fullscreen Benjamin Sesko rounds Pokatilov to make it three. Photograph: Michael Regan/UEFA/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Sesko gets some air on his celebration. Photograph: Lee Smith/Action Images/Reuters Share Updated at 16.01 EDT

16m ago 15.47 EDT 44 min United are starting to impose their class now, and excuse me while I interrupt myself. Share

17m ago 15.47 EDT GOAL! Manchester United 2-0 Sabah (Fernandes 43) Tielemans slips out to Dorgu who goes wider to Cunha, who punches a diagonal ball into the box, where Tielemans collects, spins away from goal toward the touchline and lays back to Bruno, who passes into the net. That is very nice. View image in fullscreen Bruno Fernandes celebrates with Youri Tielemans. Photograph: Lee Smith/Action Images/Reuters Share Updated at 15.50 EDT

19m ago 15.45 EDT 42 min …and again, the corner is to the back post and poorly executed, Cunha and Martinez jumping into each other’s way. Share

19m ago 15.44 EDT 41 min Mainoo is dictating a lot of United’s play and he passes forwards to Bruno, who disguises a ball out wide, but Dorgu’s shot is blocked behind… Share

21m ago 15.43 EDT 40 min Nice from Mbeumo, who shapes to cross then fizzes a square-pass to Bruno, 20 yards out … but his shot is well over the bar. So far, he’s not having one of his better days – nor did he at the weekend. Share

22m ago 15.42 EDT 38 min United look pretty well-organised tonight – their shape is good and having Sesko makes that better – but their execution hasn’t been good enough. Share

24m ago 15.40 EDT 36 min And here Sabah come again, Parris feinting to go outside Dorgu, deliberately leaving the ball behind, then going back to it and picking out Mickels at the back stick! this is a chance, but he can only bungle it wide – though, in fairness, there wasn’t much space between Lammens and the post. View image in fullscreen Joy-Lance Mickels wastes a glorious chance to equalise. Photograph: Carl Recine/Getty Images Share Updated at 15.43 EDT

27m ago 15.37 EDT 33 min Tielemans drills a luscious ball out to Bruno, who kills it and goes backwards, United again prioritising keeping the ball. And then, when it again goes to Tielemans, he finds Dorgu, whose cross is behind Sesko but, back to goal, the striker hooks it goalwards … and just wide of the near post. There are more goals in United, but they should be concerned at their inability to pen Sabah in. Share

29m ago 15.35 EDT 32 min Sabah haven’t shrunk since going behind and again, Parris cuts in, his shot blocked behind by Dorgu. The corner is well claimed by Lammens. Share

30m ago 15.34 EDT 31 min Mazraoui has seen a lot fo the ball and he digs out a cross, of which Parris makes a mess, but Dorgu’s consequent volley is blocked. Share

31m ago 15.33 EDT 30 min Parris again shows himself down the right, crosses low, and for a second dit looks like Mickels will have a tap-in, but Tielemans is there to make an important challenge. Share

31m ago 15.32 EDT 29 min I wouldn’t say the goal was coming, but United had improved a bit in the five minutes preceding it, a bit more tempo and imagination in their passing. Share

32m ago 15.31 EDT GOAL! Manchester United 1-0 Sabah (Cunha 28) Parris gives it away, passing infield to Mbeumo, and the ball moves to Sesko then Bruno, who feeds Dorgu. The low cross to the near post is good enough and Mbeumo, played onside by McCarthy, leaps to punch a close-range finish into the ground and in, off the keeper’s shoulder. That’s his first Champions League goal. View image in fullscreen Matheus Cunha finally breaches the Sabah defence. Photograph: Stu Forster/Getty Images Share Updated at 15.33 EDT

34m ago 15.29 EDT 27 min “I just noticed that Sabah have a centre back called Aden (Aidan) McCarthym” writes John Brennan. “Taking over from Thomas Delaney as the most Irish sounding non-Irishman around.” Yup, I looked him up too – he’s Saffer. Share

35m ago 15.29 EDT 25 min A ball into Mbeumo, who explodes on to it and inside, beating McCarthy and creating a shooting lane but, stumbling as he lets fly, it’s straight at Pokatilov. Share

36m ago 15.28 EDT 24 min Again, the corner comes to nothing. Without Casemiro, so far this season, they’re offering no threat form set-pieces. Share

37m ago 15.27 EDT 23 min What United have lacked so far is players beating their men. When Tielemans did it earlier, it opened things up, but they need more of it from their attackers. Meantime, though, Mainoo sweeps a lovely lofted pass forward – the kind of thing he has to do more often – picking out Bruno, unmarked on the right of the box. He’s got Sesko in the middle, but his square-ball is careless and Sabah get it behind. Share

39m ago 15.25 EDT 21 min Mazraoui is doing a fair bit of work underlapping, and here he is again, but when the ball goes into the box, there’s too much on it for Dorgu to control his header back across. Share

41m ago 15.23 EDT 19 min The corner is comfortably collected by Pokatilov. Share

41m ago 15.22 EDT 18 min Martinez and Mainoo look to bait the press but Sabah sit off, in their shape and forcing United to come up with something. So it goes into Mainoo, who plays a nice pass out wide and, when Dorgu crosses, they pick up the second ball and try to pick a route through a crowded box before Bruno shoots, the ball deflected behind. Share

44m ago 15.20 EDT 17 min Sabah attack confidently, passing through midfield, then the ball goes wide to Parris, whose speculative shot is weak and straight at Lammens. Share

45m ago 15.18 EDT 15 min Sabah will be delighted with how this is going. United need to get closer together and move the ball faster, players following passes and breaking into the box. View image in fullscreen Sabah’s Joy-Lance Mickels is challenged by Noussair Mazraoui. Photograph: Michael Regan/UEFA/Getty Images Share Updated at 15.23 EDT

46m ago 15.18 EDT 14 min The first flash of Tielemans, beating two men in midfield and spreading to Dorgu, who finds Cunha down the left side of the box. He might shoot but opts to recycle, which is probably a sensible call: control, not hopeful efforts with two defenders between him and keeper. Share

48m ago 15.16 EDT 13 min Zedaka runs at Martinez, trying to go by on the outside, but the defender is strong, making the challenge and winning a goalkick. Share

49m ago 15.15 EDT 12 min United win another corner and again, Mbeumo goes back post; it yields another, down the left this time, against the ball goes deep, and the ref spies some kind of foul, so awards Sabah a free-kick. Share

50m ago 15.14 EDT 10 min Mazraoui has a shot from the edge blocked, then Mbeumo squares for Bruno, who caresses a lovely one-touch pass back the way it came, and Mazraoui will shoot … wide of the near post. Share

51m ago 15.12 EDT 9 min Mbeumo aims the corner at Martinez, who springs at the back post, but can’t get the purchase necessary to make anything happen. Share

52m ago 15.12 EDT 8 min Mazraoui finds Cunha, outside him on the right, and his low shot is bundled behind at his near post by Pokatilov. Share

53m ago 15.11 EDT 7 min As a team, United are trying to find the balance between attacking with intensity and staying patient; against Everton, they strayed too close to the latter. Share

54m ago 15.10 EDT 5 min This has been a decent start from Sabah, who don’t look daunted at all and why should they? They’re a champion team playing one under pressure and, as the move it forward, Parris shimmies inside then dips out, fooling Dorgu, the ball clipping his shin and then his hand as he turns away. There are calls for a penalty, but even in Europe, no chance; the corner comes to nowt. Share

1h ago 15.07 EDT 3 min Some of United’s passing at Everton was really sloppy, Cunha and Mbeumo the main culprits, and they’ve already given the ball away a couple of times tonight, Sesko passing it to no one. He does, though, close down the the keeper, who swallows his insides as he tries to get the ball out of his feet, just about managing to move it wide. Share

1h ago 15.05 EDT 2 min United look to move the ball quickly but Sabah aren’t here to watch them, getting in among it. On the one hand, it increases the pressure on each pass but, on the other, it leaves gaps to hit. View image in fullscreen Sabah's Akim Zedadka moves away from Matheus Cunha. Photograph: Lee Smith/Action Images/Reuters Share Updated at 15.12 EDT

1h ago 15.02 EDT We take a moment to remember those who died and are suffering following the awful tragedy in Nepal. Share

1h ago 14.58 EDT If they offered odds on it, I’d be considering a few pennies on Marcus Rashford to score last – he’s a terrific sub, will almost definitely get on, and I’d expect the game-state to offer him opportunities. Share

1h ago 14.56 EDT Our teams are tunnelled … and here they come. Share

1h ago 14.53 EDT “Carrick is not given the credit he deserves,” says Krishnamoorthy V. “So many heavyweights have come and gone after SAF and few have been as quiet and as effective as Carrick. He should be given more freedom and a longer term to stabilise and deliver. They may not go far in this new Swiss scheme but their focus should be top four and constant presence in Big Cup.” He’s fortunate in that it’s likely to be top five for the foreseeable future. Otherwise, I’d say that if United can’t make the playoffs, that’d be a failure, probably the last 16 too – he has players more than good enough for that, because though there are defensive issues, what he has should be good enough for the league stage and even if not, his attackers should be able to outscore most opposition they’ve been drawn against. Share Updated at 15.14 EDT

1h ago 14.48 EDT Talking of United’s firepower, it makes sense to see Sesko given a start tonight. He missed the end of last season and didn’t have a proper pre-season, so bringing him along slowly made sense. My sense is Carrick’s inclination is two have three all-purpose attackers rather than a reference-point centre-forward, but i’m certain he knows that, though his stable contains a lot of really good attackers, the one with elite potential is the one who doesn’t necessarily fit his model. Sesko is a phenomenal athlete, able to finish in a variety of different ways; his best hold-up play is very good though it needs polishing, and he brings useful defensive height to a relatively short outfit. However he does present issues of balance, because he needs service, and United’s wide players aren’t really into that – Mbeumo wants to score and Cunha wants to dribble and shoot. That said, Rashford’s creativity is better than he’s given credit for and seems to have improved while he was at Barca, with Tielemans’ crossing a potentially rich avenue of provision. Share

1h ago 14.39 EDT “It feels like there has been a certain pattern to United over the years since Fergie left in that there is usually a decent/good season usually achieving Champions League qualification followed by a drop-off the following season due to the additional games in Champions League and the defeats that usually come with that,” reckons John Brennan. “I’m thinking of 23-24 under Ten Haag, 21-22 under Solskjær and, going further back, 18-19 under Mourinho. If this pattern holds (and the results so far this season suggest that it might), I can see a draw tonight followed by a comfortable win for Man City at the weekend and all of a sudden Carrick is going to be under pressure.” The drop-off you mention, I think, was also because after qualification was achieved, all those managers were denied the necessary funds to strengthen, because they’d achieved the board’s objective. I’ll be pretty surprised if United don’t win comfortably tonight because they’ve got so much firepower, but they could easily play well at the weekend and lose because any team in the world could play well against City and lose. At this point, of course results are crucial, but so are performances – I didn’t watch the Everton game and think United were hopeless. As I say below, they’re learning how to control a game – both Solskjær and Van Gaal fell down when they tried that, having not been backed in the market – and progress isn’t always linear. But they do seem to moving in the right direction. Share

2h ago 14.28 EDT It’s also worth noting that Patrick Dorgu starts at left-back tonight, for the first time under Carrick. Bought for Ruben Amorim, really he’s a specialist wing-back – not a defender because his awareness isn’t great, nor his ability to pass the ball out from the back, nor a winger because he lacks finesse and one-on-one ability – he starts at the back tonight mainly because Shaw is rested and there’s no better option. But if he’s to have a future as a starter, it feels much more likely it’ll be at the back than in attack – though, as we’ve seen he’s got a worldie in him. Share

2h ago 14.24 EDT Thinking more about that United defence, this is a big evening for Leny Yoro. He was pretty good in his first season at Old Trafford, but didn’t get to play much last; ultimately, Carrick couldn’t afford to risk him because he had a formula that worked – Maguire and Martinez, plus fast counters – with points to win and a job to secure. But if United are to get properly good, they need to close the huge spaces in their midfield that come about partly because of how deep that first-choice centre-back pairing needs to defend due to its lack of pace – for defensive reasons, but also so they can squeeze up on opposing teas. Though Yoro has actually been better at left centre-back, not right, Martínez’s playmaking is perhaps the best in the world – one of the reasons United struggled for parts of the game at the weekend is because Everton forced the ball to Maguire – so he can’t really be left out. A good game tonight won’t be enough to earn a derby spot, I don’t think, but I’m certain the plan is to upgrade on Maguire – and perhaps Martínez too. If Yoro has a good season, he can be the internal solution to solve that problem; if he doesn’t, he’ll have a problem, because United won’t be waiting. Share Updated at 14.28 EDT

2h ago 14.16 EDT Email! “Yes, there are reasons both emotional and mythological why United need to be in the Champions League,” concedes Matt Dony. “But there are equally emotional and mythological reasons why, to fans of other clubs, their Champions League return being on a Thursday night against a relative European minnow is objectively funny. It sort of doesn’t feel like a Champions League night. Not that that will matter one jot to the players and fans. And it shouldn’t, obviously. A club like United clearly belong here. It’s a footballing shame that they’ve been so far away for so long. I’m not convinced Carrick is the long-term solution, but I hope he enjoys an extended European adventure. (Just not too extended, obviously.)” Of course – one of the joys of football is the opportunity to glory in ultimately meaningless misery. Carrick’s done well so far, and though there’s not been as much progress as is required out of possession, in possession they’re doing more of the right things, with Carlos Baleba still to come in. He may not be the long-term solution because almost no one is, but he might be able to take United most of the way, even if it requires someone else to finish the job. Whoever on earth that is. Michael Carrick has earned the right to bring equilibrium to Manchester United | Daniel Harris Read more Share Updated at 14.16 EDT

2h ago 14.12 EDT The manner of Sabah’s qualification was also incredible. Get a load of this. Share

2h ago 14.08 EDT Carrick tells TNT they’ll give Sabah maximum respect. They’ve won a lot of matches, play attractive, attacking football, and they’ll be a challenge, but he’s mainly focused on United. Shaw came off with cramp at the weekend so they opted not to take a chance on him, but they wanted freshen things up and get the balance right. He’s got a good squad and thinks this is a good team, but he didn’t want to change too much as that makes things difficult. Though results haven’t been great, Carrick thinks United have improved from last season, with some good attacking and combination play. He wants his team to be ready from the first whistle and other scat, then off he goes. Share

2h ago 14.04 EDT Looking more closely at that United XI, it makes broad sense. Though I’m not sure why it’s Noussair Mazraoui not Diogo Dalot, Michael Carrick can’t afford to risk Luke Shaw, who didn’t train yesterday, given the lack of left-back alternative and derby coming on Sunday. In the centre of defence, Leny Yoro gets a necessary start, Matheus Cunha is back on the left, and Benjamin Sesko makes his first start of the season after scoring off the bench at Everton. It’s also worth noting that Mason Mount, really impressive in pre-season playing in the midfield pivot, is on the bench having injured himself – sadly, again – though the competition for places in that position is intense. Share

2h ago 13.55 EDT Teams Manchester United (4-2-3-1): Lammens; Mazraoui, Yoro, Martínez, Dorgu; Tielemans, Mainoo; Mbeumo, Fernandes, Cunha; Sesko. Subs: Darlow, Mee, Dalot, Maguire, Mount, Rashford, Zirkzee, Andrey Santos, Heaven, Lacey, Fletcher T, Amass. Sabah (4-2-3-1): Pokatilov; Zedaka, McCarthy, Dashdamirov, Puchacz; Rakhmonalev, Lepinjica; Parris, Simic, Nwachukwu; Mickels. Subs: Ramazanov, Mirzammadov, Kahibulaev, Isaev, Rustamli, Mutallimov, Almeida, Du Queiroz, Fernandes, Mukhtarov, Mbina. Share

Sports.title: French FA accuses Infantino of ‘seriously damaging’ football as it withdraws support
Sports.content:
The French Football Federation’s president, Philippe Diallo, said Gianni Infantino had “seriously damaged the image and the unity of football” as he announced the end of France’s support for the Fifa president’s re-election.

The FFF’s executive committee unanimously voted on Thursday to withdraw its backing, which had been formalised at the end of June. Diallo referred to “events during the World Cup” which had “flagrantly gone against the way we believe our sport should be run” and to Infantino’s World Cup sell-off plan, which was revealed in July and scrapped after a widespread backlash.

During the World Cup the suspension of the US forward Folarin Balogun was overturned by Fifa after lobbying from Donald Trump. The US president said he called Infantino to recommend that Balogun be allowed to play. Fifa has said the decision taken by its disciplinary committee was “a balanced measure” and “based on an explicit provision of the applicable regulations”.

Diallo outlined the reasons for the loss in confidence: “From July onwards, the conditions which led to us to support his candidacy had been disrupted. Does the withdrawal of the [sell-off] project solve the issue? I don’t think so. His initiatives during and after the World Cup have seriously damaged the image and the unity of football. As a result, we believe that trust has been broken.”

Diallo said of the initial decision to support Infantino: “It would be wrong to say that certain developments in football were not made under his mandate.” But he added: “When you are making changes to the game itself, in a unilateral and opaque fashion to sell our shared asset, that changes our appreciation.

“France is one of the founding members of Fifa, and as such we have a historical legitimacy to intervene when we feel that Fifa and its president are deviating from our vision of how world football should be run. We also have sporting legitimacy, as one of the top three teams in the world rankings over the last 10 years. We wanted to make it clear that we refuse to go in a direction which does not correspond to the general interest of our sport.”

When reports of the sell-off project came to light, the FFF expressed “doubts and deep concerns”. Uefa threatened a boycott of Fifa competitions and several European countries, including Wales and England, withdrew their support for Infantino but the FFF had not until Thursday publicly disavowed him.

Diallo indicated France would play an active part in Uefa’s search for an alternative candidate for the Fifa presidency before the 18 November deadline. The election will take place in March during Fifa’s next congress.

Before then, Diallo said, the FFF would reach out to figures it considers experts in “transparency and good governance” in football and beyond as part of France’s “contribution to the debate”, as it pushes for “far-reaching reform” of Fifa.

He cited Kevin Lamour, the former Fifa chief operating officer who was dismissed after criticising the sell-off plan, as one of the people the FFF would look to consult.

Fifa was approached for comment.

Sports.title: Football Daily | Mauricio Pochettino, Tottenham’s game of thrones and retrospective action
Sports.content:
ER, MEMORY LANE?

State-sanctioned execution of spouses and allies (Henry VIII), the Marian persecutions (Mary I), and enslavement and branding of the unemployed (Edward VI). During the 15th and 16th centuries, assorted monarchs from the House of Tudor were responsible for visiting no end of dread and terror on their subjects but it is the 44-day reign of one of their more contemporary counterparts at Tottenham that local subjects found truly unforgivable. Enthroned last February to secure Spurs’ safety following the dismissal of Thomas Frank, Igor Tudor took just one point from 15 available in his five top-flight games in charge. His subsequent deposition heralded the arrival of Roberto De Zerbi and ultimately last-day Premier League survival, but may also have denied the club’s fans a reunion with Mauricio Pochettino, a comparatively beloved former monarch who was tasked with focusing on other conquests in the Americas at the time.

“The problem was that the timings were never the best,” tooted Poch of the game of thrones played out in the kingdoms of the Seven Sisters and the New World that he claims dashed his hopes of coaching at the Geopolitics World Cup and then returning to a club he had managed for more than five years. “When I was free, I never received a contact. And then when I was working [with USA USA USA], I received a contact but I cannot make the decision to come back. It was a little bit unlucky. Maybe one day the stars will align and it can happen. If I was free, of course, I come. But I wasn’t free.” Having since signed a new four-year deal, he remains with the USA USA USA, while De Zerbi is tied to Spurs until 2031. Or possibly November.

A man who famously keeps a bowl of lemons in the office to help soak up negative energy, Pochettino might have needed several silos of the citrus fruit if things had worked out differently and he’d returned to coach a Spurs side muddying their spats in the Championship. However, it is a role the former manager of Paris Saint-Germain and Chelsea insists he would not have considered beneath him. “Tottenham … it’s the only club that always I am open to help in whatever division,” he cooed, when quizzed about his appetite for the grind of midweek trips to Lincoln City, Bolton and Stoke.

In a wide-ranging interview staged in That There Big London to mark the beginning of his second cycle as USA USA USA head coach, Pochettino stated that Chelsea should be stripped of the Premier League title they won in 2016-17, having since been found guilty of multiple and serious financial shenanigans at that time. As luck would have it, in such a scenario the honour would almost certainly be bestowed on a Spurs side that finished second in the league that season and happened to be coached by him. “If that [Chelsea’s chicanery] was true, then we deserve to be champions that year, for sure,” he parped. “They were punished, they admitted it? So that’s it. The title should be for the team that was second.” While Poch might well have an excellent point, Football Daily can’t say we recall him being such a stickler for the fastidious application of the rules when his USA USA USA team’s star striker had a ban controversially shelved by Fifa following the intervention of Donald Trump at the recent GWC.

But my plan was to go to England and follow my dream to become a coach, and that’s how it started” – Valdas Dambrauskas gets his very entertaining chat on with Nick Ames about his remarkable journey from an appearance on the Lithuanian version of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? via pub work in north London, to becoming manager of Azerbaijani champions Sabah.

And, given he also says that if he were Chelsea manager at the time, he’d admit that ‘we don’t deserve the title because we broke the rules’, it also conclusively proves he was the completely wrong man for Chelsea” – Noble Francis.

Sports.title: Why Kai Havertz’s dummy was perhaps more pleasing than a Lionel Messi waltz | Max Rushden
Sports.content:
During Covid, when sport was back but behind closed doors, I hosted a number of strange online shows to fill the void of real life. The highlight was chatting to Darren Gough about a lifesize bronze rhinoceros for 45 minutes to 15 small boxes on a Zoom call. I don’t recall who it was for and where the rhinoceros came from – but it might be in his garden.

I ended up doing virtual pre-match corporate Zoom calls for Heineken before Europa League games. It was the wifi version of Club Wembley: a Q&A happening on stage between a generic host and some random ex-pro while you’re trying to chat to your mate and eat an unidentified square of meat with some dauphinoise potatoes.

I’d be in my little square talking to Luis García in his little square about the ghost goal while an assorted group of faces and living rooms or kitchen tables would stare at you, perhaps interested, perhaps not. Did they even want to be there? Were we on mute while someone from marketing was filling a spare box on my laptop watching Death In Paradise on the TV behind me?

Certainly it was hard to create an amazing vibe with Mark van Bommel while his internet connection crashed and a little note on a Google doc appeared telling me to fill for 25 minutes with my favourite memories of the Europa League. Did these disembodied heads in front of me want the deep dive they got on Tony Parks’ heroics in 1984? How many of them knew about Gary Mabbutt playing centre mid and marking Enzo Scifo out of the game?

One of the guests was Dimitar Berbatov. You’d log on half an hour before the show and say hello, try to build some kind of electric rapport with a man in Bulgaria (I think) presumably looking to get in and get out and get back on with whatever social distancing life in Sofia had to offer.

He may have not had Akabusi levels of energy, and his economy of language was not unlike his playing style – why use a hundred words when one will do? But he was into it and did the job perfectly. I absolutely loved Berbatov as a player. Watching him pluck a goalkick out of the sky was more beautiful than watching a lot of other players banging one in from 25 yards. There’s a YouTube video called Dimitar Berbatov – the most underrated first touch ever? It begins with him standing like a lamp-post on the halfway line at Craven Cottage and stopping a crossfield ball stone dead like it’s an anvil.

View image in fullscreen Dimitar Berbatov, pictured scoring for Manchester United against Sunderland in 2009, could make football look easy. Photograph: Carl Recine/Action Images/Reuters

Back to the Zoom call: I welcome Dimitar, he says hello, I explain my admiration for him, and then say to him that he made football look easy. Did he find it easy? “Yes” he replied. Totally matter of fact. Not trying to impress – just explaining that football was easy.

And for someone like Berbatov, it is a different level to “good touch for a big man”. This is the ultimate type of grace on a football pitch. And perhaps it is reserved for tall, skilful players. I’ve probably used the word languid already but I can’t think of any other use of the word – reserved for players who are almost balletic.

Is it insane to say it’s more aesthetically pleasing than seeing a Messi or a Maradona waltz through a defence? It almost feels as if a low centre of gravity gives you an unfair advantage when it comes to technical skill. No flailing arms and legs to get in the way of you being naturally brilliant.

View image in fullscreen Argentina’s Lionel Messi dribbles away from three Dutch players in the 2022 World Cup. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

My biased brain instantly goes to Glenn Hoddle walking through the Oxford United defence with one sway, sitting the keeper down with a movement of the leg. It’s all saying: “This is easier for me than it is for you.”

Which brings us to Kai Havertz – and that dummy against Chelsea. The more and more football becomes that David Mitchell sketch, the more surprised I am that there are still moments in a game that lead to some involuntary noise from deep within.

The ball from Christos Tzolis is definitely for him. Havertz points in front to where he wants the ball. If it’s played there he can probably get a shot away first time. But when it comes, controlling the ball would have been a sensible choice. Back to goal. He could have turned and shot, or just kept the ball. There are lots of good players to pass it to.

View image in fullscreen Martin Ødegaard scores Arsenal’s second goal against Chelsea after Kai Havertz’s dummy. Photograph: Tony O Brien/Reuters

Even the way he lifts his left leg at the last second to let the ball run through to Martin Ødegaard is delightful. It’s easy to forget the pace of the game at this level. And when you’re watching on TV where it’s much easier to see the pass you also forget these guys don’t have that view.

Someone somewhere will have done a report on Havertz’s scanning abilities. He doesn’t appear to look behind to check where Ødegaard is. But awareness is hard to calculate. He just knows. And he does it all in a split second, not even. How wonderful that you can do so much without even touching the ball.

A lot of people do quite well out of repeatedly asking whether Arsenal need a centre-forward, so I don’t want to do them out of work. And Havertz isn’t perfect – he isn’t Robbie Fowler in the box. But he has scored in two Champions League finals. He did win the league last season. A lot of beautiful graceful players tend to be beautiful and graceful without delivering on the biggest occasions. Havertz does both. And when he gets it right, it looks easy to him. Imagine finding it easy.

Sports.title: Alexis Mac Allister makes his point as Liverpool fight back to defeat Atlético
Sports.content:
It was the time and place for Alexis Mac Allister to do his talking on the pitch and the disgruntled Liverpool midfielder delivered on cue. “Very sad” over Liverpool’s refusal to offer him a new contract, while Dominik Szoboszlai and Ryan Gravenberch were getting theirs, Mac Allister made Anfield very happy with a match-winning display against Atlético Madrid.

The Argentina international, one of five World Cup finalists involved in an absorbing, delicately-poised contest, vented his frustrations in the best possible and most professional way – from behind an immaculate 20-yard strike into Jan Oblak’s goal rather than a microphone. Mac Allister believes he is playing for a new deal this season and promised to give “100% to my last day” at the pre-match press conference. He was true to his word to extend Atlético’s winless sequence against English opposition in the Champions League league phase to 11 matches.

For Andoni Iraola, it was the perfect start to life as a Champions League coach after an imperfect start to the game. Diego Simeone’s switch to a 3-5-2 formation caught Liverpool cold and it was only when they regrouped in the aftermath of Marcos Llorente’s latest Anfield goal, and again during the half-time interval, that their performance level improved. Mac Allister’s timely moment, Alexander Isak’s relentless industry, Florian Wirtz’s creativity and another performance of drive and intelligence from Szoboszlai ensured the Liverpool head coach had plenty to savour.

“I have to blame myself a bit for the start of the game,” Iraola said. “Atlético surprised us with the way they approached the game. They haven’t used that system too much this season and it’s difficult if you are not ready for it, but we adjusted and played better. In the second half we were the best team. We came back for the third time [this season] and that showed the players are pushing and they have character.”

It was a night of firsts. Iraola coached a Champions League game for the first time in his career – he did take charge of 12 Europa League matches with AEK Larnaca in 2018-19 – Bradley Barcola made his first Liverpool start after a move worth up to £123m from Paris Saint-Germain and Julián Álvarez was in Atlético’s starting lineup for the first time this season since his failed attempt to join Barcelona. All appeared to have been forgiven – for now at least – as his name was cheered by the small pocket of Atlético fans when the teams were announced before kick-off and he repaid them by creating the opening goal.

View image in fullscreen Dominik Szoboszlai scores Liverpool’s equaliser late in the first half. Photograph: Dave Thompson/AP

Llorente was the scourge of Anfield yet again when Álvarez threaded a pass behind the home defence and the right wing-back raced clear on goal. The man who named his dog Anfield after scoring twice to eliminate Jürgen Klopp’s team from the competition in 2020, in the game played while Madrid was in lockdown from the Covid pandemic, lofted a confident finish beyond Alisson. It was Llorente’s fifth goal at Anfield, half of his entire total of Champions League goals. He had been kept onside by Milos Kerkez, who endured a poor night with his positioning and distribution before atoning with a key role in Liverpool’s equaliser.

Álvarez almost doubled the visitors’ lead when granted far too much time and space to take aim from almost 30 yards. Alisson, at full stretch, intervened with a superb finger-tip save. Anfield was growing restless at Liverpool’s carelessness on the ball and Atlético’s comfort on it. But the threat and control from the hosts increased.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Wirtz drew a fine save from Oblak at the end of a flowing move involving Barcola and Isak. Liverpool then drew level thanks to tenacity from Kerkez, a lovely touch from Ronald Araújo and Szoboszlai’s instinctive finish. The left-back won possession with a clean, crunching challenge on Lee Kang-in before finding Barcola. The France international was denied a goal on his full debut by Oblak’s low save but Wirtz kept the pressure on and Szoboszlai, having been halted on the edge of the area, got a second bite from Araújo’s clever flick. The midfielder’s first-time shot sailed into the far corner.

Barcola should have put Liverpool ahead when played through on goal by Wirtz early in the second half. The winger had time to measure the finish but pulled it wide of Oblak’s right-hand post. He would later depart with cramp. Liverpool were ahead one minute later when the lively Rio Ngumoha beat Llorente and his cross fell to Mac Allister via a deflection off Isak. Mac Allister told Szoboszlai to leave the ball and drilled home an unstoppable left-footed drive from 20 yards. Atlético remained dangerous and the introduction of Ademola Lookman added an extra dimension to the visitors’ attack but Liverpool defended impressively to secure a deserved victory.

Sports.title: Why David Beckham will have my vote for the US Soccer Hall of Fame | Pablo Iglesias Maurer
Sports.content:
Next spring, when the US Soccer Hall of Fame welcomes its newest class, there will be pomp and circumstance. The hall, which sits in a corner of Toyota Stadium, home of Major League Soccer’s FC Dallas, will feature the enshrineds’ signature red jackets. There will be glad-handing and speeches from players and coaches, misty-eyed reflections on their upbringings and their careers.

Many involved will be American-born soccer legends, of course. Yet every once in a while, a player whose footprint extends well beyond the borders of the United States graces the stage. Such may be the case next year when the hall potentially welcomes English legend David Beckham into the fold.

Some readers abroad – and certainly plenty of readers here in the States – will wonder why an ostensibly American Hall of Fame would admit non-Americans, something it’s done since its inception. The answer lies in the nature of the American game itself. Even our earliest heroes – Joe Gaetjens and the like – were immigrants, with Gaetjens scoring his famed goal against England in the 1950 World Cup when he wasn’t even a US citizen (he never ended up becoming one).

Advance through the decades and big-name, American-born heroes do start to emerge, but they are still outpaced by those from abroad. The history of the North American Soccer League is replete with foreign-born members of the country’s hall of fame such as Pelé, Franz Beckenbauer and Carlos Alberto. Even the Major Indoor Soccer League got its due eventually: just last year, Steve Zungul, the “lord of all indoors”, was inducted. Tatu, another foreign-born legend of the arena, seems likely to go in this year.

All of which is to say, there’s precedent for this. If you made a sizable contribution to soccer in the United States, you’re eligible – period. It’s the way it should be.

By that standard, there’s no doubting Beckham’s credentials. Perhaps the most direct analog for his contributions is the career of Pelé, who arrived stateside in 1977 and transformed the landscape of the game in this country. Like Beckham’s stay with the LA Galaxy, the Brazilian’s playing career was successful. He won a league championship in 1977 and was wildly productive throughout the entirety of his stay in the US. He did every interview, signed every autograph, more or less, and went on to found a soccer camp in New Jersey that produced thousands of soccer-mad children, more than one of whom went on to feature for the US men’s national team. He remained a presence for decades after his retirement.

Still, after all of that, professional soccer in the US more or less collapsed within seven years of his departure.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Twice weekly Sign up to Soccer Desk Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer. Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Beckham’s playing career with the Galaxy (2007-2012) was in some ways more successful than Pelé’s. Much has been made about his tumultuous arrival in the US, so expertly told by the late, great Grant Wahl in his book The Beckham Experiment. After the smoke cleared, though, Beckham was a mainstay for the Galaxy, working alongside Landon Donovan (a Hall of Famer himself) to lead the club to a pair of league titles and two Supporters’ Shields.

His true effect, though, came at a league level. Major League Soccer created an entirely new roster mechanism – the designated player rule – to accommodate Beckham’s arrival, a guideline that fundamentally changed its reality. Like Pelé, scores of uninitiated fans filled MLS stadiums to see Beckham. And just as the Brazilian did, Beckham stayed well beyond the end of his playing days, eventually founding Lionel Messi’s Inter Miami, the current standard bearer of the league.

The Hall of Fame inducts candidates in three categories: player, veteran and builder, the last of which is reserved for those whose work was primarily off the field. Beckham’s inclusion this year comes in the veteran category, where he’s nominated alongside nine other deserving candidates. The presence of his name has been the subject of much debate among the hall’s voters, of which I am one.

Arguments against his inclusion center on the fact that, in several years, Beckham’s name seems likely to come up on a list of “builder” nominees. Certainly, helping to found Inter Miami, and luring the greatest player in history to play there, is worth considering by that standard. So if he stands a good chance of making it in that way, then why not save this spot for someone else?

To me, though, voting him in now is an easy decision – why wait? Beckham’s playing career alone stacks up favorably against many members of the hall. And while he is unquestionably a “builder”, so much of that work was simultaneous with his career as a player.

His mere presence on field legitimized a still fledgeling league and led to a decade-long boom that saw it nearly double in size. This, of course, is not solely Beckham’s doing – far from it – but I could easily make an argument that Beckham’s influence on American soccer is as big as Pelé’s – and Pelé, of course, has a place in the hall.

So, English-born Beckham will be getting one of my votes for induction. In truth, three of my five selections for induction (Beckham, Tatu, Ken Cooper Sr, Tiffany Roberts and Clint Mathis) are foreign-born. That feels truly American to me.

Sports.title: Cole Palmer powers Chelsea to comeback win over Leeds in nine-goal epic
Sports.content:
Where’s the fun in doing it the easy way? Chelsea remain chaotic at the back but can drag their opponents into horrible places. It helps, mind you, to have some assistance from the referee. Jarred Gillett and Cole Palmer? They made for a killer combination as Chelsea swerved embarrassment and treated Stamford Bridge to one of life’s rarities: a classic in the third round of the Carabao Cup.

Gillett, a referee who always seems to be guessing when he makes key calls, was the villain as far as Leeds were concerned. They had just gone 2-0 up when Gillett altered the flow of the tie by pointing to the spot after Pep Chavarría made the most of slight contact from Daniel James. The subsequent conversion from Palmer was inevitable and from there so was the comeback from Chelsea, who rattled through four goals in 12 minutes before eventually reaching the last 16 by winning 6-3.

It made little sense. It could have gone down as Xabi Alonso’s first misjudgment as Chelsea’s manager. The Carabao Cup is important given the Spaniard’s side are not in Europe, but his rotation almost backfired. Chelsea were shambolic after making nine changes – the 16-year-old debutant Reggie Watson was overrun in midfield while Estêvão Willian and Jamie Gittens struggled in attack – and Alonso was in emergency mode when he made a quadruple change at half-time.

“I take responsibility,” Alonso said. “No player is to blame. It’s the decisions we took. When you don’t have this time to work with them, it’s difficult to compete at this level. I need to take my own blame for the things that happen. I need to be able to help them better. They are not responsible. After you need to react and think what’s better for the team.”

Quick Guide Championship: Ten-man West Brom win at Derby to go top Show West Bromwich Albion held on for a memorable 1-0 victory over Derby at Pride Park, after playing for more than an hour with 10 men. Aune Heggebø's early goal proved enough to take the Baggies top of the table, despite Brayann Pereira being dismissed on his debut after collecting two first-half yellow cards. Derby had started the stronger, but West Brom swept downfield to score in the 16th minute, Jimmy-Jay Morgan whipping in a low cross from the left which Heggebø [pictured] finished at the near post. The visitors were rocked by the dismissal of Pereira in the 34th minute, as he was shown a second yellow card for a clumsy challenge on Charlie Taylor. The hosts went close just before half-time when David Ozoh flashed a low ball across the six-yard box with no white shirt able to turn it in. Derby should have levelled in the 68th minute but Lars-Jørgen Salvesen headed over from Joe Ward’s cross. Late on, Nat Phillips made a great clearance after a late goalmouth scramble, summing up a performance full of grit and resolve. James Morrison's side move above West Ham to top the Championship table with 13 points from six games. Either Charlton or QPR could have joined them on 13 points, but the sides played out a stalemate at the Valley. Derby, meanwhile, slipped into the bottom three with their fourth defeat in six games. Norwich moved up to ninth in the table as they edged past visitors Birmingham 2-1 to make it three wins in four league games. Oscar Schwartau's screamer opened the scoring, the young Dane lashing an unstoppable right-footed drive past James Beadle from 25 yards out. Papa Diallo's first goal for the Canaries doubled their advantage before the break, as the Senegal winger sidefooted home from Andre Brooks' cross. Carlos Vicente pulled a goal back for the visitors, but wasted a glorious chance to equalise near the end as Chris Davies’ men suffered their first league defeat this season. Press Association Photograph: Morgan Harlow/Getty Images Europe Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Equally Alonso can take credit for responding. His moves were decisive. Reece James offered security after replacing Watson and Pedro Neto scored after coming on for Malo Gusto, who could barely complete a pass during a wretched first half. Leeds, beaten at this stage for the 14th time in 18 years, were overwhelmed once their lead was halved. Morgan Rogers and Palmer were devastating after replacing Estêvão and Gittens. Rogers had a hand in four goals and Palmer, who scored twice, seemed affronted by the notion of Leeds going through.

It finished as another thrilling attacking display from Chelsea, who have scored 16 goals in Alonso’s first five games. There are flaws to fix at the other end, though. Leeds also experimented, Daniel Farke making eight changes, but controlled the first half. They led when the Bosnia and Herzegovina centre-back Tarik Muharemovic, signed from Sassuolo last summer, headed Harry Wilson’s corner past Mike Penders in the 23rd minute.

Chelsea have already conceded 10 goals in all competitions. Leeds could have doubled their lead through Sean Longstaff. Valentín Barco and Watson, son of the former Wigan midfielder Ben Watson, were second best in midfield.

Leeds were on their way when Barco lost possession three minutes into the second half. Ethan Ampadu charged past Rogers and found Lukas Nmecha, who teed up Brenden Aaronson to make it 2-0.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Pedro Neto fires home Chelsea’s third goal at Stamford Bridge. Photograph: Adam Davy/PA

Chelsea needed a lift. Chavarría crossed from the left and went to ground. Gillett whistled and Palmer scored with 53 minutes played. “He gave out of nothing a penalty where it wasn’t even a chance for them,” Farke said. “A quality player scores and the body language of the Chelsea players was different.”

Palmer was in his element, equalising in the 55th minute after Rogers laid the ball off for his pal to stroke a casual finish past Michael Zetterer from 20 yards. Chelsea were rampant and led on the hour, Palmer and Rogers combining for Neto to finish well. Leeds looked dizzy. They readied the changes but Danny Welbeck made it 4-2 with a sharp turn and finish in the 65th minute.

Leeds kept fighting. Dominic Calvert-Lewin came on and pulled one back to remind Alonso of Chelsea’s defensive weaknesses. Chelsea responded, Rogers crossing for Barco to score his first goal for the club. The sixth followed, Barco’s mis-hit shot diverted in by Welbeck. “A crazy nuts game,” Farke said. That’s been the way for Chelsea under Alonso.

Sports.title: Scottish Premiership: Miovski hits last-gasp Rangers winner and Celtic keep 100% record
Sports.content:
A dramatic last-gasp strike from substitute Bojan Miovski gave Rangers a 1-0 Premiership win over St Mirren at Ibrox.

Back in the technical area after a two-game touchline suspension, Derek McInnes watched St Mirren’s Australian goalkeeper Jacob Chapman keep the home side at bay in the first half with a string of saves, albeit helped by some poor finishing.

Craig McLeish’s side, who lost 5-1 at Ibrox in the Premier Sports Cup last month, grew in confidence after the break and Fraser Taylor missed a great chance while the frustrated home support returned to the state of agitation which characterised the start of the season.

However, in the final seconds of normal time, Miovski, on for Djeidi Gassama, pounced in the box to grab the winner to make it four victories in a row.

Summer signing Mika Baur notched his first goal for Celtic as the Scottish champions maintained their perfect start to their title defence with a 1-0 victory away to St Johnstone.

View image in fullscreen Celtic’s Mika Baur scored his first Celtic goal at McDiarmid Park. Photograph: Steve Welsh/PA

The German midfielder struck from close range early in the second half after the debutant Hoops keeper Sam Johnstone had produced a stunning first-half save to deny Saints midfielder Joel Cotterill.

It was a night when the Celtic head coach, Martin O’Neill, was able to demonstrate the depth of his squad before Sunday’s Old Firm meeting away to Rangers in the Premier Sports Cup, with key players such as Camilo Duran, Benjamin Nygren and Kieran Tierney on the bench and defender Cameron Carter-Vickers given the evening off.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Although far from their convincing best, the Hoops did enough to close out a sixth consecutive league victory this term and their 13th in a row in total stretching back to the closing weeks of last season.
