Sports.title: Coleman: Ireland's new generation not scarred by past World Cup play-off pain
Sports.content:
Seamus Coleman insists the Republic of Ireland's new generation will not be scarred by the bitter pain of World Cup play-off defeat as they attempt to book a ticket for this summer's finals.

Ireland face the Czech Republic at Prague's Fortuna Arena on Thursday evening attempting to go one better than they did in 2009 against France and in 2017, when Denmark shattered their dreams with a 5-1 demolition job in Dublin.

However, Everton defender Coleman, who was not in the squad on that fateful night in Paris and was injured for the game with the Danes, is confident there will be no hangover, with the Czechs standing between Heimir Hallgrimsson's men and a winner-takes-all match with either Denmark or North Macedonia in Dublin on Tuesday.

Asked if the pain of those near-misses was fuelling the latest bid to make it to the finals for the first time since 2002, the 37-year-old said: "It's difficult to say if it's fuelling the players, they're all so young.

"Obviously the nation was hurt massively, but in terms of the current group of players I don't think they're dwelling too much on that hurt.

"To be honest, we're just riding the wave of the confidence we've got as a group - which I think this young group deserves - from the last two games and we're looking forward to Thursday night and then see what comes after that.

"But to see how the nation is feeling now is incredible and we've got a duty to try and make them even happier."

Image: Troy Parrott's goals inspired Ireland to stunning wins over Portugal and Hungary that secured a play-off spot

Ireland are only in Prague because they backed up a scratchy Group F victory over Armenia with an unexpected 2-0 win against Portugal in Dublin before going to Hungary and coming out on top in a five-goal thriller in which Troy Parrott scored the decisive goal with the last kick of the game.

Coleman is one of only two players - 34-year-old Robbie Brady is the other - in the current squad to have been to a major tournament, and the experience they had in earning their trip to Euro 2016 in France could prove invaluable this time around.

Image: Coleman and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson are bidding to lead Ireland to World Cup qualification for the first time since 2002

Martin O'Neill's team reached the finals by beating Bosnia and Herzegovina 3-1 on aggregate in a play-off after a hard-fought 1-1 draw in Zenica in the first leg.

Coleman said: "Maybe two years ago it would have been a lot for the young lads to take.

"But everyone now has stepped up and are prepared for what's to come and we absolutely, no doubt about it, understand it's going to be a tough game for us, but it's also going to be a tough game for them as well."

Head coach Hallgrimsson, who is without suspended defender Liam Scales and injured midfielder Josh Cullen, as ever exuded calm as he fulfilled his media duties on Wednesday morning, simply asking for more of the same from his players.

He said: "We all know by now why we got good results and good performances, and that's the key, not be over-ambitious tomorrow, stay on point, focus on why we are here and trying to improve that, not only this game, continuously."

Czech boss says Soucek still key player despite not being captain

Image: West Ham's Tomas Soucek is no longer captain of his country

Czech Republic boss Miroslav Koubek said "full-fat" Tomas Soucek remains a key player for his country despite being stripped of the captaincy.

The 31-year-old West Ham midfielder has been replaced as skipper by Wolves defender Ladislav Krejci after being removed from his position amid the fall-out from the 2-1 defeat by the Faroe Islands in October.

However Koubek, who himself took over from Ivan Hasek as head coach in December, still counts Soucek among his most important players ahead of Thursday night's World Cup play-off semi-final against the Republic of Ireland in Prague.

He said: "Tomas Soucek is an outstanding player with a great career. He doesn't have the captain's armband at this moment for reasons you all know, but nothing changes.

"It does not mean he will lose his value. He is still a 'full-fat' player, if I can use these words."

Image: Miroslav Koubek's first game in charge of the Czech Republic is against Ireland

Soucek's removal as captain has prompted speculation in the Czech media that he could even lose his place in the team, although Koubek remained coy over his team selection.

The 74-year-old said: "I don't read the newspapers, so I don't know. You will see tomorrow."

Koubek's side will welcome Ireland to the Fortuna Arena, the home of domestic champions Slavia Prague, knowing they will have to find a way to stop in-from striker Troy Parrott, who scored five goals in his country's last two qualifiers against Portugal and Hungary to get them to the play-offs.

Asked about his analysis of Heimir Hallgrimsson's team, he said: "One thing I noticed: they put a lot heart into their game. Ireland will definitely be a very tough opponent.

"But we will have a similar mindset, it will be a hard match, definitely.

"As for Parrott, he is outstanding, he is doing great. He is very fit, we know how he works. We do have some information, so now it will all be about eliminating him in a smart way. We will just have to stop him."

Krejci, however, has little doubt that it will be he and his team-mates who ultimately fight it out with either Denmark of North Macedonia for a trip to the United States, Canada and Mexico this summer.

He said: "We will make it. We will reach our goal. We will qualify for the World Cup."

Sports.title: Conor Benn hits out at 'spoiled brat' Ryan Garcia ahead of Las Vegas world title showdown - as Brit dismisses concerns over huge weight cut on eve of clash with 'insecure' rival
Sports.content:
Conor Benn hits out at 'spoiled brat' Ryan Garcia ahead of Las Vegas world title showdown - as Brit dismisses concerns over huge weight cut on eve of clash with 'insecure' rival

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Conor Benn knows there is a sizeable question hanging over him before he even gets into the ring with Ryan Garcia this weekend: can he still make 147lb?

Benn has not fought at welterweight for more than four years, having moved up through the divisions before competing at middleweight during his two-fight rivalry with Chris Eubank Jr.

Now, for the biggest fight of his career, taking on Garcia for the World Boxing Council (WBC) title under the bright lights in Las Vegas, he has to come all the way back down.

'I can't wait. It's going to be hard,' Benn told Daily Mail Sport during camp. 'I know it's going to be hard, but I believe I can do it.

'I think a lot of people are banking on the weight being an issue and me not having made 147 for four years. Ultimately, my discipline will prevail, and I'll continue to show why I can do what people say I can't do.'

Whether the weight cut affects Benn's strength and power on Saturday night will be one of the central questions of his WBC world title fight.

Conor Benn works out at the MGM Grand in Las Vegas ahead of his showdown with Garcia

Garcia has suggested Benn's move back down could leave him vulnerable, but Benn is dismissive of that concern.

'You think I've been up at middleweight, mixed it with someone who's competed at super middleweight? You think I'm worried about what a lightweight can do to me?' he said.

'You think I'm concerned in the slightest about this guy? I'm not concerned about one little thing he brings to the table… that silly left hook of his is useless. He can bring whatever he wants. It don't concern me.'

Benn's unusual route to this fight has been shaped by his rivalry with Eubank.

Their first meeting at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in April 2025 was the culmination of years of animosity between the two families, with Benn and Eubank Jr inheriting a rivalry that began with their fathers in 1990.

The fight itself was fought at a catchweight above 160lb, with Benn stepping up significantly from his previous division. Eubank won a close decision, leaving Benn to reflect on a performance in which he felt the occasion and the emotion had affected him.

Benn and father Nigel at the Mandalay Bay in Vegas - this is Benn's second fight since he renewed the family feud with the Eubanks

Seven months later, the pair met again at the same venue. This time Benn won the decision, dropping Eubank twice in the final round in a dramatic conclusion to their second fight. It left them level at one victory apiece and appeared to finally close the door on one of British boxing's most talked-about rivalries.

Benn insisted the atmosphere this week is nothing like those two nights when asked whether his hatred for Garcia compared.

'This is nothing like the Eubank fight,' he said. 'The Eubank fight, there was nothing pleasant or friendly or fake about the Eubank fight. There was a lot more raw emotion in that fight and I let that get the better of me the first time. That won't happen here.'

Garcia has been happy to trade insults with his British opponent, but Benn clearly has little time for his opponent's personality.

'He just carries on like a spoiled brat, like a big child who throws his toys out of the pram,' Benn said. 'I'm not worried about him in the slightest. If anything, I'm gonna have a bit of fun with him. He's a little bit sensitive, highly emotional, and a little bit insecure.'

There is also an uncomfortable shared history between the two men when it comes to drugs testing.

Benn's original 2022 fight with Eubank was cancelled after he returned two adverse findings for clomifene, something he has consistently denied intentionally taking. Garcia subsequently returned an adverse finding for ostarine following his 2024 victory over Devin Haney, which he also denied intentionally taking.

Both men were asked at the fight's press conference whether they had concerns that the other could use performance-enhancing drugs ahead of Saturday's contest.

Neither appeared keen to make it a central issue, with the focus instead returning to the fight itself.

Ryan Garcia, Benn's opponent, has also had controversy in his career over positive drug tests

Garcia has also questioned whether Benn's career has prepared him for this level of opposition, arguing that the Briton is taking a step too far by challenging for the world title.

JEFF POWELL IN LAS VEGAS An advance guard of a couple of hundred UK fight fans arrived here in time to see Conor Benn stage a public work-out three days before he challenges Ryan Garcia for the world welterweight title in the intimidating T-Mobile Arena. They kicked up a din as Benn went through a few minutes of snappy pad work in a temporary ring pitched between a bar waiting to serve them and the MGM Grand Casino’s sports book. While admitting he can’t wait to wolf down fish and chips after all the dieting to make the 147lbs welter limit he assured them: ‘I feel great and I’ll give my all to give you all a night to remember.’ But he refrained from removing his top to give them a glimpse of his body. Both he and Garcia looked sharp and calm in their brief appearances. The Benn faithful will be heavily outnumbered on Saturday night by the Americans and Mexicans rooting for King Ry but they are in good voice.

Benn's response was typically blunt. 'How is this too far? He quit against Tank Davis. He got outclassed by Rolly [Romero], and then got a world title shot with Barrios,' he said.

'Then there is me. Stepping up to fight the contenders up at middleweight, fight of the year up at middleweight, avenging my loss. Two big stadium shows. Just come off beating a two-time former world champion and having to make 147, which again I ain't made in four years in six weeks.

'What's he talking about? Ultimately, who cares what he thinks? I don't listen to quitters anyway.'

For all the talk, though, the immediate challenge is the scales. Benn has to get himself back down to a weight he has not made since 2022, before attempting to deal with one of boxing's fastest and most dangerous punchers.

He accepts it will not be straightforward, but he remains convinced the doubts surrounding him will only add to his motivation.

'If I'd listened to everyone that didn't believe in me, I'd be nowhere,' he said. 'But I continue to believe in me. And that's all that matters… you believing in yourself. I believe in me to get me to where I am right now, to revenge that loss against Eubank, to put on Fight of the Year against Eubank, to then fight for the WBC world title.

'I don't need nobody else to believe in me. Continue to doubt me because doubt fuels the fire.'

Sports.title: Katie Taylor is crowned undisputed champion for a THIRD time with unanimous decision victory over Flora Pili - as Irish boxing icon, 40, enjoys fairytale end to her career in front of 82,000 fans at sold-out Croke Park
Sports.content:
There will never be another night quite like this for Katie Taylor… or, for that matter, for boxing itself.

Under the lights at Croke Park, in front of 82,000 delirious fans, Ireland's greatest fighter walked into the ring for the final time and left it as a three-time undisputed world champion after defeating Flora Pili on points.

Taylor had dreamed of this moment for much of her life. She had spent more than a decade rewriting the history of women's boxing, collecting world titles, conquering America, avenging the only defeat of her professional career and becoming the undisputed champion not once, but twice.

But nothing could have prepared her for this.

The noise inside Croke Park was deafening as Taylor made her final walk to the ring, the 40-year-old receiving a hero's welcome before facing the undefeated Frenchwoman in the last fight of a career that has transformed boxing in Ireland and beyond.

And when the first bell rang, Taylor set about doing exactly what she had come to Croke Park to do.

Katie Taylor celebrated victory on her farewell fight to become a three-time undisputed champion

Taylor overcame the challenge of Flora Pili, who had been unbeaten in 12 fights as a professional

Taylor appeared in the ring with family and friends are wrapping up her career in style

From the opening round, she demonstrated her speed deploying a lightning-quick jab despite being 11 years older than her opponent.

It was in the second round Pili really felt Taylor's power after taking a strong right hand to the temple.

It got the fans excited but the Frenchwoman weathered the storm before receiving a slap across her face from her trainer in the corner as he urged her to 'wake up'.

Knowing she was down heavily on the scorecards Pili showed conviction in the seventh round but it was never going to be enough to topple the Irish champion.

As the tenth and final round rang in, both fighters touched gloves as a sign of respect. The crowd cheered their champion home as she drew the curtain on her career.

Taylor did everything she could to get the stoppage in the dying seconds of the fight but she had to settle for a points victory.

There was a moment after the final bell when Taylor simply stood and took it all in.

The noise, the tears, the Irish flags, the thousands of people on their feet inside Croke Park and the knowledge that this really was the end.

Taylor emerged to a stunning ovation at a sold-out Croke Park, with 82,000 in attendance

Taylor's husband Sean McCavanagh was among those watching on ringside at the venue

Westlife performed in the build-up to Taylor taking to the ring for the last time in her career

Michael Flatley was among the well-known faces in attendance on the historic night

She had wanted one final night. One final fight. One final chance to walk into the ring in front of her home crowd and remind the world exactly who she was.

She got all three.

Taylor leaves boxing as a three-time undisputed world champion, an Olympic gold medallist and one of the most important figures the sport has ever produced.

But her legacy cannot be measured in belts alone.

She changed women's boxing forever. She gave a generation of young girls a reason to believe that they belonged in a boxing gym. She carried Irish boxing on her shoulders for years and became a sporting icon far beyond the ring.

And perhaps most fittingly of all, she signed off where she had always wanted to be.

At Croke Park. In front of her people. With another world title wrapped around her waist.

The final chapter could not have been written any better.

Katie Taylor came home, became undisputed for the third time and walked away on top.

A champion to the very end.

Sports.title: Tyson Fury claims Anthony Joshua fight is OFF in another social media rant: Gypsy King accuses AJ of 's***ing his pants' in talks over Battle of Britain deal
Sports.content:
Tyson Fury has suggested he will no longer be fighting Anthony Joshua in another social media rant as rows over the location and contract surrounding the fight continue.

The two British heavyweights had seemed set to finally face off later this year, but Fury had suggested his rival was stalling over the contractual agreements.

Joshua's promoter, Eddie Hearn, claimed last week that talks had 're-opened' – but things, if Fury is to be believed, seem to have again gone backwards.

'So it looks like AJ has s*** his pants yet again,' Fury said on social media on Sunday. 'After 11 years, he's finally s*** his pants yet again.'

The bitter tug-of-war over their heavyweight superfight has largely centered on a debate around hosting it at London's Wembley Stadium or broadcaster Netflix's choice of Madison Square Garden in New York City.

Last week, Fury, who regularly takes to social media to express his views on potential opponents, was keen to make clear he feels Joshua is not motivated by a love of his country. Earlier this year Daily Mail Sport revealed Joshua had in fact quit the UK to move to Dubai – even as thousands tried to flee amid rising panic in the Middle East warzone.

Tyson Fury (pictured) has claimed Anthony Joshua has bailed on their potential fight

Joshua (pictured) is still yet to sign the deal to fight Tyson Fury, Frank Warren has revealed, with a deadline for Sunday

And Fury, a tax exile to the Isle of Man himself, brought up a 2020 speech at a Black Lives Matter march, where Joshua read out a letter from his friend Reece Campbell to urge attendees to stop spending money with white-owned shops and businesses.

'Show them where it hurts', Joshua had said. 'Abstain from spending your money in their shops and economies, and invest in black-owned businesses.'

Fury re-posted the video of the speech, writing: 'This is the man who loves England, absolute s*** bag! Total piece of s*** bully with zero guts! Don't let them deceive you! & Living in Dubai.'

In an address to camera, Fury accused Joshua of trying to derail their fight to avoid being embarrassed: 'If I agreed to tie both hands behind my back and wear solid cement boots, Anthony Joshua would never get in the ring with me because I'll annihilate him.

'And he's a piece of s*** bully, and that's his game—bullying people like he tried to do to Daniel Dubois, and he got knocked spark dead out.

'The latest news from them is, 'Tyson don't want to fight in England'. Why the f*** wouldn't I want to fight in England, you sausage? 'Tyson only wants to fight in America'. Are you joking or what?

'Tyson is not in charge of this fight. Tyson didn't put the money up for this fight. Tyson is not the paymaster. Netflix are and Turki Al-Sheikh. Lovely. If it's in England, even better. I'll knock the motherf***er out even quicker. Prime time England, 10 o'clock, Wembley Stadium, 100,000 people. Why the f*** wouldn't I want it in England? Doesn't make any sense, does it?

'Like I said, who do you think you are? You and your little pathetic puppet Eddie Hearn trying to save you. There's no escaping, you know. I'll come to Watford (Joshua's hometown) and I'll set about you. I'll batter you in your own front garden, you piece of s***.'

Joshua's 2020 Black Lives Matter speech was brought back up by his great boxing rival Fury

'There is no getting out of this one. There is no getting out of this one. Get ready for this fight. I've had enough of your sauce to last me 11 years. I'm battering the f*** out of you, you useless dosser, piece of s***. That's what you are. And you know it as well, and everybody else knows what you are: a coward.'

Roaring out his title of the 'Gypsy King,' Fury added: 'You's are going down, and the cash cow is getting knocked out. Because after this, he won't be able to show his face in public ever again.

'You're a useless dosser, a big bodybuilding piece of s***. Too many weights, not enough speed. When I crack a big right hook off it, you'll go over like spaghetti legs Deontay Wilder. But he's 10 times the man you'll ever be, because he's got a pair of b*****ks like King Kong, and you've got a pair of b*****ks like two f***ing garden peas, you piece of s***.'

On Sunday, Fury revealed he has turned his attention to trying to fight Oleksandr Usyk for a third time – on the back of two defeats.

'So this would only lead me to a fight with Oleksandr Usyk,' he said. 'Let's do it again. Let's run it back in November. The ball is now in your court, Oleksandr.'

He added: 'Do you want to fight me this year, 2026, or are you calling it quits? Let me know, because I'm now looking for a new opponent.'

Fury's promoter Frank Warren, who suggested that in reality boxing's longest hatching deal had to be finalised by Sunday, told Daily Mail Sport last week: 'AJ hasn't signed yet.

'Tyson signed in January. He's training in Miami for the fight in early November and doesn't care where it takes place.'

There is debate around the contract and location of the fight, with Fury supposedly agreeing the match-up earlier this year

The original agreement stipulated England, putting Wembley Stadium on alert.

But Netflix, the mega-paymasters for the broadcast, have joined their Saudi partners in insisting on New York's fabled Madison Square Garden so as to maximise US revenue.

Joshua will need at least a two-month training camp for a fight of this magnitude and ideally nine to ten weeks.

It comes after Joshua was given ten days to agree a deal on August 26 with Warren previously warning: 'Unless AJ commits by the end of next week I'm afraid this will slip away like so many of those great fights which never happened.'

He added: 'At some point everyone has to say the most important thing is that it happens. Not this bulls*** about money.

'That everyone wants the fight. Does AJ really want it? I don't know. He's been through that tragedy of the car crash which killed two of his closest friends. Only he knows what he wants.'

Much of the discussions around Wembley centre on a willingness to allow a late start time – and late curfew – to suit the American TV market. Mayor Sadiq Khan this week stated that he is keen to host the fight and find a solution.

Sports.title: Anthony Joshua's conqueror Andy Ruiz is PUMMELLED with punches and brutally beaten on his return to the ring after two years - but incredibly insists he WILL keep fighting
Sports.content:
Anthony Joshua's conqueror Andy Ruiz is PUMMELLED with punches and brutally beaten on his return to the ring after two years - but incredibly insists he WILL keep fighting

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Andy Ruiz, the man who condemned Anthony Joshua to his first ever professional defeat, suffered a horrific loss of his own on Friday night.

The 36-year-old Mexican was left bruised and bloodied as he lost to Poland's Damian Knyba on his return to the ring after two years out.

Knyba unleashed heavy punch after punch in the seventh round but Ruiz managed to ride it out, after being saved by the bell, to lose by a unanimous points decision.

Ruiz, who is now signed to British promoter Eddie Hearn, vowed to carry on despite losing his comeback fight to Knyba. The Pole now has a record of 18 wins and one defeat.

Rewind to June 2019, and Ruiz shocked the boxing world by upsetting the odds to knock Joshua out in the seventh round at Madison Square Garden.

Ruiz was a late stand-in for Jarrell Miller, who had failed a drugs test, and wasn't seen as a threat to Joshua's chances of remaining unbeaten and hanging on to his then IBF, WBO and WBA world heavyweight titles.

ANDY RUIZ IS SAVED BY THE BELL 🤯🤯🤯#TheFight | #RuizKnyba | Live NOW on DAZN and TNT ▪️ pic.twitter.com/JVQjG3KQM3 — DAZN Boxing (@DAZNBoxing) September 5, 2026

Andy Ruiz kneels down in front of the referee after being on the receiving end of heavy blows

Ruiz feels the full force of Poland's Damian Knyba during Friday's fight in New Jersey

Ruiz famously defeated the then undefeated Anthony Joshua back in June 2019

Joshua exacted revenge six months later and Ruiz has gone on to have just four more fights since due to injury problems, beating Chris Arreola and Luis Ortiz before drawing with Miller and now suffering his third loss.

Ruiz said after Friday's defeat in New Jersey: 'It was just a long layoff, and it was a great opponent.

'I didn't want to take an easy fight, so that's why I took Damian. He's a big guy. But we've got to take risks. I've still got it in me, man. I've just got to stay active and I want to fight again.

'Every time I tried to come in, he'd hold me really tight, and I just couldn't let my combinations go.

'He played a good game plan, but I'd love to run it back and do things a lot different.'

The judges scored the fight 117-110, 114-113 and 114-113 in Knyba's favour.

It wasn't the night Hearn was hoping for after signing Ruiz this summer but much of his current focus is on trying to finalise Joshua's highly anticipated fight against British rival Tyson Fury.

The bout has been proposed to take place in November after years of negotiations but the location of the fight appears to be a major sticking point.

Hearn and Joshua are said to want the fight to take place at Wembley Stadium in London while the Fury camp are reportedly leaning towards Madison Square Garden in New York City.

Sports.title: RIATH AL-SAMARRAI: This is the untold behind-the-scenes story of the rumbling Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua fight talks - and how much the pair stood to lose under disgraceful idea to stage bout in New York
Sports.content:
I remember the first time I reported that cogs were turning on a fight between Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury. It was a good while ago – almost 12 years, actually.

The date was December 2, 2014. I’d spoken that evening to Joshua’s promoter, Eddie Hearn, when both his guy and Fury were unbeaten and neither had fought for a world title.

Hearn, then and now, was bullish in spelling out his plan. ‘It is a fight I would love to make next summer,’ he told me. ‘People ask if AJ is ready to fight Fury but, to be honest, is Fury ready to fight AJ?’

It was a nice line for the back page and ultimately good for one thing alone – proving the timeless point that, in boxing, you should only believe it when you see it.

But here we are, trapped in a different version of the same dance all these years on.

Because as of Friday, the fight was on and, according to Hearn, talks had been resurrected to take it to Wembley Stadium. A day earlier it was heading to New York’s Madison Square Garden on November 20 and Joshua’s team were floating the possibility of canning the whole thing in protest.

They were furious that a contract signed three months ago, stipulating a UK venue, was being broken so that Netflix could have a cosier fit with American viewing hours. The Saudi powerbrokers for the fight, led by Turki Alalshikh, were evidently happy to side with the broadcaster, to hell with the British audience for a British fight, and ostensibly that is what sent Hearn and Joshua into a spin.

Twelve years on from when I reported that Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury were in talks to fight each other, the pair are still yet to touch gloves

Fury and Joshua are closer than ever to trading blows, with signatures on contracts, but they are still squabbling on the details

Time will tell if they get their way – Wembley conversations may have reopened, but it isn’t the only factor at play in this game of brinksmanship. Far from it.

I’ve had conversations this week with people around the deal and can flesh out a few of the details behind the chaos, which boils down to a boring three-letter word. Tax.

It’s something Hearn himself has alluded to in interviews this week – he mentioned that tax conditions in the US were unfavourable for Joshua. The information I’ve since received illustrates what that would look like in real language.

In short, it is my understanding that Joshua’s team have somewhere close to 10 million reasons not to want the fight in New York. Explained in a slightly longer form: if it is staged in London, the tax for a pair of non-UK residents would be around 20 per cent and in the US ‘withholding tax’ is around 30 per cent.

That is a significant jump with the purses involved – I’m told Joshua and Fury are in line to receive approximately $100m each (around £74m), so a $10m shortfall on the net amounts they would take back to Dubai and the Isle of Man respectively has not gone unnoticed.

As far as we can tell, Fury has not kicked up a fuss on the US tax. Publicly, anyway. But Joshua’s team viewed it as a hefty pay cut on what he signed, which fed into their wider anger that the fight was being shifted abroad.

Irrespective of which motivation weighed more, it seems that some level of sense might yet prevail – if the fight lands in the UK, that can only be a good thing. Hearn was very much in the right to paint it as a disgrace if it goes anywhere else.

But, again, we are in the realms of believing it when we see it. And especially in consideration of the individuals who hold true power behind this fight. That would be Netflix, who presumably still see greater value in the US, and the Saudi organisers, Sela, who have been steered on this fight by Alalshikh.

If fight is staged in the US, Joshua and Fury are set to pay millions more in tax. Fury and his promoter Frank Warren have not kicked up a fuss on issue - publicly at least

Turki Alalshikh (centre) claimed that he was trying to stage the fight in London back in July, though this may only have been lip service

Alalshikh, you might note, has already performed a curious role in the London saga. It was early July when he began applying pressure to City Hall, flagging that curfews in the capital would need tweaking to enable a US-friendly start time.

Writing on X, his favoured means of communication, he posted: ‘Hopefully a positive statement from the Mayor of London’s office about a later start time if Fury v Joshua is in London, as so far we have been told it is not possible.’

I might add here that the latter sentiment landed as something of a surprise to those on the receiving end – I’m told no request was made by Sela to mayor Sadiq Khan until mid-August. When those conversations did finally occur, sources tell me it was made clear by the mayor’s office that a late start wouldn’t be a hurdle. Khan has since gone public in saying he wants the fight in London.

A plausible theory, held by a few parties, is that the Sela overture was a gesture. A means of being able to claim: ‘We tried.' Lip-service, in other words, and flapping lips in boxing tend to serve no one.

Hopefully this fight proves the exception to the rule. Hopefully it does go to London. Hopefully the pressure applied by Hearn and Joshua, for whatever reason they prioritised, is decisive. Anything else would be an utter sham and a betrayal of British sport.

But this is boxing. And for more than a decade, one excuse after another has been found to keep these two fighters apart – the threshold for tedium was breached long before any contract. If that extends indefinitely, the question of New York or London might be rendered slightly irrelevant.

Sports.title: 'Seeing every boxing gym in the country packed with female fighters... that's the legacy I want': KATIE TAYLOR reflects on changing the face of her sport as she prepares to bids farewell in front of 82,000 at Croke Park
Sports.content:
'Seeing every boxing gym in the country packed with female fighters... that's the legacy I want': KATIE TAYLOR reflects on changing the face of her sport as she prepares to bids farewell in front of 82,000 at Croke Park

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

There is something beautifully fitting about the way Katie Taylor's extraordinary boxing story is coming to an end.

Thirty years ago, a little girl from Bray had to hide her hair under headgear and pretend to be a boy simply to pursue the sport she loved.

On Saturday night, that same girl – now 40, a five-time world champion, Olympic gold medallist and three-time undisputed champion-in-waiting – will walk into Croke Park for the final fight of her career, with 82,000 people watching.

It is, Taylor admits, the ending she always dreamed of.

'To be honest, I was saying after the last fight against Serrano, nothing can get bigger than MSG, so I think I'm going to just hang up the gloves,' Taylor tells Daily Mail Sport. 'The only thing that could be bigger than MSG is actually Croke Park, but that looked unlikely to happen.

'So when I got the phone call then from Brian that it was actually going to happen, I couldn't believe it. I was so excited and so emotional. This is really the fairy-tale ending I was actually looking for.'

Katie Taylor is set to bid her final farewell to boxing at Croke Park on Saturday night

Taylore takes on Flora Pili in a bid to finish her incredible career as undisputed light-welterweight champion

Taylor has spent her entire life chasing impossible things. At 10, she began boxing with her father Peter, a former Irish champion, but girls were not allowed to compete. So she found a way.

She disguised herself as a boy and fought wherever she could. When women's boxing was finally sanctioned in Ireland, Taylor made history by taking part in the country's first officially recognised female bout in 2001.

What followed was beyond even the wildest dreams of that stubborn little girl: Olympic gold at London 2012, five world titles, six European titles, undisputed crowns at lightweight and super-lightweight, and history-making nights at Madison Square Garden. Now Croke Park.

'This was an impossibility a few months ago, and I don't think people outside of Ireland really understand the importance of Croke Park and the fact that it's there. It's a part of Irish culture and it's our national stadium. Politically, it's been so hard to get this fight over the line for many years, and we're here now. It's actually happening, and not only that, but it's in front of a sold-out crowd.'

Yet beneath the excitement is the realisation that this really is goodbye. Asked about making her final ring walk, entering the dressing room for the last time and knowing there will never be another fight camp, Taylor becomes emotional.

'You're making me emotional here, Charlotte,' she laughs, trying to hold back the tears. 'Yeah, it's... I'm trying not to get too emotional, but even just talking about it, I'm starting to choke up. It's all becoming a bit too real now, honestly. Just give me a minute.'

After pulling herself together she continued: 'I have to obviously hold my emotions together because I have a very important job to do. And I'm trying not to reflect too much on the whole journey because I actually have to go in and perform, and the most important part is that I get my hand raised.

'But every now and then I do think about it, and I do get a bit emotional. I have given my life to this sport and it's everything I know and I love, so the idea of not doing it anymore hurts but I have to actually focus on not thinking too much about it. It's also too dangerous a sport to have your body in the ring, your heart out of it, thinking of retirement.'

Taylor has been a major icon for young women in the boxing community over the years

Flora Pili is intent on ruining the fairytale. The unbeaten Frenchwoman is 12-0 and will challenge Taylor for her WBO, WBA and IBF titles, with the vacant WBC belt also at stake.

'She's a young, hungry fighter. She's undefeated. She's big, she's strong, she's going to come to fight. She looks a bit awkward as well. She has long arms and will look to pressure me. She's obviously trying to ruin my night. She's trying to ruin the fairytale end, and so I have to be at my very, very best to win this fight.'

That competitive instinct remains, but the decision to retire has been coming for some time.

'What else is there to chase after?' Taylor asks.

'It’s been such an amazing journey, but it’s been a long and hard journey as well. It’s been difficult on the body, and my whole life has basically been one big training camp after training camp after training camp. Even as an amateur boxer, I gave so much of my life and so much of my time to amateur boxing. It was gruelling, and I have a lot of wear and tear on my body. There have been little niggles here and there that have popped up over the last few years, so I knew physically it was time.

'And then mentally, I think an athlete’s life is a life full of sacrifice, and usually the casualty of those sacrifices are your relationships. It’s not always the case, but it was the case for me. I found it very hard to focus on relationships when I’m actually in the middle of these big, amazing moments in my career. So I think it is the right time to bow out. I get a chance to actually invest in my marriage now, just pour my energy into that and enjoy the fruits of my labour.'

Then comes the familiar Taylor humour.

'I'll also look forward to not getting punched in the face again after this fight. It doesn't help I don't know how to actually box and move,' she jokes. 'I have to turn it into a war.'

But Taylor's greatest legacy will not be measured in belts.

Taylor's opponent Pili is 12-0 and intent on ruining the Irishwoman's fairytale ending in Dublin

When she looks back, she remembers the pioneers who helped pave the way – Laila Ali, Christy Martin, Lucia Rijker, Ann Wolfe and her childhood hero Deirdre Gogarty – but she also understands what her own journey has meant.

'I want to be remembered as a great fighter, but I also think the one thing I want to be remembered as is that I left my sport in a better place,' she says.

'I think that's probably the proudest moment of my whole career, inspiring a new generation of young female fighters, and seeing every boxing gym in the country just packed with female fighters not having the same struggles or the same obstacles that I had."

Taylor does not know exactly what comes next, although she cannot imagine staying away from boxing entirely.

'I've been involved in boxing for the last 30 years of my life, so I think it would be strange just to walk away and not have a part to play,' she says.

'I do love my sport, and I love the boxing gym environment. And I think that's something that I'm always going to be involved in but I am actually looking forward to being able to just enjoy my life after this fight.

'I've been boxing since I was 10 or 11 years of age. It's been a gruelling and tough journey. It's been an amazing journey, but it has been very, very tough. And I am looking forward to not feeling the pressure of fights again, the pressure of expectation, and not having to prepare for these brutal matches again, and just kind of enjoy life for a change.

'It's been a lot on my family too. Even my siblings’ lives were scheduled around my training growing up because of my Olympic dream. I look back and think how supportive and amazing they were. If I was in their shoes, I’d be so bitter because their lives revolved around me and my schedule. So, it will be nice to enjoy life together now.'

First, though, there is one final war. One final ring walk. One final chance to have her hand raised.

Sports.title: Hamilton: I don’t want preferential treatment from Ferrari
Sports.content:
Lewis Hamilton says preferential treatment over team-mate Charles Leclerc is not what he’s been asking Ferrari for, despite his position as a potential Formula 1 title contender in 2026.

Leclerc’s retirement from the Italian Grand Prix means he’s now 112 points adrift of championship leader Kimi Antonelli, with a maximum of 258 points to score over the last 10 rounds – assuming the final races aren’t impacted by the Iran war.

Hamilton’s deficit, meanwhile, is ‘just’ 76 points, so the seven-time world champion does have more realistic odds – however slim – to be a dark horse for the title.

However, when asked if it was time for the Scuderia to put all its efforts behind him and for Leclerc to support him, Hamilton retorted: “That's not actually really what I've been asking for.

“It's really just making sure we're executing to make sure we get the best result for the team. Instead of us working against each other and finishing fourth and fifth, maybe we can work together and get a podium, pull off more points.”

Consistency has kept Hamilton in the title race so far, as he is the only driver to have finished every grand prix in the top 10; the top six has actually never eluded him. But he’s painfully aware of the Silver Arrows’ dominance in terms of pure speed, with Ferrari yet to take a single pole position in 2026; the discrepancy largely stems from the power unit.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes, Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

“Mercedes, if you look at the last race, they were six tenths a lap quicker on the straights,” Hamilton pointed out. “Pretty much most of the other tracks, it was three or four tenths. We were losing just on the straights.

“I think we've done a really great job, given that we've had that deficit, and we continue to make improvements to the car. We've made improvements to the engine. We knew that the last [engine] upgrade wasn't going to be a silver bullet and close that gap completely. But for me, it's really positive to see us continuously stepping forward. They are just very, very quick, and it's not easy.

“As I said, rather than focus on them – they're not a focus for me at the moment – I think our focus should just be, how we can do the best and execute the best on our weekends, because there'll be weekends where they're exceptional, and there'll be weekends where they maybe drop the ball.

“As long as we just focus on our consistency and trying to optimise our weekends, maybe there's going to be a moment where we are able to capitalise on, perhaps, their shortcomings.”

Sports.title: What the drivers think of the "crazy" Madrid F1 circuit
Sports.content:
"I'll put my money on a red flag, that's for sure," said Pierre Gasly when asked what he thought of Formula 1's new Madring street circuit.

Risk and difficulty level have been the common denominators in conversation with drivers about the Spanish Grand Prix track and its layout. Well perhaps not Lance Stroll, but at least he managed a distant orbit of the topic, saying, "I think we're going to be busy, very busy." While all the drivers have tackled the track in their simulators, the only real-world reference so far, apart from a mildly controversial Ferrari filming day in July, has been a Formula 3 test late last month. It is fair to say this did not go well, with no fewer than 19 red flags and three wrecked cars.

The incidents that brought out the red flags, and triggered some unwelcome repair bills, were not concentrated in one specific area but spread out through the lap, mostly in the second sector where there are a number of chicanes and blind corners, plus the banked 'La Monumental'. One of the more intriguing facets of canvassing driver opinion on this track is the fact that so few of them are being negative about the Madring, even while comparing it with Jeddah, whose layout was revised between its first and second appearances on the calendar in response to criticism.

The impression is that the drivers cannot wait to test themselves against it.

"I think this track is going to be extremely difficult for the drivers," said Franco Colapinto. "In the simulator, putting together one complete lap could take me hours. So imagine what it is going to be like here when you only have two or three laps to do it. Finding that perfect lap is going to be very difficult.

"It has a bit of everything. If you took everything you find across the 24 races on the calendar and mixed it together, you would probably get something like this. So I'm happy and looking forward to trying it."

Tight, blind-entry corners pose a challenge because lap time can leak away with a more conservative approach Photo by: Getty Images

"It's a bit scary," said Sergio Perez. "It reminds me a bit of Jeddah. Good, proper track, [I'm] really happy to be here, and I think the atmosphere here is going to be one of the best."

Asked how punishing this track could be in response to driver error, Perez was unequivocal.

"I think very," he said. "It all depends what sort of grip level we get, but I think there is no room for error. It's very rare, depending on which corner you do a mistake, you might get away with it – but in most places, there is no margin for it."

In the consequence-free environment of the simulator, most drivers have already made the majority of their big mistakes. It's now a question of fine tuning.

"Driving-wise, I must say in the sim it was very enjoyable and very exciting," said Gasly. "I got a good read and feel of pretty much every single wall at every single corner, so actually I know what to do and what not to do.

"But I think it's going to be very challenging, especially in terms of evolution, probably a lot of track evolution, kind of slightly off-road braking zones, which are not fully straight, kind of like snaky, very twisty type of corners, many corners, a lot of blinds, banking, up and down, undulation all the way."

The Madring's bank corner isn't linear, and flows onto a section which also has a change of camber Photo by: Getty Images

Photographs and television images have a tendency to flatten out gradients so the undulations will be less apparent to those watching or reading at home. But the flow of the track is going to have a powerful effect on lap time. From the end of the first sector, all the way through the second, the circuit poses a highly technical challenge. For instance, the second chicane feeds onto an uphill gradient, so drivers must carry as much speed through as possible – but there is a wall at the exit, and the entry trajectory is complicated by steep kerbs.

In terms of risk vs reward, it bears some similarities with the chicane at the Norisring in Germany, where the quickest way through involves kissing the wall at the exit. But that chicane doesn't have aggressive entry kerbs that will guide your car into the wall if you don't get your approach right.

This is one aspect of the track the drivers will have to adapt to quickly, since the simulations may not have rendered the kerbs with total accuracy.

"I think Monaco is more unforgiving," said Arvid Lindblad. "But yeah, it's not a very forgiving track. I think all street circuits now, there's not much margin. This one definitely does not have much scope for error.

"That's probably the thing that's the hardest to simulate. From offline simulations, but also just from the sims that we drive, they get, I think, a measurement from the FIA with a photo saying, 'it looks like this, and this is this many centimetres', you know, width and length, whatever.

"But yeah, that's the hardest part to simulate. So I think that I would already say just from a driving point of view will be a challenge because they're not small kerbs, they're proper kerbs, so we'll need to attack them."

Oliver Bearman finds some cause for humour in the track layout… Photo by: Getty Images

Unlike the banked final corner at Zandvoort, which most drivers barely regard as a turn at all because speeds through there are limited by engine power rather than outright grip, 'La Monumental' is grip-limited. So there may be some experimentation before competitors converge on an ideal line. There may also be some carambolage as drivers explore the limits of a corner where they will be at full throttle – or close to it – for over four seconds.

After the F3 test, the track was jet-washed to remove the greasy layer left when freshly laid asphalt cools and some of the bitumen used to bind the aggregate leaches through to the surface. But even so, grip levels are uncertain and the track will evolve through the weekend.

It's also likely that the racing line will evolve at a different rate, producing scenarios similar to Miami where the track is very slippery away from that line – especially when the tyres shed 'marbles' of rubber during practice, qualifying and the race. This will compound the effects of any imprecision, and make overtaking tricky because a defending driver will be able to 'park the bus' on the line.

One thing that will not change this weekend is the technical challenge of many of the blind corners. Most of the turns are of the late-apex variety, requiring the drivers to commit before they see the apex.

"You're kind of swinging in from a blind spot and you've got to try and pick an imaginary spot that's a few hundred meters in front of you," explained Alex Albon.

"That's really challenging to do. It's a lot of repetition and muscle memory just to get that timing right. Because you basically can't see an apex. So now you're just using your internal body clock and almost imaginary, you're trying to focus on a reference point or something to know what's your apex point of that corner."

As with Jeddah, the blind corners will likely cause some flashpoints in qualifying as drivers on push laps come up quickly on those on in- or out-laps. The demands of the track will also have a compounding effect on disparities between cars, because those with more efficient downforce will enjoy better performance from the electrical elements of their power units.

Bridges and tunnel complicate the sight lines – and mean the outside walls are quite tight in some blind-entry sections Photo by: Getty Images

"Technically speaking, there's a lot of corners on this track that will be between 90% and 100% throttle," explained Albon. "I think for the top teams, it will be flat out. For the midfield teams and the backfield teams, a bigger lift, which has a big effect in deployment. If you can do a corner flat or not, it massively changes the way the deployment works.

"And you don't want to go in qualifying, suddenly all these corners start to become flat and your deployment starts to move around a lot. That's what we've found so far.

"The technical part will be, can you make a car that is good over the kerbs from Turn 1 to Turn 5? But you want the stiffness in the car for Sector 2 and Sector 3, because actually, the stiffer car gives you more load.

"But then you're going to sacrifice your Turn 1, Turn 2 kerb riding. And then the final thing is, is it one of those weekends where Q3, Run 2 for those guys – Q1, Run 3 for us – do you end up just sending it across the kerbs? I mean, that Turn 5, 6 feels a little bit like, I hope there's a rhythm to it and it's actually not that bad. But I think there's an angle there that you're going to just send it.

"If you get through the other side, you're going to be two or three tenths quicker. And if you don't want to take that risk, you lose out on those few tenths.

"The other thing we've seen in the simulator already is the tyres are going to be absolutely screaming."

Sports.title: Leclerc accepts blame for Italian GP clash with Hamilton: "I went too far"
Sports.content:
Charles Leclerc admitted that he went "too far" when battling against Lewis Hamilton in the opening chicane of Formula 1's Italian Grand Prix, and said he and Hamilton have since buried the hatchet over the incident.

Leclerc and Hamilton had been side by side through the opening chicane, but the Monegasque attempted to take the standard racing line on the exit of Turn 2 - which resulted in Hamilton being guided onto the gravel along the outside of the corner.

In the immediate aftermath following his own second-lap shunt at the Parabolica, Leclerc stated that "we went too far" in their battle at the opening corner. Hamilton staunchly disagreed, stating that "there was no 'we' in it" and delivered criticism about Ferrari's communication and execution of races.

After reviewing the incident with team principal Fred Vasseur and with Hamilton himself, Leclerc seemed to accept responsibility for the incident and wanted to ensure that it had not affected his relationship with his team-mate.

"I mean the rules of engagement, I think it's kind of clear that we never want to see a car of the same team in the grass," Leclerc said.

"After reviewing, we spoke with Lewis, I obviously know I went too far in Turn 2 and I said it to Lewis and I think it's very clear what we should do or should avoid going forward.

"But I won't go into much more details of what we said. The only thing I can say is that it definitely did not affect the good relationship that we have and it will not affect anything going forward. And that is the most important for me really.

Charles Leclerc, Ferrari, Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

"Then of course, I know we are driving for Ferrari and if there's one race where you don't want that to happen is in Monza and when these things happen at our home race, then it does a huge mess outside.

"However, looking at the race from outside, there's been also some friction between other team-mates and the only thing we end up speaking of is Lewis and I, which I don't think is quite right.

"But that doesn't mean we did everything perfect. I didn't in Turn 2 and for that I've been straight away very clear with Lewis after reviewing the images.

"I think the most important is that we clarified the situation, we talked, I told Lewis how I felt, Lewis told me what he felt and I think we fully agree with both of our views in hindsight when we speak without the emotions of the race.

"It happens. It's not the last time that will happen I'm sure, because it's the kind of things that happens in racing - particularly when we are starting so close to each other so often. But it's not a situation that we want to find ourselves in again so and that is very clear for Lewis and for myself."

Asked by Autosport if he felt the incident had been overblown, particularly after explaining his observation that there was "friction between other team-mates" (presumably, referring to Mercedes' pitstop split and the terse on-track battle between the Mercedes cars) over the course of the grand prix, he agreed that the "proportions" that the incident had taken were larger.

Charles Leclerc, Ferrari Photo by: Alessio Morgese

That said, Leclerc was keen not to downplay the incident, stating that it was "not acceptable" to end up seeing his team-mate in the gravel during the course of the race.

"Again I need to be careful with that because surely it's not to minimise the way that this unfolded. And as I said, it's not acceptable to see Lewis going in the gravel," he said.

"But for sure the proportions as a matter of fact are much bigger on our side compared to the two other teams that have had some... I didn't follow the whole race but the two other teams I saw that were fighting at the top, there wasn't as much noise around it.

"So surely, the proportions that it takes when you are driving for Ferrari is much bigger and particularly if we're in Monza. But that's not to minimise what happens and it's not something that should happen again."

Read Also: Formula 1 Vasseur rejects Ferrari internal crisis claims as he defends team

Sports.title: Vasseur rejects Ferrari internal crisis claims as he defends team
Sports.content:
Fred Vasseur does not deny that there were things to clear up between Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton at Monza and the Ferrari team principal has spoken to both drivers after the Italian Grand Prix, addressing what happened on track as well as some of the comments made.

What Vasseur does reject, however, is the scale the situation has taken on, with the episode becoming, within a matter of days, evidence of supposed tension within the team.

“We had some good meetings with Lewis and Charles,” Vasseur told Autosport. “They cleared things up together and I reminded them of some fundamental principles of the way I manage the team. And I will continue to stick to them.”

The point the Scuderia boss is making goes beyond what happened at Monza. Vasseur wants his drivers to accept their share of the responsibility for protecting the work of the team, in the same way that he says he does whenever something goes wrong.

“I reminded Lewis that when we won the race in Melbourne two years ago thanks to the strategy, I sent Ravin Jain onto the podium because it was right that he got the recognition. When we lost a race because of strategy, I went in front of the TV cameras and took responsibility,” he said.

“My job is to protect the hundreds of people in the team and to take responsibility. That is what I have asked the drivers to do as well: if we want to achieve results, we need to protect the team and each of us needs to take responsibility.”

Charles Leclerc, Ferrari, Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari Photo by: Sam Bloxham / LAT Images via Getty Images

Vasseur won’t silence his drivers, but felt criticism was overblown

It is not a request for silence. Vasseur is not asking Leclerc and Hamilton to stop being critical, but he stresses that a comment made in front of the media can carry far more weight than the person making it may have intended.

“I’m not asking them not to be open or not to be tough. But very often they are much calmer with us than they are when they go and speak to the press,” Vasseur explained. “Lewis told me: ‘Fred, 80% of my message was positive and they took the 20% that was negative.’ But we all know how it works. If you say the team is doing a good job and then add a ‘but’, that is the part that will become the headline. It’s part of the game.”

This is where Vasseur connects the issue to the narrative that, in his view, developed after Monza. The two Ferrari drivers came close to making contact, Hamilton was aggressive and Leclerc subsequently admitted his own mistake. But what began as an on-track incident quickly turned into questions over the management of the drivers and even the stability of the Scuderia’s leadership.

“Charles, after the discussion, said: ‘I was too aggressive.’ And for me, that’s fine. When Kimi was fighting with Russell he ended up in the gravel, just as Lewis did at the start,” Vasseur countered. “But in our case, we moved very quickly from an incident on track to talking about a crisis in the way the drivers are being managed. I think the two things need to be kept in the proper perspective.”

Ferrari gives drivers principles to follow but no rules of engagement

On the subject of “rules of engagement”, Vasseur also rejects the idea that Ferrari has no framework governing how its drivers race each other, and while there is no code capable of accounting for every inch of an on-track battle, there are clear principles and responsibilities.

“To say that there are no ‘rules of engagement’ doesn’t reflect reality,” he said. “You can’t expect contracts to cover every possible scenario you might encounter on track, because inevitably everything would become a matter of interpretation. ‘I was there’, ‘no, you were five centimetres further back’ — you don’t solve anything that way. The principles are clear and the drivers know them.”

Ferrari’s philosophy remains unchanged: two number-one drivers and equal treatment. A hierarchy may eventually be established when the championship standings make it clear that one of the two no longer has a realistic chance, but not before then.

Lewis Hamilton, Charles Leclerc, Ferrari Photo by: Ferrari

“Ferrari drivers can count on equal treatment, then there may come a point when we have to make a decision if one of them is out of the fight,” Vasseur said. “In that case, it will be my decision. But until that moment, the treatment will be equal.”

Vasseur points to the previous season as an example, when Piastri arrived at Monza with a lead of more than 30 points over Norris, and McLaren asked Piastri during the race to hand second place back to Norris.

“Imagine if McLaren had decided to put everything behind Piastri: perhaps Verstappen, who finished three points behind Norris, could have become champion,” he explained. “That’s what I told our drivers. We’ll make a decision when we’re closer to the end, why not? But today there isn’t even anything to discuss.”

Vasseur defends Ferrari engine upgrade

Another point Vasseur raises concerns the technical assessment of Ferrari. The ADUO 2 introduced by the Scuderia at Monza has, in some quarters, been portrayed as an upgrade that failed to deliver the expected results. The team principal believes that conclusion is wrong because it fails to take into account how differently engine power affects lap time from one circuit to another.

“I know it’s difficult to understand at first glance, but anyone with some technical knowledge knows exactly what I’m talking about,” Vasseur explained.

“Let me give you an example: at a circuit like Zandvoort, a power deficit of X horsepower might cost you three tenths. If we improve the performance of that engine to the point where we reduce the power deficit by a third, then go to a circuit like Monza, we may find that the lap time gap to our rivals, instead of getting smaller… gets bigger.

“That doesn’t mean the ADUO isn’t working. Even if you make a step forward of several horsepower, at Monza you can still be further away from the benchmark than you were at Zandvoort.”

Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari Photo by: Manuel Eletto / Getty Images

Behind the numbers, there is above all an issue that Vasseur considers important: respect for the work being done at Maranello.

“When I read that ‘the ADUO isn’t working’, I find that disrespectful towards the people working on the engine because it doesn’t reflect reality,” he said.

Embracing the pressure of being Ferrari boss

The Frenchman knows that being in charge of Ferrari means living permanently under a microscope. Speculation about his future has resurfaced periodically, just as it did last year, when rumours of a possible departure were circulating even though his contract extension had already been agreed.

“Somebody says I’m going to be fired this weekend, or that I was fired last night,” he said. “We’ve won two races, we can win more, and we have a clear idea of how to make further steps forward. That’s where I’m focusing my energy. Being under pressure is part of my job. It’s not something I want to waste energy on.”

Asked whether he sometimes feels “alone” in his position, Vasseur firmly rejected the suggestion.

“First of all, it’s not for me to underline whether or not I have the support of the chairman, but the communication channel is constantly open and constructive,” Vasseur affirmed. “On top of that, at almost every race weekend we’ve had representatives of the senior management from Maranello with us, from John Elkann to Benedetto Vigna and Piero Ferrari. I think that’s a really positive sign for everyone working in the team, both at the track and in Maranello.”

The pressure, nevertheless, remains. And Vasseur appears to have no intention of trying to escape it. It comes with the role of leading Ferrari. What he asks is that criticism remains criticism and a racing incident remains a racing incident, rather than every episode being turned into a symptom of a wider crisis.

Sports.title: McLaren drops H-wing concept for F1 Spanish GP
Sports.content:
McLaren is parking its H-wing concept for this weekend's Spanish Grand Prix in Madrid, with its version of the rotating Formula 1 rear wing set to return in Baku.

The Woking-based team had been working on its own interpretation of the rear wing, which rotates 180 degrees between Corner Mode and Straight Mode, after seeing Ferrari pioneer its concept during winter testing. Following a delayed rollout, the team debuted the new wing in practice at the Hungarian Grand Prix before testing it again in Zandvoort. It finally ran in competition at last weekend's Italian GP.

By all accounts the system, which McLaren has internally dubbed H-Wing, worked as intended, with the mechanism helping to reduce drag on the straights. But Autosport understands McLaren will keep the H-wing system on its low-drag wing for now, rather than retroactively adding the system to its higher downforce packages.

At the high-downforce Madring circuit, which makes its debut this weekend, McLaren is set to run the new rear wing introduced in Zandvoort, featuring striking sculpted endplates.

As teams have to carefully decide to allocate their production resources, McLaren wanted to focus on fast-tracking its H-wing concept for Monza, where the drag reduction yields a much bigger lap time benefit than on twistier circuits. It therefore decided against producing a version of the Zandvoort wing with the H-wing concept.

McLaren will run its Zandvoort wing in Madrid, featuring sculpted endplates. Photo by: Eric Le Galliot

The Monza H-wing is now set to return at the high-speed Baku street circuit at the end of September, which also places an emphasis on top speed and efficiency. Meanwhile, the team plans to produce another iteration of its higher downforce wing later on, built from the ground up to incorporate the rotating rear wing actuator.

McLaren heads into the Madrid weekend as one of the favourites to contend for victory on the challenging 5.4km circuit, off the back of two wins for Lando Norris at the Hungaroring and Zandvoort circuits.

The H-wing monikers is a nod to the letter H in the Etihad logo that adorns the rear of the MCL40's rear wing. The letter H runs along the centreline where the H-Wing's straight mode actuator is positioned. It follows a tradition set by the team's famed F-duct in 2010, which was named after the F in Vodafone along the nose where the duct was installed.

Autosport understands the Racing Bulls team, which introduced a rotating rear wing of its own in Monza as well, will also park it for Madrid as it doesn't suit the characteristics of the Madring track. It is also planning to run the wing again later on this season.

Sports.title: Audi commits to appeal against Tsunoda's Italian GP result
Sports.content:
The Audi Formula 1 team will follow through with its intention to appeal Yuki Tsunoda's lack of penalty for causing an extra formation lap in the Italian Grand Prix, Autosport understands.

Tsunoda caused an extra formation lap at the restart of the Monza race as race director Rui Marques was not comfortable with the way the Japanese driver lined up in his grid box, angled towards the pitwall.

FIA's race stewards reviewed the incident after the race, but decided not to hand Tsunoda the customary stop-and-go penalty, which would have been converted into a 30-second time penalty.

According to Article B5.9.4 of the F1 2026 sporting regulations, "any driver who caused an extra formation lap, and is then able to start the, or any subsequent, extra formation lap must enter the pitlane at the end of the lap and must start... from the end of the pitlane."

But Tsunoda's Racing Bulls team argued that its driver was not out of his grid slot and didn't impact his competitors. Race director Marques also explained that he acted out of an abundance of caution.

As a result, the team hadn't been notified by race control that Tsunoda was the cause of the extra formation lap, so it had no reason to tell its driver to start from pit exit instead.

Gabriel Bortoleto stands to gain as he finished 11th Photo by: Alessio Morgese

The stewards agreed with that interpretation of the rules, but Audi soon lodged an intention to appeal. The German team was affected by the non-penalty as Gabriel Bortoleto finished one position behind Tsunoda in 11th and would be promoted into a points-paying position if Tsunoda's verdict is overturned.

By notifying the FIA of its intention to appeal, Audi gave itself a 96-hour window to further study the rulebook, build a case and decide whether or not to follow through with the appeal. That time window closes on Thursday night and sources have now confirmed to Autosport that Audi will follow through with the appeal procedure.

It is understood that Audi feels the rulebook is black and white on drivers being penalised for causing an extra formation lap. There is an argument that because the race director felt Tsunoda's start position was enough of a reason to abort the start, Tsunoda should have started from the pitlane regardless.

Whether or not the appeal is enough to overturn Tsunoda's decision, the team is keen to get clarification from the race stewards for future occasions. The FIA has yet to set a date for the appeal hearing.
