World.title: Family of 9/11 hero to retrace his steps in final Tunnel to Towers stop
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The family of 9/11 hero Stephen Siller will mark the 25th anniversary of the attacks by retracing the FDNY firefighter's steps as he ran through the Brooklyn-Battery Tunnel toward the World Trade Center.

Frank Siller and other members of the Siller family will participate in the private walk before joining hundreds of friends and supporters at the FDNY Ten House.

The event will conclude the Tunnel to Towers "Steel Across America" tour, which has traveled since May bringing Siller's story and a 21-foot steel beam from the South Tower all across the nation.

FRANK SILLER: 'I LOVE YOU, BROTHER' -- THE 9/11 LOSS THAT INSPIRED A MISSION OF SERVICE

On the morning of 9/11 Siller had just concluded his shift with the fire department when he received word that a plane had struck the World Trade Center.

"Stephen drove his truck to the entrance of the Brooklyn Battery Tunnel, but it had already been closed for security purposes. Determined to carry out his duty, he strapped 60 lbs. of gear to his back, and raced on foot through the tunnel to the Twin Towers, where he gave up his life while saving others," the tour's website recounts.

NEW YORK JETS OWNER WOODY JOHNSON TO BE HONORED AT TUNNEL TO TOWERS GALA FOR DECADE-LONG PARTNERSHIP

Since its founding, inspired by Siller and his favorite quote, "While we have time, let us do good," Tunnel to Towers has provided more than 1,700 mortgage-free homes to the families of fallen service members and first responders, as well as to disabled veterans and first responders. The organization has also delivered housing assistance and support services to more than 20,000 homeless veterans and holds hundreds of events nationwide to honor America’s heroes and preserve the memory of those who lost their lives for future generations.

The Tunnel to Towers 9/11 Institute has helped to educate students from kindergarten through 12th grade on the "extraordinary heroism and goodness of everyday people" on Sept. 11, "while demonstrating the strength and resilience of America’s spirit." Its mobile 9/11 exhibit has traveled to nearly all 50 states as well as Canada.

To mark the 25th anniversary, Tunnel to Towers also launched its 343 Homes Initiative this year to honor the 343 New York firefighters who died on Sept. 11. According to the group, this initiative will deliver 343 mortgage-free homes to the families of fallen service members and fallen first responders as well as to catastrophically injured service members across the country.

Fox News' Peter Pinedo contributed to this report.

World.title: Donald Trump had no interest in watching the horrible NFL opener, ESPN's Taylor McGregor is a star & Danica!
World.content:
'Nightcaps' is a daily column that catches you up on the biggest sports, news and culture stories you may have missed while pretending to do work at your desk. It runs Monday–Friday on OutKick.com.

First Thursday of football season. First real Thursday of football season. You know what that means, right?

Happy unofficial start to your weekend! Around here, weekends in the fall start on Thursdays — and for good reason.

We've got football all over the globe tonight. Obviously, the big one is the Rams-Niners in Melbourne, which technically takes place tomorrow morning at 10:30 a.m.

NFL PUSHES DEEPER INTO STREAMING AS NETFLIX LANDS AUSTRALIA GAME AMID FCC, DOJ SCRUTINY

We've also got a MASSIVE college game tonight. And by massive, I mean the point spread. No. 7 Miami is currently a 59.5 point favorite of FAMU. That has to be one of the largest point spreads I've ever seen.

It's on ACC Network, for those interested!

On that note, welcome to a Thursday Nightcaps — the one where Donald Trump was most certainly NOT interested in watching last night's football game.

Lordy. What a ballgame. Not a good ballgame, by any means, but a ballgame nonetheless.

What else? I've got Aaron Rodgers stuffing poor Danica Patrick in a locker, Boston radio stations are in absolute shambles today, and ESPN reporter Taylor McGregor continues to captivate America this week.

She was dominant during Monday night's power outage in Tallahassee, and she followed it up by arguing with a parking attendant during a radio interview earlier today.

What a week.

OK, let's get this thing going. Thursday night football is finally back. No time to waste.

Grab you a TV dinner for National TV Dinner Day, and settle in for a Thursday 'Cap!

Trump had no time for last night's big game

Before we start ... man, do I miss TV dinners. The best. Obviously, I grew up in the 90s, so Kid Cuisine was my weapon of choice.

I feel like my mom fed me at least four of those a week. If I tried to even sneak one into my house nowadays for the kids, my wife would have me arrested.

MAHA moms are built different.

Hungry Man was great, too. That's the one that started it all, right? Those things weighed a literal ton out of the freezer. You could kill a man with one of those boxes.

But Lordy, they were good:

Amazing. What a commercial. They just don't make 'em like that anymore. Nowadays, it's all Big Pharma ads and insurance. We had it so good, and we just pissed it all away.

Sad.

Anyway, let's go ahead and get this class started with Donald Trump declaring last night's midterm party vs. NFL opener a triumphant SUCCESS!

Boston radio is handling the loss well today

"The Republican Midterm Convention last night, in Dallas, was a major, sold-out hit, far bigger, better, and more important than anyone thought possible," Trump said via Truth Social.

"It was really something, streaming all over the place, and really big numbers, despite going up against the NFL. The overall numbers beat the NFL. The Arena, which was really nice, beat its own attendance records. The place was packed! There were thousands of people outside who couldn’t get in. Screens were provided. I guess people LOVE TRUMP POLITICS! I’ll be there again tonight to close out the show."

Amazing. Between that declaration and the $5,000 we're all getting in a few months if we play ball, it was a great night!

Look, I have no clue if that's true. Did Trump's convention speech beat the NFL opener ... on NBC? I doubt it. I do know that those numbers aren't even out yet, so I'm not sure they're accurate regardless.

I will say ... he didn't miss much. What an awful game. A great game, because it's football, but a pretty horrible game for three quarters.

Drake Maye was a disaster. AJ Brown got hurt. Sam Darnold played five snaps and then missed the rest of the game.

Maybe stop shoving Pats-Seahawks down our throats, NFL? Ever think about that?

On that note, let's check in with Boston radio today as the Pats start the year 0-1:

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Taylor, Danica & Aaron!

Football fans are the best. We wait nine months for our teams to play again. We suffer all winter long. We yearn for game days. We spend all summer counting down to kickoff.

And then, just like that, we're immediately pissed and want the whole thing blown up. It's like clockwork, every single year.

For what it's worth ... Maye was really, truly horrible last night. Just a baffling fourth quarter out of him, and I'm not even a big Maye fan.

Even I was stunned by this throw:

As a miserable Dolphins fan who had to suffer through Tua ... that fourth quarter gave me some pretty concerning flashbacks, Pats fans.

I'm just saying.

OK, let's rapid-fire this Thursday class into a big night of FOOTBALL. First up? A quick PSA for everyone that tonight's Rams-Niners game is on NETFLIX.

That's right. You're gonna have to subscribe to another streaming app to watch the second NFL game of the season:

Look, I think it's beyond dumb to put an NFL game behind a paywall. It's ridiculous, but that's the world we now live in.

I fear it ain't going anywhere, either.

That being said ... what an incredible promo by Netflix. Fair is fair, and I'm ready to run through a brick wall after that.

It also gives me the chance to bring Minka Kelly back to class. We simply can't have a Friday Night Lights-NFL promo and NOT check in with the star of that show:

Looks like she's doing well.

Clear eyes, full hearts, can't lose!

OK, two more on the way out. How about this humdinger from Aaron Rodgers about Danica Patrick on Cam Heyward's podcast this morning:

"I dated Danica. She had just retired. She was depressed and not fun to be around. But I didn’t leave her because I was trying to be there and be a good partner. Then it was going a certain direction, obviously. There was no intimacy; there was nothing," Rodgers said in the second part of the interview, which dropped Thursday morning.

"She tells a story that she was so blindsided and getting left by you, and that he leaves a trail of blood around him. And I’m like, what are you talking about? That’s not what happened."

Lordy. Rodgers, of course, wasn't done! Apparently, Danica tried to co-sign the mortgage with him on a new house in Malibu, and he wasn't having it.

"I’m buying a house in Malibu, and she goes, ‘Do you want to buy it together?’ And I said no. And she said, ‘You know what that means then?’ And I said, ‘Yeah, that’s the way things are going.’ She said, ‘Well, let’s get counseling.’ Then we got counseling. Then COVID hits and we’re stuck together."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

My God. COVID was bad enough. Now you're putting Aaron Rodgers and an apparently "no fun" Danica Patrick in the same house together?

Sounds like a blast!

OK, that's it for today. Good work, everyone. Long class, but an important one.

Here's ESPN's newest star, Taylor McGregor, getting a parking ticket while doing a live radio hit.

See you tomorrow.

World.title: Jimmy Kimmel says show won’t air James Talarico interview on TV, citing FCC threats
World.content:
Jimmy Kimmel announced on Wednesday night that his show would not air his upcoming interview with Texas’ Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico on television, citing the Trump administration’s threats against ABC.

Kimmel said that during President Donald Trump’s administration, the Federal Communications Commission “has threatened me, threatened our show, threatened our network, ABC, our affiliates, our local stations, based on simple, traditional editorial decisions, guest bookings it would seem they don’t like.”

“Out of consideration for our local stations, especially our ABC affiliates in Texas, who would have to deal with this nonsense, my interview tomorrow with James Talarico will not air on television,” he said.

The interview, set for Thursday, will be posted on the YouTube channel for “Jimmy Kimmel Live!” instead, he said. Talarico, a Democratic state representative in Texas, is locked in a competitive Senate race with Republican state Attorney General Ken Paxton.

Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico. Brandon Bell / Getty Images file

The Talarico campaign and the FCC did not immediately respond to NBC News’ request for comment. ABC Entertainment declined to comment.

FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez, who was appointed by former President Joe Biden, condemned “FCC intimidation” in a statement reacting to Kimmel’s announcement.

“No host, local affiliate, or network should have to weigh federal retaliation before booking a guest for a newsworthy interview,” Gomez said in the statement. “Any attempt to pressure broadcasters into self-censorship undermines both press freedom and the public’s right to hear from candidates in their communities seeking public office.”

Kimmel’s announcement marks the latest apparent instance in which pressure from the administration has affected content aired on an entertainment show. Stephen Colbert said in February that CBS did not air his interview with Talarico out of fear of the FCC.

“He was supposed to be here, but we were told in no uncertain terms by our network’s lawyers, who called us directly, that we could not have him on the broadcast,” Colbert said at the time.

CBS said in a February statement that “the show was provided legal guidance that the broadcast could trigger the FCC equal-time rule for two other candidates.”

Trump has publicly targeted Kimmel in the past, calling multiple times for the comedian to be fired.

About a year ago, ABC pulled Kimmel’s show following the comedian’s comments about conservative activist Charlie Kirk, who was assassinated in September of last year. The show returned nearly a week later, and Kimmel said in his monologue that “it was never my intention to make light of the murder of a young man.”

The FCC, under Chairman Brendan Carr, announced in April that Disney’s eight local television stations owned and operated by ABC needed to file broadcast license renewals early. The Walt Disney Co. sued over the decision last month.

In January, the FCC issued a memo saying that late-night and daytime talk shows must adhere to the equal time rule, which requires broadcasters to offer equal opportunities to other qualified candidates who are running for the same office. The memo marked a change in the FCC’s position. Twenty years earlier, a decision found that late-night and daytime talk shows were exempt from the rule.

Trump himself was interviewed by Kimmel in 2015, when he was running for president. Kimmel recalled the interview during his Wednesday show.

“At that time, when he was the one sitting next to me, he seemed to have no problem with the idea of talk show hosts interviewing candidates,” he said. “In fact, he was very eager to come back for another interview, which he did just before he became the nominee in 2016.”

“But for some reason, and I can’t seem to figure out what that reason is, something has changed,” he said, tongue in cheek.

World.title: Rhode Island Gov. Dan McKee loses Democratic primary to businesswoman Helena Foulkes
World.content:
Rhode Island Gov. Dan McKee has lost his Democratic primary to former CVS executive Helena Foulkes, NBC News projects, after facing a significant spending disadvantage and voter discontent with his tenure.

In an election season that has seen a wave of anti-incumbent energy, McKee, 75, becomes the first governor to fall in a primary this year — and the first in eight years.

Public polling had shown McKee, who was running for a full second term, trailing by double digits heading into Tuesday. And Foulkes, 62, outspent him on the airwaves by 3-to-1, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact.

The primary was a rematch of 2022, when Foulkes narrowly lost to McKee, who had replaced Gov. Gina Raimondo after she was selected for President Joe Biden’s Cabinet in 2021.

McKee’s 2023 decision to close the Washington Bridge, a commuter thoroughfare in Providence, hung over his campaign. The bridge closure came after state engineers discovered major structural problems that could have eventually caused it to collapse. Three years later, the bridge remains under construction.

Dan McKee; Helena Buonanno Foulkes. Getty Images

An Emerson College poll in August found that 63% of likely Rhode Island voters disapproved of McKee’s handling of the Washington Bridge, with just 18% saying they approved.

In her campaign ads, Foulkes said the state had “the worst roads and bridges.” She also touted her plans to boost the state’s economy and housing market.

McKee has defended his decision to close the bridge, saying he prioritized safety over politics, and he has said construction will be completed by 2028.

The last time a sitting governor lost a primary was in 2018, when Kansas Republican Jeff Colyer was defeated by then-Secretary of State Kris Kobach, who was endorsed by President Donald Trump. Hawaii’s Neil Abercrombie was the last Democratic governor to fall in a primary, losing by 35 points to David Ige, who was a state senator at the time, in 2014.

Eleven House members and two senators have lost primaries this year.

Given the heavy focus on local issues, the Rhode Island primary did not attract the level of national attention other Democratic contests around the country — which centered on fierce ideological and generational battles — have attracted this year.

Still, Foulkes does have connections to powerful Democrats. Thomas Dodd and Chris Dodd, her uncle and grandfather, were both U.S. senators from Connecticut. And former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., who was a college roommate of Foulkes’ mother, campaigned for her.

Foulkes will be the heavy favorite in the general election in the blue state, which has not elected a Republican governor since 2010. Kamala Harris carried it by nearly 14 points in the 2024 presidential election.

World.title: ‘We felt defeated’: Lindsay Clancy juror provides new details about the lone holdout
World.content:
A juror in Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial provided new details Thursday about the lone holdout on the panel, including that he acted out the killings on a water bottle during deliberations.

Nick Dargie, 25, was one of the three men on the 12-person jury tasked with determining whether Clancy should be held criminally responsible for the 2023 strangulation deaths of her three young children: Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months old. He told “Good Morning America” on Thursday about his frustrations with the holdout juror, who has yet to be publicly identified.

“I think we felt defeated,” Dargie said about the case’s conclusion. “We spent seven weeks on this trial, almost two months of, you know, all of our lives dedicated to it.”

He is among at least five jurors — and the first male — who have spoken out about the case and what happened inside the deliberation room at Plymouth Superior Court last week. After more than 38 hours, the jurors could not reach a unanimous decision, forcing Judge William Sullivan to declare a mistrial after they deadlocked three times.

On Thursday, defense attorney Kevin Reddington filed a renewed motion to find Clancy not guilty by lack of criminal responsibility on each of the three charges, arguing that the prosecution did not prove, beyond a reasonable doubt, that Clancy was not in psychosis at the time of the killings.

Dargie told “Good Morning America” that toward the end of deliberations, the holdout juror would not engage in discussions with others or provide evidence that supported his reasoning, instead choosing to scroll on his phone.

Ultimately, Dargie said, he confronted the holdout juror after the man mimicked the killings, tying an exercise band entered into evidence around an empty water bottle and pulling it tight. Dargie said he is not sure why the man did that.

“I was shocked. It didn’t make any sense to me,” Dargie said. “We’re not in here to play detective or it’s not a game of Clue. This is serious.”

Nick Dargie on "Good Morning America." ABC News

Throughout the trial, Clancy’s defense attorney argued that she was in a state of psychosis when she strangled the children with exercise bands and therefore was not aware of what she was doing. The prosecution, however, argued she was not actually experiencing postpartum psychosis and planned the killings ahead of time.

Three women on the jury told NBC Boston that the 11 jurors agreed to find Clancy not guilty by lack of criminal responsibility. The holdout wanted to convict, they revealed, but admitted he expressed doubt in the prosecution’s case.

“It was definitely frustrating, mainly frustrating when [the holdout juror] explicitly said, ‘You know, I don’t know if the prosecution or the defense proved their case,’” Dargie told “GMA.”

Reddington in the motion also pointed to the fact that in this case, every juror except one — who did not apply the reasonable-doubt standard — came to that same conclusion.

“No rational jury could find beyond a reasonable doubt that she had no mental disease or defect when the Commonwealth’s own proof established that she did,” the motion said, noting the 11-1 jury split.

And at first, Dargie said, a number of jurors thought Clancy was guilty of the crimes, and at times the jury’s votes differed day to day.

A female juror who spoke with CBS Boston anonymously said many people on the jury were initially “firm in their beliefs,” and that she was one of the people who, at first, agreed with the holdout and thought Clancy was guilty.

She explained how there was so much “gray area” and doubt in the case, and that ultimately, she switched her tune because she thinks Clancy is mentally unwell and that she’d get better help in a state mental health facility than in prison.

Dargie told “GMA” that “once we laid out all of the evidence and how we saw it, that really brought everyone kind of on the same page, except for this one juror.” The female juror chalked it up to one person being unable to let go of their convictions.

When that one juror didn’t agree with the group, Dargie said, he asked him to show evidence that “helped to prove what he was saying, but he couldn’t.” That’s what led the jury foreperson to send a note to the judge about the holdout during deliberations, explaining that he wasn’t meeting the burden of reasonable doubt the prosecution must overcome.

Dargie acknowledged that it’s fair for someone to have a differing opinion, but said this particular juror would not engage and could not “find something to support his view.”

Now, prosecutors must decide whether they want to retry Clancy. The next hearing for the case is scheduled for Sept. 29.

Dargie, who was serving in the military overseas, said he’s “haunted” by the case. Specifically, he said, the recording of the 911 call made by Clancy’s then-husband, Patrick Clancy, when he found the dead children that night is seared into his memory. The recording was played in court and was not released to the public.

Patrick Clancy on the stand. David L. Ryan / The Boston Globe via Getty Images file

“I’ve never heard something like that, like a scream like that, come out of someone’s mouth,” Dargie said of the recording. “It’s horrifying.”

The anonymous female juror told CBS Boston that she will “never be the same after that 911 call.”

Dargie also rejected online conspiracy theories that Patrick Clancy was actually the one who carried out the killings, noting that if anyone had heard the 911 calls, they would change their mind.

“I think if they tried the trial again the way they did, I think nine times out of 10, I think the jury would come back with not guilty by reason of insanity, no doubt,” Dargie said.

World.title: Spice Girls fans feel duped after social media tease wasn’t for tour, but a music re-release
World.content:
Spice Girls fans are telling you what they want — what they really, really want — and it’s a tour that they aren’t getting any time soon.

The disbanded girl group excited their followers on Wednesday with a social media post teasing a big announcement for the following day. A short clip posted to Instagram showed an issue of “The Stage” magazine left on a set of stairs before zooming into a clasified  seeking Spice Girls Fans who are a “superfan, a collector, a music lover.”

“No sheet music required but you will need a vinyl or cd player,” the ad said.

Fans immediately jumped to speculation on what it could be, with many hoping for a possible reunion.

“If it’s a world tour, I’m selling my house to buy tix,” one Instagram commenter wrote.

Another wrote, “please say it’s @spherevegas,” referring to the popular Las Vegas venue where the Backstreet Boys are currently in residency.

But some should have slowed it down and read the sign.

On Thursday, the Spice Girls account announced a re-release of “all the singles” with b-sides and surprises “from the vault” on CD and vinyl. A previously unreleased demo of a song called “Do You Think About Me” was also made available on streaming services Thursday.

The full collection will release in November and ranges in price from $128.99 to $380.99, according to the band’s website. The re-release is meant to honor the 30th anniversary of their single “Wannabe,” the hit that changed the trajectory of their lives.

It was a blow to the ‘90s band’s most loyal fans, who were ready to promise they would be there in the stands.

“Negotiating with my husband on my price cap for Spice Girls tickets today was for NOTHING,” one woman wrote in the comments.

“Guys we want two things- Spice World on streaming platforms and a tour with the full line-up,” another Instagram user wrote. “Please make it happen.”

“I hear the millennial sigh of devastation from across the world,” one person said.

00:15 Spice Girls drop a cryptic video spurring reunion rumors 00:00 00:00

The Spice Girls have been asked repeatedly about a tour in recent years in interviews, but it appears that a reunion performance with all five original members is a pipe dream. There was a small tour across the U.K. and Ireland in 2019 that didn’t feature Victoria Beckham, aka Posh Spice.

Beckham expressed her excitement to go watch her former bandmates even if she wasn’t going to be on stage. The fashion mogul has said in the last year that she hasn’t performed in years and doesn’t feel that she is the strongest singer or dancer.

She told Andy Cohen on his radio show in October that she didn’t think she could even make a world tour work with the demands of her business.

“Before I was in the Spice Girls, I was so self-conscious and they made me feel that I was good enough, but being on stage, I realized as fun as it is, you know, it’s not ultimately what I want to do anymore,” Beckham said.

Melanie Brown, or Scary Spice as she’s known to fans, reiterated that a tour was not happening in an interview with Hello! magazine published in April.

“I’m 50. You can’t be nagging everyone to go on tour if they don’t want to,” Brown said. “I laid that to rest when I turned 50.”

But the women are still close friends.

All but Beckham were in attendance for Melanie Chisholm’s wedding earlier this year. And though she couldn’t be there for Sporty Spice on her big day, Beckham designed the singer’s wedding dress, according to Vogue.

All five women were together earlier this year, according to social media. Beckham’s youngest son posted a video on Instagram in February of the Spice Girls singing their song “Viva Forever” around a dinner table while he played guitar for him. The video has been watched more than 13 million times.

“Love you all,” Beckham wrote in her son’s comment section.

World.title: Trump's $5,000 payment would reignite inflation, economists say
World.content:
President Trump's vow to send $5,000 to every U.S. adult if the Republican Party keeps control of Congress in the midterm elections would drive up the federal deficit, reignite inflation and alarm investors, according to economists.

After Mr. Trump raised the idea of such a dividend on Wednesday night at the Republican National Committee's midterm convention, Vice President JD Vance told Fox News that the U.S. would fund the payment using tariff revenue collected by the Trump administration, and that it would be aimed at the middle class.

Those tariffs are generating about $125 billion in annual revenue — one-tenth of the $1.25 trillion that would be required to pay $5,000 to each of the nation's roughly 245 million U.S. adults,, Erica York, senior economist with the Tax Foundation's Center for Federal Tax Policy, told CBS News.

Because tariff revenue would fall short, the U.S. would likely need to issue government debt to pay for the dividends, raising the federal deficit to $3 trillion, up from its current level of about $1.8 trillion, York estimated.

Why the dividend would drive inflation

The one-time payments would also likely stoke inflation by fueling a surge in consumer spending, as did the multiple federal stimulus checks during the pandemic.

Economists say those payments contributed to consumer prices reaching a 40-year high in June 2022.

A $5,000 giveaway would also rattle financial markets, York said. With the nation's debt recently surpassing $40 trillion for the first time, Treasury bond buyers would likely demand higher yields to offset increased fiscal risks, she added.

"If financial markets are already concerned about U.S. budget deficits, which are historically large and are projected to grow, and the message that you're giving is, 'We don't really care. We're almost going to double our deficits' — that's madness," York said of Mr. Trump's proposal.

Offering such a payment to Americans would be "fiscally dangerous," Maya MacGuineas, president of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, a nonpartisan think tank that favors reducing the U.S. deficit, said in a statement on Thursday.

"It's hard to understand how anyone could look at our current fiscal and economic situation and think we need to borrow another $1.2 trillion to send everyone cash," she said.

The White House said that Mr. Trump has "consistently proven his doubters wrong."

"The doomers and naysayers have consistently doubted President Trump: when he pledged to create the historic Trump Accounts, lowered prescription prices with Most Favored Nations, secured the border with no crossings, cleaned up our streets, ended taxes on tips, grew real wages, renegotiated broken trade deals and reshored key manufacturing back to the United States," White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said in a statement to CBS News.

Piling on debt

Many fiscal hawks have urged lawmakers to start addressing the mounting federal debt, which has doubled in less than a decade due to multiple tax cuts and COVID-related spending, among other factors.

Adding $1.25 trillion in debt to the nation's ledger is "completely detached from fiscal reality," York said.

Rising U.S. debt has pushed up the nation's interest costs, with the U.S. government now spending more on servicing its debt than on national defense or Medicare. Investors are demanding higher Treasury yields due to the worsening federal fiscal outlook. That, in turn, is pushing up borrowing costs for consumers, including mortgages, auto loans and personal loans.

"The bond market is already nervous about inflation and America's $40 trillion debt," Heather Long, chief economist at the Navy Federal Credit Union, said in an email. "This would likely cause borrowing costs to jump even further."

Long added that because of those issues, Wall Street is "largely ignoring" the Trump administration's dividend plan, writing it off as unlikely to gain traction with Congress, which would need to approve it.

During his Wednesday speech, Mr. Trump also proposed other ways to lower the cost of living for Americans, which polls show is a key campaign issue ahead of the November elections. That includes possibly eliminating credit card swipe fees, which he said could save the typical family about $1,200 a year.

But the $5,000 payment has garnered the most attention, likely because many consumers say they're struggling with the cost of living, with gas prices remaining above $4 a gallon and inflation still elevated.

Consumer Price Index data for August, set to be released on Friday, is expected to show inflation rose at an annual pace of 3.3%, well above the Federal Reserve's annual target of 2%.

While a $5,000 payment might initially help struggling consumers, such a program would soon backfire by driving inflation even higher, York told CBS News. The COVID stimulus checks caused inflation to rise by 2.6% during the pandemic, according to 2023 research from the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis.

"We would be stimulating the economy in a really massive way with $5,000 payments, when the economy is not really calling for that," she said. "You're really kind of worsening the problem that you're supposedly trying to address with this proposal."

World.title: How much interest can a $15,000 6-month CD earn now?
World.content:
A 6-month CD could be a smart place to park your $15,000 right now. Flavia Morlachetti/Getty Images

If you still have a tax refund that you haven't yet figured out what to do with or simply have built your savings to a milestone $15,000 amount, you may find yourself exploring your savings account options right now. And with inflation still pronounced, an interest rate hike from the Federal Reserve looming for later in September and credit card balances growing, where you keep your money now is more important than usual. That's especially true for amounts such as $15,000, which will need to be leveraged strategically in today's unique economic environment.

A certificate of deposit (CD) account, however, could be the perfect albeit temporary home for this money. With a 6-month CD, for example, savers will be able to take advantage of today's elevated interest rate climate without having to worry about losing access to their funds for an extended period. CDs have fixed rates, allowing savers to precisely determine their interest-earning potential. And they're FDIC-insured up to $250,000 per account, providing ample protection for a $15,000 deposit. Then, in six months, once today's market uncertainty has shaken out, savers can revisit their savings strategy, but with more money.

How much more money will they actually be working with at that point, however? Below, we'll break down the interest-earning capacity a $15,000 6-month CD could provide savers who take action now.

Earn more interest on your money by opening a CD account here.

How much interest can a $15,000 6-month CD earn now?

While CD interest rates will look similar from lender to lender, they won't be identical. That's why it's so important to shop around before locking your money into an account, especially with a CD, which will require you to pay an early withdrawal fee to regain access prematurely. Using three of the top 6-month CD rates available this September, here's how much interest savers can expect to earn if they keep the account frozen up to the maturity date:

$15,000 6-month CD at 4.00%: $297.06 upon account maturity

$297.06 upon account maturity $15,000 6-month CD at 4.15%: $308.09 upon account maturity

$308.09 upon account maturity $15,000 6-month CD at 4.20%: $311.76 upon account maturity

For context, these returns aren't materially improved from what they were in July, when rates were only slightly lower. They are still higher than what they were in May, though they're below the 4.40% savers were able to secure in September 2025. In other words, if you can find a 6-month CD with a rate around 4.20% or higher right now, it's worth locking, especially if you have $15,000 you want to deposit. There's no guarantee that rates will rise further, even if it looks that way right now. In the interim, however, you'll lose out on the interest you could already be earning.

World.title: August CPI report could spark the Fed's first rate hike in over 3 years
World.content:
A key inflation reading tomorrow could determine whether the Federal Reserve issues its first interest rate hike in more than three years.

The August Consumer Price Index report, scheduled for release at 8:30 a.m. ET on Friday, is the last major inflation snapshot Fed officials will receive before announcing their next interest rate decision on Sept. 16. Economists expect prices last month rose 3.3% on an annual basis, reflecting an easing after reaching a three-year high of 4.2% in May.

The August report could help Fed officials determine whether the recent easing reflects an ongoing trend, or whether inflation is becoming stubbornly entrenched amid high fuel prices caused by the Iran war. Its primary tool for taming inflation, one of its core mandates, is to raise borrowing costs, which helps cool spending.

At the Fed's previous meeting, nearly half of its policymakers said they would support a rate hike later this year. If officials vote to raise their benchmark rate next week, it would mark the first increase since July 2023, when the central bank was battling the highest inflation in more than four decades.

"It's clear that the swing voters at the Fed are paying close attention to this inflation data," Heather Long, a chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, said of the CPI report.

"I think that's what's really giving it heightened meaning," she added.

On Thursday, the Labor Department said the producer price index — which captures inflation before it reaches consumers — rose 5.4% in August from a year ago, up from 4.8% in July. U.S. oil prices topped $100 a barrel Thursday on renewed fighting in the Middle East, while President Trump has intensified a trade war with Canada, a sign tariffs still could push up costs.

The Fed's swing voters include Fed Governor Christopher Waller, who said in a speech earlier this month that he would consider a rate hike "if inflation comes in hot." But he added that if the August CPI shows progress toward the Fed's 2% goal, he would be willing to hold rates steady.

Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh has been more guarded in his communication about the Fed's next moves. However, last month while speaking at the Fed's annual conference in Jackson Hole, he said the Fed will "have work to do" if inflation doesn't drop toward the central bank's 2% target at a "sufficient speed."

What's the likelihood of an interest rate hike?

The Fed has held its benchmark rate at its current range of 3.5% to 3.75% since December 2025.

However, investors are bracing for an increasing likelihood that the central bank will raise rates as it grapples with ongoing price pressures stemming from the war in the Middle East. Markets are now pricing in a 70% probability the Fed will increase its benchmark rate to 3.75% to 4% at its Sept. 16 meeting, according to CME FedWatch, which bases its forecast on 30-day Fed funds futures prices.

Prices at the pump also remain elevated, with diesel hitting an all-time high of almost $6 a gallon on Thursday. Other factors are also fueling inflation, including tariffs, rising health insurance costs and AI expenditures, experts told CBS News.

"The [CPI] report is unlikely to alter the message of limited inflation progress and should provide sufficient support for the Fed to hike rates at the September meeting," Stephen Juneau, a U.S. economist at the Bank of America Securities, said in a research note Thursday.

What is the inflation report expected to show?

Economists polled by FactSet expect that inflation rose at an annual rate of 3.3% in August, slightly below the 3.4% pace recorded in July.

However, Gregory Daco, chief economist at EY-Parthenon, said the Fed will pay closer attention to core inflation — which excludes more volatile energy and food categories — to monitor whether higher energy prices are passing through to goods and services.

Economists polled by FactSet expect that core CPI rose 2.4% on an annual basis last month, which would extend a downward trend that started in June.

"Traditionally, the Fed used to think along a framework that would assume supply shocks were infrequent and short-lived, and therefore it could look through those supply shocks," Daco said.

"That's no longer a reality. We have more layered supply shocks, and therefore the Fed has to think carefully about the potential pass-through of these higher commodities prices, higher supply chain costs, higher transportation costs into core items."

World.title: Prosecutor who withdrew from dismissed Adani bribery case fired, sources say
World.content:
A federal prosecutor who withdrew from the criminal case against Indian billionaire Gautam Adani shortly after senior Justice Department officials moved to dismiss the charges has been fired, several sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.

Andrew Tyler, an acting assistant chief in the fraud section of the Criminal Division, was removed on Tuesday over allegations of ethical violations, two of the sources said, without providing further details.

After this report was published, a source with knowledge of the matter, however, disputed those claims, saying Tyler was never accused of any wrongdoing or provided with a reason for the termination. His dismissal letter, like many others that department employees have received, stated he was being removed under Article II of the Constitution.

The source said that his firing was an act of retaliation over Tyler's decision to withdraw from the Adani case. The source said that Tyler removed himself from the case in order to fulfill his ethical duties as a prosecutor and added that Tyler conducted himself ethically on all of the cases he handled, including the Adani case.

Another source who previously worked with Tyler concurred, and described him as a dedicated employee who had worked at the Justice Department for most of his career.

His Linkedin profile shows he started as an intern in the tax and criminal divisions. After a brief stint as a law clerk in the Superior Court for the District of Columbia, he returned to the Justice Department, where he started as a clerk before becoming a trial attorney and eventually an assistant chief.

His termination was first reported by NBC News.

Adani and other executives at his renewable energy company were indicted at the end of the Biden administration in a wide-ranging foreign bribery and securities fraud scheme which alleged they paid off Indian government officials to obtain lucrative solar energy supply contracts.

In May, Trent McCotter, who is now the acting deputy attorney general, ordered the case to be dismissed. The decision came after Adani's attorneys at Sullivan & Cromwell including Bob Giuffra met with department officials about the case.

In one meeting at the Justice Department about the Adani case, Giuffra made a presentation that disputed evidence of the alleged bribery scheme, according to sources familiar with the matter and records reviewed by CBS News. One slide claimed that one of Adani's companies is "powering India's progress," and another slide said the Trump administration "would not have brought the case."

Giuffra also said at the meeting that if prosecutors were to drop the charges, Adani would be willing to invest $10 billion in the American economy, sources told CBS News.

The motion to dismiss the case was only signed by politically appointed Justice Department officials, and not by the career prosecutors involved in the case.

Shortly afterwards, Tyler and one of his co-counsels, Shy Jackson, filed motions to withdraw from the case — an act that was widely viewed as a quiet form of protest.

U.S. District Judge Nicholas G. Garaufis, in the Eastern District of New York, initially refused to drop the charges. He said the Justice Department had not provided an adequate factual basis for doing so.

He demanded more information from the Justice Department, and also asked Adani to submit a sworn statement answering questions about whether there was a quid pro quo. Adani denied the existence of one.

Garaufis ultimately agreed to drop the charges against Adani and several of his co-defendants last month, but he has steadfastly refused to drop the charges against the remaining defendants on the grounds that the Justice Department has provided "no new reasons to dismiss counts one and five, and no additional facts to support the reasons given for the requested dismissal."

Judge Garaufis also accused McCotter of improperly interfering in the case, saying he had "eschewed the professional opinions of innumerable officials from various federal offices and replaced them with his singular judgment."

Tyler is the second federal prosecutor to be fired this month amid disagreements with senior department officials over a high-profile criminal case.

Earlier this month, the department fired Matthew Evans, a prosecutor in Minnesota who was investigating ICE officer Christian Castro over the shooting of a Venezuelan immigrant earlier this year.

His firing came shortly after ProPublica reported that Evans told attorneys for the man who was shot, Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis, and other victims to prepare for Castro to only be charged with making false statements. That would result in lesser penalties than criminal charges that Castro had violated people's constitutional rights under color of law.

Several sources told CBS News that Evans is now under investigation.

World.title: Anthropic says scientists used AI for possible biological weapons development
World.content:
Anthropic said Thursday it blocked scientists who used its Claude AI models "in ways that could support biological weapons development."

The revelation was shared in a lengthy report that also divulged other harmful activity involving surveillance, scams, conventional weapons development and propaganda. The cases in the report are examples of "the most notable and novel threat activity" identified by Anthropic so far, the company said. Threat actors included criminals, suspected state-sponsored groups, spyware vendors and state propaganda institutions, the report said.

Anthropic shared five cases involving activity that had the potential to support the development of biological weapons. It called biological misuse "one of the most serious risks of frontier AI models."

The company said the cases identified "provide evidence of capability" of the AI models, but "cannot concretely demonstrate that such capability would ever be used to develop biological weapons in the real world."

The people involved in these cases are working scientists, whom Anthropic chose not to identify. The company said it can't "assert that they intended harm."

"When we detected and investigated these cases, we banned the users' accounts and incorporated our investigative findings into our frontier model safeguards, enforcement, and threat intelligence processes to better prevent, detect, and disrupt these activities in the future," the report says.

Recent, more advanced models like Claude Fable 5 contain stronger safeguards than earlier models and restrict access to "a wide range of dual-use biological research queries," the report says, noting that the biological capabilities of AI can be used both for beneficial and harmful purposes.

"The same information that can be used to develop a biological weapon could also be used to develop, for example, a vaccine or a cure for a disease," the company said.

Propaganda and surveillance

Anthropic also said that it identified and removed accounts using Claude for influence operations campaigns to shape public opinion, including three Iranian state-aligned accounts.

In these cases, each operation was run by an actor working within or on behalf of an Iranian state propaganda institution, the company said. Claude was used to build content, make posts seem like they were from independent news sources and to proliferate content across social media platforms like X, Instagram and TikTok.

One Iran-nexus threat actor used Claude to develop targeting recommendations against U.S. naval forces in the region, Anthropic said. The same account designed software for a domestic mass-surveillance platform for Iranian state systems.

Claude was also used to build and run surveillance operations by actors in China and West Africa, and in some cases, to identify targets. Anthropic said it identified cases where AI was being used in place of an engineering workforce.

In China, three accounts aligned with the PRC municipal security service used Claude for surveillance and transnational repression, including a municipal bureau that profiles overseas activists and organizations.

World.title: Why you shouldn't bank on Trump's $5,000 dividends happening
World.content:
Washington — President Trump pledged to give every American adult $5,000 if Republicans keep the House and Senate in November, framing it as a dividend made possible by the country's "tremendous economic success."

But the president's pledge at the Republican National Committee's midterm convention has political and logistical hurdles. And Mr. Trump has yet to follow through with other universal cash payments he's promised to Americans thus far, with the Trump Accounts for babies born during his time in office being an exception.

The Census Bureau says there are about 245 million U.S. citizens over 18, so if the Trump administration gave $5,000 to every adult U.S. citizen, it would cost over $1.2 trillion. CBS News has asked the White House for details on the president's plan, including whether the money would come in the form of a check or some other way.

Here are the reasons why Americans might not want to count on that $5,000.

The payments would have to pass both chambers of Congress

Giving $5,000 to each American adult would require an act of Congress. Republicans already control both chambers, so if Mr. Trump wanted to prove he's serious — and wanted to gain goodwill with voters — he could have already demanded that Congress take it up, or he could draft legislative language now.

Asked by Fox News' Laura Ingraham why not give Americans the money now, while the GOP has majorities in both chambers, Mr. Trump blamed Democrats.

"Because they can't — I'll tell you what — because the Democrats can't do it," he responded in a brief clip posted on social media. "Because with them it's negative growth. With us, it's so positive."

So far, Republican leaders in Congress aren't jumping on an idea that would add to the national debt, which last month surpassed $40 trillion. And House Speaker Mike Johnson has pledged spending cuts after the midterms should the GOP retain control.

Polling isn't favorable for Republicans to keep both chambers. Republicans face particularly strong headwinds in the House, where only a few district flips would lose them the chamber. Democrats are outperforming Republicans on the generic ballot.

It's unlikely a Democratic-controlled House or Senate would approve the $5,000 payments.

Americans never received DOGE dividends

The president expressed openness to some form of "DOGE dividends" to Americans at the beginning of his term, when billionaire entrepreneur Elon Musk was overseeing the implementation of the administration's government downsizing.

"There's even a — under consideration, a new concept where we give 20% of the DOGE savings to American citizens and 20% goes to paying down debt," Mr. Trump said at the FII Priority Summit in Miami in February of last year.

DOGE savings came in well under projections, and the idea died out.

Mr. Trump pledged tariff refunds that never arrived

The president already vowed tariff dividends last year for Americans. He said a dividend of "at least $2,000" a person would arrive for everyone except for high-income Americans.

The government has not, however, paid taxpayers directly. Companies are receiving tariff refunds after the Supreme Court ruled some of Mr. Trump's tariffs were illegal. Some of those companies have vowed to share their financial relief with consumers, but they aren't required to do so.

The money generated from tariffs hasn't come close to $5,000 per adult

Vice President JD Vance told Fox News the money would come from tariff revenue. But the government isn't generating enough tariff revenue for that to work. The money the U.S. has raked in through tariffs hasn't come close to the more than $1.2 trillion that would be needed to pay each American adult $5,000.

According to the Bipartisan Policy Center, the U.S. has brought in about $210 billion from gross tariff and other excise taxes in 2026. That only amounts to about $857 per eligible person, not to mention the U.S. government has already had to return much of its tariff revenue to companies. Over half of the revenues generated by tariffs in 2026 have been eaten up by refunds to companies, the Bipartisan Policy Center says.

According to the Cato Institute, a $5,000 check for each American adult would be between 60% to 75% of the total revenue the Trump administration's tariffs are projected to generate over 10 years.
