Fowler calls the current GOP an "unprecedented party" centered around an administration dominated by decisions made by Trump, often seemingly for his own benefit. This includes constructing a ballroom, renaming landmarks to spite allies and putting his face on a coin. Voters say they want the Republican-controlled federal government to focus on issues like rising gas prices and the war in Iran. If the GOP adjusts its course, there's potential for a shift in voters' viewpoint, Fowler says. ➡️ Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) made a surprise appearance at the midterm convention in a 64-second video introducing Sen. Dave McCormick (R-Pa.).

at the midterm convention in a 64-second video introducing Sen. Dave McCormick (R-Pa.). ➡️ Here's what to expect on the second night of the convention.

Sponsor Message

Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins is set to face the state Supreme Court today to explain why he should not be held in contempt of court. Hoskins faces two conflicting court rulings regarding a Republican redistricting plan that could influence the outcome of the midterm elections. He has chosen to follow the ruling he prefers while ignoring his state's Supreme Court, which last week rejected the Republican map that could help the GOP win a House seat.



🎧 The court mandated that the new map be approved by voters in November before it can take effect and said Hoskins has intentionally delayed the process, according to Jason Rosenbaum of NPR network station St. Louis Public Radio. The primaries have already taken place under the Republican plan, and now, election officials are uncertain about which congressional districts voters will belong to in the midterms.

Today marks one year after a gunman fatally shot Charlie Kirk during a talk at Utah Valley University. His death galvanized many in the Republican Party but has left questions about his movement's future. A little more than a decade before he died, Kirk founded Turning Point to engage more young people in conservative politics. Over the next 10 years, he became a key figure among Generation Z and millennial conservatives. As his young supporters reflect on the past year, they describe a complex reality: Rather than uniting, the movement faces uncertainty about its future, struggles to rally around a new leader and grapples with the same divisions that affect the broader Republican Party.

Sponsor Message

Apple's new CEO John Ternus yesterday unveiled a new foldable device called iPhone Duo. The design marks the most radical change to the iconic phone since the company introduced it nearly 20 years ago.



🎧 Ternus takes on his role at a time when Apple has been criticized for losing some of the "wow factor" of the Steve Jobs era, NPR's John Ruwitch says. While foldable phones have been around for years, Apple has had the advantage of learning from the market's successes and failures. And Ruwitch says one of the things Apple does best is enter markets late with well-designed, user-friendly products.

Today's listen

toggle caption Monica Schipper/Getty Images/Getty Images North America

Olivia Rodrigo is one of pop music's biggest stars. Now, she's using her fame to speak out about political rights. Last month, her inaugural Daisy Chain Fields music festival, which featured an all-women lineup, raised $20 million for 10 organizations supporting women and girls. In an interview with Morning Edition, Rodrigo tells host Leila Fadel that she felt it was important to hold the festival now because many people are feeling discouraged by efforts to strip away their rights. "I think that the people who want to keep us down are really relying on us feeling alone and overwhelmed," she said. "And I think the antidote to that is joy and community." At the festival, she performed her single "Serena Joy" on stage for the first time. The song is named after a character in Margaret Atwood's The Handmaid's Tale who wrote about the threat to all of our human rights. Listen to Rodrigo perform the song live and read more about her politics.

Life advice

Navied Mahdavian for NPR

Conflict in relationships is not always a bad thing. In fact, it can be necessary for maintaining a close and authentic connection with loved ones. Conflict resolution facilitator Priya Parker has shared strategies for starting and ending a disagreement while minimizing discomfort for everyone involved. And in true Life Kit fashion, the team has made Parker's advice easily digestible by putting it in comic form.

Sponsor Message

💬 To decide whether it's worth it to engage in a conflict, ask yourself if you care enough for this person, whether you still long for this relationship, whether the conflict challenges a core value and whether saying something could alter the situation.

💬 Before you fight, make sure you understand what the conflict is really about. It can help make sure you and your loved one have the right conversation.

💬 Ease feelings of discomfort by taking deep breaths and shaking out your limbs. Also, stay focused on the present and avoid rehashing past arguments.

💬 After an argument, try to reflect on what you discussed together, without judgment.

For more advice on how to handle conflict in your relationships, listen to this episode of NPR's Life Kit. Subscribe to the Life Kit newsletter for expert advice on love, money, relationships and more.

3 things to know before you go

toggle caption Imen Ben Youssef/AFP

The artificial intelligence company Anthropic has developed an interactive tool to test how AI could impact the U.S. economy. A researcher from the company resigned yesterday, saying he feared that AI could be disastrous to humanity. Kelly Rogers abruptly announced her resignation as the leader of the Education Department's special education office after less than four months in the position. In this week's installment of Far-Flung Postcards, NPR's Hannah Bloch sends greetings from Paris, where the floating Olympic cauldron is still rising in the nighttime sky two years after the 2024 Paris Games.

This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

World.title: One year after Charlie Kirk's death, Turning Point USA faces an uncertain future
World.content:
One year after Charlie Kirk's death, Turning Point USA faces an uncertain future

toggle caption Alex Brandon/AP

When Jacob York found out that Charlie Kirk had been fatally shot, he was at baseball practice. Standing in the outfield, he broke down in tears. That night, he decided that Kirk's organization, Turning Point USA, should have a chapter on his campus. So he got to work starting one himself.

"I feel like there [were] many of us who had that wake-up call," said York, 21, who attends Olivet Nazarene University, a small Christian school south of Chicago.

"I think I submitted the request to start a chapter six times," he recalled. "There were so many requests that it kept saying, 'Oops, try again later.'"

Sponsor Message

Kirk's death one year ago on the campus of Utah Valley University was as stunning for his followers as it was painful. A little more than a decade earlier, he had founded Turning Point with the goal of getting more young people involved in conservative politics. By the time he died at age 31, he had become one of the most revered figures on the right, especially among Generation Z and millennial conservatives.

From students like York all the way to the upper echelons of the Republican Party, Kirk's death was seen as a call to action. In the days following the shooting, Turning Point reported an initial surge of interest among college and high school students looking to start chapters.

His widow, Erika Kirk, spoke about that momentum in her first public remarks, just days after his death.

"If you thought that my husband's mission was powerful before, you have no idea," said Erika Kirk, who has since taken over as Turning Point's CEO. "You have no idea what you've just unleashed across this entire country, and this world."

But, as Charlie Kirk's young supporters reflect on the past year, some paint a more complicated picture of the organization he left behind. Rather than a unified and growing coalition of young voters, they describe a movement facing questions about its future — one that has yet to fully coalesce around a new leader and that is grappling with the same issue divides causing friction within the Republican Party more broadly.

Sponsor Message

Fractures amid growth

The fractures have been felt acutely by young conservatives like 23-year-old Dino Fantegrossi.

"Charlie Kirk got it. He spent all of his time on college campuses talking to people my age, whether he agreed or disagreed with them," said Fantegrossi. "He knew — because he was so plugged in — what bugged young people, what needed to be addressed. There's no one else that was quite at that level of plugged in."

Fantegrossi, a recent graduate of the University of Arkansas, had led his school's Turning Point chapter for more than two years. That is until last spring, when he decided to break with the organization and start a new group, Young American Revival, which he said aims to be "a positive vehicle for students to take out their frustrations in a manner that actually brings about change within our state."

toggle caption Melissa Majchrzak/AFP via Getty Images

"One of the big problems that has happened since Charlie's death is that I think a lot of the youth have kind of felt lost," said Fantegrossi. "They're not really sure how to channel their frustrations, and that oftentimes — when it's not put in check or pointed in a positive direction — can manifest itself in some very nasty ways."

In a statement, Turning Point spokesman Andrew Kolvet acknowledged that the group is facing "a confluence of challenges" but attested that "the organization is still growing in nearly every conceivable way," saying it's "a testament to Charlie's enduring legacy."

Turning Point says in a fact sheet that it saw "unprecedented expansion" in the 2025-2026 school year, with over a million involved students across 3,500 high school clubs and 1,500 college chapters.

"In many ways the challenges our students and chapters face have never been more obvious or pronounced, but so too are the opportunities," Kolvet said.

A missing leader for young conservatives

At the time of his death, Kirk was seen as one of the most influential voices within the conservative youth space and broader Republican Party. Supporters have credited him for the gains that then-candidate Donald Trump made with young voters in the 2024 presidential election, a crucial bloc that helped propel him to a second term.

Sponsor Message

Kirk's influence extended into Trump's second administration, as Kirk maintained close relationships with top White House officials while continuing to engage with the Make America Great Again movement's newly expanded youth coalition.

For his followers, his influence meant their views had a direct pipeline to the president. For the administration, he was a trusted messenger on policy decisions, even when they split the MAGA base, as with the strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities in the summer of 2025.

toggle caption Joe Raedle/Getty Images

But for as much as Kirk was revered on the right, he was reviled on the left, facing pushback for comments disparaging immigrants and transgender people and questioning the qualifications and capabilities of women and Black Americans. He also amplified conspiracy theories about COVID-19 and falsely claimed the 2020 presidential election was fraudulent.

The criticism did not faze Kirk, as he visited campuses across the U.S. to debate his positions at "Prove Me Wrong" events that were central to the image he cultivated for himself as a defender of free speech, free markets and limited government. It was the same type of event he was taking part in last year when he was assassinated at Utah Valley University.

"He was unique in terms of his connection to a not-insignificant number of younger people," argued John Della Volpe, a Democratic pollster who has spent decades researching young Americans.

Della Volpe, who observes and conducts focus groups of Gen Z voters, said Kirk's death could be another factor fueling a growing belief among young people that they lack political agency.

"His name is mentioned on an ongoing basis, literally every single month. But it's framed as 'He was someone who understood me, who heard me,'" Della Volpe added. "People feel like he listened to them and he's been taken from us. So therefore, why does it matter anymore?"

Sponsor Message

The divides playing out within Turning Point

That kind of direct connection has felt missing for many of Kirk's followers. Turning Point leaders vowed to continue holding campus visits in Kirk's stead, organizing more formal events that largely veered away from direct debate and instead featured a range of keynote speakers, including the group's new leader, Erika Kirk, and Vice President Vance. But the events have drawn mixed and, at times, lackluster turnout.

Filling Kirk's shoes isn't the only challenge facing Turning Point. There's also the daunting task of keeping young conservatives engaged at a time when many of them are unhappy with party leaders.

That includes Trump, whose youth coalition has increasingly soured on him. At the start of his second term, 92% of Trump voters under 35 approved of his job as president, according to data from Pew Research Center. By late April 2026, that support had dropped to 57%.

toggle caption Pool/Getty Images

Student organizers say the Iran war and the administration's relationship with Israel have been major tension points. Gen Z and millennial Republicans are much less likely than older generations to hold favorable views on both topics.

To Hazel Roberts, 18, a first-year student at Grand Canyon University who started a Turning Point chapter back in high school, these intraparty rifts are a painful reminder of why Kirk's leadership mattered.

"That's what Charlie loved about Turning Point. We could all have different perspectives and not hate each other for it, and we can talk about it. And since Charlie's passing, there has been a lot of hate from the right," she said. "Charlie was the glue that held us together."

Misinformation about Turning Point could cloud its future

The divides go past just policy rifts, and for some student activists on campus, they had made organizing efforts more of a challenge.

"The conspiracies revolving around Charlie Kirk's assassination [have] really tanked the credibility of Turning Point," said Alex BirdSong, 19, a junior at Georgia State University, referring to the slew of unfounded claims made by right-wing influencers, namely podcaster Candace Owens, to millions online over the past year.

Sponsor Message

BirdSong, who joined his school's Turning Point chapter following Kirk's death and now serves as its president, hopes that this school year he can help change how people think about the organization.

"We've had people come up to us who are Candace Owens fans and get mad at us for being Turning Point, and so that's what the climate is," he explained. "It's going to be a huge challenge for Turning Point and the right if, one, the right can't unify and, two, if the [Trump] administration can't get the controversies under wraps."

Some students admit that the confluence of challenges has caused momentum to fizzle.

toggle caption Win McNamee/Getty Images

"I would say the interest in conservative organizations is low right now, even if it did rebound when Charlie Kirk got shot," said Max Williams, 20, a junior at the University of Richmond, where he leads the school's Turning Point chapter. "I think that Charlie not being there, the Trump administration not being popular right now — I think that it is definitely slowed down a bit and maybe even is going in the opposite direction."

Williams said there's a part of him that's not excited to participate in organizing on campus again this year, as he too has grown frustrated with Trump.

"Some of this stuff is just infuriating, and you can't defend any of it. And I don't even try anymore," he added.

His plan for talking with students on campus: Emphasize the issues they care about, instead of focusing on Trump.

But without Kirk, that might not be as easy as it once was.

World.title: Democrats blast $5,000 payment promise ahead of Trump, Vance speeches in Dallas
World.content:
Democrats blast $5,000 payment promise ahead of Trump, Vance speeches in Dallas

toggle caption Justin Sullivan/Getty Images

At the Republican midterm convention in Dallas, President Trump made a stunning and implausible pledge: to send every American adult a $5,000 cash dividend. But only if his party maintains control of the House and the Senate in November's midterms.

"If the Republicans win, you win with us," Trump said to applause. "And it will be called the 'Trump dividend'. Congratulations. Now all we have to do is win."

That's a big "if." Republicans are facing significant political headwinds.

"We might not win," Trump admitted.

Sponsor Message

Quick math puts the bill for this proposed "dividend" at more than $1 trillion. Plus, it's illegal to pay or be paid to influence voting.

House Democrats in Dallas Thursday to counter program the convention quickly attacked the announcement.

Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., called the president a "known liar."

"The dividend is not happening," Garcia added. "[Trump] promised a dividend on tariffs. That didn't happen. He promised a dividend on DOGE. That didn't happen. He promised some strange, new dividend from Air Force One, what six months ago? That never happened."

"There's no one in the country that thinks somehow this new dividend is actually going to happen," he said.

Trump's address last night was a wide ranging, rally-style speech where he did everything from defend the Iran war to criticize the fashion sense of one Republican Senate candidate. He attacked Democrats as communist and extremists and begged Republicans to vote in November as if he were on the ballot.

"Please pretend that I'm running," he said. "If we don't have the majorities, so much can be lost."

Trump spoke for an hour and 44 minutes, far longer than scheduled.

He will deliver closing remarks tonight as well.

"But I'm not doing a big deal like this," he joked. "I gave you a lot of material. I don't have to do it twice."

Sponsor Message

The two-night event, hatched by Trump, was meant for Republicans to energize the base ahead of the midterms.

"It took a little imagination to think of it," Trump said of the first ever Republican midterm convention.

In a preview of what to expect tonight, the focus on Trump was clear as the event kicked off Wednesday, with a lineup of Republican lawmakers, candidates and everyday Americans, praising the president and his policies. It was capped off by Trump's headlining speech.

Speaking to an arena with whole sections of empty seats, Trump rallied the party faithful.

"The midterms are not supposed to be won by [the party of] the sitting president, and we're going to change that," Trump said, promising to visit the states and districts of every Republican facing a close race.

Tonight, Trump will share the convention's final hour with Vice President Vance. By the time Republicans hold their next convention in 2028, Trump will no longer be the center of the party's attention. There will be a new nominee and de facto party leader charting a course for Republicans.

The program tonight will include a tribute to the late republican activist Charlie Kirk, who was assassinated one year ago, and an observance of the 25th anniversary of the September 11th attacks, which is Friday.

MAGA celebrities and cabinet members will also grace the stage tonight. Former White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt is set to speak, along with Donald Trump Jr. and Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

Over the course of the convention, 19 Republicans in competitive House and Senate races will deliver short stump speeches. Many of them have used the stage to position the Republican Party as the party of the American people, painting Democrats as aligned with "socialism" and "communism."

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who is running to represent the state in the US Senate made those points, but also used his speech to ask for money.

"I need your prayers, your vote and your support," Paxton said. "If we lose Texas, we lose the common sense revolution. If we lose the common sense revolution, we lose America."

His Democratic opponent, state Rep. James Talarico has a campaign cash advantage but Trump's Super PAC, MAGA Inc. just committed to spend $10 million, propping up Paxton and hitting Talarico. A Republican shouldn't be in a tight race in Texas, but Paxton has been plagued by scandal and weak fundraising.

Sponsor Message

Trump, in his remarks, urged Texans to vote for Paxton despite what the president considers to be his flaws.

"Some may not like the way he dresses. I don't," Trump said as part of a lengthy and lighthearted critique of the man he endorsed.

NPR's Stephen Fowler contributed reporting.

World.title: Poilievre tells U.S. TV Canadians are 'wounded' and 'confused' to be in America's crosshairs
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is telling Americans their northern neighbours are feeling "wounded" and "confused" over how Canada and its economy became a key target for U.S. President Donald Trump.

"I think we feel a little bit wounded," Poilievre told reporters on the U.S. network CNBC on Thursday during a trip to New York where he is advocating for a return to normal trade relations.

"We're kind of confused as to how it is, suddenly, that Canada ended up in the crosshair."

The Conservative leader said Canada and the U.S. have a deeply interconnected economic relationship that has delivered peace and prosperity for decades and the only way forward should be tariff-free trade.

"Both countries are going to have their grievances," he said. "America had buy-America policies that prevented us from selling into subnational procurement markets and tariffs on our softwood lumber.… But the bottom line is: let's sit down and work them out for the mutual benefit of our people."

WATCH | Poilievre appears on CNBC:

In a statement Poilievre said he went to New York to fight against tariffs and for jobs on both sides of the border.

He said he will be meeting with investors and business leaders but his "main audience is the American people" to which he is making the case "that both our countries can be safer, richer and more affordable if we trade freely."

Poilievre also said he will stay in New York for the 25th anniversary of 9/11 on Friday, to honour the victims and highlight "how Canadians and Americans stood together after the terrorist attacks."

'Politics ends at the border': Poilievre

That national spirit was on display during Poilievre's CNBC interview, when he refused to be goaded into answering a question about whether he believed Prime Minister Mark Carney was acting in good faith during the recent round of trade negotiations.

"I'm not going to attack my prime minister on foreign soil. It's just not something I'm going to do," he said. "My mission here is to fight for my country, not to score political points domestically. Politics ends at the border."

Poilievre said Canada needs to leverage the "single biggest asset Canada has in the U.S., which is our friendship with the American people who overwhelmingly love Canada."

Co-host Joe Kernen said he respected Poilievre for refusing to criticize Carney while abroad, noting that politicians in opposition in the U.S. do not maintain that standard.

"You actually have a little bit of class," Kernen said.

When Kernen pressed Poilievre on Canada's economic performance over the last decade, the Conservative leader also avoided criticizing the country, saying Canada has had "a lot of good public policy successes by different levels of government."

Going forward Poilievre said rivals and risks to the U.S. are "slowly mounting" and rather than combat them on their own, the U.S. should rebuild the Western alliance that won the Cold War rather than fighting with friends.

"I think the United States would be better off if it united with those countries that believe in free speech, free markets, free trade and free people," he said.

"We could build an incredible North American fortress with the resources that we have on this continent, but it's going to take a collaborative relationship to do it."

World.title: Separatists dominating Alberta referendum conversation online: report
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

On the morning of Alberta Day this year, also known as the first of September, one of the most influential separatist social media accounts in the province sprung into action to mark the occasion.

The anonymous account known as Rise of Alberta, which has amassed almost 100,000 followers on X with a consistent flow of independence content, began the day with a dramatically backlit Alberta flag to celebrate the province’s future as a “free and independent country.”

Then came a clip of Premier Danielle Smith talking about the referendum, a shot of a celebratory Alberta Day drone show against a dark sky, and, finally, a link to a site where you could buy a “classic, handcrafted” Alberta flag blanket that comes in a variety of sizes and starts at $75. (They are made, the site notes, in the U.S.)

According to a new analysis from the Centre for Media, Technology and Democracy's Media Ecosystem Observatory, co-led by McGill University and the University of Toronto, the account is the most influential player in the raging online debate about Alberta independence that is dominated by a loose network of grassroots citizens, passionate advocates and anonymous social media accounts. Some of whom are also selling home decor.

“I think this is, in many ways, what modern political campaigns look like,” says Chris Ross, a senior analyst with the Observatory, pointing to the increasingly blurred lines between social media influencing, commerce and regular old politics.

“The general public needs to wrap our heads around this and think, ‘OK, this is becoming more normal, so how should we think about this?’” Ross added.

“And should we be giving it more scrutiny?”

Unlike in, say, Quebec, there is no elected party campaigning for sovereignty in Alberta, which has left the campaign for independence largely in the hands of a leaderless group of individuals with a wide range of beliefs and allegiances.

Passionate network

Online, the study suggests this has manifested as a passionate network of influencers, memes and online spaces devoted to the cause.

The analysis, released Thursday, paints a picture of an online conversation dominated by the separatists, in contrast to real world polling which suggests that support for independence has remained consistent at roughly a quarter of the population.

Among those with the biggest sway identified in the report, the pro-independence influencers outnumber their critics almost two to one, and receive roughly eight times as many likes, comments and shares.

In order to capture the online conversation, researchers collected all the posts on five social media platforms — Instagram, X, YouTube, TikTok and Bluesky — that included the word “Alberta,” plus related terms such as “referendum,” “sovereignty,” and “separatist.” (Facebook was not included because the site does not allow the search of specific terms in the same way.)

They then screened-out the accounts of politicians and media organizations, as well as those that fell below a certain threshold for engagement.

The result was 114 political influencers that were responsible for roughly half of the total social media engagement on this topic since the beginning of 2025. The report names the 40 most significant accounts, defined as those with more than 50,000 engagements on the posts collected as part of the study.

“The independence movement is, obviously, not a fan of Canada’s federal institutions, so I think modern technology allows for this guerrilla-style campaign strategy that really does end up in front of people’s eyes on their feeds,” Ross said.

The account driving the most engagement was Rise Of Alberta, whose posts on X have received over two million engagements over the last year and a half. (There was no response to the requests for comment that CBC News sent to the Rise Of Alberta accounts on X and Facebook.)

The top seven accounts are all similarly pro-independence, and include the personal accounts of notable figures in the movement, such as Keith Wilson, head of the Alberta Transition Council, and Jeffrey Rath, spokesperson for the Alberta Prosperity Society.

But the list also includes an account called Tablesalt, which has recently posted about everything from tariffs to home invasions to criticism of Jason Kenney, while misteristersunshinebaby, which describes itself as “born in Canada before it became the 51st state,” is ninth.

The most influential federalist account belongs to Thomas Lukaszuk, the founder of the Forever Canadian petition, which ranks eighth, with just over 181,000 interactions since the beginning of 2025. The account of former premier Jason Kenney, who has become a very public defender of confederation, ranks 32nd.

Chatter about Alberta separation of any kind is an outsize driver of online engagement, Ross noted. “There is just something about the spectacle of a province potentially leaving Canada that is naturally very interesting,” he said. “It’s like rubbernecking at a car accident.”

But the separatists have emotion on their side, he noted, as they appeal to the anger and fear that many of their followers feel about Alberta’s relationship with Ottawa.

Social media influencers have become a major source of political information more broadly in Canada, Ross points out, and some users have also come to prefer the more conversational tone of the separatist camp, compared to the missives from mainstream government or political institutions, who tend to lean federalist.

“There’s something deep in the human brain that likes seeing these off-the-cuff takes more,” he said.

Piggybacking on COVID

Another big part of the pro-separatists’ success is that they didn’t have to build their network from scratch, says Jean-Christophe Boucher, an associate professor of political science at the University of Calgary.

The independence influencers “piggyback on a network that was built, at least since COVID,” says Boucher, who was not involved in the writing of the report but has worked in monitoring online influence campaigns.

Some of the influencers on the list were also active during the trucker convoy in Ottawa and during the contested ostrich cull in British Columbia, he says, both of which were magnets for activists concerned about what they saw as government overreach.

“That capacity to already have an audience, to have people excited and engaged on these issues is a huge benefit for them,” Boucher said. “Whereas the federalist camp has to build everything from scratch.”

While the data isn’t clear on whether online posts have the ability to influence what people believe, Boucher argues that the dominance of separatist content online has the potential to affect mobilization and voter turnout.

“It gives the pro-separatist camp the perception, a false perception, that they’re mobilized,” Boucher said. “The odds that they will go vote will increase… because they think they’re winning.”

World.title: Canada, Ukraine forge 100-year pact built on drones and defence
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada and Ukraine were bound together more tightly on Thursday with the signing of a long-term strategic and political partnership that lays the foundation for the construction of millions of drones to defend both countries.

The countries signed a declaration to establish a 100-year partnership that stretches across defence and security, trade and investment, as well as energy and critical minerals.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said the war in Ukraine is at a turning point where some of its uncrewed systems are now reaching hundreds of kilometres inside of Russia.

He also acknowledged the heavy toll Russia's stepped-up missile and drone campaign is having on Ukraine, especially Kyiv which has been under relentless night and day bombardment.

WATCH | Carney says he's still speaking with Trump about issues including Ukraine: Canada ready to support Russia-Ukraine ceasefire where U.S. can play 'decisive role': Carney | Duration 2:17 Speaking alongside Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Thursday, Prime Minister Mark Carney said a cessation of hostilities between Russia and Ukraine offers a possible 'shorter-term solution' to global issues around access to energy and agricultural goods.

"Canada will always stand in solidarity with Ukraine," Carney said alongside Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Calgary.

"Canadians understand in our bones the importance of your struggle. There is no qualification to our commitment. Because your cause — freedom, democracy, sovereignty — is our cause."

Ripping a page out of Ukraine's wartime experience, Canada plans to create its own drone marketplace where individual military units can reach out to companies to quickly fulfil their needs.

"This is a key part of our plan to build the industrial capacity to produce millions of drones within the next two years," Carney said.

At the moment, the Canadian military has only 2,000 drones — of all types — in its inventory.

The governments also plan to partner Canadian and Ukrainian companies to build drones.

"As a result, Canadian industry will learn from the most battle-tested developers on earth," Carney said.

Canada and Ukraine are also forging a long-term partnership to jointly produce uncrewed systems, counter-drone technologies, munitions and artificial intelligence technology.

Zelenskyy called it a "very important package" and a decision that could affect the lives of Ukrainians.

"I'm very happy to be here among friends," the Ukrainian president said prior to the signing of the agreement. "Thank you for your support, supporting Ukraine, Ukrainians, our children, our sovereignty."

Carney also announced that Canada will contribute to the Ukraine Energy Security Fund to repair energy infrastructure, increase storage capacity and power hospitals. To help Ukrainians get through the winter, Canada will provide over $430 million in loan guarantees for gas purchases.

In addition, Canada is putting $350 million toward an air defence package. The U.S.-Israeli war with Iran has created a shortage of air defence missiles that has directly affected Ukraine.

World.title: Kimmel says interview with Democratic candidate won't air on his network show, cites FCC threats
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

ABC late-night talk show host Jimmy Kimmel said an interview with Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico on Thursday will air on YouTube and not during the network broadcast, citing threats from the ‌Federal Communications Commission.

In January, the Republican-led FCC said that daytime and late-night TV talk shows are no longer considered "bona fide" news programs that are exempt from equal time rules that require them to give airtime to opposing candidates.

Kimmel noted that for decades talk shows ​have been free to interview political candidates without being subject ​to those rules.

Talarico is running in Texas against Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton in a race that could decide control of the U.S. Senate in November.

Kimmel's interview with Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico will air on You Tube. (Joel Angel Juarez/Reuters)

Kimmel noted that he ​had previously interviewed U.S. President Donald Trump as a candidate in 2016.

"Now that ⁠he is president, his FCC ⁠threatened me, threatened our show, threatened our network ‌ABC, our affiliates, our local stations, based on simple traditional editorial decisions — guest bookings it would seem they don't like," Kimmel said on Wednesday's broadcast.

ABC declined to comment.

The FCC did not immediately respond to a request for comment. But Anna Gomez, the Commission's sole Democrat, said in a Thursday statement on social media that Kimmel's decision to keep the interview off-air "shows just how far this Administration's campaign of censorship and control has gone."

Gomez condemned the latest "intimidation" from her agency — and added that she hopes "courts will soon make clear that the FCC has no place dictating editorial choices or what viewers are allowed to see."

FCC Chair Brendan Carr ordered early reviews in April of Disney's eight company-owned ABC ⁠stations, even though the licence renewals were not scheduled to be considered before October 2028. The FCC had not ordered an early review in more than 50 years before April.

The reviews were ordered a day after ‌Trump urged ABC to fire Kimmel. Disney filed suit to block the early reviews in August, saying Trump is trying to punish the network over its content.

The FCC is also investigating ABC daytime talk show The View, which discusses U.S. politics, after saying it is subject to the equal ​time rules following an interview with Talarico in January. Disney said that since February the program has not invited any political candidates to ⁠appear, citing the FCC's "pressure campaign."

In February, former CBS late-night host Stephen Colbert said the network's lawyers barred ⁠him from airing an interview with Talarico on his show and instead aired it on YouTube, ⁠where ⁠it has been seen more than 9.5 ​million times.

Trump has repeatedly urged broadcasters to drop comedy or news programs he dislikes, or which have joked ​about or criticized him or his ⁠administration. He has also called on the FCC to strip stations of licences after criticizing news and other programming.

Broadcast stations need FCC licences to use public airwaves. While licence revocations are extremely rare, critics say the threat of losing a licence can pressure broadcasters and raise concerns about government interference in editorial and programming decisions. Networks have ⁠broad First Amendment protections over programming ‌choices.

World.title: Orange Shirt Day founder says her truth is being 'pushed aside' by controversial shirts
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The founder of Orange Shirt Day says she was sick to her stomach when she learned orange shirts with slogans like "Dig deeper" and "Still no proof" were being sold online.

Holding back tears and speaking from Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc in B.C., which announced a discovery of potential unmarked graves near a former residential school site in 2021, Phyllis Webstad said her campaign was being used in a "hateful way."

"I've been trying to understand why they believe that it's OK to hurt people," she said.

In 1976, Webstad wore a present from her grandmother, an orange shirt, on her first day at a residential school at St. Joseph's Mission, in Williams Lake, B.C. The shirt was taken from her by school officials and never returned.

Webstad founded Orange Shirt Day on Sept. 30, 13 years ago, to honour Indigenous children who were forced to attend residential schools.

In late August, Rebel News announced it was selling orange T-shirts on its website for the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation and that the shirts are about "challenging the identity politics that Canadians are increasingly pressured to accept and standing up for the whole truth in our complex Canadian history."

Statements printed on the shirts include "Still no proof," "You can't handle the truth," "Buried Truth" and "Dig Deeper," as well as "Canada was built not stolen."

Webstad called the sales a direct attack on her work with the Orange Shirt Society.

"It's my truth and what I know is the truth," Webstad said.

"It seems like this truth is not being respected. It's not being understood. It's being pushed aside."

Orange T-shirts with various slogans were posted to the Rebel News store at the end of August. (Rebel News Store)

In an emailed statement, Ezra Levant, founder and owner of Rebel News, pointed CBC News to a video on its website launching the sale of the shirts, saying their reporter "approaches these issues with compassion."

"The stated purpose of the National Truth and Reconciliation Day is noble – to honour residential school survivors and their communities by recognizing the lasting impacts of Canada's residential school system, so Canadians can better understand its legacy as part of our ongoing journey toward truth, healing, and reconciliation," Levant quoted what was said in the video.

In the video, the Rebel News reporter goes on to say "But five years later, Canadians are still being told that there are some truths they're not allowed to question."

Levant added in the statement that Rebel News staff are "dedicated to freedom of expression including the right to seek the truth" and "these orange shirts are a response for people who are forced to wear orange shirts at school or at work, as part of an 'official' political narrative."

"No Canadians should be compelled to support any political view, including Orange Shirt Day’s politics."

In the video promoting the shirts, the Rebel News reporter says "what's more than likely underneath the apple orchard soil at the Kamloops site is probably an old septic plot."

Webstad pointed to the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation, which has so far documented more than 4,000 deaths of Indigenous children in Canada's residential school system.

WATCH | B.C. regional chief speaks on residential school denialism: ‘Denialism is not an academic debate. It’s hate speech,' says regional chief | Duration 1:32 Regional Chief of the British Columbia Assembly of First Nations Terry Teegee said violence, anti-Indigenous rhetoric and hate speech are linked to residential school denialism and that, if left unaddressed, denialism ‘undermines truth and reconciliation.'

She said her own auntie, Agness Jack, shared a personal story about what it was like living in the Kamloops Indian Residential School in a book published in 2001, Behind Closed Doors: Stories from the Kamloops Indian Residential School.

Webstad also said her grandmother and her grandmother's 10 children including Webstad's mom were all forced to attend residential school.

"My mother was so traumatized that she could not take care of me; thank God my Granny was there, thank God my auntie was there," said Webstad.

"I want to say that we aren't liars. Indian Residential School survivors are not liars. Have some respect and give us the space and time to do what we need to do as individuals, as family, as a community, as a nation."

The orange shirts available on the Rebel News website are listed in youth sizes as well as adult.

"That is a whole new level of every word in the book: disgusting, unbelievable, sickening. Where are their minds?" said Webstad about the youth sizes.

MPs and ministers condemn shirts

Last week, the Liberal Indigenous Caucus published a statement that said merchandise "that mocks survivors' experiences and dismisses their truths is reprehensible and beneath any organization."

A request for comment from Conservative MP Billy Morin, the party's shadow minister of Indigenous Services, was not returned by time of publishing.

Morin told APTN News last week, “I find it racist and I find it absolutely disgusting that they’re attempting to make a profit off the pain and suffering of residential schools."

Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty, who is a member of the Waswanipi Cree Nation in northern Quebec, said people across the country have raised concerns about the shirts to her.

"Not just people living in my riding but also from Canadians who are appalled about this really disgraceful and grotesque attempt to exploit human suffering for financial gain," said Gull-Masty.

Gull-Masty's mother and grandmother were both forced to attend the La Tuque Indian Residential School in Quebec.

Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty, a member of Waswanipi Cree Nation in northern Quebec, says she heard concerns from people all over Canada about the shirts being sold online. (Marie-Laure Josselin/Radio-Canada)

Gull-Masty said she expressed her concerns to Justice Minister Sean Fraser, but didn't say what avenues the government would explore. She said she felt Fraser understood how serious the matter is.

"I think this is one of the areas where we are seeing behaviour that is not only being perpetuated more commonly but it is reaching a level that is unacceptable," said Gull-Masty.

In a statement to CBC Indigenous, a spokesperson for Fraser said, "Seeking to profit from Indian residential school denialism is deeply disgraceful and represents a cruel and grotesque attempt to exploit human suffering."

"Residential school denialism is a serious and distinct issue, and our government has said this issue warrants dedicated further parliamentary study," the statement said.

"Any legal response should be developed carefully in consultation and co-operation with Indigenous Peoples and the communities most affected."

Earlier this year, Canada's Senate voted down an amendment to Bill C-9 that would have criminalized residential school denialism, by making it illegal to wilfully promote "hatred against Indigenous Peoples by condoning, denying or downplaying the Indian Residential Schools System."

Webstad said she supports the idea that residential school denialism should be added as hate speech to Canada's Criminal Code.

"I believe what Rebel News is doing right now is what is needed to convince our Canadian government that yes, a law needs to be passed," said Webstad.

Shirts designed to provoke conflicts in schools, says academic

Sean Carleton, an associate professor in history and Indigenous studies at the University of Manitoba, said he feels the shirts monetize anti-Indigenous racism and deliberately profit off of pain and suffering.

"Thousands of Indigenous children died, we know that," said Carleton.

"So what [Rebel News] is trying to do is cast doubt, shake public confidence and are trying to convince Canadians that maybe we shouldn't care about Indigenous people and reconciliation anymore."

Carleton said the easiest way to understand denialism is to look at the Truth and Reconciliation Commission's simple formula.

Sean Carleton, an associate professor in history and Indigenous studies at the University of Manitoba, says the shirts monetize anti-Indigenous racism, and deliberately profit off of pain and suffering. (Submitted by Sean Carleton)

"We've got to have truth first," he said.

"Truth will lead to healing and justice. Healing and justice will lead to reconciliation. Denialists know that and what they're trying to do is keep us stuck in the truth part."

Carleton said he believes the inclusion of youth sizing is a tactic designed to provoke conflicts within schools where parents may be influenced by denialist rhetoric and use their children to challenge school policies.

He said the slogans on the shirts not only defend the colonial status quo but promote colonization as a compassion project, and said they question survivors' lived experiences.

NDP MP Leah Gazan tabled a private member's bill in Parliament last fall to criminalize residential school denialism.

In a letter to the Indigenous Liberal Caucus on Tuesday, Gazan said anti-Indigenous racism and denialism are growing and have now resulted in "the production of merchandise denying genocide and mocking the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation. We must respond to this as what it is – the incitement, monetization and promotion of hate."

Gazan called on the Indigenous Liberal Caucus to table her bill as a government bill.

A national 24-hour Indian Residential School Crisis Line is available at 1-866-925-4419 for emotional and crisis referral services for survivors and those affected.

World.title: Man, 27, charged in stabbing inside Edmonton Sikh temple
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Nearly three weeks since two men were stabbed inside a Sikh temple in Edmonton, police have laid criminal charges in the case.

In a news release Thursday, police said Austin Sim-Pelletier, 27, has been charged with two counts of assault causing bodily harm, two counts of possession of a weapon for a dangerous purpose, and mischief.

Sim-Pelletier was charged on Sept. 4 and his next court appearance is scheduled for Friday, police said.

“This investigation is complex and involves numerous investigative steps that we are still diligently working to complete,” Staff Sgt. Eric Stewart, with the EPS Investigations Branch, said in the statement.

In a news conference Thursday, Stewart said the accused remains in custody in a federal institution.

Stewart said the charges against him were not announced immediately as the investigation continued.

He noted that there was no concern for public safety as the accused remained in custody on a previous warrant for his failure to report to an Edmonton halfway house in the hours before the attack.

"We first wanted to work with the community, we want to work with our victims to ensure that we are providing them the support they need," he said.

"And also we wanted to make sure that we conducted a thorough investigation."

He said police have been in contact with both victims in the stabbing and have confirmed they are recovering from their injuries. He said the attack has been traumatic for members of the temple community and he thanked their staff for being exceptionally helpful during the course of the investigation.

Stewart said police continue to investigate a possible motive, but there is no evidence to support hate crime related charges at this time.

'Like any other investigation, we work by obtaining evidence," he said, "This investigation is still ongoing."

The attack

Police said the accused, who had been released from a federal prison outside the Edmonton region the day before, entered the Nanaksar Gurdwara on Aug. 21 during morning prayers.

Police said the man entered attempted to access the prayer area when he was confronted by staff.

The victims, aged 51 and 75, were taken to hospital with non-life threatening injuries after the attacker was wrestled to the ground by temple attendees and arrested by patrol officers.

The violent incident inside the sprawling temple on the northeastern outskirts of the city has prompted widespread condemnation from political leaders and Sikh community advocates and raised questions about the release of federal offenders who may pose a risk to public safety.

Sikh communities have documented a rise in recent discriminatory threats and attacks.

Police in Edmonton have laid charges in the stabbing of two worshippers at a Sikh temple in the city's northeast on Aug. 21. (Sam Brooks/CBC)

During a news conference last month, police said the suspect had a “significant” history of violent crime dating back more than a decade.

Court records shed light on his extensive history with the justice system.

Documents show his most recent conviction was for an assault on a peace officer in Calgary in September 2024, for which he was issued a six-month sentence. He was also found guilty in an aggravated assault on a woman in August 2024 and was sentenced to 28 months, court records show.

Statutory release 'not a choice'

In her statement condemning the attack last month, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said the stabbings should serve as a reminder of the need for federal bail and parole reform.

In a statement to CBC News on Aug. 24, the Correctional Service of Canada (CSC) stated that the suspect had been discharged from custody on statutory release — a policy which means federal officials have little leeway over his removal from custody.

“Statutory release is not a choice or discretionary decision by CSC — it is required by law after an offender serves two-thirds of a fixed-length federal sentence, with the offender being supervised in the community under conditional release,” the statement reads.

Statutory release requires the Correctional Service of Canada to release most federal prisoners into the community under supervision.

Unlike day and full parole, statutory release is not subject to decisions by the Parole Board of Canada but inmates released under the federal policy are required to report regularly to a parole officer and remain subject to conditions.

Most offenders qualify, with the exception of those serving a life sentence or an indeterminate sentence because of a dangerous offender designation issued by the court.

'Where the chain breaks down'

Michael Spratt, an Ottawa-based criminal defence lawyer with APG LLP, told CBC News last month that statutory release laws are "very, very effective" overall, but questioned systemic enforcement when breaches occur.

When an offender breaks release conditions — such as failing to report to a halfway house — infractions are reported quickly, Spratt noted.

He said public scrutiny should focus on how fast law enforcement responds to issue warrants and apprehend individuals in breach, he said.

“The public is rightly concerned when someone does offend on statutory release or on bail," Spratt said.

"We often focus on the tragedy of the offence, but we don't focus on the police response … quite often that's where the chain breaks down.”

World.title: Lindsay Clancy's lawyer asks judge to find her not guilty of murder following mistrial
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

WARNING: This article contains details about violence against children and attempted suicide.

Lindsay Clancy's lawyer on Thursday asked the judge who oversaw the Massachusetts woman's murder trial to declare her not guilty by reason of insanity, saying ‌prosecutors had failed to prove that, despite being mentally ill, she knew killing her three young children would be wrong.

Defence attorney Kevin Reddington made the request to Judge William Sullivan six days after the trial ended in a deadlock, and as a fourth member of the 12-member jury went public to describe how a ​single juror had prevented the panel from reaching a unanimous verdict.

The ​jury in Plymouth, Mass., deliberated for seven days before Sullivan declared a mistrial on Aug. 4, following repeated reports by the jury that it was deadlocked.

Prosecutors have yet to say if they plan to ​retry Clancy. But Reddington argued that Sullivan should decide the matter himself, saying prosecutors did not present evidence during the ⁠six-week trial ⁠that would allow a jury to find Clancy guilty ‌of the first-degree murder charges she faces.

WATCH | After Lindsay Clancy mistrial, what happens next? ‘Impossible case’: Breaking down the Lindsay Clancy mistrial | Duration 5:33 The National’s Erica Johnson asks attorney and professor Margo Lindauer to break down why a mistrial was declared in the Lindsay Clancy case and what could happen next.

Reddington argued that even the prosecution's expert witnesses agreed Clancy suffered from a serious mental illness at the time. He said the evidence at most showed that she retained the ability to perform familiar tasks, but not that she could appreciate the wrongfulness of her actions.

"No rational jury ⁠could find beyond a reasonable doubt that she had no mental disease or defence when the Commonwealth's own proof established that she did," Reddington wrote in the motion, referring to the prosecution.

He asked the judge to hear arguments on his motion during a hearing ‌scheduled for Sept. 29. A spokesperson for Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz did not respond to a request for comment.

Clancy, 36, has admitted to strangling her three children with exercise bands on Jan. 24, 2023, in the basement of their home in the Boston suburb of Duxbury. She then cut herself with a knife ​and jumped from a second-storey window, leaving her paralyzed.

WATCH | Trial put focus on maternal mental health: The Lindsay Clancy trial and maternal mental health | Duration 2:13 The trial of Massachusetts mother Lindsay Clancy has put a spotlight on maternal mental health, which some medical experts say may be the only positive outcome in the tragic case. Her legal team argues that she shouldn't be held criminally responsible for the murder of her three children because she was suffering from bipolar disorder and postpartum psychosis.

Holdout 'wouldn't engage' with other members: juror

Reddington at trial sought to convince jurors she should ⁠be found not guilty by reason of insanity, known in Massachusetts as lack of criminal responsibility, saying she suffered from postpartum psychosis ⁠when she killed Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and eight-month-old Callan.

In his motion, Reddington said 11 of the 12 ⁠jurors ⁠had been prepared to find her not guilty ​by reason of lack of criminal responsibility but could not return a verdict due to a single juror who, despite acknowledging having reasonable ​doubt, would not agree to find Clancy ⁠not guilty.

One of the jurors, Nick Dargie, said in an interview with ABC's Good Morning America that aired Thursday that the holdout juror, who has not been publicly identified, often "wouldn't engage" with other members of the jury.

"I think if they tried the trial again the way they did, I think nine times out of 10, I think a jury would come back with not ⁠guilty by reason of insanity," Dargie ‌said. "No doubt in my mind."

World.title: August was Earth's hottest month, European climate agency finds
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Earth cooked to its hottest month on record in August, blowing far past a key climate threshold due to the dangerous double whammy of human-caused climate change and a supersized El Niño, according to the European climate service Copernicus.

August's sizzle also helped push the globe and Canada to swelter through the hottest Northern Hemisphere summer scientists have measured.

Last month the world averaged 16.96 C, which technically was one-hundredth of a degree Celsius more than the all-time global mark set in July 2023. But because that's also the uncertainty level, it's considered a tie, said Samantha Burgess, strategic climate lead for Copernicus.

"It is now time to stop acting surprised that our warming planet keeps getting warmer. This is occurring exactly as forecast by scientists literally decades ago," Texas A&M University climate scientist Andrew Dessler said in an email.

"The interesting question is not whether we will keep breaking heat records (we will), but whether we're going to do anything about it or just stand there while the climate train runs us over."

This graphic shows that August 2026 was the hottest month ever recorded globally. (C3S/ECMWF)

Globally, August was 1.65 C above pre-industrial levels, far exceeding the longer term 1.5 C threshold set by the 2015 Paris climate agreement. The eight hottest months on record have all been from July 2023 on, according to Copernicus data.

"Our climate system is really operating well outside the range we would have expected just a decade ago," Burgess said Wednesday from a United Kingdom that has been beset with heat waves.

WATCH | Millions across Europe facing record temperatures from major heat wave: Millions across Europe facing record temperatures from major heat wave | Duration 2:21 Much of western Europe saw another scorching day on Saturday amid a deadly heat wave that has already broken temperature records in Britain, France and Spain. The heat is moving east across the continent, with one expert warning Switzerland's glaciers are set to lose a massive amount of ice due to the heat wave.

"We've transitioned from climate being very abstract and perhaps impacting the Global South or faraway places to climate impacting and disrupting our daily lives with schools closing, hospitals being overwhelmed, roads melting, train lines buckling. And the reality is we will get more of these conditions that we've seen this summer."

Global monthly ocean temperatures in August tied a March 2024 all-time record for the warmest month recorded, while Aug. 22 set a record for the hottest day recorded in the world's seas, according to Copernicus.

An extra-hot summer hits

"This summer has really been exceptional. We've seen records that existed for close to 100 years be broken, in the U.S. in particular," Burgess said.

The U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) on Wednesday announced that for the first time, summer in the lower 48 states was hotter than during the peak of the devastating Dust Bowl in 1936.

Until humanity stops burning colossal amounts of coal, oil and gas, the pollution this causes will keep baking our planet, and extreme heat will keep smashing all-time records, killing millions and costing trillions. - United Nations climate chief Simon Stiell

June through August of 2026 in the contiguous United States averaged 23.54 C, nearly four-tenths of a degree warmer than the mark set 90 years earlier. Globally, this past summer also tied with 2024 for the hottest on record, according to Copernicus.

That records are regularly getting broken, and that August and not July — which is traditionally warmer — set an all-time record, are signs that human-caused climate change is accelerating, Berkeley Earth climate scientist Zeke Hausfather said.

Fossil fuels, El Niño blamed

Several scientists said while El Niño is a factor, this natural and temporary warming of parts of the Pacific that warps and warms weather globally is nowhere as big a cause as the heat-trapping gases emitted as humans burn coal, oil and natural gas.

"While El Niño is starting to ramp up the heat, the underlying driver remains our relentless burning of fossil fuels. Climate change makes every El Niño hotter, and until we stop burning coal, oil, and gas, these record-shattering months will simply keep on coming," said Friederike Otto, a climate scientist at Imperial College London.

Burgess said El Niño generally adds only one- or two-tenths of a degree Celsius to the global temperature with the overwhelming rest of the heat coming from the burning of fossil fuels.

WATCH | 1,000 additional deaths amid record-breaking heat wave: France records 1,000 additional deaths amid record breaking heat wave | Duration 3:54 France reported around 1,000 additional deaths last week as a record smashing heat wave spreads across Europe. The numbers are expected to climb as more data is collected.

This El Niño is forecast, however, to break records for strength in the coming months. And as temperatures continue to rise, heat waves, storms, floods and wildfires will get more frequent and more dangerous, said Texas Tech climate scientist Katharine Hayhoe.

According to Hausfather, "it is increasingly likely that 2026 ends up beating 2024 as the warmest year on record, and almost certain that 2027 beats both, potentially reaching as high as 1.8 C above pre-industrial levels on the back of an unprecedentedly-strong El Niño event."

Some days may hit an even higher climate threshold: 2 C above mid-1800s, Burgess said.

"Until humanity stops burning colossal amounts of coal, oil and gas, the pollution this causes will keep baking our planet, and extreme heat will keep smashing all-time records, killing millions and costing trillions, hitting transport and health systems, and pushing up prices for household basics like food," United Nations climate chief Simon Stiell said.

"This is the spiralling price of humanity's fossil fuel addiction, and the global climate crisis it is fuelling."

World.title: Court orders Colombia’s government to remove images of slain “narcoterrorists”
World.content:
A Bogota judge ordered Colombia’s government to remove images and videos of President Abelardo de la Espriella walking through the remains of slain suspected guerrillas from its social media accounts.

The judge also ordered the government to remove images and videos of the body bags containing the lifeless remains of four members of organized crime group ACSN who were killed in La Guajira.

According to the judge, the images could be harmful to minors.

The decision was celebrated by congressman Santiago Osorio (Green Alliance), who sued the government over the controversial social media posts.

The State and the National Government cannot engage in a contest with crime to see which of the two is the most cruel; in this regard, the Office of the President of the Republic, Mr. Abelardo de la Espriella, were ordered to promptly remove images that may have reached the cell phones of children across the country, showing a state displaying corpses as trophies. Congressman Santiago Osorio

Th publications were previously rejected by the Ombudsman’s Office, whose director, Iris Marin, urged the government not to “compete with armed groups over who instills the most fear, who humiliates the adversary the most, or who turns death into a display of power.”

In the first video, De la Espriella and Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora walked through rows of body bags, displaying the remains of 23 alleged members of FARC dissident organizations EMC who were killed in the southern Guaviare province.

Among those killed in Operation Azarias were two minor victims of forced recruitment by the guerrillas.

The videos sought to promote the government’s hardline security policy, which vows to kill “narcoterrorists” who refuse to surrender.

World.title: US, Colombia sign memorandums of understanding amid “rebirth” of relations
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio hailed the “rebirth” of bilateral relations as they signed memorandums of understanding on nuclear energy and rare earths.

The two leaders met in Barranquilla, where De la Espriella lives, as part of Rubio’s tour through allied countries in the Andean region.

The president and the secretary of state hailed the improvement of ties that were severely disrupted when former President Gustavo Petro was in office.

During a joint press conference, Rubio stressed the need for security in the region, claiming that “the same networks, the same criminal groups that, although they commit their crimes here, they also commit crimes in the U.S., and they damage our people.”

De la Espriella said that as part of the “Barranquilla Agreements,” he asked the US for support for his hardline security policy.

We have proposed to the government—and today I reiterated this proposal to the secretary—the 21st-Century Patriot Plan to modernize aircraft, radars, drones, helicopters, anti-drone systems, air defense, mobility, intelligence, cyber defense, special forces, and maintenance and operations. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president promised to “start spraying, we are going to target the laboratories, the precursors, the trafficking routes, the drug trafficking kingpins, the armed narco-terrorist organizations—we are going after the money launderers, their criminal assets, and those international networks that pose a grave danger not only to the hemisphere but also to humanity.”

Rubio did not openly commit any US support other than the memorandums of understanding.

The unbinding agreements were part of Rubio’s wish list as the US seeks new sources for rare earths and miners that can be processed outside of China, which the US Government sees as its rival.

With the nuclear energy agenda, Colombia seeks to “strengthen its capacities” with US support. Both governments “reaffirm their commitment to international development and the peaceful use of nuclear energy.”

In order to create policy regarding the memorandums, De la Espriella would need congressional support, which he has yet to seek openly.

World.title: De la Espriella lifts Colombia’s 10-year gun ban
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella lifted a gun ban that had been in place since 2015.

According to De la Espriella, the decision seeks to give “good citizens” a way to defend themselves against “criminals.”

“For years, law-abiding citizens were restricted, while criminals continued to arm themselves to the teeth illegally. That has to change,” said the president on social media platform X.

99.9% of crimes committed with weapons are committed with unlicensed, illegal weapons. Anything said beyond the mathematics is just opinion. Mathematics is an exact science. So I am pleased to sign this decree. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president said that those who want to carry guns legally must comply with strict regulations and can’t have criminal records.

The ban reactivates previously approved gun licenses and allows citizens older than 25 to purchase approved hand guns from Colombia’s State military industry.

In order to be given a license, a potential gun owner must undergo fitness tests and convince the military authority that his position in society merits a firearm.

The decision has long been awaited by conservative and far-right elements in society, who have claimed that the gun ban made them sitting ducks for extortionists, particularly in the countryside.

Experts consulted by newspaper El Colombiano warned that lifting the gun ban could increase deadly violence, particularly considering Colombia’s violent history and evidence obtained in countries where guns are legal.

“There is no evidence showing that these countries have seen a decrease in theft, extortion, and threats following these measures,” said the director of the Central University’s Security Observatory, Andres Nieto. “On the contrary, the evidence does show an increase in violence among citizens,” the scholar added.

The ban was initially imposed by former President Juan Manuel Santos in 2015 and has since been upheld by his successors.

World.title: Liberal Party joins Colombia’s far-right to form majority coalition
World.content:
The Liberal Party announced that it had joined the congressional coalition of Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella.

The party, which also supported De la Espriella’s presidential bid, said that it would join the coalition after “extensive deliberation and arduous debate among representatives, senators, and leadership” of Colombia’s oldest political party.

It is worth noting that the discussions between representatives and senators over the past several weeks have revealed disagreements among some members of our caucuses with the current administration, but they also acknowledge President Espriella’s ability to work toward stimulating economic growth, building a talent pool to provide real opportunities for Colombians, and restoring security and respect for institutions. Liberal Party

The liberals’ decision gives the government broad support in Congress and marginalizes the opposition led by the leftist Historic Pact Party.

In the senate, De la Espriella’s right-wing coalition can count on the support of 63 of 103 lawmakers. In the House of Representatives, the coalition consists of 123 of 183 lawmakers.

The Historic Pact, which won the elections and became the biggest party in Congress, was abandoned by the left-liberal Green Alliance party and can count of the support of 28 senators and 44 representatives.

The opposition party has been able to make temporary anti-government alliances with, for example, the far-right Democratic Center party of former President Alvaro Uribe.

World.title: Colombia’s president appoints controversial new spy chief
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella appointed retired army General Jorge Andres Zuluaga as director of the National Intelligence Directorate (DNI) despite pending criminal investigations.

Zuluaga, who spent 30 years with military intelligence, is best known for his participation in Operation Jaque, which liberated former presidential candidate Ingrid Betancourt, three American military contractors and 11 soldiers.

Throughout his career, the 61-year-old former general was deputy commander of the now-defunct Charry Solano intelligence school, commander of the Regional Intelligence #5 and the director of the National Army’s Technical Intelligence Center (CITEC).

Zuluaga received training in the United States and was a diplomatic aide at the Organization of American States.

He was removed as CITEC director in 2014 after prosecution investigators found out that he received intelligence illegally obtained from “Andromeda,” a clandestine intelligence unit that operated from a Bogota internet café.

In October 2024, war crimes tribunal JEP ordered the Prosecutor General’s Office to investigate Zuluaga for his alleged participation in the extermination of the leftist Patriotic Union party when he was the CITEC’s director between 2004 and 2005.

The prosecution has yet to decide whether or not to formally charge the retired general with the crimes he allegedly committed.

Zuluaga, who became a member of the far-right Democratic Center party after he was ejected from the army, has always sustained that he acted within the boundaries of the law.

World.title: Colombia’s government clashes with ombudsman over De la Espriella walking among corpses
World.content:
Colombia’s chief ombudsman, Iris Marin, clashed with the national government after she criticized President Abelardo de la Espriella for walking among the corpses of people killed by the military.

In a public statement, Marin reiterated that “in recent days, we saw the president of the Republic walking among the bodies—in white body bags—of people who were killed during Operation “Azarías” in Guaviare.”

“I don’t recall ever seeing a president walking among the dead and taking pride in those deaths,” said the ombudsman, whose office is independent from the government.

The state and the government cannot allow themselves to be drawn into a competition to see who can be the cruelest. They cannot compete with armed groups over who instills the most fear, who humiliates the adversary the most, or who turns death into a display of power. Ombudsman Iris Marin

According to Marin, the military has the right to kill citizens, but must do so with respect for the Constitution and International Humanitarian Law, and is responsible for “the way that the State exercizes power and communicates its results.”

In a response, Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara said that the Ombudman falsely equated the State with “narcoterrorist groups as if it wer competing with them in cruelty.”

“Such an equivalence is inappropriate,” said Lara and called on the Ombudsman’s Office to be “an ally of the victims and of our mission to protect them and to liberate them from the terror regime of crime.”

Marin told Lara that she trusted that “the President and the Government will reflect on the way they communicate operational results, as I requested in my statement.”

De la Espriella’s stroll through the 23 body bags, including those of two minors, was also fiercely criticized in independent and foreign media.

World.title: Judge orders Colombia’s military to suspend air strikes on illegal armed groups
World.content:
A court ordered the government and the military to suspend air strikes on suspected members of illegal armed groups while studying the risk of harm to child forced recruitment victims.

In a preliminary sentence, the Bogota family court in response to a lawsuit that was filed by a civilian who claimed the State ignored its obligation to protect children when carrying out air strikes on illegal armed groups.

TO ORDER the PRESIDENCY OF THE REPUBLIC, the MINISTRY OF NATIONAL DEFENSE, the GENERAL COMMAND OF THE MILITARY FORCES, the NATIONAL ARMY, the COLOMBIAN AEROSPACE FORCE, and the NATIONAL NAVY, through the appropriate channels and within the scope of their respective authorities, that, pending a decision on the merits in this constitutional protection action, they refrain from conducting offensive air operations against targets regarding which there is certain, objective, or reasonably verifiable information regarding the presence of children or adolescents recruited or used by armed groups, until the necessary precautionary and protective measures have been adopted and verified, and it has been determined, based on the available information and applicable operational protocols, that there is no less harmful operational alternative that would allow the legitimate military objective being pursued to be achieved Bogota family court

According to Radio Caracol, at least 107 minors were killed in air strikes on illegal armed groups since they were resumed by former President Ivan Duque in 2018.

The sentence comes a day after President Abelardo de la Espriella announced the military killed 23 “narcoterrorists” in the deadliest air strike during the peace process that started in 2016.

The president vowed to resume bombing campaigns that were all but suspended by former President Gustavo Petro as he sought peace and demobilization talks with multiple illegal armed groups, a strategy rejected by the new far-right government.

Following the killing of at least three children in an air strike carried out in August, Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora blamed guerrilla organizations for the deaths, claiming they were recruiting children for human shields and combatants.

World.title: Evacuations ordered in Chile as wildfires run amok
World.content:
Chile’s National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred) Wednesday ordered the evacuation of 14 communes in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, including Nacimiento, Purén, and Contulmo, which have all been particularly affected by the forest fires.

In messages broadcast through the Emergency Alert System (SAE), the authorities also called on residents to leave their homes to avoid further damage to their health.

It has already been a week since the first wildfires ran amok in south-central Chile despite efforts to contain them. High temperatures, dryness, and strong winds add to the plight of local people and some 5,600 firefighters deployed in the area while helping flocks in from abroad.

”We are entering this part of the week which is the most complex.
