World.title: Privy Council introduces free visa process for parties attending London appeals
World.content:
Visa

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Commonwealth citizens travelling to London to attend Judicial Committee of the Privy Council (JCPC) proceedings can now access a free, streamlined visa application process.

The initiative, developed by the JCPC in collaboration with the United Kingdom (UK) Home Office and Ministry of Justice, is available to appellants, respondents and members of their legal teams who are attending appeals in person.

The process does not extend to wider family members, the JCPC said in a statement on Thursday.

Once a hearing date has been confirmed, counsel must use the JCPC portal to indicate who will attend the hearing in person and whether they require a visa.

The JCPC will then verify the applicant’s connection to the case before issuing an invitation letter and providing further guidance on the visa application process.

Visa applications will continue to undergo the UK’s usual database checks, and the Home Office may request additional information in some cases, the JCPC said.

JCPC Registrar Laura Angus said the new process reflects the committee’s commitment to open justice, transparency and continuous improvement.

“The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council is very pleased to be able to confirm the UK Government’s offer of this service to parties attending appeals in London. We listen to our users’ feedback and this decision underlines the JCPC’s commitment to open justice, transparency and continual improvement. We also routinely offer hybrid hearings for parties who prefer to take part in appeal hearings virtually,” Angus said.

World.title: CASINO CAUTION
World.content:
AS the Casino Gaming Commission (CGC) shores up its anti-money laundering defences ahead of the planned opening of Jamaica’s first casino at Princess Grande Jamaica Resort in Hanover early next year, the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) has issued a warning on key red flags to look out for.

FATF, the global illicit-finance watchdog, published a list of new gaming scams in a report on Wednesday, which it said was based on surveys conducted and included contributions from more than 80 jurisdictions.

The document titled ‘Red Flag Risk Indicators, Risks of Gaming and Gambling’, stated that the industries have changed significantly over recent years and continue to evolve through the expansion of online, cross-border, multi-product, and multi-payment platforms.

FATF said the work offers an updated analysis of money laundering risks posed by the casino sector as well as risks posed by the broader gambling and gaming sectors.

Red flag indicators in customer behaviour at brick-and-mortar casinos included attempts to influence or bribe venue staff to ignore their activities or bypass thorough customer due diligence checks and offering tips and other incentives.

Some casino customers were found to only want to deal with one staff member and avoid other staffers. These schemers use third parties to place cash into redemption terminals and purchase gaming chips, or place bets in an attempt to anonymise gambling.

The report outlined that the schemers also tend to request that winnings be paid in cash up to the threshold amount, but they never return to collect the balance. They also make purchases or attempts to purchase winning claim instruments from another customer and then present it as their own.

The report warned that eyebrows should raise if a player attempts to present a casino value instrument from an unknown source or if they are behaving in an unusual way on premises. It also warned of players acting on behalf of a third party and taking instructions from mobile phones or other customers on the premises.

Other red flags include customers who are reluctant or refuse to provide up-to-date identification documents or inconsistencies in personal information.

The report pointed out that some casino customers also opt to produce documents that are unclear or doctored and prove difficult to authenticate.

Where betting patterns are concerned, some customers were flagged for inconsistent spending that do not match their customer profile, including their known income and background.

In the report, FATF said it examined the scope of the risks associated with brick-and-mortar casinos, sports and novelty betting, other non-casino gambling — including scratch cards, arcades, bingo, lotteries, and slot machines outside of casinos.

“Findings indicate that certain payment methods associated with gaming and gambling activity such as cash, e-wallets, mobile money, and virtual assets are vulnerable to a range of money laundering risks. The variety of payment methods accepted by online gaming and gambling operators increasingly allows rapid, anonymous, cross-border transactions and conversion of value into different forms,” read page two of the 10-page document.

The operators and platforms covered in the report varied in nature and most of the risk indicators provided were related to land-based and online casinos and, to a lesser extent, betting. It was found that land-based operators have similar indicators as do online platforms.

In a statement on Wednesday, Giles Thomas, the president of FATF, said without robust safeguards, these sectors can attract gateways for fraudsters, professional money launderers, and organised criminal networks.

“I urge all governments to take note of the risk factors we have set out today, and put in place appropriate risk-based responses — from strengthening oversight and cracking down on illegal and offshore operators to boosting international co-operation and deepening public-private collaboration,” the FATF president said.

At a recent Jamaica Observer Monday Exchange officials of the CGC declared that they have been engaging in training with the Major Organised Crime and Anti-Corruption Agency (MOCA), the Financial Investigations Division (FID), and the Jamaica Customs Agency in an effort to ensure that strong anti-money laundering guardrails linked to casino gaming are in place when Jamaica gears up to claim its stake in an industry that generated more than US$320 billion worldwide last year.

The partnership with MOCA and FID is one based on capacity-building and information-sharing, support, and investigations.

Damion McKenzie, senior director of enforcement and investigations at the CGC, told Observer editors and reporters the entity recognises that, “Casino gaming is unique here, so some of the typologies and some of the crimes that happen in casinos, they might not be familiar with them. Our initiatives are to ensure that they are aware of those types of instances that can happen in a casino,” said McKenzie as he pointed out that the training of the law enforcement agents included them acquiring an understanding of the workings of slot machines and vulnerabilities.

The commission’s Chief Executive Officer Cleveland Allen emphasised that the entity is committed to properly regulating the casino gaming industry by ensuring that a multi-pronged approach is taken towards monitoring the sector in order to better protect the financial ecosystem.

“We operate in a space where we don’t have all the resources and all the knowledge, but remember, we operate in a large financial ecosystem. Our approach is focused on keeping us off the blacklist and on the right side of FATF,” Allen said.

He underscored that with Jamaica no longer being on the FATF list of countries that are assessed as having strategic deficiencies in their anti-money laundering/countering the financing of terrorism (AML/CFT) regimes, dubbed a grey list, the CGC is prepared to do all in its powers to help to ensure Jamaica does not find itself back on that list.

In June 2024, then Minister of Finance Dr Nigel Clarke said he was proud to share that FATF, at its plenary in Singapore, welcomed Jamaica’s significant progress in improving its AML/CFT regimes.

As a result, FATF said that Jamaica was no longer subject to an increased monitoring process. With the island acknowledging the importance of remaining off the grey list, the CGC said it plans to ensure there are tight guardrails to protect Jamaica’s good standing with FATF.

Jamaica was placed on the FATF grey list in 2020, which signalled to international financial institutions to take special care when transacting with entities and individuals from the island.

One of the drawbacks of this is that it is more expensive to carry out transactions with countries on the list.

Other red flag indicators to look out for at casinos and other gaming establishments:

*Sudden changes in customer’s betting patterns.

*Co-ordinated or unusual betting activity, including hedged bets, betting on all outcomes and consistent losses to other players in peer-to-peer settings.

*Structuring of deposits into smaller amounts to fall under reporting thresholds.

*Use of short-odds bets and other low-risk mechanisms to justify withdrawals.

*Players making numerous large withdrawals without engaging in significant gambling activity.

*Customers appear to play frequently together, with one always winning and the other always losing.

*Suspected collusion in gambling activities, including gambling on both likely outcomes.

*Customer tries to circumvent note insertion limits by playing multiple machines simultaneously.

*Customer frequently plays games with low returns but with lower risks and a higher chance of winning.

*Customer repeatedly collects winnings just below a customer identification threshold.

*Non-genuine play patterns – wagers are low while large sums are deposited and withdrawn.

World.title: Gov’t looking to add speed to school repairs
World.content:
This file photos shows some of the damage Hurricane Melissa did to Edwin Allen High School last year.

THE Government could look overseas for contractors to speed up the repair and rebuilding of schools devastated by Hurricane Melissa last October.

More than 600 educational institutions sustained damage from the Category 5 storm with 309 severely damaged and ranked priority one for repairs and reconstruction.

At a post-Cabinet media briefing at Jamaica House in St Andrew on Wednesday officials of the Ministry of Education said 57 of those severely damaged institutions were fully repaired when the new school year began on Monday. The ministry said another 95 schools will be fully repaired by the end of September, and another 34 repaired by the end of December.

Education Minister Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon told the media briefing that school repairs were hampered by a shortage of grade one contractors and the ministry will, among other things, explore hiring external contractors to fill gaps while ramping up efforts to upskill local contractors.

Morris Dixon admitted that the current situation is far from perfect and argued that the need for contractors was even more imperative given the mandate placed on the National Reconstruction and Resilience Authority (NaRRA) — the specialised body established to coordinate and accelerate post-disaster rebuilding and long-term infrastructure resilience after Hurricane Melissa.

She pointed out that while the Administration is committed to continue the work to rebuild schools it has been constrained by the number of grade one contractors available in Jamaica.

“When the budget for the project is above a particular amount, you have to use a grade one contractor, and we’re limited with the number of grade one contractors, so that’s a constraint,” Morris Dixon explained.

“We need those contractors for the schools, we need them for the homes, we need them for the businesses, we need them for that beautiful vision that Prime Minister [Dr Andrew Holness] laid out in his budget presentation. And so, one of the things that we are working on, separately, in a different part of the ministry on the skills side, is an initiative between HEART NSTA/Trust and the Development Bank of Jamaica (DBJ)…we have to work to get those who are at grade two up to grade one through financing and otherwise, because that’s a key element of it. And so DBJ is at the table with us, trying to work through that, because our goal is to give the money to the Jamaicans,” Morris Dixon disclosed.

“What we’re looking at is, how we can work with young people who want to be contractors, put them in groupings, provide funding, and provide incubation to them so that we can get more in the pipeline of grade one contractors. Using external sources is something that we’ll have to look at. For example, for the STEM (science, technology, engineering, and mathematics) schools, we have done international tenders, and so in some of the big projects, we’ll have to do some international tendering. We’ll see what comes out of that…but right now, our commitment is to our local contractors using them. But of course, they have to show that they can deliver,” Morris Dixon said further.

The education minister, in the meantime, said work was continuing apace to rehabilitate schools listed as priority one which were severely damaged by Melissa with almost continuous afternoon rain in Westmoreland slowing down the process.

“It’s not perfect. Where we are now is not perfect, and we have a lot of people working. We have many contractors. For our very severely damaged schools, which is about 309 schools that were severely damaged… the bills are high. A lot of them are over $100 million, $200 million, $300 million, a billion dollars almost in some instances,” Morris Dixon said.

According to Morris Dixon, the hurricane is being used as an opportunity “to get better school plants, at least in the west”.

Meanwhile, permanent secretary in the Ministry of Education Dr Kasan Troupe said the new school year got off to a fair start on Monday with 92 per cent of schools having all students while two per cent of schools will have to be augmented with temporary learning spaces and utilise some amount of rotation.

“That’s tremendous given what we have been through, and I want to thank all my principals, all my chairmen and board members, and of course, all the teachers,” Troupe said.

She told the media briefing that the ministry has ensured that all schools have been given their operational funds along with furniture and other resources.

“We sent out 30 per cent of the increased grants into our schools in June. The second tranche of that is due in September, the first Friday in September and two weeks ago, we ensured that all the funds were out in all our schools, so we are ahead of time because we understand what it means for our principals to have monies to get the work done. That amounted to $3.05 billion that we have disbursed to our schools, and that will treat with the operations, that will treat with the nutritional support for the learners, and of course, an additional $75 million we sent out to our schools to impact 275 schools to treat with canteen repairs,” Troupe said.

“As it relates to furniture, 41 schools indicated that they need additional support. We are responding to that, but in preparation for this year, we spent $300 million to get furniture out into our schools. So before we started, we distributed over 17,000 pieces, and whilst we were wrapping up on the last weekend, there were 8,000 pieces that we were distributing across our schools,” added Troupe.

According to the permanent secretary, another 20,000 pieces of furniture are being prepared for distribution to the system.

She said the ministry is spending more than $700 million in resourcing high schools with books and more than $300 million in primary schools, making that approximately $1.1 billion of expenditure in providing books for public schools.

World.title: 450 set for Caribbean Music Awards performance
World.content:
450...preparation has been good. We’ve been putting in the work and making sure everything is right.

Dancehall artiste 450 is gearing up to make his debut performance at the highly anticipated Caribbean Music Awards (CMA).

The fourth annual ceremony and showcase will take place on Saturday, September 19 at the National Academy for the Performing Arts (NAPA) in Port of Spain, Trinidad and Tobago.

For 450, the opportunity to perform on the regional stage represents another significant moment in his career.

“It feels like a big moment for me. The CMA is a major platform for Caribbean music, so it feels like another chapter of the story that my team and I are grateful for,” 450, who is also nominated for Album of the Year, told the Jamaica Observer.

V’ghn, Freetown Collective, Jah Mason, 1T1, and Theomaa are among the artistes slated to perform. The line-up represents a cross section of Caribbean music, spanning soca, reggae, dancehall, bouyon, and contemporary Caribbean sounds.

After three years of staging the awards in New York City, organisers are bringing CMA to the Caribbean for the first time since its inception. The move will also see the celebration expand beyond a single awards night into an immersive weekend of activities.

The weekend is expected to feature networking opportunities, industry discussions, cultural showcases, and opportunities for fans to interact more closely with artistes and other players in the Caribbean music industry.

450 said preparations are well under way for his performance, with his team focused on ensuring his CMA debut makes an impact.

“Preparation has been good. We’ve been putting in the work and making sure everything is right,” he shared.

While not revealing too much about what he has planned, the entertainer promised a high-energy performance featuring some of the songs that have connected with his fan base.

“Energy, good vibes, and some of the songs they know and love. I’m representing Jamaica and dancehall music,” 450 said.

The appearance comes during what the artiste describes as a strong year of career growth, particularly as he continues to introduce his music to audiences outside Jamaica.

“It’s been a really good year. I’ve been able to reach new audiences, perform on bigger international stages, and continue growing the music. There’s still more to accomplish, so mi nah slow down,” he said.

With the final quarter of 2026 under way, 450 has no plans to ease the pace. Beyond his upcoming CMA performance, the dancehall artiste is working on new material and further expanding his international presence.

“I’m working on new music, more visuals, and some exciting international projects. More to come soon,” he added.

World.title: Contractor says all his 7 school jobs almost complete
World.content:
Inside a newly completed grade six classroom with a new roof, ceiling, lighting and ceiling fans at Petersfield Primary School in Westmoreland..

PETERSFIELD, Westmoreland — While several schools in western Jamaica still have a long way to go to repair damage inflicted by last October’s Hurricane Melissa, Petersfield Primary in Westmoreland is now 98 per cent complete. There are only a few doors and windows left to be installed.

The Petersfield project is one of seven being undertaken by Archistruct Limited. Others include William Knibb High in Trelawny and five schools in St Ann. According to owner and managing director of the 14-year-old company Chadwick Lawrence, all the schools are almost 100 per cent repaired.

“The minister [of education] did say she’s holding us accountable, so I take that one seriously. I couldn’t afford to disappoint her,” he told the Jamaica Observer Wednesday.

With a degree in engineering and a master’s in construction project management, Lawrence is supported by a team of qualified construction professionals.

“It is no secret sauce; it’s just a matter of management and execution of tasks based on schedule and procuring materials on time. That is what I do. We use a lot of people from the area, as well as people from different areas, as needed. At Petersfield, we did a lot of night and day work to get it finished,” Lawrence explained when asked the secret to his success in having the schools ready for September.

“It boils down to one expression: Construction is about the joy of creating. It is nice to just see the students inside the classroom; it’s a genuinely nice feeling to see the students in the classroom learning and the teachers teaching in a comfortable space. When you talk with the teachers and the principals and they tell you that they are happy with the product they have received because it’s better than it was before… that really brings the joy of creating,” he said.

The company has been strategic in its approach.

“In terms of the scheduling and procurement of materials, we had ensured that we did that beforehand as we went along. We were doing seven schools, so we were able to buy in bulk and to get everything on spot before we needed it. Now we are at 98 per cent complete and we are happy to say that it is a good September morning. All the kids are out and about, parents and teachers are happy, and we’re just glad to see a satisfied customer,” Lawrence told the Observer.

School board chairman and Custos of Westmoreland Reverend Hartley Perrin, who had initial concerns, is among those pleased with the results at Petersfield Primary.

“I had my doubts. I was very concerned about the progress, or lack thereof… But then, all of a sudden, it started to pick up as if they stepped on the accelerator. They were working longer hours and they seemed to have employed more people. I’m pleased to see the work that has been done and the quality of it. Even the painting is of good standard,” the Custos beamed.

But it has not all been smooth sailing. The type of windows needed for the school projects is not available in Jamaica. The original structures had aluminum window blades.

“We’re doing some… we discussed with the principals and they have agreed to other options for the type of windows,” said Lawrence.

At all seven schools, his team is now adding little touches that make a world of difference.

“We work closely with the principals and teachers. Even now, we are at different locations doing what we call commissioning. There are little things that might be needed — a teacher may need a nail there or a piece of board there for a pin-up board [to place teaching aids] — and we’re there now putting those things in place to make the space as comfortable as possible,” said Lawrence.

At Petersfield, his company has a separate contract to build a new administrative and classroom block. Lawrence confirmed that all materials are on-site and the bending of steel began Wednesday morning.

World.title: THE ULTIMATE TEST
World.content:
World 100m champion Oblique Seville headlines Jamaica’s team for the inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championships in Budapest, Hungary. (Photo: AFP)

Technical Leader Maurice Wilson says Jamaica’s athletes will be ready for the inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championships which starts tomorrow at the National Athletics Center in Budapest, Hungary.

A 32-member team, with 27 athletes set to contest individual events for Jamaica, was named by World Athletics on Monday, based on world rankings for the first of what is set to be an annual end-of-season all-star competition.

Wilson described the event as “a fantastic initiative”, which he said has the potential to take the sport to another level.

“There are changes to the arrangements,” he told the Jamaica Observer, where athletes’ representatives will have “a more hands-on” duty, as national federations such as the Jamaica Athletics Administrative Association (JAAA) will only be responsible for naming relay coaches.

Wilson and Michael Frater have been named by the JAAA to take charge of the mixed 4x100m and 4x400m teams, with the athletes being able to have their personal coaches with them.

“Every major professional sport has annual championships,” Wilson said. “So track and field should not be an exception, and this is something we need.”

Winners of the individual events will receive a bye to the 2027 World Championships as well as US$150,000 (over $23 million) while winning relay teams will share US$80,000 (just over $12 million). Just about every participant will take home a cash prize.

There will also be a US$100,000 ($15.5 million) bonus for breaking a world record, while the champions will get a trophy rather than the traditional gold, silver, and bronze medals.

Newly crowned Diamond League 100m champions Oblique Seville and Tina Clayton have been included in Jamaica’s 32-member team that will compete at the three-day event.

In addition to Seville on the men’s side, Commonwealth Games champions Navasky Anderson, Romaine Beckford, and Demario Prince were also named.

Commonwealth Games champion Sanique Walker and women’s 4x100m relay gold medallists Jodean Williams and Lavanya Williams were also named.

Team Jamaica

Men



Navasky Anderson, Romaine Beckford, Orlando Bennett, Ackeem Blake, Bryan Levell, Tyler Mason, Demario Prince, Oblique Seville, Christopher Taylor

Women

Rushell Clayton, Tina Clayton, Lamara Distin, Brianna Lyston, Ashanti Moore, Ackera Nugent, Nickisha Pryce, Demisha Roswell, Shiann Salmon, Megan Simmonds, Ackelia Smith, Jonielle Smith, Sanique Walker, Danielle Williams, Jodean Williams, Lavanya Williams

Relays

Zandrion Barnes, Kadrion Goldson, Rohan Watson, Assinie Wilson, Shana Kaye Anderson

World.title: Grace Back-To-School Bites: Grace Vienna Sausage Mac & Cheese + Grace Corned Beef Pinwheel Sandwiches
World.content:
This simple recipe brings together the familiar taste of Grace Mac & Cheese with hearty Grace Vienna Sausages for a satisfying meal the whole family can enjoy.

Grace Vienna Sausage Mac & Cheese

Creamy, cheesy and easy to prepare, Grace Vienna Sausage Mac & Cheese is a comforting option for busy back-to-school days. This simple recipe brings together the familiar taste of Grace Mac & Cheese with hearty Grace Vienna Sausages for a satisfying meal the family can enjoy.

World.title: ‘My heart broke’: Education minister orders probe after student denied restroom
World.content:
Minister of Education, Skills, Youth and Information, Senator Dr. the Hon. Dana Morris Dixon, addresses the post-Cabinet press briefing held on September 9 at Jamaica House. (Photo: JIS)

KINGSTON, Jamaica — The Ministry of Education, Skills, Youth and Information is to receive an official report from the school where a student was denied the opportunity to use the restroom and soiled herself.

Portfolio Minister, Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon, made the disclosure during the post-Cabinet press briefing on Wednesday at Jamaica House.

“When I saw that story, of course, as many Jamaicans did, my heart broke,” Morris Dixon said. “My heart was breaking for that student when I heard the story, and so I understand the outrage. I understand how Jamaicans feel and how they feel it as if it were their child, because I felt similarly that that was my child.”

“As minister, I have to have all the facts, and it’s for that reason that I’ve asked for an investigation of what took place, so that I can get an official report on it with all the facts on the table. And then we will take action after that,” she added.

The minister said she spoke with the child’s father on Wednesday, noting that the ministry will provide the necessary support needed.

“I had a good conversation [and] noted that all of Jamaica feels concerned and that we’re worried about his daughter. We conveyed our love for her and that at the ministry we’ll provide whatever support she may need. There was indication that there may be need for some emotional support and some counselling support,” Morris Dixon said.

“In the ministry we’ll do that. We have psychologists on retainer, so any child in our system that needs support, we in the ministry, we pay for the psychologist or if they need a psychiatrist, we also pay for it. So, we’ll provide whatever support that child needs, and the children of Jamaica are at the centre of our decision-making,” she added.

The minister also revealed that she spoke with the principal of the school on Wednesday, adding that it was important to listen to all sides.

“I had a good conversation with the principal, and she assured me that the children are at the centre of all of her policies. And that everything she does is with them in mind. She also went through what happened on the day. She’s indicated we will get the official report from the school, and as I said, we’ll meet with the Board, we’ll meet with the parent, with the school, and in the ministry we’ll get to the bottom of it, and we will take action that is needed,” she added.

Morris Dixon pointed out that many schools have a difficult balancing act, noting that “out of safety for the children and out of other incidents that may have happened, you have to make a call as a teacher”.

“So, I understand the difficulty in that call. But when there are emergencies, we have to act differently. So even when we have the set bathroom breaks, if a child is ill between those bathroom breaks, we have to give them the time to go to the bathroom. And the good thing is when I spoke to the principal, the official rules at the school match with the ministry’s expectations and so what we have to do as a ministry, is to check if the rules were broken,” she said.

— JIS

World.title: Kazakhstan can’t sing its way into Eurovision in 2027
World.content:
Those requirements are set out in the EBU’s statutes, which were relaxed in June to allow broadcasters from some countries outside Europe to become full members.

“Khabar Agency is a valued Associate Member of the EBU, and we appreciate its long-standing engagement with the Union,” the statement added.

The broadcaster, controlled by Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Culture and Information, took the country to Junior Eurovision five times between 2018 and 2022, finishing as runner-up twice. Associate membership, however, does not provide an automatic route into the senior contest.

A small portion of Kazakhstan (albeit an area larger than Greece) lies within geographical Europe, bolstering its claim that it should be able to compete. The EU is the country’s largest trading partner.

That said, geography is hardly a deal-breaker. Australia has competed through special invitations since 2015, finishing fourth in May earlier this year. Canada went further this summer: CBC/Radio-Canada became a full EBU member after the rule change and will make its Eurovision debut in 2027. Canada qualifies because it holds observer status with the Council of Europe and meets the EBU’s public-service-media criteria. Russia frequently competed in the past, until it was kicked out of the competition following its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, despite most of its vast territory being in Asia.

The rejection lands as Eurovision wrestles with another set of geopolitical rules. Five broadcasters boycotted the 2026 contest over the participation of another non-European country, Israel, over its conduct in the Gaza Strip. Dutch broadcaster AVROTROS has already said it will sit out again in 2027.

World.title: Bernie Sanders, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez invited to Paris for Gabriel Zucman’s tax-the-rich summit
World.content:
Zucman’s Paris event — currently billed as the “Summit Against the International Oligarchy” — is nominally focused on three themes: media and online platforms, artificial intelligence and taxing billionaires.

But it won’t have an impact on the California contest, as voters there head to the polls on Nov. 3.

Instead, it appears to be an opportunity to thrust wealth inequality and tax justice back into the public debate ahead of the next French presidential election, whose first round takes place in April of next year. The event, whose co-organizers include Nobel laureate Joseph Stiglitz and best-selling author Thomas Piketty, will kick off just a few days after the launch of Zucman’s similarly titled book, “Against the International Oligarchy.”

Ocasio-Cortez, Sanders, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani — whom Zucman met in April — and top Mamdani aide Morris Katz were all invited, according to Pierre Natnaël Bussière, Zucman’s strategy and communications adviser.

Representatives for Sanders and Ocasio-Cortez did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Paris Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire — who modeled parts of his campaign earlier this year on Mamdani’s — is slated to speak at a gala following the summit.

While Grégoire has been trying to keep his focus local and beef up his image as a Paris-first leader, the unequal distribution of wealth and the growing proportion of wealth derived from inheritance are issues that affect housing prices and purchasing power in Paris — two key priorities for Grégoire.

Anthony Lattier contributed to this report.

World.title: Macron’s space summit showed Europe isn’t ready for takeoff without the US
World.content:
Things had already started to look bad a few days before the summit when American space companies such as SpaceX decided to ditch the event after White House pressure, accusing France of “anti-competitive practices” and disregarding the perspectives of U.S. industry. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz also skipped the event, despite it being co-chaired by France and Germany.

French officials downplayed the importance of the U.S. absence, stressing that the summit would provide Europe with an opportunity to step up its game on space.

But several participants said that the summit's goals were unclear and that it lacked political commitments from countries other than France to boost public investment in the space sector.

Good idea, bad execution

“I had mixed feelings,” said Ezequiel Sánchez, the executive president of PLD Space, one of the companies selected by the European Space Agency to develop European launchers.

“We were all expecting the rabbit out of the hat,” said Sánchez, noting that the summit was “a good idea,” but with a “bad implementation.”

The lack of public funding comparable to the levels delivered by the U.S. loomed large at the summit.

World.title: EU prosecutors should go after sanctions busters, top diplomat suggests
World.content:
Kaja Kallas is pictured at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France on June 16, 2026. | Christophe Verhaegen/AFP via Getty Images

Kaja Kallas wants the European Public Prosecutor’s Office to be given a mandate to squeeze Russia’s war machine.

BRUSSELS — The EU’s top diplomat has proposed giving the bloc’s own organized crime prosecutors responsibility for bringing cases against companies and individuals that help Russia get around sanctions and fuel its war in Ukraine.

Kaja Kallas, the EU’s high representative for foreign affairs and security policy, suggested handing oversight of sanctions circumventions cases to the European Prosecutor’s Public Office (EPPO). The Luxembourg-based agency would investigate those shipping sensitive trade goods that could be used by Moscow’s war machine or laundering money for the Kremlin.

Kallas floated the idea at a meeting with ambassadors from EU member countries on Wednesday, two diplomats with knowledge of the discussion said — although she stopped short of making concrete proposals at this stage.

World.title: Farage donor scandal turns spotlight on UK polling industry
World.content:
Since the sting video first aired last week, former employees and clients of JL Partners have told POLITICO that the company carried out other polls where the funder was not declared — while similar lapses have occurred at other well-known British polling companies.

Rules set out by the British Polling Council, the industry watchdog, specify that all research carried out by pollsters which enters the public domain “must include reference to the… client commissioning the survey” as well as dates, methodology and sample size.

JL Partners did not respond to requests for comment on these fresh claims. The company told Channel 4 News in response to the report about their work for Reform UK last week: “Despite there being no concern about the accuracy of our work, the report did reveal weaknesses in our procedures.”

The British Polling Council said in a statement about the Channel 4 News report that it was “clear there have been breaches” of the watchdog’s rules, adding: “We are seeking further information from the BPC member concerned.”

Reform UK denies any wrongdoing in relation to the sting, which is now under investigation by the Met Police.

Tory leadership races

Johnson’s firm conducted polls on three occasions during the Tory leadership elections in 2022 and 2024 which received press coverage without disclosing who paid for them either in the media reports or in the company’s published tables.

World.title: Lagarde rejects far-left Mélenchon’s debt-cancellation plan
World.content:
She pointed to Article 123 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, which prohibits the ECB and national central banks from financing governments. The provision was agreed to and ratified by all EU member countries, Lagarde stressed.

Lagarde also dismissed the proposal on economic grounds, citing “very, very solid economists,” including former International Monetary Fund chief economist Olivier Blanchard, who can “demonstrate easily” that such a move would be “financially dangerous.”

Mélenchon renewed his call in August for the ECB to freeze pandemic-era government debt, arguing that the move would create additional fiscal space for France. Public debt amounts to more than €3.5 trillion, or 117.5 percent of French GDP, and the issue has become a top concern for voters.

Ahead of today's rate decision, Mélenchon also criticized the ECB’s widely expected hike, warning on X that “the ECB is leading us straight into the wall.”

Lagarde also used the press conference to dismiss renewed speculation about an imminent announcement that she would leave the ECB early. Rumors have swirled for months, after she left open the possibility of playing a role in the French presidential campaign.

World.title: Lagarde brushes off exit gossip as ECB raises rates
World.content:
Lagarde has since floated an early ECB exit to play a role in the French presidential campaign. She continues to refuse to rule out leaving before the end of her term, although has said she will stay at least until the end of the year.

At today's meeting, the ECB raised its key deposit rate for the second time this year, as energy prices driven by the Middle East war threaten to keep inflation above target through 2028.

The hike was widely expected after inflation topped the 2% price-stability target for six straight months, reaching 3.3% in August as energy inflation surged to 14.3%. Oil topping $100 a barrel after fresh escalation in the Middle East suggests little relief is in sight.

ECB staff lifted the inflation forecast for 2027 to 2.5%, from 2.3%, and for 2028 to 2.1% from 2% — enough to put it just above the ECB’s 2% target. “The outlook remains highly uncertain, with risks to the upside for inflation,” the ECB said in a statement.

Lagarde kept the door open to further rate hikes but offered no guidance on the path ahead, as policymakers weigh persistent inflation against the economic fallout from the war and rising government borrowing costs.

The eurozone economy has so far held up surprisingly well. The ECB raised its growth forecasts for 2026 and 2027 to 0.9% and 1.4%, respectively, “mainly reflecting the greater than expected resilience of the euro area economy.”

World.title: German foreign minister urges voters to back Ukraine, NATO as far right surges
World.content:
The call comes after the AfD won 43.8% in the regional election in Saxony-Anhalt, more than doubling its 2021 result and leaving Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democrats a distant second at 17.2 %.

Wadephul argued Thursday that the way forward was not to retreat from Germany’s commitments, but to do a better job of explaining why they matter.

He cast the challenge in stark historical terms, invoking the collapse of Germany’s democracy between the two World Wars. “Germany knows from the Weimar Republic what could happen if Democrats are not ready to defend their system,” he said. “We have to show that we have learned our lesson.”

The Weimar Republic, Germany’s first parliamentary democracy, was progressively hollowed out amid economic crisis, political paralysis and growing support for anti-democratic forces before Adolf Hitler was appointed chancellor in 1933.

As for the results of Sunday's vote, they were not only the AfD’s strongest-ever showing, but the highest vote share won by any party in the state since German reunification.

During the campaign, AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund repeatedly presented spending abroad as money missing at home. He told regional broadcaster MDR that Germany was “giving away money all over the world” and pointed specifically to support for Kyiv: “Every minute, €20,000 goes to Ukraine. That is all money we are missing.”

World.title: NATO allies successfully thwart Russian undersea cable sabotage operation
World.content:
NATO allies have caught Russian submarines training to carry out undersea cable sabotage using a secret weapon that leaves no trace, Reuters has reported citing two Western officials.

 

This clandestine Russian operation was carried out by the highly secret GUGI, the Russian undersea warfare directorate, in Arctic waters near Norway's Svalbard territories.

Britain said it had tracked and deterred three Russian submarines on an alleged month-long "covert operation" near vital undersea cables and pipelines connecting the Norwegian archipelago.

Following Euronews reporting on the operation that was announced in April, the discovery of the weapon, the location of the operation, and the US involvement have now been disclosed.

This joint operation between the UK, Norway, and the US successfully tracked and diverted Russian vessels before they could complete their exercise.

Secret weapon training

While Russia didn't damage any cables, it carried out this exercise to simulate the deployment of the secret weapon, in the event of a conflict with NATO, officials told Reuters.

They refused to give any details over the weapon or technology used by Russia.

While the confrontations were taking place at sea, UK and Norway officials faced Moscow with their findings in an attempt to deter Russia of using the secret technology.

Targeting essential infrastructure

Undersea fiber-optic cables that are as thick as a garden hose are the main conduit by which almost all of the world's internet traffic is channeled.

They are critical to global internet connectivity and financial transactions, which have increasingly made them targets for disruption of countries' communications.

In this image from a video provided by Russian Defense Ministry Press Service on Thursday, 21 May 2026, a Russian nuclear submarine is escorted by boats during drills. Russian Defense Ministry Press Service

Russia's Defence Ministry did not comment on the topic as the Kremlin has consistently denied conducting sabotage in NATO countries.

"Through our joint operation, we ​sent a clear message to Russia that they cannot operate covertly," Norway's Defence Minister Tore Sandvik said to Reuters.

"We have made it unequivocally clear to Russian authorities that any attempt to target our critical infrastructure will be detected and met with consequences," he said. "It is in no ​one's interest to escalate tensions in the High North."

Increasing undersea Russian threat

Since the 2022 destruction of three of the Nord Stream subsea pipelines supplying Germany with Russian, NATO allies shifted their focus to undersea critical infrastructures.

Gradually more ships have been seen mapping undersea elements including pipelines, power cables and telecoms fiber-optic cables since 2023.

While it's not illegal to conduct such surveys in international waters, some experts say it could be preparation for sabotage.

"In the last 25 ⁠years, Europe did two ​things simultaneously. It dramatically expanded the extent to which it relies on seabed infrastructure, and it dramatically shrunk its capacity to protect that infrastructure," Bruce Jones, a senior ​fellow with the Brookings Institution told Reuters. "It's belatedly rebuilding now, in the face of a burgeoning Russian threat."

Contacted by Euronews, NATO refused to discuss specific details of the operation.

World.title: Giorgos Mazonakis: Arrests and new evidence amid probe into Greek star's death
World.content:
The investigation into the sudden death of Giorgos Mazonakis, one of the most popular Greek singers of the past three decades, is at the centre of public debate in Greece and Cyprus.

 

In a significant development on Thursday evening, Greek authorities arrested the two doctors linked to the private medical practice in central Athens where Mazonakis had gone for scheduled plasmapheresis before suffering cardiac arrest.

A case file has been opened against them for the Greek criminal offence of exposure resulting in death. The case is now expected to proceed through the prosecutorial process.

The death of the 54-year-old artist remains the leading story in the news in both countries, where Mazonakis enjoyed huge popularity, while media outlets across the Balkans are also following the case.

Attention has now shifted to the circumstances that preceded his death. Giorgos Mazonakis had gone to a private medical practice in central Athens for a scheduled plasmapheresis, a specialised therapeutic procedure to remove blood plasma, before suddenly collapsing.

The authorities must now answer a series of critical questions: what exactly had been planned, whether the procedure had in fact begun, who was in charge of it, what medical assessment had preceded it, and whether the premises had the required licence, the appropriate equipment and specialised staff.

At the same time, the forensic examination is expected to determine the cause of death and help clarify whether there is any link to what happened at the practice.

Three decades on the Greek music scene

Giorgos Mazonakis was born in Nikaia, Piraeus, in 1972 and stood at the forefront of Greek music for more than 30 years.

He began singing professionally at a young age. In 1992, while performing at a night-time venue in Patras, he was spotted by the record company PolyGram and the following year released his first album.

In the years that followed, he became one of the most recognisable figures in contemporary Greek laïko music, a pop-folk Greek music style from the 50s and 60s, delivering a string of commercial hits and maintaining a constant presence on the country's nightlife and live music circuit.

Beyond Greece, Mazonakis had a strong fanbase in Cyprus and among Greek diaspora communities, with performances in Germany, Australia and the United States.

In recent years, he has also been a judge on the popular programme The Voice of Greece.

His appeal extended beyond Greek-speaking audiences, particularly in the Balkans. He had appeared in Sofia as early as 2012 and returned for a concert in 2023, while in December 2024, he performed in Tirana.

News of his death was reported immediately by media outlets in Bulgaria and Albania.

What police are examining

One of the main issues authorities are seeking to clarify is what exactly happened before the cardiac arrest and whether the scheduled treatment had begun.

According to reports in Greek media, the doctor said to have been responsible for Mazonakis's treatment testified that the plasmapheresis had not yet begun and that his condition deteriorated abruptly while preparations for the procedure were under way.

The same reports, citing her testimony, say that Mazonakis had visited the practice the previous day as well. The doctor is said to have described his condition as already compromised and to have referred to difficulties with his speech.

Authorities are therefore expected to examine which symptoms had been recorded, what tests had been carried out, what medical history had been taken and on what basis it was considered that the planned procedure could go ahead.

The doctor's husband, who is also a doctor and in whose name the medical practice is registered, is reported to have told investigators that he had not personally treated Mazonakis and that his wife had undertaken the singer's treatment.

New findings from the police investigation have raised further questions about what happened inside the practice.

On Thursday, police carried out a lengthy search of the premises and seized digital devices, files, medical products and other material. A subsequent search was also carried out at the doctors' home.

According to Greek National Television, ERTnews, paramedics told investigators that the plasmapheresis machine was operating when they arrived at the practice. An initial technical examination is also reported to have shown that, during its most recent operation, the machine had remained switched on for 45 minutes. A more detailed examination is expected to establish when exactly it had been in use.

Police are also examining a discrepancy in the timeline. The doctor is reported to have said that Mazonakis arrived at around 16:30, while the emergency services had already been called shortly beforehand. Investigators believe the singer had been at the practice for at least three hours.

Following the examination of the new evidence, the two doctors were arrested and a case file was opened against them for exposure resulting in death.

Greek health minister: 'A very arduous procedure'

A separate inspection is underway into the licensing and operating conditions of the premises.

Greek Health Minister Adonis Georgiadis said that the facility was registered as a simple internal medicine practice and not as a clinic.

In his initial comments, he stated that, in such a practice, performing plasmapheresis is not permitted, according to him, and he ordered an immediate inspection by the Athens Medical Association.

On Thursday, he returned to the issue, describing plasmapheresis as a "very heavy" procedure which, he said, is carried out "only in a hospital setting".

The minister has stressed from the outset that the precise causes of death and whether there is any liability will have to emerge from the forensic and wider investigation.

'Specialised medical procedure'

During Thursday's inspection of the practice by police and representatives of the Athens Medical Association, two plasmapheresis machines were found. According to Greek Media, the machines had not been identified during Association inspections in 2024 and 2025, while questions remain over whether the relevant authorisation was in place

Athens Medical Association president Giorgos Patoulis had earlier said that the premises were licensed as an internal medicine practice and that the Association had no record of such equipment.

He also stressed that plasmapheresis is "a specialised medical procedure" which requires not only appropriate machinery but also specialised staff and specific standards.

The doctors' lawyer, however, has maintained that the machines had been duly declared to the Medical Association and that the practice was operating lawfully.

Greek media reports are also raising questions about the regulatory framework governing specialised medical procedures in private practices. The Central Health Council is expected to examine the issue and the conditions under which such therapeutic interventions may be carried out.

What is plasmapheresis?

Therapeutic plasmapheresis (therapeutic plasma exchange) is a procedure in which blood passes through a special device that separates and removes the plasma, while the red and white blood cells and platelets are returned to the body. The plasma that is removed is replaced by a special solution.

According to doctors Konstantinos Giannakas and Thanos Dimopoulos of the Therapeutic Clinic of the University of Athens, who spoke to the Athens-Macedonian News Agency, the method has specific therapeutic indications, including for certain serious haematological, neurological, and immunological diseases.

It requires an assessment of the patient's condition beforehand and continuous monitoring of blood pressure, heart rate and oxygen saturation. It is generally considered safe when carried out under the prescribed conditions, but it can cause adverse effects, ranging from a drop in blood pressure and hypocalcaemia to, more rarely, allergic reactions, bleeding or arrhythmias.

World.title: Youth losing critical skills and AI 'hollowing out' capabilities, PISA founder says
World.content:
The picture of student performance in Europe is "really concerning", with a recent report showing young people are losing essential skills that are "particularly important for the times we live in", Andreas Schleicher, the founder of the OECD's renowned PISA tests, has told Euronews.

 

The results of the 2025 standardised test, taken by 15-year-olds across 91 countries, were released this week, and found that performance in reading and mathematics had reached record lows across OECD countries.

The assessment measures students’ ability to apply reading, mathematics and science skills to real-world problems.

"We see that young people not only have lower literacy skills, but we are seeing a decline in students' capacity to triangulate and to critically reflect on information, to engage with more complex texts," said Schleicher, adding that these are essential skills in the world of artificial intelligence (AI).

"This technology is not necessarily accurate and therefore that intuition to check and verify should be really present," he added.

He also described a vicious cycle in which young people's use of such tools, which "are not designed to make us think harder", is further "hollowing out exactly the capabilities that we need". This was reflected in the PISA results: Students not using AI tend to be higher-performing.

"The bottom line is quite simple: You don't get fit by watching sports. You get fit by doing sports," Schleicher said. "And the same is true with learning. Learning doesn't come through the consumption of content; learning comes by engaging with ideas to compare and contrast. And AI can hollow out that very process. That's what we observe."

One factor at play is that the speed at which new technologies such as AI have advanced in many countries outpaces education systems' ability to reform. "Humans have always been better at inventing new things than using them wisely," Schleicher said.

However, the OECD assessment also found that guided, active use that forces cognitive friction — for example, challenging AI's output — translates to better learning outcomes.

"There are really interesting examples of countries where AI is used to make pupils think harder, to make them think about the right questions, to give teachers powerful tools to help students learn better," Schleicher said, adding that the education system needs to "shift gears away from a consumptive use of AI to a more creative use."

Small countries stand out

Schleicher has become one of the most influential voices in global education since he created the PISA test during the 1990s.

"We started work on this because, in the 90s, we measured success in education mainly by how much was spent on education and for how many years pupils sat in a classroom, which actually tells us very little" about the skills produced, he explained.

The assessments provide data-driven comparisons of national education systems across the world, and highlight major discrepancies, even within Europe. The latest results show that pupils' scores in seven EU countries were significantly above the OECD average, while in 13 member states, they were considerably below it.

"The biggest declines were recorded in large European countries, like France, Germany, and Spain. The most interesting solutions were found in the small, dynamic economies," Schleicher said.

An example is Estonia: Its students ranked first in Europe and in the global top ten in all three domains of the assessment. "It's a clear example of a country that is engaging with the digital world in a cautious but very thoughtful, very productive way," Schleicher explained.

Advice for parents and teachers

When looking to the future, Schleicher stressed that the focus should shift away from teaching skills that are easy to digitise, to more human skills such as "ethical decisions" and "our capacity to navigate complex human relationships".

He noted that students can no longer be "passive consumers" of education, but should become active learners. This raises questions in many parents' minds after the test results came out: What can they do?

"For parents, the answer is really simple. One of my real concerns is that parental interest in education in Europe has dramatically declined."

He explained that the solution is less about "doing three hours of homework with your child at the kitchen table" and more about "showing your child that what they are working on in school really matters to you".

Children whose parents ask them how their school day went, he noted, are two school years ahead in their test results.

Meanwhile, teachers' job should expand from being a good instructor to being "a great coach, a good mentor, a great facilitator" who takes a "genuine interest in who your students are and who they want to become and to accompany them on that journey".

However, in a Europe where many countries are suffering from teacher shortages, he stressed that the education system must "give teachers more time and more to play that much more important role."

World.title: 3D printing to colonise Mars after the Moon: the biomaterials tested by scientists
World.content:
As the return of humans to the Moon and their long-term stay there come ever closer thanks to the Artemis programme over the next few years,which will also feature the first lunar habitat module developed in Italy, the scientific community is already working on the prospect of colonising Mars.

 

Researchers at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) have developed an innovative formula for 3D printing housing structures on the Red Planet, combining three elements: gelatine, yeast and regolith.

What is Martian regolith

The study, led by civil engineer Jishen Qiu, was published in the journal Chem Circularity and reported by Interesting Engineering. (source in Italian)

The most striking innovation is undoubtedly Martian regolith, the layer of rocky material, made up of fine dust, sand, pebbles and rock fragments, that covers the entire surface of the planet.

The compound devised by the Hong Kong researchers would use it as a structural base to give volume and mass to the construction.

To this "local" raw material are added a very special yeast, engineered with adhesive proteins (modelled on the natural glue mussels use to cling to rocks) and gelatine, which acts as a binder and nutrient for the yeast.

In the HKUST experiments the researchers also tried to harness Mars' frozen climate as a natural freeze-dryer to save energy and avoid melting the minerals.

During processing in the 3D printer they therefore used low temperatures and reduced atmospheric pressure to encourage the sublimation of ice into vapour, generating a solid, lightweight foam.

Tests in simulated environments ultimately confirmed that the new compound resists compression at a level comparable to lightweight concrete, making it ideal for building multi-storey, fully recyclable structures.

However, several challenges remain regarding the sustainability of this Martian architecture, including the ability of micro-organisms to survive in the planet's environment and its dependence on resources sent from Earth.

From biomaterials for circular architecture to NASA projects

The use of yeast in 3D manufacturing technologies has a precedent in the laboratories of the Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden, as documented by MaterialDistrict (source in Italian).

The Swedish team has created a hydrogel made from yeast and cellulose to produce biodegradable architectural components. This approach also shows how adding value to food-industry waste can foster circular architecture both on Earth and in space missions.

In parallel with academic research, the aerospace sector is developing industrial-scale 3D printing for space habitats. As reported by Rinnovabili.it (source in Italian), NASA has allocated around 57.2 million dollars in recent years to the Olympus Project, dedicated to building permanent infrastructure on the Moon and Mars.

One of the practical developments of these technologies is Mars Dune Alpha, a 150-square-metre structure produced by 3D printing in Houston. NASA has used this habitat module in the Chapea analogue missions to test human life on Mars, laying the foundations for future human colonisation of space.

World.title: Podcast: Eco-anger, France in space, world's first photograph
World.content:
A climate expert experiences eco-anxiety firsthand after living through France's hottest summer on record. France tries to find its place in the new space race. And the story of the earliest known photograph still visible today.

Advertising

Eco-anxiety is on the rise in France after a summer of unprecedented heatwaves led to wildfires, scorched crops and the deaths of at least 7,000 people as well as livestock and birds. Juliette Decq, a climate adaptation consultant, says fear is a normal response to the reality people are now facing. A mother of two young children, she experienced that reality firsthand when her own home became unsafe. She talks about her anger over France’s lack of preparedness, not least in schools, but also about the solidarity she witnessed in her local community as they helped people protect themselves. Eco-anger, she says, can be a force for change. (Listen @0')

Historically a leader in Europe’s space programme, France is reassessing its role in space. Although French astronaut Sophie Adenot is currently on the International Space Station, France’s space ambitions haven’t focused on human space flight. But as the US and China ramp up their Moon missions and space becomes increasingly industrialised, France is looking to find its place. Space policy analyst Xavier Pasco explains how Europe is positioning itself as a regulator in a rapidly changing sector that has, until now, remained largely unchecked. (Listen @20'10'')

French inventor Nicéphore Niépce took the earliest surviving photograph in July 1827: a scene from a window that might have taken days to make. He fell into obscurity, and the photo itself was lost. Now it's returning to France, as part of a celebration of 200 years of photography in his honour. (Listen @14'15'')

Episode mixed by Cecile Pompeani.

Spotlight on France is a podcast from Radio France International. Find us on rfienglish.com, Apple podcasts, Spotify or your favourite podcast app.

Several people were killed and others injured in a tourist bush crash near the alpine village of Susch in Switzerland's eastern canton of Graubünden.

Several people were killed and others injured in a tourist bush crash near the alpine village of Susch in Switzerland's eastern canton of Graubünden, police said on Thursday.

Local police said that emergency response teams had been dispatched to the site of the crash.

Dutch media reported that the bus was carrying tourists from the Netherlands.

"These ​are Dutch ‌customers of [Dutch tour operator] OAD. We cannot yet say how many ​people ⁠have been killed or injured," a spokeswoman for Dutch travel association ANVR told the newspaper De Telegraaf.

De Telegraaf reported that 48 people were aboard the bus. The number has not been confirmed by police.

The crash occurred on the road between Susch and the nearby village of Zernez, where the bus collided with a guardrail, according to Swiss broadcaster SRF.

The broadcaster reported that multiple helicopters were deployed as part of rescue operations.

World.title: Digital data leeches: trading on our profiles
World.content:
US tech companies gather, link, and sell more and more information about their users. The scandal involving the dating app Grindr shows how easy it is for highly sensitive data to fall into the wrong hands.

Everyone has secrets. Things they wouldn't tell just anyone – except, perhaps, their dating app. What sort of partner they're looking for. Where they go to look for them. Their sexual preferences, maybe, or details about their health.

This information is meant to help the app find suitable matches. Selling the details on to other companies is not in the users' interest.

But this is what allegedly happened with Grindr, a dating app explicitly aimed at the LGBTQ+ community. Around 12,000 app users in Britain sued the company, which they said had shared highly sensitive personal information with advertisers — even, in some cases, a user's HIV status.

The lawsuit, filed in 2024, was settled earlier this week. Grindr has agreed to pay the claimants a total of 26 million pounds (€30 million; $35 million) – but stresses that this is not an admission of liability. Grindr continues to dispute the allegations, there has been no legal judgement.

Grindr, a dating platform aimed at (mostly men in) the LGBTQ+ community, is alleged to have passed on sensitive personal data Image: Andre M. Chang/ZUMAPRESS.com/picture alliance

What happens to the data you entrust to apps?

This latest case is just one of many that raise the bigger question of what actually happens to the information we entrust to our apps on a daily basis.

For users, an app is primarily just a helpful product. But they are often supported by cloud services, analysis tools, advertising networks and other service providers. They save and transfer data, link and analyse it — often contrary to our interest.

Jan Penfrat, a digital policy expert, says that many of the big tech companies want to "make it as difficult as possible for users and regulatory authorities to understand what data is gathered on our devices by which players, and for what purpose."

Penfrat works for European Digital Rights (EDRi), a European network of NGOs and experts that campaigns to defend fundamental rights and freedoms in the digital realm.

We all know what it's like: An app, a messenger service, for example, is quickly installed, and when it asks if it has permission to use personal data, users will often just click "yes."

Phone numbers are stored on servers — without approval

But the devil is in the detail. When you install WhatsApp, for example, you give it access to all the contacts in your smartphone. The phone numbers are transferred to the server — including those of people who don't use WhatsApp themselves, and who have not given permission for their contact details to be passed on.

"All of this flows into an enormous profile," says Penfrat.

Designed to fail: What dating apps really want from you To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Companies like Google then offer so-called "targeting" products based on this data.

"This means a car or clothes manufacturer can say: I'd like to address these target groups, and I want my advertising to appear in their Google search, Google Mail, or any of the hundreds of millions of third-party websites with integrated Google advertising," Penfrat explains.

Selling data profiles

Google is just one of many companies that offer data profiles. Two types of data feed into these profiles. One is the data that every user voluntarily discloses when they state something in their profile, or upload private photos.

But in addition, many big tech companies have for years now made assumptions based on the data they receive.

"If they have access to my location data and know where I usually am at night, they can assume that this is my home address," Penfrat says.

Who is in control of your data? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"If, for example, it's in a very expensive part of town, they can immediately make assumptions about my income. If they see: Oh, he has geolocation switched on and he regularly goes to a gay club, then he's probably a member of the LGBTQ community. And all this goes straight into the profile."

Strict regulation in Europe

The EU already has one of the strictest data protection regulations in the world. The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) aims to protect people's personal data and privacy.

Other EU digital laws such as the Digital Markets Act or the Digital Services Act are intended to prevent big tech companies misusing their power over businesses and users. US businesses also have to abide by these laws if they offer their services to people in Europe, or observe their behavior.

The EU Commission has imposed numerous fines as punishment for violations of these regulations. In 2025, it fined Apple €500 million euros ($580 million). Meta, the company that operates Facebook, was fined another €200 million ($232 million).

EU Commission spokesman Thomas Regnier in July 2026, announcing that the EU would fine Google 890 million euros Image: Virginia Mayo/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

Google had to pay €890 million ($1.03 billion) in fines this year. That sounds like a lot — but a look at the net profit of the Google corporation Alphabet puts it into perspective. In 2025, Alphabet's net profit was around €117 billion ($136 billion).

"So these are sums that a company like Google or Amazon will make in just a few days," says Penfrat. "They just include it in their budget."

Dependency on US digital services

As a result, it is not that easy for the EU to implement truly effective controls. The tech giants have global infrastructures, huge financial resources, and complex business models. European agencies first have to get past these.

Europe's quest for digital independence To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Added to this is Europe's dependency on cloud services, operating systems, platforms and increasingly also AI infrastructure that, at least to date, have been provided in large part by US companies.

Penfrat criticizes Brussels for lacking the political will needed to take firmer action against these companies, and to better equip European data protection authorities.

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: Canada, Ukraine pledge 100-year partnership
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Canada would provide Ukraine with a "very important" air defense package.

Canada and Ukraine on Thursday signed a declaration vowing to keep a 100-year partnership between the two countries.

It comes as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy visits the country for talks with Prime Minister Mark Carney and other Canadian officials.

Zelenskyy and Carney said that Canada had pledged to help shore up Ukraine's air defense.

"Earlier today, Canada and Ukraine finalized an agreement to deliver critical air defense interceptors (through) the United States Jumpstart mechanism," Carney said.

He said that the package would amount to some 350 million Canadian dollars ($260 million, €218 million).

The prime minister said that Canada had provided the equivalent of 26 billion Canadian dollars ($19 billion, €16 billion) in support for Ukraine.

"We've provided support for the energy systems and beyond. We'll provide more support," he said.

Zelenskyy expressed his graitude for what he described as a "very important" air defense package.

"I'm so thankful," Zelenskyy said. "This is very important package of air defense and this is crucial."

Speaking ahead of his meeting with Zelenskyy, Carney also emphasized Ukrainians' historical role in contributing to European settlement in the prairies of Canada's western provinces.

"Ukrainians help build ​this province, ⁠this country. Canada will help rebuild Ukraine when peace comes," he said, referring to Alberta, of which Calgary is the largest city.

Canada is home to over a million people of Ukrainian descent.

Zelenskyy and his wife Olena arrived in Canada late on Wednesday Image: Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

Zelenskyy visits Canada after Norway

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy arrived in Calgary late on Wednesday for "important meetings ​and agreements" with Canadian officials.

His visit comes on the heels of his attendance at King Harald V's funeral in Norway, where his plane had been delayed by a drone incursion.

The Ukrainian leader is in the middle of a flurry of trips and meetings to shore up his country's defenses for the cold winter months.

"The main focus will be on supporting Ukraine in protecting our skies and preparing for the winter," Zelenskyy said in a social media post before leaving.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a statement that the visit "will focus on shared priorities between Canada and Ukraine, including deepening defense, economic, and energy cooperation."

Carney's statement added Canada "remains steadfast in our commitment to support Ukraine's defense, recovery, and reconstruction."

Zelenskyy had also signaled a desire to meet with US President Donald Trump on the matter before the end of September.

Since Russia's invasion in 2022, Moscow has consistently increased attacks on fuel and heating infrastructure in Ukraine in the autumn and winter.

What is happening on the battlefield?

Ukraine struck a Russian oil refinery in the Yamalo-Nenets region overnight, as well as a seaport in Dagestan, Zelenskyy said. He added that other unnamed sited critical to Russia's war industry had also been hit.

Alexander Gusev, governor of Russia's Voronezh region, said that one woman in the town of Borisoglebsk had been killed by falling drone debris overnight and that at least 19 drones had been destroyed while flying over the region.

The Russian Defense Ministry said a total of 448 Ukrainian drones were shot down overnight.

In Ukraine, Russian attacks hit buildings owned by a major food producer in Dnipro, killing at least two according to local officials.

Two Azerbaijani crew members were killed in a drone attack on a cargo ship in the Ukrainian region of Odesa, Ukraine's infrastructure ministry said.

Azerbaijan's foreign ministry also confirmed the information, adding that two further members of the crew were taken to hospital in Chornomorsk, Ukraine.

While Baku did not mention who was responsible for the attack, Ukraine blamed Russia for the drone strike.
