World.title: Woman's death linked to 'highly potent' synthetic opioid first in ACT
World.content:
The ACT Coroner's Court has found the overdose death of a 42-year-old woman is the first in Canberra with an established linked to a novel psychoactive substance.

The woman's body was found at her home in Ainslie in July 2022 by her housemate who called emergency services.

Post-mortem testing found quantities of a range of drugs in her blood including protonitazene.

A highly potent synthetic opioid, or New Psychoactive Substance (NPS), protonitazene is estimated to be at least 100 times more potent than heroin.

Coroner Ken Archer said the woman had been using illicit drugs — predominantly heroin — for several years prior to her death and had overdosed while riding a bus a few days prior to her death.

"While she sought opportunities for drug counselling, the complexity of her dual diagnosis of deteriorating mental health and ongoing addiction issues required a holistic response to her health needs," Coroner Archer said.

"[She] was not able to engage with support services at a level and for a period that enabled such a response to be developed.

" Her response was to withdraw from support and her engagement with treatment services was limited. "

Police found items "consistent with drug usage" in the home including uncapped syringes, an empty clip seal bag with presumed drug residue, cannabis seeds, naloxone hydrochloride dihydrate (a single dose nasal spray for opioid overdose), fentanyl test strips and a sharps container.

They also found a large number of prescription medications and three bottles of methadone.

During a raid of a home as part of an unrelated investigation into a Canberra-based drug syndicate, police found the deceased's name in a notebook that appeared to contain a 'tick list' of customers along with a large amount of synthetic opioids.

Drug-checking service CanTEST has been present in the ACT since 2022. (Supplied: CanTEST)

The forensic pathologist who conducted the post-mortem indicated that protonitazene present at even low levels can be highly potent and "may have added to the degree of respiratory depression" but concluded it wasn't possible to say if the substance on its own was the cause of death.

Coroner Archer accepted this view, finding the woman had died of multiple drug toxicity, with aspiration of vomit a contributing cause.

Matters of public safety

Last month, police issued a warning after five people died within a fortnight from suspected drug overdoses linked to opioid use.

Researchers have also raised concerns about a rising number of deaths nationally, linked to novel substances.

Coroner Archer noted drug checking service CanTEST posts alerts about potentially dangerous drugs or additives, but the taking of blood samples from people who have died is delayed by the scheduling of post-mortem examinations.

Coroner Ken Archer said there were constraints to quickly identifying cases where novel psychoactive substances had contributed to death. (ABC News: Michael Barnett)

He said the ACT Government Analytical Laboratory is working on establishing a capability to detect NPS in blood samples including a "fast toxicology" capability, but it's not clear how long that work might take.

"There is not an integrated public notification system that arises from known outcomes from toxicological testing for NPS in the coronial space," Coroner Archer said.

"Warnings are issued on an ad hoc basis by the [Australian Federal Police] where patterns of NPS detection in death cases suggest a greater prevalence of NPS in drugs apparently distributed within the ACT," he said.

Five people in ACT die from suspected overdoses in a fortnight Health and emergency services have issued a warning about the presence of potentially lethal drugs circulating in the territory.

"It is noted that it is difficult to determine how long the drugs in which the NPS are found remain within the relevant distribution cycle for that drug that apply at the time of detection."

Coroner Archer said the delays affect the power of public messaging.

"For example, batches of heroin brought to the ACT from Sydney or Melbourne that contain NPS might move through the supply chain at varying rates depending on batch size and the demand for the product of the particular supplier," he said.

"A dangerous circumstance that arises is that heroin that is known to produce a greater 'high' can become popular in the market place.

"Heroin with higher purity levels or heroin with NPS added can produce that effect.

"Both circumstances created significant dangers for even experienced users".

Coroner Archer extended his condolences to the woman's family and apologised for the delay in finalising the findings.

World.title: Horses hop on steam train for unique ride through Flinders Ranges
World.content:
It is not unusual to see South Australia's oldest operating heritage railway full of tourists, but rather rare to see horses among its passengers.

Based in Quorn in the Flinders Ranges, the volunteer-run Pichi Richi Railway recently opened its carriages to more than 30 four-legged guests.

Horses were loaded onto the train. (ABC Rural: Isabella Kelly)

It was the third time horses had boarded the train since the once-regular service ceased in 2008.

Jenni Reschke and her horses used to be regular passengers.

"It's been a while, and I just always thought about it," Ms Reschke said.

Jenni Reschke initially reached out to a few friends to come on her first ride in 2022. (ABC Rural: Isabella Kelly)

Ms Reschke got in touch with some of the Pichi Richi Railway train drivers a few years ago to see what it would take to bring back the horse rides.

She reached out to some friends to gauge interest, and in 2022 she organised the train ride of a lifetime for about 13 people and their horses.

"It was really great, so I said, 'That's so fun, I'll do it again,'" Ms Reschke said.

The horse passengers seemed pretty chuffed with their scenic train ride. (ABC Rural: Isabella Kelly)

Since then, she has run the event every two years.

"I ended up asking a few more friends, so last time [in 2024] I reckon we had about 23 people," she said.

" I just bring them up here to our beautiful country and I love showing them around. I'm a bit of a show-off. "

The Pichi Richi route is surrounded by colourful wildflowers. (ABC Rural: Isabella Kelly)

When it came time to continue the event this year, there was even more interest.

"The word sort of got out a bit more … and we've ended up with 32 horses," she said.

Hold your horses

Pichi Richi volunteer Senga Reed said the extra cargo attracted a lot of interest.

"It's an unusual experience, and it's good for the passengers," she said.

Senga Reed says passengers are always excited to find out they will be joined by horses. (ABC Rural: Isabella Kelly)

" They love it when they find out that they've got the horses on board, it's extra special. "

She said the heritage railway experience was always "very popular", horses or not.

The area has blossomed with wildflowers. (ABC Rural: Isabella Kelly)

"We get people from all over the world coming to travel on the train, and we get a lot of repeaters as well," she said.

"It's fantastic when you get to see people coming back, and they come a few times, then they start volunteering themselves."

Jenni Reschke brought a couple of her horses along for the ride. (ABC Rural: Isabella Kelly)

After heavy rain, this year's ride among fields of wildflowers was a far cry from the last.

"Two years ago we were in a very heavy drought, very solid. It was so dry," Ms Reschke said.

"The land is still beautiful, but it's very, very harsh.

"And this year we've just been so blessed, it's so, so different."

World.title: Crows' quest for premiership glory just beginning as they prepare to take on Lions
World.content:
A week is a long time in footy, but an hour can feel like a lifetime.

In the space of 30 minutes last Saturday, Adelaide coach Matthew Nicks jumped from zero to hero, whilst hours earlier at the SCG the Lions went from premiership favourites to staring down a straight sets exit.

When the Bulldogs piled on three rapid fire goals to erode the Crows' 20-point lead, the tension at Adelaide Oval was palpable; but after Izak Rankine snapped a magical goal to seal Adelaide's first finals victory in nine years, everything changed.

The home crowd rose as one to give their embattled senior coach a standing ovation; drawing a smile from the man whose future was publicly in the spotlight and uniting a football club that has been fractured since its 2017 grand final collapse.

Izak Rankine sealed Adelaide’s first finals victory in nine years with a spectacular goal from a ridiculous angle. (AAP: Matt Turner)

Adelaide premiership player and former board member Rod Jameson couldn't hold back his emotions post-game on ABC Sport.

"'Get stuffed' is probably what you want to say," he said.

"It's been against the odds.

"I feel really happy for Matthew Nicks that he's actually got one … so what's the narrative now next week?"

That's the big question in a relentless news cycle. Despite the pressure valve being released, Adelaide's quest for glory is just beginning with an upcoming semi-final at the Gabba to face a Lions side who handed them their biggest loss of the season back in round 7.

But the heat has certainly shifted to the qualifying final losers Fremantle and Brisbane, with both teams facing the daunting possibility of becoming the 13th side in 13 years to be eliminated in straight sets.

Matthew Nicks claimed his first AFL finals win since he began coaching the Crows. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

Reigning premiers Brisbane were stunningly blown away by an undermanned Swans. Sydney's passion was unrelenting; winning the tackle count by 15, contested possessions by 19 and beating the Lions at their game with a whopping six goals to one from centre bounce.

"They were desperate from the start, and all you want as a fan is the effort … that was perfect finals footy," dual premiership winning Swan Ryan O'Keefe said on ABC Sport.

"When was the last time 36 scoring shots were kicked against an opposition in a final? That's unbelievable."

It’s a blueprint that will build belief for the Crows ahead of Saturday’s semi and could dictate the result. Adelaide is one of the best pressure sides in the competition. The six times they have lost pressure differential this season they’ve been defeated, whilst the Lions are 13-0 when winning it.



Adelaide’s other advantage is their forward firepower, with the team averaging 109 points per game in their last five matches. The Lions conceded 14 goals to key forwards last week, have leaked 100 points eight times this season and are sitting 13th for points against per game.



"The defence is the difference this year," premiership Magpie Luke Ball said after the Lions loss at the SCG.

"It looked too easy to score against them. They're going to have to defy history."

Lachie Neale starred for the Brisbane Lions with 42 disposals. (AAP: James Ross)

The final and most pivotal factor is likely to be the midfield. The Lions kicked five goals to none from centre bounce back in their round 7 mauling on top of 27 extra points from stoppage. Lachie Neale starred with 42 disposals and Will Ashcroft had 36 touches and a goal.



It's a concern for the Crows who conceded three unanswered goals from the middle against the Bulldogs on Saturday night. They made up for it in their defence with Josh Worrell nabbing a career high 34 disposals and a massive 19 intercepts. Adelaide kept the Bulldogs to a 14 per cent inside 50 to goal efficiency.



Brisbane are no strangers to doing it the hard way. This is the eighth consecutive year they’ve made it to a preliminary final or semi-final with a record of 3-2 in the latter.

The Crows, meanwhile, have got the monkey off their back, snapping their September shackles and now can take a swing at the reigning premiers at a venue they haven't won at since 2018.

"I don't think it can be understated how much pressure was on this side coming into this contest," All-Australian midfielder Josh Francou said after the elimination final.

"They were challenged and in the end they got the job done and in the end they go to up to Brisbane with a free hit."

You can hear ABC Sport call the semi-final between Adelaide and the Brisbane Lions from 5:30pm CST on 891 ABC Adelaide and on ABC Listen.

World.title: High-frequency 'pingers' trial to keep whales out of shark nets
World.content:
For the first time in 15 years, acoustic alarms attached to shark nets off Queensland's coastline are changing pitch.

Authorities hope the new, high-frequency 'pingers' will more effectively prevent whales from becoming trapped in nets.

About 50,000 humpbacks pass by Australia's east coast each year, with the southern migration currently in full swing.

Sam Fary (left) from Queensland's shark control program, with James Turner from Future Oceans. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross)

Shark control program operations coordinator Sam Fary said about "0.02 per cent" of the whales would interact with the nets — but there was always room for improvement.

"This is a higher frequency, something that we haven't used before … this is world-leading research in this space," Mr Fary said.

The five-week trial is being conducted in waters off Noosa Heads, as part of a collaboration between the University of Queensland, the state government and the alarm supplier, Future Oceans.

These acoustic alarms deter whales, but there are also separate alarms attached to nets that deter dolphins. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross)

How does it work?

James Turner from Future Oceans said the pingers sent a sound into the water that is understood to be heard by whales and dolphins.

Shark Control Management Plan expanded A multi-million-dollar shark control investment — the biggest in the program's history — looks to protect beachgoers. But some are questioning if it's even legal.

"They acoustically illuminate things like fishing nets and drum lines … whales are actually moving away from whatever the gear the pingers are attached to," Mr Turner said.

"The University of Queensland did some trials and decided that one of the frequencies was going to be even better than the frequency that the government's been using for the past 15 years in the pingers."

A whale spotted frolicking in waters off Queensland's Gold Coast. (Supplied: Sea World)

Mr Turner said the technology was constantly evolving, and they hoped to soon be able to understand the sounds the whales made.

"Researchers think that they can start to break down the sequences and the signals whales are using," he said.

" And if we learn what are deterrent signals or an alert signal to them, then we can replicate those. "

Keeping watch

Researchers from the University of Queensland will be at Noosa Heads for the trial.

University of Queensland researchers will be surveying the site for the duration of the trial. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross)

Riona McNamara said they would be set up for 10 hours each day.

"We're watching the shark nets and observing any whales that track close to them," she said.

" People are really inquisitive about what we're doing and yeah, perfect position to watch the nets and the whales migrating through. "

UQ's Ashleigh Bourke, Riona McNamara, Christin Mundell and Oscar Heaselgrave will monitor the nets. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross)

Humpbacks and High-rises chief executive Olaf Meynecke, whose conservation organisation monitors whale movements, said previous studies had not demonstrated similar pingers to be a sufficient deterrent.

"These shark nets have clearly proven to be lethal for a lot of non-target species, and their effectiveness [in deterring sharks] is questionable," Dr Meynecke said.

He said there were approximately 60 entanglements along the east coast each year, but the number could be higher due to inaccurate reporting.

"If we take out the shark nets during the whale season, we won't have any entanglements of whales. It's simple as that," he said.

The researchers will actively monitor the shark nets for the duration of the trial. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross)

Primary Industries Minister Tony Perrett said the trial reflected the state government's commitment to swimmer safety.

"Queensland's shark control program plays an important role in protecting beachgoers, and we are always looking at ways we can improve the program with contemporary technology and science," Mr Perrett said.

World.title: Greens co-founder weighs in on party split over koala park carbon credits
World.content:
Australian Greens founding figure Bob Brown has backed the three senators who took the rare step of crossing the floor to vote against the party but does not believe the split weakens the leader's authority.

He acknowledged that those who voted with Labor "in a way" chose "the lesser of two evils" but ultimately sided with those who crossed the floor.

"It's a very big moral issue that's at stake here and, were I in the Senate, I would have made the same decision," Mr Brown said.

Forestry looks for new markets The forestry industry is considering its future after the announcement of a Great Koala National Park.

At the heart of the issue is the development of the Great Koala National Park on the New South Wales Mid North Coast.

A crucial hurdle is the successful registration of the project under a federal government scheme known as the Improved Native Forest Management [INFM] method.

The INFM allows state governments to earn carbon credit units by ceasing planned logging in defined areas of "multiple-use public native forests that would otherwise be used for commercial forestry," according to the government's website.

Those credits can then be sold to organisations that want or need to offset emissions.

Greens leaders say issue divisive among 'good hearts' and 'reasonable minds'

Loading...

The issue divided environmentalists and the Greens, but ultimately the party struck a deal with Labor to support the scheme after securing changes, including restrictions to stop coal and gas projects from using offsets.

On Thursday, Greens senators Nick McKim, Vanessa Bleyer, and Jordon Steele-John defied the usually cohesive bloc to vote with the Coalition on a disallowance motion.

That motion was voted down in the chamber, 27 to 34.

Liberal senator Andrew McLachlan also crossed the floor to vote with Labor.

In the lead-up to the vote, Senator McKim told the chamber that he, Senator Bleyer and Senator Steele-John strongly disagreed with the INFM method.

"Labor is holding koalas hostage … and threatening their extinction unless they can profit from their habitat," Senator McKim said.

Nick McKim told the chamber that he strongly disagreed with the INFM method. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

But he acknowledged there were different views in the party room.

"I want to be very clear that people of good heart and clear mind, both in our party room and in the environment movement, can and have come to different positions on this issue," he said.

Greens leader Larissa Waters expressed a similar sentiment, and acknowledged "reasonable minds, with good hearts, can differ on the outcome."

She explained her vote as protecting 176,000 hectares of native forest and the habitat of 12,000 koalas.

The ABC requested further comment on Thursday night from Senator Waters and several other members following the vote, but they all either declined or were unavailable.

Asked on 7.30 last night whether he thought the Greens leader's authority had been "fatally weakened" by the split, Mr Brown responded, "no, I don't".

Bob Brown says he would have crossed the floor too. (Supplied)

Labor accuses opposing Greens of 'ludicrous fearmongering'

Mr Brown accused Labor of seeing "forest as a commodity to be traded one way or another for their corporate supporters".

"I do have a great deal of alarm that we are now setting in place a system … where unless money is to be made out of the environment, we won't get future national parks," he said.

But the Assistant Minister for Climate Change, Josh Wilson, described that claim as "ludicrous fearmongering".

"This is a method that rightly attributes value to the carbon storage that occurs when native forests keep growing and aren't subject to harvesting or logging as is currently the case," he said.

"There's no trade-off here".

Josh Wilson accused the Greens of "fearmongering". (ABC News: Briana Shepherd)

But Mr Brown pushed back, arguing the best way to tackle climate change was to "stop logging forests and have the carbon come out of the atmosphere into those forests".

"It's perverse, it's wrong, and history will show us that it's extremely costly as climate change comes to change the lives of everybody," he said.

Energy Minister Chris Bowen said the motion was a "test" for the Greens.

"The majority of the Greens passed that test," he told Afternoon Briefing.

"If you believe in ending native forest logging or moving away from it and reducing it, then you vote for this method."

World.title: Governance dispute between University of Queensland and student union boils over
World.content:
A dispute between the University of Queensland (UQ) and its student union has reached a boiling point, with the university applying for a transition plan due to governance concerns.

The University of Queensland Union (UQU) has accused the university of attempting to interfere with funding allocated to the union due to its positions on social and political issues.

Under federal legislation, higher education providers can charge students a Student Services and Amenities Fee (SSAF) to support services and amenities for students, with a portion allocated to student-led organisations.

When universities believe student-led organisations are failing to comply with legislative governance requirements, they can apply for the organisation to be granted time to fulfil those requirements in the form of a transition plan.

UQ Union has alleged the university is targeting its funding due to positions on social and political issues. (Supplied)

The union has alleged in a "Hands Off Our Union" social media campaign that UQ is attempting to override UQU's independence by withholding funding.

"The University of Queensland is holding your student fees for ransom by threatening to withhold funding so they can dictate how we run our student union," a petition on social media read.

"Our job is to be a body where students can come together and organise to defend our rights against the university, and fight for progressive reforms against the government. That's exactly why the university administration is threatening our funding.

"They want us to be passive, apolitical, and unable to express any opposition to their agenda."

University points to governance concerns

A UQ spokesperson told the ABC the university had not proposed cuts to UQU funding.

Federal legislation requires universities to allocate at least 40 per cent of SSAF money to student-led organisations, with UQU receiving a total of $9.2 million in 2025.

In its SSAF Allocation Report for 2025, UQ noted it had assessed that the union had failed to fulfil a legislative requirement for "corporate governance policies and procedures established and adhered to".

The same report noted UQ had submitted a transition plan application to the Department of Education for approval on June 29.

The University of Queensland says it has sought the plan to give the union time to meet governance requirements. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

A spokesperson for the education department confirmed UQ's application had been received.

UQ is required to ensure that any student-led organisation receiving SSAF funding meets the governance requirements detailed in section 20 of the Higher Education Support (Student Services, Amenities, Representation and Advocacy) Guidelines 2022 (SSARA).

SSARA governance requirements: The governing body of the student-led organisation makes decisions independently from the higher education provider; and

the organisation keeps and publishes annual audited accounts that record the organisation’s income and expenditure, including in relation to transactions between the higher education provider and the organisation; and

the organisation has, and complies with, policies and procedures in place that relate to record keeping, risk management, fraud prevention and financial controls.

Transition plans can be sought if universities believe their allocation of 40 per cent of SSAF funding to student-led organisations does not comply with the above guidelines.

"The purpose of a SSAF transition plan is to provide a framework though which providers can meet their legislative requirements," the education department spokesperson said.

A spokesperson for UQ said its application for a transition plan involved the university working with the union to introduce improved governance standards, with funding remaining in the hands of students.

The spokesperson said recommendations had been made to the union and if approved by the department, the transition plan would see the university and union work in collaboration.

Federal legislation requires higher education providers allocate at least 40 per cent of SSAF funding to student-led organisations. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

Funding should 'remain in student hands'

The spokesperson for UQ said the university had a legislative responsibility to ensure SSAF funding "is governed appropriately".

"To support the union to meet the government requirements, the university has put forward recommendations for the union to consider.

"The university has not proposed any cuts to the UQU funding."

The spokesperson did not confirm what those recommendations were, or what governance concerns they held.

In a press release, UQU president Alyssa Roser said "student money should remain in student hands".

"The university wants to keep this quiet and to prevent the student body from having any say or control over this process," Ms Roser said.

"An independent student union cannot properly hold a university to account if the university can use its funding relationship to influence how the union operates."

Union president Alyssa Roser says student money should remain in student hands. (ABC News: Giulio Saggin)

The UQ spokesperson said the university supported "lawful free speech".

"We remain committed to working constructively with the UQU in the interests of all students."

UQU's most recent publicly available annual budget is from 2024, and it has not published meeting minutes since May last year.

The clash between UQ and the student union comes as UQ staff walked off the job on Tuesday in relation to a separate pay dispute.

UQU's student executive leadership team declined to answer specific questions.

World.title: Fears for historic show's future after years of cancelled events
World.content:
Fears are growing for the future of the 153-year-old Royal Launceston Show, which, after cancelling three years in a row, is now at risk of having its charity status revoked.

The show, which has run since 1873, scrapped its main 2024, 2025 and 2026 events citing financial difficulties and other challenges.

But it has also failed to file its 2024 and 2025 annual information statements with the federal government's Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission (ACNC).

The ACNC said the annual statements give government and the public details about a charity's activities, operations and finances over a 12-month period.

Its website, where the show society is registered as the "Royal National Agricultural and Pastoral Society of Tasmania", shows the "charity is reporting late".

"Usually, historically, when an organisation has been repeatedly late filing financial reports or other required documents, it's a sign that something is amiss," economist Saul Eslake said.

An ACNC spokesperson said if a charity fails to submit the required annual information statements for two reporting periods, it risks becoming a "double defaulter" and having its charity registration revoked.

They said this would see the Australian Taxation Office (ATO) remove entitlements to charity tax concessions.

Independent economist Saul Eslake says it's not a good sign when an entity is late filing financial reports. (ABC News: Jordan Young)

Losing concessions could make existing problems worse

University of Tasmania's accounting discipline lead Donovan Castelyn said a general situation in which a charity loses its tax concessions "could pose a significant risk to the bottom line".

"It might be very hard for the entity to continue existing or providing the services that it was established to do, to the point that it might not exist in the future," he said.

The ACNC could not comment publicly on a particular charity.

The Royal Launceston Show board told the ABC it is "focused on ensuring financial reporting obligations are properly completed" and would not comment further while that work is underway.

Operating losses

The Royal Launceston Show board said a key reason for the 2026 cancellation was the "financial and operational requirements" necessary to host the event.

The woodchopping competitions were a staple of the Royal Launceston Show. (ABC News: Sallese Gibson)

Its most recent available financial report, from December 2023, showed its total assets outweighed its liabilities.

But its operating losses had grown from $205,935 in 2022 to $327,639 in 2023.

The report also stated the ATO had, after the end of the financial year, "reinstated an alleged debt" of $80,334.

It said the directors believed the debt had been retracted by the ATO in 2017, which is why it had previously been written off.

The available financial reports do not establish if they were ultimately required to pay the debt.

An ATO spokesperson said it cannot comment on the matter.

The Devonport Show has long been on hiatus. (ABC News: Sallese Gibson)

Auditor suggested company insolvent

The Royal Launceston Show's bottom line seems to have improved in recent years compared to the previous decade.

Back in 2019 it reported total assets of only $22,158, against total liabilities of $524,951.

Several shows across Tasmania have folded or are doing it tough.

For each year from 2015 to 2018, the board noted "there are not reasonable grounds" to believe it can pay its debts and discussions were taking place with potential funders and creditors.

In 2019, an auditor said the company's financial position and trading outcomes "cast considerable doubt over its ability to continue as a going concern".

"The company lacks the capacity to pay its current debts," the auditor said.

"I have not been presented with any evidence supporting the fact that the company is not insolvent under the law as at the date of signing this report.

"I have however been advised of a possible solution to this problem."

This may have been a reference to a contract the show society had entered into, to relinquish its 99-year-lease on the Inveresk Showgrounds in 2020 for $1.3 million.

"The proceeds will be used to clear all debts and to commence the development of a replacement ground to accommodate events including the annual Launceston Show," the report said.

The 2026 Royal Launceston Show has been cancelled, following cancellations in 2024 and 2025. (ABC News: Laura Beavis)

This may have helped, with net assets outweighing liabilities each year from 2020 to 2023.

No suitable ground

Following pandemic cancellations in 2020 and 2021, the event was held at Quercus Park in Carrick in 2022 and 2023, when it celebrated 150 years.

However, the show society board said another reason for the 2026 cancellation was the "absence of a suitable ground space".

Launceston Mayor Matthew Garwood said the council has contacted the show society over several years about its future and the challenges around finding a suitable location.

"Ultimately, the operation and financial position of the Show Society are matters for the organisation itself," he said.

"But council absolutely recognises the importance of the Royal Launceston Show and what it has meant to our community."

Launceston Mayor Matthew Garwood says he recognises the importance of the Royal Launceston Show. (ABC News: Georgia Hogge)

'Sense of loss'

It is not the only country show to face challenges.

The Devonport Show operated for 108 years but has been on hiatus since 2016.

Lesley Young hopes the Launceston Show can return one day. (Supplied: Lesley Young)

Lesley Young, who is "president of a very small committee that's trying to hold things together", said its main challenges were rising costs and dwindling public support.

But she believed the event was as important as ever, particularly to bridge "the divide between the city people and country people".

"We need to showcase the work that farmers do, the importance of agriculture, whether it be where your beef and lamb comes from or where your carrots and spuds come from," she said.

"And also the opportunities that there are for younger people to get involved in the workforce."

She said she was hopeful the Royal Launceston Show would return, despite its difficulties.

"You'd like to think that the Launceston [Show] could get up and going again," she said.

Mr Eslake agreed.

"I think most people in and around Launceston and across northern Tasmania would feel that if this show were never to be staged again, there'd be an understandable sense of loss about that," Mr Eslake said.

World.title: Free canola field lets tourists take selfies without trampling crops
World.content:
As an agricultural export, Australia's canola fields are big business.

Harvested for its oilseed, it is a $5 billion industry with product consumed locally and exported across the globe.

But it is the picturesque yellow backdrop created by the fields of flowers that has people travelling long distances to catch a glimpse or take a selfie.

Canola fields are vast between Temora and Coolamon. (ABC News: Lauren Pezet)

Canola is also in full flower across New South Wales's central west. (ABC Rural: Emily Middleton)

Bright yellow fields are lining roads across central and southern NSW. (ABC News: Lauren Pezet)

"Tourists love it," said Craig Sinclair from Temora Shire Council in the New South Wales Riverina.

"There's something about the colour yellow I think that really makes people feel a sense of joy and happiness."

Protecting crops

But that photogenic popularity has long caused a headache for farmers, and the biosecurity risk from trespassers remained a major issue.

"Fungal disease can easily occur when they come in from another property or there's also weeds that can easily get caught up on people's clothes or their shoes," said FarmLink Research CEO Shaughn Morgan.

"By walking into another property, they could actually cost the farmer their livelihood.

Trespassers are still a problem for farmers trying to protect their crop. (ABC News: Lauren Pezet)

Keep out signs are distributed by Canola Trail councils for farmers to put on their roadside fences. (ABC News: Lauren Pezet)

After years of trying to educate the public about the risks and distributing "keep out" signage, Temora Shire Council and the non-for-profit group FarmLink Research has teamed up to create a public field allowing tourists to safely and legally get amongst it for free.

Temora's public canola field gives visitors free access to walk through, take photos and look at a crop up close. (ABC News: Lauren Pezet)

Tourists are able to legally enter Temora's public canola field to take photos. (ABC News: Lauren Pezet)

Yellow Bloom Rd is a canola field open to the public for free. (ABC News: Lauren Pezet)

"Rather than people jump fences and get into paddocks that they shouldn't be in, why not actually put a paddock that people could go and visit and actually go and touch, feel, ask questions, be able to get photos taken?" Mr Morgan said.

Now in its second year and with flowering starting earlier than usual this season, Mr Sinclair said interest was growing.

"It's a particularly good year this year for canola," he said.

"There's blooms all around the countryside here in the Riverina and we're seeing lots of visitors coming from Sydney, from Canberra, some people just coming just for the day from Sydney to walk across the canola."

Craig Sinclair says canola is a huge drawcard for attracting new visitors to the broader area. (ABC News: Lauren Pezet)

'Life-giving' tourism

Temora has also joined forces with the surrounding Coolamon and Junee shires on a tourism campaign that contributed to a significant increase in the amount of money spent in those areas during the spring flowering.

The Hello Yellow campaign is reaching new visitors. (ABC News: Lauren Pezet)

Spending at business in Canola Trail shires jumped around 20 per cent during a 2025 marketing campaign. (Supplied: Canola Trail)

Hot air balloons operate in the Temora region specifically during canola's flowering season. (Supplied: Canola Trail)

Last year, for the month of September, spending was up about 20 per cent on the previous year, with $4.6 million worth of revenue coming from tourism.

"Canola is the drawcard," Mr Sinclair said.

"That is the thing that has a limited window every year, the sort of six-week flowering season, and that is the bright lights that gets people here.

"But once they're here, there's so many other things that keep them here."

Canola is harvested for its oilseed. (ABC News: Lauren Pezet)

The canola fields always put on a show in the lead up to spring. (Supplied: Canola Trail)

For local small business owners like Debbie Davidge, that draw card has been "life-giving".

"It puts a pep in our step. It gives us a reason to get out of bed. It's something that we discuss with people," she said.

Debbie Davidge says the popularity of the canola crops is "life-giving" for local businesses. (ABC News: Lauren Pezet)

Ms Davidge said her shop and café had been flat out since the public field opened this season.

"[Visitors] are just mesmerised by it," she said.

"Even in what we consider not a great season, people from away that have never seen this before are just amazed at what the country can produce and how it can look."

Trespassing a threat to food security

Shaughn Morgan said it was concerning that people continued to jump fences and wander on to private canola farms despite having legal alternatives.

"Food doesn't come from supermarkets, it comes from farms and it scares me that there are many people out there that don't realise the important role that farmers play within the sector to be able to ensure that their food is made," he said.

"The good thing about coming out along this road here, this trail, is to be able to actually see what it is that we're able to provide to the community and be able to show where the food is coming from."

Shaughn Morgan says trespassers can cost farmers their livelihoods with the damage they can cause to crops. (ABC News: Lauren Pezet)

For the farmers waiting to harvest their crop, Mr Morgan said the signs were "positive" but time would tell.

"Until it actually comes to the day where you actually are able to harvest, anything's possible," he said.

"A sudden frost could come, the rain may not occur, there are so many variables with the weather."

World.title: ‘Chilling’: AI giant Anthropic says it blocked possible efforts to build biological weapons
World.content:
TechnologyAI ‘Chilling’: AI giant Anthropic says it blocked possible efforts to build biological weapons Dustin Volz September 11, 2026 — 6:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Anthropic said it had disrupted several potential plots this year by scientists who used its leading artificial intelligence models to conduct research that could have helped develop biological weapons. In a report describing misuses of its AI models, Anthropic said it could not determine whether the research served a legitimate or nefarious purpose because valid biological inquiry — the kind that can lead to breakthroughs like vaccines — can also help engineer dangerous pathogens. In the face of that uncertainty, Anthropic said it erred on the side of caution because the consequences of missing malicious activity could be severe. The potential for cutting-edge AI models to facilitate the development of known or entirely new biological pathogens is among the gravest concerns experts have about a technology that is developing so rapidly that even its leading architects doubt whether humans will be able to fully control it. AP “You are not seeing someone in a comic book kind of way say, ‘Hey, I want to build a biological weapon to kill everybody,’” Jacob Klein, the head of threat intelligence at Anthropic, said in an interview. “It’s an incredibly nuanced situation.” The potential for cutting-edge AI models to facilitate the development of known or entirely new biological pathogens is among the gravest concerns experts have about a technology that is developing so rapidly that even its leading architects doubt whether humans will be able to fully control it.



Compared with the threat of catastrophic cyberattacks or AI agents that fail to align with human intentions, biological misuse has gained less attention as an existential risk of AI, in part because past examples have generally been shown only in research settings rather than in the real world. Andrew Weber, a senior fellow on the Council on Strategic Risks who reviewed Anthropic’s report before its release, said the findings were “chilling examples of state-sponsored biological weapons developers tapping into the rapidly advancing capabilities” of leading AI models. Related Article AI ‘Could kill us all’: Anthropic insiders say AI has more than 10% chance of ending humanity – soon The lengthy report Anthropic published on Thursday catalogued a litany of misuses of its AI models, including the chatbot Claude, over the past eight months. Some examples were similar to past disclosures from Anthropic and other AI labs, including suspected Chinese and Iranian government-linked actors targeting dissident and diaspora communities for surveillance. The report also highlighted cases of Russian state media using Claude to generate online propaganda masquerading as independent reporting, including fabricated claims about an election in Moldova.



Anthropic documented another genre of abuse it said was new: attempts to use Claude to develop software for conventional weapons design and development, including firearms, missiles, armed drones and bombs. It detailed three cases in China, two in Russia and one in Yemen. The report does not identify by name which parties were involved in the Yemeni case, but the context makes clear that it is referring to the Iran-backed Houthi militia. AI use by terrorist networks is a growing concern among US security officials. But among all the categories of threats shared in the report, none may be as worrisome as the biological research cases. Anthropic did not disclose the names of researchers or institutions that it blocked, their countries of affiliation or the specific biological agents at issue, in part because of its uncertainty about their aims. The lengthy report Anthropic published on Thursday catalogued a litany of misuses of its AI models, including the chatbot Claude, over the past eight months. AP Photo/Patrick Sison Still, Anthropic said the scientists circumvented its controls intended to prevent users from blocked regions from gaining access to its AI models and worked to “obfuscate the purpose of their research to evade our safeguards.” The company banned accounts associated with the research.



In one example from May, a scientist sought Claude’s help with writing a grant application for funding to conduct research intended to experiment on the chikungunya virus, a mosquito-borne malady that can lead to months of severe pain and other symptoms. Such research, known as gain of function, can be legitimate and lead to vaccine development, but it can also create superbug versions of viruses. In this instance, the scientist wanted to engineer mutations to the virus that would make it more harmful as it repeatedly infected live animals. Anthropic said it believed the particular research was worrisome in part because it could discern that the work was intended to be performed at a military research institute. The findings are ‘chilling examples of state-sponsored biological weapons developers tapping into the rapidly advancing capabilities.’ Andrew Weber, a senior fellow on the Council on Strategic Risks “What we don’t know is if the research was meant to be weaponised,” Klein said. “But a military institution doing gain-of-function research is concerning.” Anthropic said evaluations from last year of its older models demonstrated that they were not yet able to meaningfully assist in conducting dangerous biological research. Its current models are more able to complete complex scientific research, the company said, which spurred tighter safeguards intended to restrict access to a wide range of dual-use biological research queries.



Susan Monarez, a microbiologist and public health expert who oversaw a review of national biosecurity preparedness in the Obama administration, also reviewed the Anthropic report before its publication. She said the findings provided real-world evidence to support concerns that bad actors were trying to covertly use advanced AI “to improve their chances of building biological pathogens that could cause significant harm.” Related Article Analysis

AI ‘We must be stopped’: Why Australia needs to listen to the experts on AI Monarez, who briefly served as the director of the Centres for Disease Control and Prevention last year, said AI held enormous promise to usher in an era of medical breakthroughs that save and extend lives. But the same abilities that make that possible, she added, could also “let bad actors hide in plain sight, using seemingly legitimate research to create pathogens we may not see coming and may not be able to stop once released.” Weber of the Council on Strategic Risks, who also served as the assistant secretary of defence for nuclear, chemical and biological defence programs during the Obama administration, called for limiting access to AI tools capable of this level of biological research to trusted researchers only. “The fact that Russia, China and North Korea continue to develop prohibited biological weapons makes it imperative that we deny their researchers access to these extraordinarily capable models,” he said.



This article originally appeared in The New York Times. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

World.title: ASX set to slump, Wall Street falls as oil climbs to its highest mark since May
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to slump, Wall Street falls as oil climbs to its highest mark since May Stan Choe Updated September 11, 2026 — 6:27am ,first published 5:23am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Oil prices keep climbing as the war with Iran keeps clogging the global flow of crude, and they leaped Thursday to their highest levels since before the summer. That worsened worries about inflation and cranked up pressure within the bond market, helping to send stocks lower again on Wall Street. The S&P 500 fell 0.6 per cent for a fourth straight loss, its longest such streak since June, though it’s not far from its all-time high set last month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 316 points, or 0.6 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite sank 0.7 per cent. Oil climbed to its highest mark since March. AP The Australian sharemarket is set for another day of heavy losses, with futures at 6.13am AEST pointing to a loss of 81 points or 0.9 per cent, at the open. The ASX shed 1 per cent on Thursday. The Australian dollar was lower at US71.56¢. US stocks sank under the weight of rising oil prices. Brent crude, the international standard, climbed another 6.3 per cent and briefly topped $US108 per barrel for the first time since May before settling at $US107.63.



Related Article Energy Australia softens local gas supply rules, easing fears in Asia It’s jumped from less than $US72 in early July as hopes fade that the war with Iran will allow oil to flow freely again from the Middle East anytime soon. President Donald Trump said on Wednesday that oil prices likely won’t come down until after the US midterm elections in November. The jump has vaulted the price for a gallon of regular gasoline to an average of nearly $US4.28 across the United States, according to AAA. That’s up nearly 34 per cent from a year earlier and is not only costing people more at the pump but also through higher prices for all kinds of products that move by truck to store shelves. A report on Thursday said inflation at the US wholesale level accelerated to 5.4 per cent last month from 4.8 per cent in July, and retailers could eventually pass such increases in prices onto shoppers. A report is coming on Friday that will show how much inflation US consumers are feeling. The typical move to rein in high inflation is for the Federal Reserve to raise its main interest rate, the federal funds rate. Such a move then filters out through the rest of the bond market, makes it more expensive for US households and businesses to borrow money, slows the overall economy and undercuts prices for investments. That hopefully would remove some of inflation’s fuel.



A report on Thursday suggested the US job market may remain solid, with fewer workers applying for unemployment benefits last week. That could give the Fed more confidence that the economy could withstand higher interest rates. Following Thursday’s reports, traders see a roughly 73 per cent chance the Fed will raise the federal funds rate at its meeting next week. That’s up from the 61 per cent probability seen the day before, according to data from CME Group. That’s also despite Trump’s consistent lobbying for interest rates to go lower rather than higher. The Fed’s counterpart in Europe, the European Central Bank, raised its own interest rates on Thursday in hopes of getting inflation in check. It cited “the conflict in the Middle East” and how it “continues to generate inflation pressures.” It all pushed the yield on the 10-year Treasury up to 4.95 per cent from 4.83 per cent late Wednesday, which is a significant move for the bond market. It’s up from just 3.97 per cent before the war with Iran began and is back to where it was in the autumn of 2023. That was after the Fed cranked the federal funds rate higher to get super-high inflation coming out of the COVID pandemic under better control.



Higher yields mean investors can make more money putting their money into bonds, which can in turn make investors less willing to pay high prices for stocks and other investments that are riskier than bonds. Some investors see a 5 per cent yield on the 10-year Treasury as the next potential flashpoint. But strategists at Bank of America’s Research Investment Committee suggest 7 per cent may be the more important threshold, pointing to peaks for expensive stocks around that point in the past. Related Article Opinion

Bonds Trump’s ‘top bond salesman’ is getting a reality check Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist In the meantime, the rising 10-year Treasury yield is making mortgages more expensive and hurting the housing industry. One report on Thursday said the average long-term US mortgage rate hit its highest level in over 14 months, while a second one said sales of previously occupied US homes fell in August to their slowest pace in more than a year. That helped sent stocks of homebuilders lower, including drops of 3.5 per cent for Lennar and 2.4 per cent for D.R. Horton.



Elsewhere on Wall Street, Macy’s fell 4.7 per cent even though the retailer reported stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. While raising its forecast for earnings this fiscal year, it warned that “there are macroeconomic and geopolitical factors that could influence” how much its customers feel comfortable spending. Macy’s said it received $US116 million ($162 million) in tariff refunds from the government — $US98 million during the quarter and another $US18 million after the quarter ended. Macy’s CEO Tony Spring told The Associated Press Thursday that it’s using some of the proceeds to lower prices on certain items like furniture and other big-ticket purchases. All told, the S&P 500 fell 44.66 points to 7,591.70. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 316.56 to 52,064.10, and the Nasdaq composite sank 171.62 to 26,081.72. In stock markets abroad, indexes slipped across much of Europe and Asia. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng dropped 1.3 per cent for one of the world’s biggest moves. World.title: This rising indie rock star has done his 10,000 hours, and it shows
World.content:
CultureMusicReview This rising indie rock star has done his 10,000 hours, and it shows Annie Toller and and John Shand September 11, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Nate Amos’ earworms are always catchy but rarely too sweet. This Is Lorelei, The Singer in My Band ★★★★ By the time his first official, label-anointed album came out in 2024, Nate Amos had done his 10,000 hours. Over the years he’d uploaded scores of releases to Bandcamp under the name This Is Lorelei – work that, until recently, was just a side project to his long-running art-pop outfit Water From Your Eyes. Now, it’s coming into its own. The years of compulsive attention to craft have paid dividends: his latest album, The Singer in My Band, is a tight, affecting collection of songs, flitting deftly between power-pop, alt-country and pop-punk.



There are goofy moments – like single Billy Came Back, a zippy jangle-pop tale of a local karaoke legend blowing back into town – but gut punches too, especially in the resonant, open-stringed numbers that fill the album’s second half. The arrangements are always catchy but rarely too sweet: even the earworm hook and cascading harmonies of highlight Oh No Now My are paired with a taut, digitally tortured guitar solo. This Is Lorelei’s Nate Amos has taken his one-time side project to centre stage. Eve Alpert Though billed as a road album, written and recorded amid a relentless touring schedule, The Singer in My Band was finished at Amos’ family home with cameos from his father and sister, both professional bluegrass musicians. It feels like a grounding moment in his trajectory – a return to centre as a solo artist, led by songwriting-first principles. Annie Toller



A sophisticated sense of mischief fuels the jazz group’s new album. Zela Margossian Quintet, Remedy ★★★★ You know that feeling when you revisit a home from your past, to find the furniture changed and walls repainted, so any familiarity or nostalgia are jumbled with an unsettling newness? This third Zela Margossian Quintet album is like that.



The familiarity of the snaking melodies of Margossian’s Armenian roots, and of her rigorous classical training being entwined with jazz’s open-endedness, are still there, but her compositions are even more sophisticated and varied, with a delightful sense of mischief sometimes creeping in. The band, meanwhile, is joined by guest artists on four pieces, swelling the already expansive palette of colours generated by Margossian’s piano, Stuart Vandegraff’s saxophones, Jacques Emery’s bass, Alexander Inman-Hislop’s drums and Adem Yilmaz’s array of percussion. Phil Slater’s trumpet cries gently over a lament called Indifferent World – a reality with which we’re all familiar. The stateliness of Jenny Eriksson’s viola da gamba features on What If, the title possibly asking what would happen were that instrument added to this already exotic band. The answer? A dreamy timelessness. Virna Sanzone applies her plush voice to the Armenian lyrics of How I Wish, and flamenco guitarist Damian Wright makes Kintsugi glisten like sunlight on water. World.title: Sex, drugs and a legend redefined: it’s time to meet the real Marianne Faithfull
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Marianne Faithfull died last year, directors Iain Forsyth and Jane Pollard had been working on a film about her for four years. Watching Broken English, named for the hit album she made in 1979, you can see what a compelling subject she was. A ’60s survivor, still probably best known to an older generation as Mick Jagger’s ex-girlfriend and the subject of scandal, she emerges as a formidable woman who was also a singer, writer and actor, the kind of liminal artist who popped up in collaborations with professional fans from Metallica to Nick Cave. In her ’70s, she is in a wheelchair, hooked up to an oxygen tank: the result of long COVID. Whatever, she still commands the room. Broken English isn’t so much an account of her life as a response to it, pitched somewhere between documentary, essay and fiction. Archive footage is sprinkled between interviews with Faithfull herself. These are set within an imaginary “Ministry of Not Forgetting”, the questions asked by “an archivist” played by 1917 star George MacKay. Derek Jacobi narrates the film and Tilda Swinton plays the head of the ministry, who at one point lists Faithfull’s many achievements before concluding: “And yet, to the world at large, she’s still just Mick Jagger’s girlfriend. Well, f--- that.” Tilda Swinton stars in the unconventional documentary. In his role as archivist, MacKay wears an earpiece to hear the directors urging him to push a point or drop it, depending on Faithfull’s answers. Clearly, they never aimed to cover Faithfull’s entire life. The juiciest scandal from her Stones era is left out. Her youthful heroin addiction is in there, but the gruesome details of her life on the street that she described in her autobiography aren’t. And while her first husband, John Dunbar, appears with her, Jagger does not. “I didn’t know how to make him a part of it,” Pollard says with a short laugh. “I really enjoyed reframing it, looking at that period of her life from the perspective of her childhood, growing up in a commune.”



With the Stones, she says, “they all felt they were all working towards something that felt really important”. But, as Faithfull reflects herself, that wasn’t how she was seen. She was cast as a rock’n’roll casualty. She was the woman arrested in a drug raid wearing only a fur coat. For the tabloids, she was a terrific story. The filmmakers set out to tell a different story. Their approach to the years Faithfull spent with Jagger, for example, was to shift their gaze away from the usual catalogue of disasters. We learn how Faithfull took Jagger to see the Royal Ballet with Rudolf Nureyev, knowing he would love it; we see that she joined in a poetry event with the Beat poets and became a lifelong friend of Allen Ginsberg. Marianne Faithfull with George MacKay in Broken English. Madman Films “All these cultural things that she was absorbed in and that she was sharing with Mick, things that felt a lot more relevant and interesting than just who at the end of the day she was going to bed with,” Forsyth says. “I hope that as much as the film is a story about a life, it’s just as much a film about how we choose to tell that story.” Forsyth and Pollard are best known to Australian audiences for their inventive 2014 film about Nick Cave, 20,000 Days On Earth. They first became interested in Faithfull because Cave and his musical partner Warren Ellis knew her well; Ellis worked with her as a producer and toured with her, playing in her band. “In the year before the lockdown, we would chat to Warren a lot,” says Pollard. “He was working on the poetry album She Walks in Beauty with her when she got COVID and went into a coma. He was just heartbroken, in the studio working on the poems, not knowing if she would ever hear them. I think at that point, our hearts found her in a different way. We began to care about her a lot, just vicariously, through him.” Marianne Faithfull with her friend and collaborator Warren Ellis. Rosie Matheson



The interviews with MacKay at the Ministry of Not Forgetting were among the first things they did, afraid that Faithfull’s precarious health would collapse again. After that, they worked on the film’s mosaic structure of memories and other interviews, showing her assembled segments as they went along. From the start, they expected that by the time they finished the work, she would no longer be with them, but they never intended it as an obituary. “The film needed, in some way, to acknowledge her passing, but not to change,” says Forsyth. “We were so determined it wasn’t going to be like a standard text with dates. That felt so at odds with it; it’s so alive with her humour and artistry and brilliance – with her defiance, actually.” George MacKay is 34. He had worked several times with Pollard and Forsyth on art projects, but he knew almost nothing about Marianne Faithfull. “I knew one or two of her songs without knowing they were hers,” he says. He threw himself into research. When he saw how she was pilloried and derided in the press during her Stones period, he was aghast. “It was awful, just on a human level, what was said about her,” he says. “The misogyny she came up against was so intense.” Although he worked from a script, he says the interviews felt like improvisations. “Because Marianne had never seen those scripts – and you have to follow wherever the interview goes.” The Ministry of Not Forgetting sounds as if it could have come from a Harry Potter novel, but it is a key idea for the filmmakers. “Not forgetting was a deliberate act, to make remembering active,” says Forsyth.



“If you choose not to forget, you make the effort. Whereas remembering something is an accident. Do I remember where I left my car keys?” Pollard chips in. “It’s also about learning lessons. The act of remembering seems loaded with a kind of sentimentality; it feels wistful in a way, whereas not forgetting is a recalibration. It has an urgency.” Broken English was billed at last year’s film festivals in Sundance and Venice as a documentary, but Forsyth isn’t sure that holds. “For us, the idea of going into a project saying ‘we are going to make a documentary’ just seems so alien, so limited from the start,” he says. “I think we were going into it thinking, ‘We are going to make a film that tells a story, and we want to make the best film and tell the best story we can.’ For me, ‘non-fiction’ works as well as anything because the story we’re telling is not fiction, although we might be using some of the devices of fictional storytelling. I think the story we’re telling is full of emotional truth. Which is not the same as journalistic truth.” Related Article Cinema Crash to classic: How Practical Magic’s box-office hex marked the spot for Nicole Kidman and Sandra Bullock For Pollard, the real discoveries in the film are the expressions that flicker across Faithfull’s face as she looks at the old footage of her younger self, beautiful and damaged but still holding up her end of things. “There’s a piece from Weekend World in 1974 or ’75, an interview she probably should have said ‘no’ to, when she had just come out of rehab,” she says. Watching it, Faithfull initially looks dismissive of that young idiot, opining on life. “Then she starts to align with her. And I’m looking from face to face, and I’m seeing the same eyes, I’m seeing the same smile, and I’m seeing the same willingness to be open. We all can all read a face – and cinema is the best way for us to do that. That’s when the film is revelatory.” Broken English opens nationally on September 17.

World.title: Blood, lies and cartels: Five new crime books to read this month
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The noir label has been tenuously attached to all manner of crime fiction of late. But rather than being identified by a landscape (think rural or outback noir), or geography (Nordic noir), or even a setting (domestic noir), the real deal features a hapless character who is always on the outer and for whom things are never going to turn out well. Just Like the Night by Michael Caleb Tasker Michael Caleb Tasker, author of the impressive first novel Just Like the Night (Allen & Unwin, $35), knows this only too well since he has written a PhD thesis exploring the existential roots of noir fiction. Meet 12-year-old Sera sitting in an El Paso hotel room while her father Ray stacks the decks in preparation for an elaborate sting. “There’s a fine line between being a magician and a card sharp,” he tells her. Despite being as sharp as a knife himself, Ray is routinely rumbled and roughed up. As father and daughter drive the length and breadth of the US, eventually decamping to Sydney, Sera wonders “how he made her feel safe while he was still covered in blood”. Fast forward a few decades and Sera is coming to the end of her prison sentence. On her own in a cell, “she’s up early before the sun, face washed, push-ups done and bed made, waiting like there was something to wait for”. To discover what that something might be, Tasker takes us on a round trip to discover what unfolded when Sera and Ray came to Australia, what has happened to them since, and how Sera manages her parole when she discovers that her estranged daughter is being used and abused by the kind of bad man her father never was. Just Like the Night is tightly written, occasionally violent and very noir, especially the haunting conclusion. The Damned by Matt Rogers If violence is not your thing then look away now since The Damned by Matt Rogers (Simon & Schuster, $40) is a veritable bloodbath. While initially a tad hesitant, after reading this sentence “Quadriceps flare beneath faded gym shorts as he balances two hundred and forty pounds of authentic Japanese straw on one shoulder”, I was in. Logan Booth (he of the flaring quadriceps) is a contract killer of Reacheresque proportions and this is his third outing.



Unlike Lee Child’s Reacher, Booth has an offsider, a diminutive, gay, recovering meth addict, whose love and loyalty to Logan ensure we know from the start the latter is a “good guy” despite his propensity to off people at an alarming rate. The fact that the president of the United States wants Logan dead is another tick in his favour. This time, the flaring quadriceps are headed to Colombia to rescue a former lover before Logan finds himself up against a nasty cartel determined to take him out. The violence inflicted on both sides is surprisingly inventive and beautifully choreographed once you get over the gore factor and the prose style. This is the kind of propulsive crime that might make you burn the soup. I did. The Burn by Jessica Mansour-Nahra Jessica Mansour-Nahra’s The Burn (Hachette, $25) is of a different order of flammable magnitude. Set in 2030, it imagines an Australia emerging from a five-month lockdown caused by rampant wildfires on a national scale. It’s a timely scenario given the disasters affecting Europe during their summer and dire warnings of worse to come. After months of enforced isolation writing uplifting social media posts for her university employer’s website, Carmen is suspiciously reluctant to leave her featureless apartment and a dying pothos plant. But her three former high school chums have different plans: a camping trip on the idyllic south-east coast that has so far escaped the fires. What could possibly go wrong? Lots apparently, but there will also be time for Carmen to ruminate on her chequered sexual history and “her broken, disparate family”. This includes her Finnish scientist father who has remarried and is deeply concerned about the fate of the walrus, her distant scientist mother somewhere in the Indian Ocean with her new German husband, and her horse-loving older sister Anna with whom she has always had a taut and tricky relationship. There’s a lot to work through. While Burn is labelled as a psychological thriller, and it is indeed that, there are also telling reflections on the power of social media for good and evil. As it emerges, it’s not just bushfires we have to worry about.



Every Time She Wakes by Petronella McGovern Nevertheless, bushfires also figure in Petronella McGovern’s latest suburban thriller, Every Time She Wakes (Allen & Unwin, $35). University careers counsellor, Suzanne Vitale, is sleepless and fretting at 2.30am when the Rural Fire Service arrives to evacuate her and her family ahead of the firestorm. Bundled into a van, it’s not long before Suzanne suspects they are being abducted rather than rescued begging the question: why? There’s scant time to consider the options as the van crashes and Suzanne wakes up. Although it might be assumed that it was all a bad dream, McGovern is playing trickier plot games. While there’s a clue in the fact that Suzanne’s eldest daughter Frankie is studying a unit on “Metaphysics, Reality, Time and Possibility”, it might be more helpful to think Groundhog Day meets Sliding Doors. Like most domestic protagonists, Suzanne’s got a lot to figure out about her life and work. This includes how best to handle student complaints concerning a repulsive radio shock jock named Rowdy Mac who has made a bankable career demeaning women. Bells ringing anyone? Rowdy’s been hiring Suzanne’s students as interns, before he moves on to Suzanne’s daughter and her best friend who is a social media influencer. This is another book with something to say about the contemporary media landscape. Given that Suzanne has to relive the bushfire scenario again and again until she gets it right, it’s tricky to summarise a plot that effectively works backwards rather than forwards. Thankfully it all makes sense in the end although you may be left wondering just how she did it. McGovern, that is. You Know What You Did by K.T. Nguyen American author K.T. Nguyen is also playing inventive mind games in her psychological thriller You Know What You Did (No Exit Press, $33) which is heavy on the psychology and light on the thrills. Annie Shaw is a budding artist with a teenage daughter, an entitled war-reporter husband and a Vietnamese mother hoarding all manner of detritus in the carriage house of their large estate. Annie also suffers from punishing bouts of a disgust-driven obsessive-compulsive disorder that is painfully realised. She takes a lot of very hot showers.

World.title: The Coalition is betting that people mistrust Albanese more than big tech
World.content:
PoliticsFederalDigital hygiene Opinion The Coalition is betting that people mistrust Albanese more than big tech Waleed Aly Columnist, author and academic September 11, 2026 — 5:03am

September 11, 2026 — 5:03am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Of course we’re talking about censorship. It could be no other way when a government tries to regulate the internet. We saw it a couple of years ago when the Albanese government tried to pass laws to deal with online misinformation and disinformation. We’re seeing it this week as it tries to take on the social media companies’ algorithms. In the former case, the government ultimately abandoned the cause. In this case, I can’t imagine any such backdown. But the debate will take a very familiar shape: the government legislating in an extremely tricky area with the stated aim of preventing harm, opposition parties accusing it of trying to remake the internet in its political image. The government’s social media pitch is trying to do two things at once. Dionne Gain There are some genuine free-speech issues at play here. There are also some red herrings. That’s because the Albanese government’s bill is trying to do two quite separate things. One, to give social media users the ability to opt out of the algorithm that feeds them suggested content. Two, to stem the torrents of what it calls “seriously harmful” online content that has people veering off into extremist misogyny or being led into having eating disorders. The objection of censorship is meaningful to the second, but it’s totally irrelevant to the first. The problem is that it’s being used to reject the whole lot. And I suspect that’s going to create a political problem down the track, especially for the Coalition, which has now officially declared it opposes the legislation.



To force social media companies to let their users switch off their algorithm doesn’t stop anyone saying or publishing anything. It doesn’t even stop social media companies producing offering to feed you content via their algorithms. It means only that you’re not compelled to be subjected to that. The relevant idea here isn’t censorship, but choice. The threat here is to the business model of the tech giants in the (unlikely) event lots of people opt out. But it is not to speech. Related Article Social media Algorithm shake-up will hurt right-wing parties, censorship fight heats up It’s far more fraught, though, to legislate that social media organisations must ensure a “safe online environment”, where people are “protected from seriously harmful material”. What’s “seriously harmful”? The bill has a list of horrible things: content encouraging child sex abuse, sexual violence, death and rape threats, encouraging suicide or self-harm, supporting terrorism, or promoting illicit drug use. But the real controversy is over what comes next. The bill would allow the minister simply to declare other things to be seriously harmful, too, and it would be so. That’s the thrust of the Coalition and One Nation’s objection: it puts the declaration of harm in the hands of the government of the day, “a blank cheque for political censorship to the minister”, in Angus Taylor’s phrase. Say she wants to designate anti-immigration content seriously harmful. Or climate-change denying content. Or anti-Israeli content. This sort of thing, they say, is entirely possible under the law, and would silence political debate. There’s half a point here. The government retorts that whatever the minister adds to the list, the senate can take away with a vote. That’s something, but it’s not as much as it seems. It puts the onus not on the government to get a majority, but on its opponents to do so. Any government will probably have a significant presence in the senate. To have a majority against it will require something close to a total alliance from all the non-government senators. In the current parliament, for instance, it would need something akin to an alignment between the Coalition, One Nation and the Greens to reverse the minister’s decision. That means that if a minister’s decision is very political – appealing to true believers on the left or the right – it will be very hard to reverse.



But it’s only half a point because this is easy enough to fix. You simply require any additions to the “seriously harmful” list to be passed through the parliament like any other amendment. That means that instead of them being at the whim of government, they’d express the will of the parliament. At least in theory, they’d capture the will of the public more broadly. I suspect nakedly partisan attempts to regulate online content wouldn’t be able to get through all that. Related Article Opinion

Meta Things seemed so much better in Back to the Future II Waleed Aly Columnist, author and academic If I had to guess, I’d say that’s what the Albanese government will do. It’s an easy enough compromise to make, and it immediately dilutes the most powerful free speech objection. But that’s where things would get really interesting. Because if the Albanese government made that sort of change, what would the other parties do? One Nation is easy enough to predict. It doesn’t want a single thing to change. The algorithm suits it perfectly. It lives in a world where social media influencers tell you the truth, and the ABC doesn’t. It is completely unmoved by any campaign to “fix our feeds” because it doesn’t see anything broken. For that reason, it doesn’t even need to get into intricate arguments about what is and isn’t censorship. But the Coalition is in a bind. It clearly accepts the dangers of social media on some level. It’s easy to forget that Peter Dutton proposed the teen social media ban before Labor did. Its Shadow Minister for Communications and Digital Safety has spoken of “dreadful algorithms” which are engines of “insidious psychological manipulation”.



But its deputy leader is Matt Canavan, who has dismissed any suggestion at all that the algorithm is a problem. That’s why the Coalition has to lean so heavily on the idea of censorship. It’s not so much that the Coalition are free speech purists - after all they began this week arguing for a law to ban burning the Australian flag. It’s that on an issue like this one, censorship is the only argument that allows them to reconcile the opposing positions within. As long as you can say Labor’s solution is an attempt at thought control, you don’t need to decide whether social media algorithms are dangerous or not. It’s banking, then, on people mistrusting the Albanese government more than it mistrusts big tech. And if the teen social media ban shows us anything, it’s that Labor quite likes that match-up. And if in the meantime it has shown a willingness to make changes, to address legitimate free-speech concerns, the Coalition might once again find itself marooned on its own divided island – unclear on what to fight for, and against whom. And, unable to decide on what it really thinks of social media, there’s a real risk it takes the fight to itself. Waleed Aly is a broadcaster, author, academic and regular columnist. He is the author of the current Quarterly Essay, Time of Monsters: What future for liberalism? The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.
