World.title: Tensions erupted between two Sydney councillors. They might have to attend mediation
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWSydney councils Tensions erupted between two Sydney councillors. They might have to attend mediation Megan Gorrey September 11, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An inquiry into allegations of dysfunction and maladministration at a Sydney council is poised to urge state government intervention that would require councillors to lift their performance, but has stopped short of recommending they get the sack. Draft recommendations from the Office of Local Government’s long-running inquiry into Liverpool City Council suggested Local Government Minister Ron Hoenig should consider issuing the organisation with performance improvement orders – a mechanism that gives councils the chance to resolve governance, performance or financial problems before actions such as suspension. Liverpool Mayor Ned Mannoun. Dion Georgopoulos Commissioner Ross Glover, whose report from last year’s hearing is due to be released imminently, also suggested in his draft recommendations that Liberal Mayor Ned Mannoun and his long-time political rival, councillor Peter Ristevski, attend mediation to repair their fractious relationship. The tensions between Mannoun and Ristevski, who was a Liberal and independent before joining the Family First Party last month, were among matters scrutinised during the 52-day public inquiry.



It examined councillors’ conduct as well as the council’s handling of finances, property purchases, more than $150 million in state government grants for infrastructure, and staff employment – including its revolving door of 10 acting or permanent chief executive officers in eight years. Related Article Sydney councils Inside the ‘brutal’ civil war tearing apart a Sydney council A spokeswoman for Hoenig said on Thursday the minister had received the final report from the inquiry and was closely considering its recommendations. Glover distributed more than 40 draft recommendations – related to elected officials, council staff and the Office of Local Government – to parties to the inquiry for their feedback in late August. The draft document does not include a recommendation for the council to be sacked or suspended; however, the commissioner’s findings and final recommendations are contained in the final report.



Among the draft recommendations is a suggestion that Hoenig consider whether performance improvement orders be issued and, if so, whether a temporary adviser should be appointed to help the council meet its requirements. Councils can be suspended if they fail to comply with the orders. The draft document also recommends that Mannoun and Ristevski participate in a “structured mediation process” conducted by a person “with appropriate skills and experience in resolving interpersonal conflict, including in the workplace environment, the cost of which is to be borne by the council” within three months of the commissioner’s final report being tabled in parliament. Liverpool councillor Peter Ristevski gives evidence at the NSW Office of Local Government inquiry. Liverpool Council inquiry He suggested changes to legislation that would require a council’s governing body to have a two-thirds majority when deciding to pursue a no-fault termination of the general manager. The commissioner also recommended the council implement a process to audio-visually record parts of council meetings held in closed session; review recruitment processes and policies to include guidance as to when it would be appropriate to make direct and temporary appointments; and arrange training for councillors on conflicts of interest and respectful debate in meetings.



Liverpool Council declined to comment on the draft recommendations. Hoenig told a budget estimates hearing this month the cost of the inquiry was $4 to $4.5 million. Related Article Sydney councils This Sydney council was meant to pick a new deputy mayor. A jaunt to the UK got in the way The inquiry was triggered by an interim report that was provided to Hoenig in 2024 and prompted him to describe the allegations against council as “the worst I’ve ever seen”. He signalled his intent to suspend councillors and tried to postpone that year’s election until the inquiry was completed. The report was part of a broader investigation into the council’s recruitment and staffing processes, which the government said unearthed “matters sufficient in seriousness and volume” to warrant an immediate public hearing.



The council launched action against Hoenig in the NSW Land and Environment Court in a bid for the election to go ahead as scheduled. Judge John Robson found the interim report failed to observe the requirements of procedural fairness as it was published without giving named individuals an opportunity to respond. But he said the government had not unduly influenced the probe, clearing the path for the inquiry to go ahead. World.title: ‘It doesn’t matter who puts the jumper on’: How the Swans replaced the irreplaceable
World.content:
SportAFLSydney Swans ‘It doesn’t matter who puts the jumper on’: How the Swans replaced the irreplaceable Jonathan Drennan September 11, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Away from football, Sydney Swans chairman Andrew Pridham has built a successful career in finance, a world in which assessing risk and preparing for the consequences are essential tools of the trade. When the Swans suspended five key players on August 18 for breaching club standards, Pridham was well aware it would likely end their season, and admitted publicly the club had “effectively torpedoed” its premiership chances. It was, he believed, a necessary step. Charlie Curnow kicked five goals in an outstanding performance in the qualifying final victory over Brisbane. Getty Images The Swans arrived at the SCG last Saturday to take on back-to-back premiers Brisbane in a qualifying final without Riley Bice, Nick Blakey, Isaac Heeney, James Jordon and Chad Warner. The corresponding magnets on the whiteboard of coach Dean Cox were impossible to replace. Heeney is ranked second in the league for score involvements while Warner is ranked first for goal assists. Blakey is one of the best rebounding defenders in the game, with Bice a key emerging talent, while Jordon can nullify the opposition’s best players as a tagger.



Outside of the Swans, little was expected of their replacements: Caiden Cleary, Angus Sheldrick, Jake Lloyd, Harry Cunningham and James Rowbottom. All were talented, but unheralded. Reliable veterans such as Lloyd and Cunningham, raw youngsters like Cleary and Sheldrick and finally, the selfless Rowbottom, who was carrying a hand injury. The talent of the suspended “Pullman Five” players could never be replaced, but those in the club’s inner sanctum were quietly confident they could make up for it in other ways. “How easy is this?” Swans forward Logan McDonald played the game of his life. AFL Photos Few could have predicted what transpired next. The Swans simply blew the Lions away with a performance built on resilience, pressure and, above all, relentless work ethic. Pridham is a lifelong fan of the Swans, but had never seen anything like it. “Without question, it was our best ever performance on the SCG, and I don’t think anyone would doubt that against the odds,” Pridham said.



“It’s just a credit to the players and the coaches ... the circumstances leading into it clearly were very challenging for everybody. “I’m talking about very challenging loss of sleep, just confusion as to how this has happened and all that sort of stuff. ‘Without question, it was our best ever performance on the SCG.’ Andrew Pridham “And I think to be able to gather themselves, I think it certainly unified the group that, if you’re out there representing the club, that’s really, really important. “You’re putting the jumper on, It doesn’t matter who puts the jumper on. Once you’re out there, you’ve got to play your role.



“So I think what it showed is, as a club, but certainly the players and the coaches, we’re very resilient. We’re very unified. And I think they were relentless ... I think that what has been forgotten a bit, we’ve actually still got a very, very good team.” According to Champion Data, the Swans made 24 tackles in the third quarter to Brisbane’s 10, highlighting an ability to sustain immense pressure. James Rowbottom celebrates with former coach John Longmire AFL Photos via Getty Images At the centre of the effort was Rowbottom, one of the club’s quiet leaders and potentially, a captain in waiting. The UNSW commerce student finished the game with seven tackles and six centre clearances. Finals football demands sacrifice, and Rowbottom epitomised it for the Swans. Gerard Healy, a member of the Swans’ team of the century, pointed to a memorable performance by Errol Gulden, who finished the game with 34 disposals and a goal, but believed it was Rowbottom’s selflessness against Brisbane that provided the platform for others to shine.



“It was manic pressure and ultimately pressure can unravel even the greatest teams,” Healy said. “If the greatest teams like Brisbane aren’t going to apply the same sort of level of pressure and meet the oncoming pressure head on, well, they’re going to fall over – no matter how much skill they have. “Everybody wants to focus on Errol [Gulden], and he was brilliant, obviously. But from the very first minute, Rowbottom – who, if you think back to the start of the year, there was a question mark on his future. And I remember saying on radio, I was going to sell my life membership if they traded Rowbottom. “Rowbottom is, in my view, such a pivotal piece of that Swans club and team. His performance was amazing, and I was very proud of the way he went about it.” Six members of the Swans team that defeated Brisbane had never played finals football. Harry Kyle and Billy Cootee only made their club debuts this season, while Cleary, Sheldrick, Jesse Dattoli and Tom Hanily had not previously experienced the pressure of September football.



Related Article AFL 2026 ‘Brought me back into footy’: How Barry Hall’s kids reconnected him with the Swans Two years ago, forward Logan McDonald played on an injured ankle in the grand final and was powerless as the Swans slumped to an agonising 60-point defeat to the Lions. McDonald then sat out the whole of last season. On Saturday against Brisbane, he stood up when his team needed him most, kicking a career-high six goals alongside fellow forwards Charlie Curnow and Tom Papley who finished with five majors each. “I just sat there in awe,” Healy said. “It was therapeutic, it was inspiring, it was all those things. “And I was just thrilled for the playing group and the club – and football, in many ways – because it had received a big black eye ... I thought the club always was going to take some time to rebuild its position and in many ways, that’s still true, but they made a good start last weekend.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: ‘Chilling’: AI giant Anthropic says it blocked possible efforts to build biological weapons
World.content:
TechnologyAI ‘Chilling’: AI giant Anthropic says it blocked possible efforts to build biological weapons Dustin Volz September 11, 2026 — 6:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Anthropic said it had disrupted several potential plots this year by scientists who used its leading artificial intelligence models to conduct research that could have helped develop biological weapons. In a report describing misuses of its AI models, Anthropic said it could not determine whether the research served a legitimate or nefarious purpose because valid biological inquiry — the kind that can lead to breakthroughs like vaccines — can also help engineer dangerous pathogens. In the face of that uncertainty, Anthropic said it erred on the side of caution because the consequences of missing malicious activity could be severe. The potential for cutting-edge AI models to facilitate the development of known or entirely new biological pathogens is among the gravest concerns experts have about a technology that is developing so rapidly that even its leading architects doubt whether humans will be able to fully control it. AP “You are not seeing someone in a comic book kind of way say, ‘Hey, I want to build a biological weapon to kill everybody,’” Jacob Klein, the head of threat intelligence at Anthropic, said in an interview. “It’s an incredibly nuanced situation.” The potential for cutting-edge AI models to facilitate the development of known or entirely new biological pathogens is among the gravest concerns experts have about a technology that is developing so rapidly that even its leading architects doubt whether humans will be able to fully control it.



Compared with the threat of catastrophic cyberattacks or AI agents that fail to align with human intentions, biological misuse has gained less attention as an existential risk of AI, in part because past examples have generally been shown only in research settings rather than in the real world. Andrew Weber, a senior fellow on the Council on Strategic Risks who reviewed Anthropic’s report before its release, said the findings were “chilling examples of state-sponsored biological weapons developers tapping into the rapidly advancing capabilities” of leading AI models. Related Article AI ‘Could kill us all’: Anthropic insiders say AI has more than 10% chance of ending humanity – soon The lengthy report Anthropic published on Thursday catalogued a litany of misuses of its AI models, including the chatbot Claude, over the past eight months. Some examples were similar to past disclosures from Anthropic and other AI labs, including suspected Chinese and Iranian government-linked actors targeting dissident and diaspora communities for surveillance. The report also highlighted cases of Russian state media using Claude to generate online propaganda masquerading as independent reporting, including fabricated claims about an election in Moldova.



Anthropic documented another genre of abuse it said was new: attempts to use Claude to develop software for conventional weapons design and development, including firearms, missiles, armed drones and bombs. It detailed three cases in China, two in Russia and one in Yemen. The report does not identify by name which parties were involved in the Yemeni case, but the context makes clear that it is referring to the Iran-backed Houthi militia. AI use by terrorist networks is a growing concern among US security officials. But among all the categories of threats shared in the report, none may be as worrisome as the biological research cases. Anthropic did not disclose the names of researchers or institutions that it blocked, their countries of affiliation or the specific biological agents at issue, in part because of its uncertainty about their aims. The lengthy report Anthropic published on Thursday catalogued a litany of misuses of its AI models, including the chatbot Claude, over the past eight months. AP Photo/Patrick Sison Still, Anthropic said the scientists circumvented its controls intended to prevent users from blocked regions from gaining access to its AI models and worked to “obfuscate the purpose of their research to evade our safeguards.” The company banned accounts associated with the research.



In one example from May, a scientist sought Claude’s help with writing a grant application for funding to conduct research intended to experiment on the chikungunya virus, a mosquito-borne malady that can lead to months of severe pain and other symptoms. Such research, known as gain of function, can be legitimate and lead to vaccine development, but it can also create superbug versions of viruses. In this instance, the scientist wanted to engineer mutations to the virus that would make it more harmful as it repeatedly infected live animals. Anthropic said it believed the particular research was worrisome in part because it could discern that the work was intended to be performed at a military research institute. The findings are ‘chilling examples of state-sponsored biological weapons developers tapping into the rapidly advancing capabilities.’ Andrew Weber, a senior fellow on the Council on Strategic Risks “What we don’t know is if the research was meant to be weaponised,” Klein said. “But a military institution doing gain-of-function research is concerning.” Anthropic said evaluations from last year of its older models demonstrated that they were not yet able to meaningfully assist in conducting dangerous biological research. Its current models are more able to complete complex scientific research, the company said, which spurred tighter safeguards intended to restrict access to a wide range of dual-use biological research queries.



Susan Monarez, a microbiologist and public health expert who oversaw a review of national biosecurity preparedness in the Obama administration, also reviewed the Anthropic report before its publication. She said the findings provided real-world evidence to support concerns that bad actors were trying to covertly use advanced AI “to improve their chances of building biological pathogens that could cause significant harm.” Related Article Analysis

AI ‘We must be stopped’: Why Australia needs to listen to the experts on AI Monarez, who briefly served as the director of the Centres for Disease Control and Prevention last year, said AI held enormous promise to usher in an era of medical breakthroughs that save and extend lives. But the same abilities that make that possible, she added, could also “let bad actors hide in plain sight, using seemingly legitimate research to create pathogens we may not see coming and may not be able to stop once released.” Weber of the Council on Strategic Risks, who also served as the assistant secretary of defence for nuclear, chemical and biological defence programs during the Obama administration, called for limiting access to AI tools capable of this level of biological research to trusted researchers only. “The fact that Russia, China and North Korea continue to develop prohibited biological weapons makes it imperative that we deny their researchers access to these extraordinarily capable models,” he said.



This article originally appeared in The New York Times. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

World.title: ASX set to slump, Wall Street falls as oil climbs to its highest mark since May
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to slump, Wall Street falls as oil climbs to its highest mark since May Stan Choe Updated September 11, 2026 — 6:27am ,first published 5:23am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Oil prices keep climbing as the war with Iran keeps clogging the global flow of crude, and they leaped Thursday to their highest levels since before the summer. That worsened worries about inflation and cranked up pressure within the bond market, helping to send stocks lower again on Wall Street. The S&P 500 fell 0.6 per cent for a fourth straight loss, its longest such streak since June, though it’s not far from its all-time high set last month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 316 points, or 0.6 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite sank 0.7 per cent. Oil climbed to its highest mark since March. AP The Australian sharemarket is set for another day of heavy losses, with futures at 6.13am AEST pointing to a loss of 81 points or 0.9 per cent, at the open. The ASX shed 1 per cent on Thursday. The Australian dollar was lower at US71.56¢. US stocks sank under the weight of rising oil prices. Brent crude, the international standard, climbed another 6.3 per cent and briefly topped $US108 per barrel for the first time since May before settling at $US107.63.



Related Article Energy Australia softens local gas supply rules, easing fears in Asia It’s jumped from less than $US72 in early July as hopes fade that the war with Iran will allow oil to flow freely again from the Middle East anytime soon. President Donald Trump said on Wednesday that oil prices likely won’t come down until after the US midterm elections in November. The jump has vaulted the price for a gallon of regular gasoline to an average of nearly $US4.28 across the United States, according to AAA. That’s up nearly 34 per cent from a year earlier and is not only costing people more at the pump but also through higher prices for all kinds of products that move by truck to store shelves. A report on Thursday said inflation at the US wholesale level accelerated to 5.4 per cent last month from 4.8 per cent in July, and retailers could eventually pass such increases in prices onto shoppers. A report is coming on Friday that will show how much inflation US consumers are feeling. The typical move to rein in high inflation is for the Federal Reserve to raise its main interest rate, the federal funds rate. Such a move then filters out through the rest of the bond market, makes it more expensive for US households and businesses to borrow money, slows the overall economy and undercuts prices for investments. That hopefully would remove some of inflation’s fuel.



A report on Thursday suggested the US job market may remain solid, with fewer workers applying for unemployment benefits last week. That could give the Fed more confidence that the economy could withstand higher interest rates. Following Thursday’s reports, traders see a roughly 73 per cent chance the Fed will raise the federal funds rate at its meeting next week. That’s up from the 61 per cent probability seen the day before, according to data from CME Group. That’s also despite Trump’s consistent lobbying for interest rates to go lower rather than higher. The Fed’s counterpart in Europe, the European Central Bank, raised its own interest rates on Thursday in hopes of getting inflation in check. It cited “the conflict in the Middle East” and how it “continues to generate inflation pressures.” It all pushed the yield on the 10-year Treasury up to 4.95 per cent from 4.83 per cent late Wednesday, which is a significant move for the bond market. It’s up from just 3.97 per cent before the war with Iran began and is back to where it was in the autumn of 2023. That was after the Fed cranked the federal funds rate higher to get super-high inflation coming out of the COVID pandemic under better control.



Higher yields mean investors can make more money putting their money into bonds, which can in turn make investors less willing to pay high prices for stocks and other investments that are riskier than bonds. Some investors see a 5 per cent yield on the 10-year Treasury as the next potential flashpoint. But strategists at Bank of America’s Research Investment Committee suggest 7 per cent may be the more important threshold, pointing to peaks for expensive stocks around that point in the past. Related Article Opinion

Bonds Trump’s ‘top bond salesman’ is getting a reality check Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist In the meantime, the rising 10-year Treasury yield is making mortgages more expensive and hurting the housing industry. One report on Thursday said the average long-term US mortgage rate hit its highest level in over 14 months, while a second one said sales of previously occupied US homes fell in August to their slowest pace in more than a year. That helped sent stocks of homebuilders lower, including drops of 3.5 per cent for Lennar and 2.4 per cent for D.R. Horton.



Elsewhere on Wall Street, Macy’s fell 4.7 per cent even though the retailer reported stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. While raising its forecast for earnings this fiscal year, it warned that “there are macroeconomic and geopolitical factors that could influence” how much its customers feel comfortable spending. Macy’s said it received $US116 million ($162 million) in tariff refunds from the government — $US98 million during the quarter and another $US18 million after the quarter ended. Macy’s CEO Tony Spring told The Associated Press Thursday that it’s using some of the proceeds to lower prices on certain items like furniture and other big-ticket purchases. All told, the S&P 500 fell 44.66 points to 7,591.70. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 316.56 to 52,064.10, and the Nasdaq composite sank 171.62 to 26,081.72. In stock markets abroad, indexes slipped across much of Europe and Asia. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng dropped 1.3 per cent for one of the world’s biggest moves. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: This rising indie rock star has done his 10,000 hours, and it shows
World.content:
CultureMusicReview This rising indie rock star has done his 10,000 hours, and it shows Annie Toller and and John Shand September 11, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Nate Amos’ earworms are always catchy but rarely too sweet. This Is Lorelei, The Singer in My Band ★★★★ By the time his first official, label-anointed album came out in 2024, Nate Amos had done his 10,000 hours. Over the years he’d uploaded scores of releases to Bandcamp under the name This Is Lorelei – work that, until recently, was just a side project to his long-running art-pop outfit Water From Your Eyes. Now, it’s coming into its own. The years of compulsive attention to craft have paid dividends: his latest album, The Singer in My Band, is a tight, affecting collection of songs, flitting deftly between power-pop, alt-country and pop-punk.



There are goofy moments – like single Billy Came Back, a zippy jangle-pop tale of a local karaoke legend blowing back into town – but gut punches too, especially in the resonant, open-stringed numbers that fill the album’s second half. The arrangements are always catchy but rarely too sweet: even the earworm hook and cascading harmonies of highlight Oh No Now My are paired with a taut, digitally tortured guitar solo. This Is Lorelei’s Nate Amos has taken his one-time side project to centre stage. Eve Alpert Though billed as a road album, written and recorded amid a relentless touring schedule, The Singer in My Band was finished at Amos’ family home with cameos from his father and sister, both professional bluegrass musicians. It feels like a grounding moment in his trajectory – a return to centre as a solo artist, led by songwriting-first principles. Annie Toller



A sophisticated sense of mischief fuels the jazz group’s new album. Zela Margossian Quintet, Remedy ★★★★ You know that feeling when you revisit a home from your past, to find the furniture changed and walls repainted, so any familiarity or nostalgia are jumbled with an unsettling newness? This third Zela Margossian Quintet album is like that.



The familiarity of the snaking melodies of Margossian’s Armenian roots, and of her rigorous classical training being entwined with jazz’s open-endedness, are still there, but her compositions are even more sophisticated and varied, with a delightful sense of mischief sometimes creeping in. The band, meanwhile, is joined by guest artists on four pieces, swelling the already expansive palette of colours generated by Margossian’s piano, Stuart Vandegraff’s saxophones, Jacques Emery’s bass, Alexander Inman-Hislop’s drums and Adem Yilmaz’s array of percussion. Phil Slater’s trumpet cries gently over a lament called Indifferent World – a reality with which we’re all familiar. The stateliness of Jenny Eriksson’s viola da gamba features on What If, the title possibly asking what would happen were that instrument added to this already exotic band. The answer? A dreamy timelessness. Virna Sanzone applies her plush voice to the Armenian lyrics of How I Wish, and flamenco guitarist Damian Wright makes Kintsugi glisten like sunlight on water. World.title: Sex, drugs and a legend redefined: it’s time to meet the real Marianne Faithfull
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Marianne Faithfull died last year, directors Iain Forsyth and Jane Pollard had been working on a film about her for four years. Watching Broken English, named for the hit album she made in 1979, you can see what a compelling subject she was. A ’60s survivor, still probably best known to an older generation as Mick Jagger’s ex-girlfriend and the subject of scandal, she emerges as a formidable woman who was also a singer, writer and actor, the kind of liminal artist who popped up in collaborations with professional fans from Metallica to Nick Cave. In her ’70s, she is in a wheelchair, hooked up to an oxygen tank: the result of long COVID. Whatever, she still commands the room. Broken English isn’t so much an account of her life as a response to it, pitched somewhere between documentary, essay and fiction. Archive footage is sprinkled between interviews with Faithfull herself. These are set within an imaginary “Ministry of Not Forgetting”, the questions asked by “an archivist” played by 1917 star George MacKay. Derek Jacobi narrates the film and Tilda Swinton plays the head of the ministry, who at one point lists Faithfull’s many achievements before concluding: “And yet, to the world at large, she’s still just Mick Jagger’s girlfriend. Well, f--- that.” Tilda Swinton stars in the unconventional documentary. In his role as archivist, MacKay wears an earpiece to hear the directors urging him to push a point or drop it, depending on Faithfull’s answers. Clearly, they never aimed to cover Faithfull’s entire life. The juiciest scandal from her Stones era is left out. Her youthful heroin addiction is in there, but the gruesome details of her life on the street that she described in her autobiography aren’t. And while her first husband, John Dunbar, appears with her, Jagger does not. “I didn’t know how to make him a part of it,” Pollard says with a short laugh. “I really enjoyed reframing it, looking at that period of her life from the perspective of her childhood, growing up in a commune.”



With the Stones, she says, “they all felt they were all working towards something that felt really important”. But, as Faithfull reflects herself, that wasn’t how she was seen. She was cast as a rock’n’roll casualty. She was the woman arrested in a drug raid wearing only a fur coat. For the tabloids, she was a terrific story. The filmmakers set out to tell a different story. Their approach to the years Faithfull spent with Jagger, for example, was to shift their gaze away from the usual catalogue of disasters. We learn how Faithfull took Jagger to see the Royal Ballet with Rudolf Nureyev, knowing he would love it; we see that she joined in a poetry event with the Beat poets and became a lifelong friend of Allen Ginsberg. Marianne Faithfull with George MacKay in Broken English. Madman Films “All these cultural things that she was absorbed in and that she was sharing with Mick, things that felt a lot more relevant and interesting than just who at the end of the day she was going to bed with,” Forsyth says. “I hope that as much as the film is a story about a life, it’s just as much a film about how we choose to tell that story.” Forsyth and Pollard are best known to Australian audiences for their inventive 2014 film about Nick Cave, 20,000 Days On Earth. They first became interested in Faithfull because Cave and his musical partner Warren Ellis knew her well; Ellis worked with her as a producer and toured with her, playing in her band. “In the year before the lockdown, we would chat to Warren a lot,” says Pollard. “He was working on the poetry album She Walks in Beauty with her when she got COVID and went into a coma. He was just heartbroken, in the studio working on the poems, not knowing if she would ever hear them. I think at that point, our hearts found her in a different way. We began to care about her a lot, just vicariously, through him.” Marianne Faithfull with her friend and collaborator Warren Ellis. Rosie Matheson



The interviews with MacKay at the Ministry of Not Forgetting were among the first things they did, afraid that Faithfull’s precarious health would collapse again. After that, they worked on the film’s mosaic structure of memories and other interviews, showing her assembled segments as they went along. From the start, they expected that by the time they finished the work, she would no longer be with them, but they never intended it as an obituary. “The film needed, in some way, to acknowledge her passing, but not to change,” says Forsyth. “We were so determined it wasn’t going to be like a standard text with dates. That felt so at odds with it; it’s so alive with her humour and artistry and brilliance – with her defiance, actually.” George MacKay is 34. He had worked several times with Pollard and Forsyth on art projects, but he knew almost nothing about Marianne Faithfull. “I knew one or two of her songs without knowing they were hers,” he says. He threw himself into research. When he saw how she was pilloried and derided in the press during her Stones period, he was aghast. “It was awful, just on a human level, what was said about her,” he says. “The misogyny she came up against was so intense.” Although he worked from a script, he says the interviews felt like improvisations. “Because Marianne had never seen those scripts – and you have to follow wherever the interview goes.” The Ministry of Not Forgetting sounds as if it could have come from a Harry Potter novel, but it is a key idea for the filmmakers. “Not forgetting was a deliberate act, to make remembering active,” says Forsyth.



“If you choose not to forget, you make the effort. Whereas remembering something is an accident. Do I remember where I left my car keys?” Pollard chips in. “It’s also about learning lessons. The act of remembering seems loaded with a kind of sentimentality; it feels wistful in a way, whereas not forgetting is a recalibration. It has an urgency.” Broken English was billed at last year’s film festivals in Sundance and Venice as a documentary, but Forsyth isn’t sure that holds. “For us, the idea of going into a project saying ‘we are going to make a documentary’ just seems so alien, so limited from the start,” he says. “I think we were going into it thinking, ‘We are going to make a film that tells a story, and we want to make the best film and tell the best story we can.’ For me, ‘non-fiction’ works as well as anything because the story we’re telling is not fiction, although we might be using some of the devices of fictional storytelling. I think the story we’re telling is full of emotional truth. Which is not the same as journalistic truth.” Related Article Cinema Crash to classic: How Practical Magic’s box-office hex marked the spot for Nicole Kidman and Sandra Bullock For Pollard, the real discoveries in the film are the expressions that flicker across Faithfull’s face as she looks at the old footage of her younger self, beautiful and damaged but still holding up her end of things. “There’s a piece from Weekend World in 1974 or ’75, an interview she probably should have said ‘no’ to, when she had just come out of rehab,” she says. Watching it, Faithfull initially looks dismissive of that young idiot, opining on life. “Then she starts to align with her. And I’m looking from face to face, and I’m seeing the same eyes, I’m seeing the same smile, and I’m seeing the same willingness to be open. We all can all read a face – and cinema is the best way for us to do that. That’s when the film is revelatory.” Broken English opens nationally on September 17.

World.title: Blood, lies and cartels: Five new crime books to read this month
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The noir label has been tenuously attached to all manner of crime fiction of late. But rather than being identified by a landscape (think rural or outback noir), or geography (Nordic noir), or even a setting (domestic noir), the real deal features a hapless character who is always on the outer and for whom things are never going to turn out well. Just Like the Night by Michael Caleb Tasker Michael Caleb Tasker, author of the impressive first novel Just Like the Night (Allen & Unwin, $35), knows this only too well since he has written a PhD thesis exploring the existential roots of noir fiction. Meet 12-year-old Sera sitting in an El Paso hotel room while her father Ray stacks the decks in preparation for an elaborate sting. “There’s a fine line between being a magician and a card sharp,” he tells her. Despite being as sharp as a knife himself, Ray is routinely rumbled and roughed up. As father and daughter drive the length and breadth of the US, eventually decamping to Sydney, Sera wonders “how he made her feel safe while he was still covered in blood”. Fast forward a few decades and Sera is coming to the end of her prison sentence. On her own in a cell, “she’s up early before the sun, face washed, push-ups done and bed made, waiting like there was something to wait for”. To discover what that something might be, Tasker takes us on a round trip to discover what unfolded when Sera and Ray came to Australia, what has happened to them since, and how Sera manages her parole when she discovers that her estranged daughter is being used and abused by the kind of bad man her father never was. Just Like the Night is tightly written, occasionally violent and very noir, especially the haunting conclusion. The Damned by Matt Rogers If violence is not your thing then look away now since The Damned by Matt Rogers (Simon & Schuster, $40) is a veritable bloodbath. While initially a tad hesitant, after reading this sentence “Quadriceps flare beneath faded gym shorts as he balances two hundred and forty pounds of authentic Japanese straw on one shoulder”, I was in. Logan Booth (he of the flaring quadriceps) is a contract killer of Reacheresque proportions and this is his third outing.



Unlike Lee Child’s Reacher, Booth has an offsider, a diminutive, gay, recovering meth addict, whose love and loyalty to Logan ensure we know from the start the latter is a “good guy” despite his propensity to off people at an alarming rate. The fact that the president of the United States wants Logan dead is another tick in his favour. This time, the flaring quadriceps are headed to Colombia to rescue a former lover before Logan finds himself up against a nasty cartel determined to take him out. The violence inflicted on both sides is surprisingly inventive and beautifully choreographed once you get over the gore factor and the prose style. This is the kind of propulsive crime that might make you burn the soup. I did. The Burn by Jessica Mansour-Nahra Jessica Mansour-Nahra’s The Burn (Hachette, $25) is of a different order of flammable magnitude. Set in 2030, it imagines an Australia emerging from a five-month lockdown caused by rampant wildfires on a national scale. It’s a timely scenario given the disasters affecting Europe during their summer and dire warnings of worse to come. After months of enforced isolation writing uplifting social media posts for her university employer’s website, Carmen is suspiciously reluctant to leave her featureless apartment and a dying pothos plant. But her three former high school chums have different plans: a camping trip on the idyllic south-east coast that has so far escaped the fires. What could possibly go wrong? Lots apparently, but there will also be time for Carmen to ruminate on her chequered sexual history and “her broken, disparate family”. This includes her Finnish scientist father who has remarried and is deeply concerned about the fate of the walrus, her distant scientist mother somewhere in the Indian Ocean with her new German husband, and her horse-loving older sister Anna with whom she has always had a taut and tricky relationship. There’s a lot to work through. While Burn is labelled as a psychological thriller, and it is indeed that, there are also telling reflections on the power of social media for good and evil. As it emerges, it’s not just bushfires we have to worry about.



Every Time She Wakes by Petronella McGovern Nevertheless, bushfires also figure in Petronella McGovern’s latest suburban thriller, Every Time She Wakes (Allen & Unwin, $35). University careers counsellor, Suzanne Vitale, is sleepless and fretting at 2.30am when the Rural Fire Service arrives to evacuate her and her family ahead of the firestorm. Bundled into a van, it’s not long before Suzanne suspects they are being abducted rather than rescued begging the question: why? There’s scant time to consider the options as the van crashes and Suzanne wakes up. Although it might be assumed that it was all a bad dream, McGovern is playing trickier plot games. While there’s a clue in the fact that Suzanne’s eldest daughter Frankie is studying a unit on “Metaphysics, Reality, Time and Possibility”, it might be more helpful to think Groundhog Day meets Sliding Doors. Like most domestic protagonists, Suzanne’s got a lot to figure out about her life and work. This includes how best to handle student complaints concerning a repulsive radio shock jock named Rowdy Mac who has made a bankable career demeaning women. Bells ringing anyone? Rowdy’s been hiring Suzanne’s students as interns, before he moves on to Suzanne’s daughter and her best friend who is a social media influencer. This is another book with something to say about the contemporary media landscape. Given that Suzanne has to relive the bushfire scenario again and again until she gets it right, it’s tricky to summarise a plot that effectively works backwards rather than forwards. Thankfully it all makes sense in the end although you may be left wondering just how she did it. McGovern, that is. You Know What You Did by K.T. Nguyen American author K.T. Nguyen is also playing inventive mind games in her psychological thriller You Know What You Did (No Exit Press, $33) which is heavy on the psychology and light on the thrills. Annie Shaw is a budding artist with a teenage daughter, an entitled war-reporter husband and a Vietnamese mother hoarding all manner of detritus in the carriage house of their large estate. Annie also suffers from punishing bouts of a disgust-driven obsessive-compulsive disorder that is painfully realised. She takes a lot of very hot showers.

World.title: The Coalition is betting that people mistrust Albanese more than big tech
World.content:
PoliticsFederalDigital hygiene Opinion The Coalition is betting that people mistrust Albanese more than big tech Waleed Aly Columnist, author and academic September 11, 2026 — 5:03am

September 11, 2026 — 5:03am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Of course we’re talking about censorship. It could be no other way when a government tries to regulate the internet. We saw it a couple of years ago when the Albanese government tried to pass laws to deal with online misinformation and disinformation. We’re seeing it this week as it tries to take on the social media companies’ algorithms. In the former case, the government ultimately abandoned the cause. In this case, I can’t imagine any such backdown. But the debate will take a very familiar shape: the government legislating in an extremely tricky area with the stated aim of preventing harm, opposition parties accusing it of trying to remake the internet in its political image. The government’s social media pitch is trying to do two things at once. Dionne Gain There are some genuine free-speech issues at play here. There are also some red herrings. That’s because the Albanese government’s bill is trying to do two quite separate things. One, to give social media users the ability to opt out of the algorithm that feeds them suggested content. Two, to stem the torrents of what it calls “seriously harmful” online content that has people veering off into extremist misogyny or being led into having eating disorders. The objection of censorship is meaningful to the second, but it’s totally irrelevant to the first. The problem is that it’s being used to reject the whole lot. And I suspect that’s going to create a political problem down the track, especially for the Coalition, which has now officially declared it opposes the legislation.



To force social media companies to let their users switch off their algorithm doesn’t stop anyone saying or publishing anything. It doesn’t even stop social media companies producing offering to feed you content via their algorithms. It means only that you’re not compelled to be subjected to that. The relevant idea here isn’t censorship, but choice. The threat here is to the business model of the tech giants in the (unlikely) event lots of people opt out. But it is not to speech. Related Article Social media Algorithm shake-up will hurt right-wing parties, censorship fight heats up It’s far more fraught, though, to legislate that social media organisations must ensure a “safe online environment”, where people are “protected from seriously harmful material”. What’s “seriously harmful”? The bill has a list of horrible things: content encouraging child sex abuse, sexual violence, death and rape threats, encouraging suicide or self-harm, supporting terrorism, or promoting illicit drug use. But the real controversy is over what comes next. The bill would allow the minister simply to declare other things to be seriously harmful, too, and it would be so. That’s the thrust of the Coalition and One Nation’s objection: it puts the declaration of harm in the hands of the government of the day, “a blank cheque for political censorship to the minister”, in Angus Taylor’s phrase. Say she wants to designate anti-immigration content seriously harmful. Or climate-change denying content. Or anti-Israeli content. This sort of thing, they say, is entirely possible under the law, and would silence political debate. There’s half a point here. The government retorts that whatever the minister adds to the list, the senate can take away with a vote. That’s something, but it’s not as much as it seems. It puts the onus not on the government to get a majority, but on its opponents to do so. Any government will probably have a significant presence in the senate. To have a majority against it will require something close to a total alliance from all the non-government senators. In the current parliament, for instance, it would need something akin to an alignment between the Coalition, One Nation and the Greens to reverse the minister’s decision. That means that if a minister’s decision is very political – appealing to true believers on the left or the right – it will be very hard to reverse.



But it’s only half a point because this is easy enough to fix. You simply require any additions to the “seriously harmful” list to be passed through the parliament like any other amendment. That means that instead of them being at the whim of government, they’d express the will of the parliament. At least in theory, they’d capture the will of the public more broadly. I suspect nakedly partisan attempts to regulate online content wouldn’t be able to get through all that. Related Article Opinion

Meta Things seemed so much better in Back to the Future II Waleed Aly Columnist, author and academic If I had to guess, I’d say that’s what the Albanese government will do. It’s an easy enough compromise to make, and it immediately dilutes the most powerful free speech objection. But that’s where things would get really interesting. Because if the Albanese government made that sort of change, what would the other parties do? One Nation is easy enough to predict. It doesn’t want a single thing to change. The algorithm suits it perfectly. It lives in a world where social media influencers tell you the truth, and the ABC doesn’t. It is completely unmoved by any campaign to “fix our feeds” because it doesn’t see anything broken. For that reason, it doesn’t even need to get into intricate arguments about what is and isn’t censorship. But the Coalition is in a bind. It clearly accepts the dangers of social media on some level. It’s easy to forget that Peter Dutton proposed the teen social media ban before Labor did. Its Shadow Minister for Communications and Digital Safety has spoken of “dreadful algorithms” which are engines of “insidious psychological manipulation”.



But its deputy leader is Matt Canavan, who has dismissed any suggestion at all that the algorithm is a problem. That’s why the Coalition has to lean so heavily on the idea of censorship. It’s not so much that the Coalition are free speech purists - after all they began this week arguing for a law to ban burning the Australian flag. It’s that on an issue like this one, censorship is the only argument that allows them to reconcile the opposing positions within. As long as you can say Labor’s solution is an attempt at thought control, you don’t need to decide whether social media algorithms are dangerous or not. It’s banking, then, on people mistrusting the Albanese government more than it mistrusts big tech. And if the teen social media ban shows us anything, it’s that Labor quite likes that match-up. And if in the meantime it has shown a willingness to make changes, to address legitimate free-speech concerns, the Coalition might once again find itself marooned on its own divided island – unclear on what to fight for, and against whom. And, unable to decide on what it really thinks of social media, there’s a real risk it takes the fight to itself. Waleed Aly is a broadcaster, author, academic and regular columnist. He is the author of the current Quarterly Essay, Time of Monsters: What future for liberalism? The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: Tensions erupted between two Sydney councillors. They might have to attend mediation
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWSydney councils Tensions erupted between two Sydney councillors. They might have to attend mediation Megan Gorrey September 11, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An inquiry into allegations of dysfunction and maladministration at a Sydney council is poised to urge state government intervention that would require councillors to lift their performance, but has stopped short of recommending they get the sack. Draft recommendations from the Office of Local Government’s long-running inquiry into Liverpool City Council suggested Local Government Minister Ron Hoenig should consider issuing the organisation with performance improvement orders – a mechanism that gives councils the chance to resolve governance, performance or financial problems before actions such as suspension. Liverpool Mayor Ned Mannoun. Dion Georgopoulos Commissioner Ross Glover, whose report from last year’s hearing is due to be released imminently, also suggested in his draft recommendations that Liberal Mayor Ned Mannoun and his long-time political rival, councillor Peter Ristevski, attend mediation to repair their fractious relationship. The tensions between Mannoun and Ristevski, who was a Liberal and independent before joining the Family First Party last month, were among matters scrutinised during the 52-day public inquiry.



It examined councillors’ conduct as well as the council’s handling of finances, property purchases, more than $150 million in state government grants for infrastructure, and staff employment – including its revolving door of 10 acting or permanent chief executive officers in eight years. Related Article Sydney councils Inside the ‘brutal’ civil war tearing apart a Sydney council A spokeswoman for Hoenig said on Thursday the minister had received the final report from the inquiry and was closely considering its recommendations. Glover distributed more than 40 draft recommendations – related to elected officials, council staff and the Office of Local Government – to parties to the inquiry for their feedback in late August. The draft document does not include a recommendation for the council to be sacked or suspended; however, the commissioner’s findings and final recommendations are contained in the final report.



Among the draft recommendations is a suggestion that Hoenig consider whether performance improvement orders be issued and, if so, whether a temporary adviser should be appointed to help the council meet its requirements. Councils can be suspended if they fail to comply with the orders. The draft document also recommends that Mannoun and Ristevski participate in a “structured mediation process” conducted by a person “with appropriate skills and experience in resolving interpersonal conflict, including in the workplace environment, the cost of which is to be borne by the council” within three months of the commissioner’s final report being tabled in parliament. Liverpool councillor Peter Ristevski gives evidence at the NSW Office of Local Government inquiry. Liverpool Council inquiry He suggested changes to legislation that would require a council’s governing body to have a two-thirds majority when deciding to pursue a no-fault termination of the general manager. The commissioner also recommended the council implement a process to audio-visually record parts of council meetings held in closed session; review recruitment processes and policies to include guidance as to when it would be appropriate to make direct and temporary appointments; and arrange training for councillors on conflicts of interest and respectful debate in meetings.



Liverpool Council declined to comment on the draft recommendations. Hoenig told a budget estimates hearing this month the cost of the inquiry was $4 to $4.5 million. Related Article Sydney councils This Sydney council was meant to pick a new deputy mayor. A jaunt to the UK got in the way The inquiry was triggered by an interim report that was provided to Hoenig in 2024 and prompted him to describe the allegations against council as “the worst I’ve ever seen”. He signalled his intent to suspend councillors and tried to postpone that year’s election until the inquiry was completed. The report was part of a broader investigation into the council’s recruitment and staffing processes, which the government said unearthed “matters sufficient in seriousness and volume” to warrant an immediate public hearing.



The council launched action against Hoenig in the NSW Land and Environment Court in a bid for the election to go ahead as scheduled. Judge John Robson found the interim report failed to observe the requirements of procedural fairness as it was published without giving named individuals an opportunity to respond. But he said the government had not unduly influenced the probe, clearing the path for the inquiry to go ahead. World.title: New Zealand First unveils plans for dramatic overhaul of immigration system
World.content:
New Zealand First is wanting to make sweeping changes to the country's immigration laws.

The party unveiled over a dozen new policies on Friday as part of a dramatic overhaul of the immigration system ahead of November's general election.

Part of the reforms put forward include a referendum on enacting an annual cap of 20,000 resident visas issued each year.

The party also wants to update birthright citizenship requirements, so only the children of citizens are automatically entitled to New Zealand citizenship at birth.

NZ First leader Winston Peters said population growth should not outpace an ability to build the country.

"New Zealand First will substantially reduce non-essential immigration and restore the principle that immigration is a privilege, not a right," he said.

"New Zealand is more than an economy. It is a nation with its own history, institutions and way of life. Immigration policy should strengthen social cohesion and encourage integration into a shared national community."

The party wants to change settings for asylum seekers, where any person who seeks asylum while in New Zealand on a working-class visa would be ineligible.

Asylum claimants would not be able to use a temporary work rights granted during the assessment period as a stepping stone to another visa.

Qualifying periods for permanent residents and citizenship would also be more rigourous with the required period to qualify for citizenship from five years to a minimum of 10 years. The qualifying period for permanent residence will be extended from two to five years under the proposed reforms.

NZ First would increase the cost of applying for New Zealand citizenship and permanent residence "to reflect its value and to better fund the wider immigration system".

A 10-year welfare stand-down period would be implemented for all visa holders, meaning non-citizens would be ineligible for jobseeker, accommodation supplement, or any other benefits during their first 10 years in New Zealand.

The party said it would bring in a 24-month amnesty for overstayers to self-deport, with no restrictions on applying to return. But any overstayer found after that period has lapsed would be deported and ineligible to apply for any visa in the future.

World.title: Pensioner hit in the pocket by two MSD botch-ups not confident it won't happen again
World.content:
Pensioner loses confidence after welfare payment error Morning Report Download MP3 3m

A pensioner who was sent into a panic when his welfare payments were wrongly stopped says he has no confidence it won't happen again.

Ministry of Social Development (MSD) chief executive Debbie Power conceded "we got it wrong" after a review released on Thursday found more than 30,000 payments were incorrectly suspended due to two separate but related problems following a law change last year.

Those affected included 2400 main beneficiaries, some of whom were left thousands of dollars out of pocket before they were backpaid.

The total arrears bill is at least $2.5 million.

Tom Evison, who is 84, was left $200 short for a week when his Winter Energy Payment and Disability Allowance were stopped.

"I have rent to pay, and power bills and food and so on, so I work out how to afford it based on what I know's coming in," he said.

"And if it stops coming in, then it's a bit of a panic. I don't like frights."

Ministry of Social Development chief executive Debbie Power. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Evison is fearful of another fright, after learning what went wrong at MSD.

"I don't have a lot of confidence it won't happen again," he said.

"People can make mistakes, but you need somebody among the dozens of staff that they have, whose job it is to check decisions and make sure that if there's a mistake, somebody catches it."

Power fronted media on Thursday, taking full responsbility and apologising.

She acknowledged the anxiety and stress people had suffered, and committed to doing better.

Social Development Minister Louise Upston issued a statement.

She also apologised, saying what happened was unacceptable and expressing disappointment in MSD.

Upston did not give media interviews.

Tom Evison said that was a bad look.

"She seems to be running away from the problem," he said.

"She just shows us a clean pair of heels as she's disappearing and won't talk to people, which isn't very good when there's an election coming up."

Social Development Minister Louise Upston. RNZ/Nick Monro

Why were payments wrongly stopped?

A law change, which was rushed through Parliament under urgency last year, required many beneficiaries to confirm their circumstances annually to ensure they remained eligible for their payments.

Two major problems surfaced, which triggered the MSD review.

The Winter Energy Payment for pensioners should have been exempt from that "confirming your circumstances" process, but it was not, which meant thousands missed out on payments they should have received.

Secondly, processing delays caused by a high volume of people confirming their circumstances meant some paperwork was not checked in time, so their benefit payments stopped.

MSD apologised and everyone was backpaid, but none would receive further compensation because that was not authorised under the law, the review said.

World.title: Why it took over a century for Auckland to get its CRL
World.content:
City Rail Link: A century in the making Morning Report Download MP3 4m

After a decade of delays, cost blow-outs and disruption to business and commuters, Auckland's City Rail Link (CRL) is finally due to open this weekend.

But in fact the story of the CRL goes back not just a decade, but over a century.

Graeme Carter edits the New Zealand Railway Observer and said governments had avoided investing in passenger rail since 1912.

"An organisation called the Northern Railway League proposed a tunnel between Auckland and Morningside. There's again another proposal in 1918 and in 1923 it attracted government attention.

"It's interesting that there's been several developments over the century and they've all basically followed the same route."

Carter has just published a history of the CRL's long and complex history. A striking theme in the article was how successive governments opted to invest in Auckland's motorway infrastructure rather than commuter rail.

"That went back to the 1950s and 1960s, there was a considerable push for motorway development [which was] a world-wide trend for most major cities.

"Auckland looked to Los Angeles for a lead -- Los Angeles was investing very heavily in motorways -- and the Auckland commuter system was deliberately run down from the 1950s through to the 1990s."

A statue of Sir Dove-Myer Robinson in Aotea Square. RNZ

Prior to today's successful project, the closest Auckland came to having an underground rail network came in the mid-1970s.

Dubbed "Robbies Rapid Rail" after then-Auckland Mayor Sir Dove-Myer Robinson, the project would have seen an underground rail loop in the city and track extensions to Auckland Airport and the North Shore. The Muldoon government derailed the plan, and preferred to invest in the city's motorway system.

More than a century after that initial plan to build a rail link in Auckland, Auckland Mayor Len Brown secured a deal with Sir John Key's government to begin work on the CRL. Today, he's cock-a-hoop.

"I feel lot of pride for our council and feel really happy for the people of Auckland. This has been a long wait."

Brown said there's an important lesson in the CRL's long history.

"We were always going to have to do this - the longer you delay an inevitable infrastructure requirement, the more expensive it's going to be for future generations to put it in place."

Simon Bridges, who was minister of transport at the time, said there was disagreement about the project within government, and tough discussions with Auckland Council.

"Not exactly acrimony but disagreement [between] council and government and as a new, incoming transport minister I thought it was a good idea to try and smooth some of that over."

Construction of the CRL has been marred by delays and multiple cost blow-outs. The initial projected cost of $3.4 billion ballooned to $5.5b.

Former Minister of Transport Simon Bridges. RNZ / Angus Dreaver

Simon Bridges recalled being told about one price hike just as the government agreed to pick up half the tab for the project.

"Officials came to me, I think from Treasury and a bunch of departments, and they said, 'Look, the cost has gone up'.

"I can't quite remember whether I've got this exactly right but it was $400 million, literally on the night we were about to sign. I rang Len Brown up and I think it was news to him as well."

But despite the hefty cost Bridges, who is now chief executive of the Auckland Chamber of Commerce, said it would be worth it and Aucklanders would feel like they're living in a "first-class international city".

"You could argue some of the set-up wasn't perfect, Covid certainly slowed it down and added cost. [CBD businesses] I think were dealt a hard blow and probably weren't dealt with fairly enough," he said.

"[But] it is transformative -- no one is going to regret it once it's open and if we go forward five, 10 years I think it will be very hard to find a person who would say 'we shouldn't have done that'."

Former Auckland Mayor Phil Goff. RNZ / Zach Cornelisen

Phil Goff, who was mayor of Auckland for much of the CRL's construction, said the biggest challenge he faced was pushing through a billion-dollar design change that would "future proof" the CRL by enabling it to accommodate nine car trains rather than just six.

"The rapid rise in rail transport meant we would have reached capacity not many years after the tunnel had been completed.

"Now that would have been a disaster because at that point you would have had to bring back tunnelling equipment to extend the platform, you'd have to close the CRL down, a little bit like the Harbour Bridge where you built it in 1960 with four lanes and within a few years you needed eight lanes."

Goff said the CRL was something Aucklanders could be proud of.

World.title: Cybersecurity experts raise alarm after back-to-back data breaches
World.content:
Cybersecurity expert on ZenTech data breach Morning Report Download MP3 4m

The education ministry says a data breach at an online learning platform may have included private information of students and teachers.

Mathspace confirmed last week that hackers had downloaded information on students, their parents or guardians, and school staff.

It comes as cybersecurity experts raise the alarm after back-to-back data breaches at two New Zealand companies, ZenTech and Thankyou Payroll.

In a special bulletin to school leaders, the ministry said the breach has impacted more than a million Mathspace users across New Zealand and Australia.

"We believe that the breach may have included private information, such as names and email addresses of students and teachers who have used the tool."

It says schools that have paid a subscription may be affected, as well as individuals who've signed up to the free version.

The ministry advised affected schools to review the Office of the Privacy Commissioner's guidance on privacy breaches.

"Each school is responsible for assessing its own circumstances and determining what actions are required under the Privacy Act 2020."

It advised schools and individuals to reset passwords and consult their IT administrators.

The ministry said Mathspace had alerted the Office of the Privacy Commissioner and the National Cyber Security Centre.

Likelihood of breaches increasing - expert

Police are investigating a breach at health research company Zenith Technology, also known as ZenTech, in which a large number of files related to clinical trials may have been stolen.

Soon after the ZenTech breach was made public, payroll company Thankyou Payroll notified its users that they had been exposed by a global security breach involving open source analytics tool Metabase.

Ben Van Der Weerd, an undergraduate cybersecurity researcher at Victoria University, said both companies made attractive targets.

"Payroll companies in specific, they have a lot of people on file, they have lot of 'PII' or 'personally identifiable information', and this data goes for a lot of money on the dark web and can enable quite a lot of further attacks and phishing," he explained.

"Now they know where you live and they've got your IRD number and full name, so they might say 'oh, you didn't pay enough tax on this pay rate exactly 3 months ago under this IRD number, log into the portal to pay your tax' and that would get quite a few people."

A company like ZenTech, on the other hand, had high-value data that could be used to negotiate for a ransom.

"Health companies as well, they're more likely to pay a ransom," he said.

"If you were hosting a website for your cafe, if you breach that there's not a lot of return for the hackers, but if you breach something that has a lot of people's biological data or financial records, that's going to get you somewhere."

The office of ZenTech - Zenith Technology in Dunedin. RNZ / Tess Brunton

Dr Abhinav Chopra, a cybersecurity expert at the University of Auckland, said even if a ransom couldn't be negotiated, the patient data would be valuable on the dark web, as it was fundamental personal information that couldn't be updated like a password or email address.

"They have information about their bodies and their allergies, they've got clinical information, which is information that cannot be changed, so the dataset is quite static and can be used by a number of buyers on the black market," Chopra said.

"So this is data that can get them good money either way, both from ransom or they sell the data on the black market."

He said the hackers who targeted ZenTech were previously known to use phishing.

"From what I've learned about the hackers, the last incident [they were involved in] they did some phishing to get the credentials of a person, and then logged into a privileged account and from there moved to get access to their dataset," he said.

"But I'm not saying that happened to ZenTech."

He said the attack was a reminder that cyber attacks were becoming more likely, even for relatively small companies.

"We have to be serious about the likelihood [of cyber attacks]. When you do your likelihood-cross-impact, impacts have been high but most of us have been saying, 'oh, well the likelihood is low'. But since the Waikato DHB, all those likelihoods have increased," he said.

World.title: Former Auckland Sky World employees allege humiliation, poor treatment by boss
World.content:
Months after the owner of Auckland's Sky World was ordered to pay her $150,000 for unpaid work and emotional distress, ex-employee Sasha Lee says she is yet to see a cent.

Now other former employees have come forward to RNZ, alleging humiliation and distress caused by the sole director of Sky World owner JNJ Management, James Kwak, along with being made to perform tasks they had not been trained for while working at the Queen St complex.

When approached by RNZ, a spokesperson for JNJ Management denied the claims made by the former workers and said further comment would not be made due to "ongoing legal processes".

Sky World - a labyrinth-like building with rocket lifts and staircases to seemingly nowhere - was once a popular destination in the central city, home to Borders bookshop and Planet Hollywood.

What the exterior of Sky World looked like in the early 2000s. ASHLEY ALLEN / SUPPLIED

Foot traffic dropped dramatically after the Covid-19 lockdowns and today, the bulding is largely empty with many shuttered shops.

In 2017, RNZ reported the building remained open without a warrant of fitness for more than a year despite a "high risk" to public safety.

The ERA case

In May, Lee - a former personal assistant to Kwak - took her case to the Employment Relations Authority (ERA) and said while she was a personal assistant on paper, her work included acting as general manager for MetroLanes bowling and taking care of tenant-related matters (JNJ looked after several hospitality businesses within the centre).

Lee also worked on business sale and refurbishment projects and attended weekly governance meetings.

She claimed she was unjustifiably dismissed due to a lack of consultation from JNJ before duties were removed from her role.

The ERA found she was not consulted about changes to her role and so an announcement sent to all employees about a newly-hired HR manager had come as a shock and caused her considerable stress.

It found Lee had been unjustifiably disadvantaged by the removal of management duties from her role.

Documents from JNJ did not explain why Lee's position was proposed to be redundant and the ERA said it did not explain the savings it needed to make or how it would help JNJ.

Inside Sky World in 2025. MARIKA KHABAZI / RNZ

There was no mention of alternatives to redundancy, or other cost savings that could be made.

Lee claimed she was not paid for additional hours worked, while JNJ submitted she was on a fixed salary and all hours were fully compensated in that way.

The ERA found she did work additional hours and notes from her work diaries showed the nature of her work went far beyond a PA position.

It found she was also owed 378 hours of accrued annual leave.

When Lee was made redundant, she had limited family support in New Zealand and struggled with depression.

The ERA found the dismissal affected her sleep and caused anxiety.

Lee told RNZ she was yet to receive any payment and understood JNJ had filed a challenge in the Employment Court.

As there were ongoing legal proceedings she didn't want to comment further at this stage.

'Shouted and sworn at'

Overlooking where the food court used to be. MARIKA KHABAZI / RNZ

Steven Yang, who worked as assistant facility manager at Sky World during 2022, alleges Kwak, shouted, swore and "humiliated" him in front of other employees.

"He was continuously very aggressive, short tempered, shouting and swearing toward me and others during business hours," he said.

"During a meeting in 2023, he began swearing at me in front of my colleagues. I felt so belittled and embarrassed - it caused me great humiliation and distress."

The event led him to immediately resign.

"I couldn't breathe in the office so as soon as he yelled at me in front of everyone I resigned straight away."

Yang said he found the job through an  on a Korean website and was surprised by the state the building was in.

"I was surprised a building in the CBD was falling apart.

"It's a s… building. Really no good."

Rubbish and debris tossed into a corner of Auckland's Sky World building in 2025. MELANIE EARLEY / RNZ

Former property assistant manager Krista* worked at Sky World in 2022 and said she was made to carry out several different roles without any prior consultation or notice.

She said she was first brought on to try and help carry out the sale of Sky World, but after a few months her hours were reduced from four days to just two, without notice.

Krista said soon after her mother, back in Korea, died.

"The owner [Kwak], declined my bereavement leave and my pay hours were reduced."

She said she ended up quitting over the way the bereavement leave was handled and took her case to the ERA to resolve it.

Krista said Kwak ended up paying her bereavement leave and unpaid wages, so she dropped the ERA case.

Leigh*, who also began working at Sky World in 2022 as an IT technician, said despite his employment agreement and lack of experience in other areas he was asked to do the work of a handyman, security, operation manager and bartender.

He said he was asked to work at MetroLanes, a bowling alley inside the complex, where he had to maintain the bowling lanes and set up booking systems.

"There was lots of multi-tasking and lots of jobs outside of my agreement. I helped support and boost the business.

"He got me to do jobs that an outside contractor was meant to do, to save money."

Leigh often said he worked very long hours for no extra pay.

"I found the job on TradeMe, I didn't hear back for weeks, and I sort of forgot about it until they called me back.

"I remembered the place and visiting it when I was growing up, so I thought it would be cool to work there."

Bookstore Borders was inside Sky World until 2012. (File photo) ASHLEY ALLEN / SUPPLIED

When Leigh began working, he found the "IT department" was just him.

"So I just started having to do all sorts of work. I was doing things I was not trained for. I was told to be the operations manager of MetroLanes so I had to get a new food hygiene grade. That was a lot of paperwork.

"I had to set up their website, deal with creditors, it was really frustrating for me, but I was doing quite well, things were moving."

But Leigh said the long hours, and continued pressure impacted his home life, and he found himself becoming increasingly stressed.

"Every day it was something new. It was meant to be 40 hours a week but I was there pretty much all the time.

"I had to quit because I think if I continued any longer my partner would have left me because I was bringing all these issues home."

Leigh said he wanted Kwak to stop treating employees, especially younger ones, in such a way.

JNJ denies allegations by former workers

The exterior of Sky World. MARIKA KHABAZI / RNZ

In an emailed response to RNZ, an unnamed spokesperson for JNJ Management and Kwak said the allegations by former workers were all "strongly refuted".

"JNJ Management Limited places the utmost importance on the well-being and fair treatment of all our employees, and we are committed to upholding ethical and compliant workplace practices."

World.title: Dave Rennie rings the changes for All Blacks' final Springboks Test
World.content:
All Blacks coach Dave Rennie has named Richie Mo'unga in his side to play the Springboks in the fourth Test in Baltimore on Sunday (NZT), the No.10 being one of five players to make their first starts in the series.

The Springboks lead the series 2-1 and while they have only made two changes to their starting 15 from the third Test, Rennie has made a number, calling in prop Fletcher Newell, lock Patrick Tuipulotu, flanker Ethan Blackadder and centre Anton Lienert-Brown to also make their first starts for the series.

In all, there are eight changes from the starting side that lost to the Springboks 29-24 in Soweto last weekend, as the All Blacks attempt to draw the series. One of them also involves a position swap, with Tupou Vaa'i shifting from lock to the side of the scrum.

Codie Taylor will captain the side after being dropped for the third Test, while prop Ethan de Groot and lock Josh Lord return to the 23 after missing the second and third Tests because of concussion. De Groot will start the match while Lord is on the bench with Sam Darry and Patrick Tuipulotu forming the second row.

Codie Taylor has been named All Blacks captain for fourth Test against Springboks. © Photosport Ltd 2026 www.photosport.nz

Josh Moorby comes in on the left wing, replacing Leroy Carter, who missed a few crucial tackles in the third Test in Soweto last weekend and drops out of the 23.

Injuries have forced Rennie's hand, with skipper Ardie Savea, Luke Jacobson and Quinn Tupaea ruled out while lock Fabian Holland is also unavailable because of illness.

But he has made other changes as well, with Mo'unga replacing Ruben Love at first five being a strong talking point.

Rieko Ioane and Beauden Barrett are named on the bench as back cover, as Lienert-Brown takes Tupaea's place in the run-on side.

Peter Lakai will play at No.8, joining Blackadder and Vaa'i as the new loose forward combination, while the front row is different too, with Taylor and De Groot returning and Tyrel Lomax dropping to the reserves with Newell preferred as a starter.
