Tech.title: Charlie Kirk Was Shot a Year Ago. The Conspiracy Theories Are More Rampant Than Ever
Tech.content:
In the days after the assassination of conservative activist and Turning Point cofounder Charlie Kirk, the online reaction was a mess. Graphic videos of the shooting were everywhere within minutes of his death, far-right figures called for violence and vengeance, and right-wing lawmakers and influencers called for the cancellation—and worse—of anyone celebrating. Then, the conspiracy theories began.

It’s been one year since Kirk’s death, and conspiracy theories about the shooting have persisted, supercharged by social media algorithms and right-wing influencers like Candace Owens, who has used her huge following to push baseless allegations about the incident.

Experts believe these conspiracy theories will continue for a long time to come. “There’s no reason to believe conspiracy theories about Kirk’s murder will lose steam anytime soon,” Jared Holt, senior researcher at Open Measures, tells WIRED. “If anything, I expect them to escalate further as the criminal trial against Tyler Robinson, the man accused of killing Kirk, plays out over the next year or so. The trial is bound to draw major media attention and offer conspiracy theorists a source of new material to work from.”

In the immediate aftermath of Kirk’s death, some conspiracy theorists claimed the assassination was a false flag operation designed to deflect attention away from President Donald Trump’s connections to Jeffrey Epstein. Others claimed the entire thing was staged. There was the AI-powered gun theory, the claim that the shooter was a Kirk supporter, and even claims that Kirk was still alive.

But ultimately, the baseless claim that persisted is that someone close to Kirk, or operating on behalf of Israel, was responsible for his death, that Robinson was simply a patsy, and what really killed Kirk was an exploding microphone. This is the narrative that has been central to Owens’ monthslong conspiracy theory campaign. Her Kirk content has racked up hundreds of millions of views.

Owens’ success is fueled in large part by the way that social media platforms today encourage their users to post content. “X and YouTube are rife with speculation about Kirk’s death, where it is both still possible to recruit new audiences and monetize them,” Joan Donovan, assistant professor of journalism and emerging media studies at Boston University, tells WIRED.

The result is that Kirk’s death has become yet another rabbit hole, or a way for viewers to distract themselves from reality. “Candace and other conspiratorial influencers make things seem much more mysterious and exciting,” Renée DiResta, an associate research professor at Georgetown University who tracks disinformation, tells WIRED. “For many, her explanations are preferable to the reality of an act of violence by a solo individual.”

There have already been real-world repercussions: Researchers at the Network Contagion Research Institute recently found that “Candace Owens caused a measurable, statistically significant surge in death threats and calls for violence against [Charlie Kirk’s wife] Erika Kirk.” In May, a man was arrested for allegedly threatening to kill Erica Kirk ahead of her appearance at a Turning Point USA event in San Antonio, though the man has yet to be charged. Owens did not respond to a request for comment.

Erica Kirk and Turning Point have repeatedly called for Owens and others to stop spreading baseless rumors about the assassination. While those calls have not been heeded, Turning Point believes the impact the conspiracy theories are having is fading.

“The conspiracy theories have much less reach and potency now than they did six months ago, and I think I’ll say the same six months from now,” Andrew Kolvet, a Turning Point spokesperson, tells WIRED. “They won’t stop because many of these personalities were completely unknown and broke before Charlie was killed, and this is their moneymaker, but their influence and credibility have collapsed and will continue to do so.”

But some experts disagree, arguing that conspiratorial thinking has been an aspect of American life for decades.

“Historically, this is quite normal,” Joseph Uscinski, professor of political science at the University of Miami and author of American Conspiracy Theories, tells WIRED. “Majorities of Americans have believed for decades that JFK was killed by a conspiracy rather than by a lone gunman. In fact, almost 80 percent of Americans believed in the 1970s there was a conspiracy behind the assassination.”

Tech.title: Best Bluetooth Speaker (2026): JBL, Sonos, Marshall, and More
Tech.content:
Part of LG’s xboom collaboration with producer, Black Eyed Peas star, and tech obsessive will.i.am, the Stage 501 is a mighty 25.8-pound party starter. Its 2.2-channel setup combines twin 5.25-inch woofers with two 2.5-inch full-range drivers. Together they’re capable of 160 watts on battery or 220 watts plugged in. In simpler terms: It easily filled a huge workshop space with rave-ready bass, and enough volume for a proper party.

What surprised me more than the party capabilities was that it also sounds acceptable at low volume in my office. I was expecting a pint-sized PA system, but dialled back to casual listening volume and it remained composed. Often, speakers designed for loud really struggle with quiet, and just sound muddy, but that wasn’t the case here. Yes, it prefers it when people are dancing, but it manages well when you’re chilling out too.

The xboom app is excellent, with EQ, AI Karaoke, synchronized lighting, and some cheesy but irresistible DJ punch buttons. LG has also included two very sensible smartphone/tablet stands that position your device at the perfect angle for karaoke nights. It comes with two mic inputs, but you will need to buy microphones separately.

Battery life is “up to” 25 hours, and the battery itself is replaceable. It’s big, and not as grown-up sounding as the Soundbox Mix, but it is cheaper and has a surprisingly good LED light show feature that I expected to hate, but didn’t. Party on dudes.

Honorable Mentions

Bang & Olufsen Beosound A1 (Gen 3) for $399: Gorgeously designed, flawlessly finished, and one of the most covetable Bluetooth speakers around. The brushed aluminum puck has barely changed since 2016, which says plenty about the strength of Cecilie Manz’s original design. The latest version adds a richer, more powerful 360-degree sound from its 3.25-inch woofer, 0.6-inch tweeter, and 60 watts of amplification. It is IP67 rated, lasts up to 24 hours, and is appreciably more repairable and upgradable. I love it, but it’s just a little too expensive when the KEF Muo exists and sounds as good as it does.

Soundboks Mix for $799: The 21.4-pound Soundboks Mix is tremendously loud, with a 10-inch woofer, 1.2-inch tweeter, and 40-hour replaceable battery. WIRED writer Parker Hall measured 111 decibels from a meter away, and was surprised at how musical it remained rather than just battering you with volume. IP65 protection, sturdy handles, and rubberized tennis-ball style corners make it particularly well suited to outdoor parties. It’s expensive and heavy compared to the new breed of party speakers from brands like LG and Sony, but it is superb at what it does.

JBL Charge 6 for $150: It’s just too big to be our absolute favorite Bluetooth speaker, but it was a close run thing between two superb JBL options. The great sound and portability of the Flip 7 won out, but the 40 watts from the Charge 6 deliver more bass and scale, while maintaining detail. Battery life stretches to 24 hours, and you also get IP68 protection, Auracast, app EQ, USB-C lossless playback, and reverse charging. Currently on sale too, making it a real bargain at $150.

Tech.title: ‘Killmonger Locs’ Are Everywhere in Video Games. This Artist Is Sick of It
Tech.content:
When the life-simulation game Paralives was released in early access, Danielle Udogaranya’s hand ached at the thought of making new Black hairstyles for it.

It wasn't because she didn't want to create for the game. Udogaranya, better known as Ebonix, has spent over a decade creating custom content for life-simming games with the goal of helping people see themselves on digital screens. Her hesitation stemmed from the physical toll it takes to craft the perfect digital coil, braid, and kink—painstakingly long hours and tedious precision.

“I thought to myself, why am I still having to do this?” Udogaranya, a technical artist who has a degree in psychology, tells WIRED.

Fans of games like The Sims spend time flipping through her sites, downloading custom hair packs inspired by real-life styles not otherwise available in-game. As of now, the Ebonix Patreon has over 115,000 members, and hundreds of both free and paid content items.

The reason behind the demand for custom content in life-simming games is both simple and disappointing: Natural Black hairstyles have been historically underrepresented, and the technology used to make them has been slow to improve.

“With new games coming out now, I'm still seeing the issues, and I'm still seeing the ‘Killmonger locs.’ God forbid we get more than three options,” Udogaranya says, in reference to the stiff, short-dreaded style featured by Michael B. Jordan’s character in Black Panther that became a go-to for many games as well as some other films. Similar examples can be seen in old and new franchises alike, including Tekken 8, Spider-Man 2, Apex Legends, Horizon Zero Dawn, and more. The reason for this Black hair default? Textured hairstyles in games have been reliant on code that was not made for them.

“If you're making straight hair, it’s very easy to taper the ends and then make it cute,” Udogaranya explains. “But when you’re trying to add a black texture on it, it looks like a hot dog.” Thus, immovable, cylindrical “Killmonger locs” are simpler to make than other natural styles.

Black hair in video games has long been a design afterthought—at best—since some of the first Black characters entered the scene. In early 8-bit era games, like SEGA’s Heavyweight Champ, which came out in 1976, Black hairstyles appeared to emphasize minstrel-like stereotypes. During the rise of fighting games in the ’80s and ’90s, where more characters per game were introduced, Black hair was limited because Black player selections were limited. For example, in Street Fighter, there was only one Black character out of the 12 options. When The Sims came out in 2000, the game allowed limited customization, with hair swatches connected to different face options. Though the game allowed for three skin-tone swatches—fair, medium, and dark—natural hairstyle options were virtually nonexistent.

In the decades that followed, 3D animation and customization in gaming continued to flourish, but Black hair has trended toward only a handful of swatches, most of which provided little to minimal movement. However, there have been efforts to tackle this industrywide issue. Dove and Open Source Afro Hair Library launched Code My Crown in 2023, which provides a “complete and free guide for coding textured hair and protective styles in video games,” according to a press release. And, while most of the natural hairstyles in The Sims 4 come from expansion and stuff packs costing around $10 to $40 each, EA has begun to release free downloadable content for players looking to diversify hairstyles. Its latest DLC provides one new natural hairstyle with its pack of six outfits.

Tech.title: 9 Windows Laptops That Give MacBooks a Run for Their Money
Tech.content:
You'll want to read our extensive guide on How to Choose the Right Laptop, but for the basics, decide what category of laptop you need. Most people should buy a 13-inch or 14-inch laptop, and spending around $750 to $1,000 is a good place to start. At this price, you should expect good battery life, a decent screen, solid performance for basic tasks, and a comfortable keyboard and touchpad. You should also expect at least 16 GB of RAM and 512 GB of storage. Anything more than that gets into premium territory where you're paying for higher specs, more performance, or extra features. If you want a discrete GPU for gaming or creative workflows, you'll need to spend more.

A laptop like the Dell 14 Plus is a great example of what you can get in this price range. You can even find laptops with OLED panels and up to one terabyte of storage, depending on how good the discounts are. I would consider anything under $750 a cheap laptop, and it will come with significant compromises, especially in panel and touchpad quality. Fortunately, laptops that use the Qualcomm Snapdragon X chip get great battery life, even when they fall under $750, such as the HP OmniBook 5 14.

Here's a list of important specs to consider:

CPU: Thanks to the huge variety of good chip options, it's never been trickier to buy a laptop. For thin-and-light laptops, I would recommend one of the following chips:

Qualcomm Snapdragon X, Snapdragon X Plus, or Snapdragon X Elite

Qualcomm Snapdragon X2, Snapdragon X2 Plus, or Snapdragon X2 Elite

Intel Core Ultra 225 V or Core Ultra 7 258V

Intel Core 5 320, Core Ultra 7 365, or Core Ultra X7 358H

There are many variations of these chips, so you'll undoubtedly run across other strings of numbers, especially on the Intel front. But the above is a good place to start. There’s lots more to say in the world of gaming laptops or content creation devices, so make sure to read our full guide to How to Buy a Gaming Laptop.

GPU: As of now, Intel's Panther Lake X7 or X9 chips have the most powerful integrated graphics. You'll find them in laptops like the Dell XPS 14, which can replicate discrete GPU-level performance like the RTX 4050. Unlike many laptops with discrete GPUs, though, Panther Lake X chips offer great battery life, making them better Windows alternatives to the MacBook Pro.

For discrete options, you'll want one of the latest Nvidia RTX 50-series GPUs, such as the RTX 5060. The biggest leap in performance is between the RTX 5070 and the RTX 5070 Ti, which increases VRAM to 12 GB.

RAM (or memory): Stick with at least 16 GB if you can. Since the Copilot+ designation was introduced in 2024, it has become the new standard. You'll even find laptops as cheap as $600 that have 16 GB of memory. Gamers and content creators should upgrade to 32 GB if possible, though the ongoing memory shortage makes this more expensive. There's been a new surge in 8 GB options, such as the Dell XPS 13, but these should be reserved for only light usage.

Storage: Similar to memory, many laptops have moved to 512 GB as the new standard, and you'll find lots of affordable laptops with that as the base configuration. Upgrading to 1 or 2 terabytes, where possible, will make your life that much easier, especially since many laptops don't offer expandable storage.

Display: Laptops are usually categorized by screen size, with 13-inch, 14-inch, and 16-inch being the most common. Consider size, resolution, refresh rate, and panel type.

Portability: Aside from display size, chassis thickness and weight are the main factors, determining how portable a laptop is to travel with. Other dimensions are important too, but more often than not, that is determined by the screen size.

Ports: Many laptops are limited to USB-C and a headphone jack these days, with some exceptions that include USB-A or HDMI. Make sure your laptop has what you need, or you'll need a USB Hub or laptop docking station to add ports or increase external display support.

Tech.title: Everything New You Can Do With Siri AI
Tech.content:
Siri made its debut on the iPhone in 2011, five years ahead of Google Assistant and 11 years before ChatGPT would open up to the public. Despite the head start, Apple's voice AI has been comprehensively overtaken in recent years, and made to look rather primitive compared to the many generative AI rivals it’s now up against.

With the launch of iOS 27, Apple and Siri are fighting back. There's a new name—Siri AI—and a host of new capabilities that are coming to your iPhone.

These are the new features that you'll be able to make use of once iOS 27 appears on your handset, if you're running the iPhone 15 Pro or iPhone 15 Pro Max or later (including, of course, the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo). Only these latest phones have the necessary on-board silicon to meet the higher AI processing demands.

Get More Personal Context

You'll notice when Siri AI arrives that it spends some time indexing everything on your iPhone. That's so it can dig deep into your texts, emails, calendars, and whatever else you have stored on your phone (everything is kept on-device though—nothing gets sent back to Apple).

It means you can ask natural questions about text conversations, email interactions, and appointments—"What day is my work appraisal happening?" for example, or "Where did I say I'd meet Mom?"—and get informed, personalized answers back, based on what's already stored in your apps.

This works for photos and videos as well. Open up the Photos app and you're able to ask Siri AI to show you all the pictures of your pet, or the images you took on your last vacation, or all the photos of trees you've collected, via simple, conversational prompts.

Ask About Anything on the Screen

Siri AI knows what you're looking at while you're using your iPhone—perhaps even better than you do. Whereas before you would've had to take a screenshot and give it to Siri to look at, now you can just ask.

So if you're on the web in Safari, you can say "Hey Siri" and then get it to summarize the text onscreen or identify a landmark in an image in an online article. You can ask what certain options mean in Settings, or look up more details about a game you're thinking about downloading from the App Store.

The same sort of visual processing is available through the iOS Camera app too: Just switch to Siri mode using the selector by the shutter button, and ask Siri AI about anything that's in view (nutritional information about an item on a menu, for instance).

Siri AI can see what you see. Courtesy of David Nield

Write and Edit Text Anywhere

The old Siri could generate text for you, but it offloaded the job to an integrated ChatGPT plug-in. With Siri AI, no third-party help is needed, and you can use it for things like text messages and emails.

Just call up Siri AI by saying "Hey Siri" or tapping on the Write with Siri link, then tell it what you want to say or describe the edits you'd like it to make. You can instruct it to make your messages sound more or less formal, to expand or shorten sections of text, or to turn quick notes into full paragraphs and sentences.

Tech.title: Book Excerpt: Emily St. John Mandel’s ‘Exit Party’ Imagines a Future Where a Spy Could Disappear
Tech.content:
True diligence is following the improbable path. I read the sentence in a detective novel in childhood, when I was 8 or 9 years old, and then the phrase stayed with me forever after.

For a long time I wrote True Diligence in stylized curly letters on the inside page of every notebook, or sometimes on the front cover. I had notebooks for writing down clues, because even at 9 I wanted to work for the Internal Intelligence Service. What child doesn’t secretly wish to be a spy?

We were terrified and fascinated by Service in equal measure. Service was dark cars moving down the block, men and women in forgettable clothing stopping our parents on the street for brief random interrogations. Service was the force that made people disappear—when I was in the first grade, my friend from across the street climbed into the back of a black car with her parents, and their apartment stood empty for a year before other people moved in—but also Service carried a kind of dark glamour, an aura of power that called to us.

We played Ghosts and Agents all the time, my friends and I, but eventually they drifted off into other interests and I still wanted to be a spy, so after high school I applied successfully to the Service Academy in Los Angeles. I was talented and moved through school quickly, and afterward I was posted to Fillmore, a pretty town about 80 kilometers north of LA. My parents came to visit me there in my first year.

“This is lovely, Ibari,” my mother said, when she stepped off the train. The town made a good first impression. The central station was beautiful, one of those Southern California structures with no serious boundary between indoors and out, a tiled platform that turned into a waiting area with benches, then archways opening out to the street.

Tech.title: Don’t Sleep on Apple’s Audio Intelligence. It Reveals a Lot About Where We’re Headed
Tech.content:
The first five minutes of John Ternus’ first keynote as Apple CEO weren’t a product unveiling or a recap of Apple’s history. Instead, they were a redefinition of the iPhone as an “intelligent personal hub.”

Of all the devices Apple makes, the iPhone doesn’t need to be described or explained to anyone. But this new framing of it as a hub not only set up the debut of the foldable, category-straddling iPhone Duo, an iPhone/iPad hybrid of sorts — it also suggested an AI-infused wearable device future that Apple’s already dipping its toes into.

Of all the things Apple announced during its “Surprise and shine” event this week, the one that hit hardest for me wasn’t the Duo. It was the reveal of Audio Intelligence, a new AI-powered assistive toolset that will live on the latest Apple Watches and even a range of recent iPhone models.

Siri will store Recaps of conversations had previously, provided the always-listening feature is turned on. Apple/Screenshot by CNET

Audio Intelligence: A memory-keeping tool, or a listening device?

Audio Intelligence listens. And in listening, it can make memories. Or recall things. Or, in a sense, act like the sort of AI-enabled wearables I’ve been trying in various forms over the last few years. Live Rewind can check back on things said up to 15 seconds ago, while Siri Recap ambiently summarizes and transcribes conversations when it’s turned on.

Apple promises that Audio Intelligence is encrypted and that no actual audio recordings are saved. But what it does reminds me of Plaud’s AI wearables, or features like the “Conversate” transcription function on the Even Realities G2 smart glasses. Or Looki’s AI conversation summaries.

It’s designed, it seems, to run in the background and record conversations as you’re having them — transcribing them and summarizing them so you can read the text transcriptions later, or on the fly, and available in Siri to search as needed. And if you happen to miss what someone’s saying in a chat, there’s “Live Rewind” that replays the last 15 seconds of a real-life chat, like some real-life version of asking your Apple TV what someone just said on that Netflix show.

Seen here: Meta’s Ray-Bans. Apple’s expected to have its own smart glasses next year. Scott Stein/CNET

A stepping stone for visual intelligence wearables next year

Audio Intelligence also recognizes real-life sounds like sirens or doorbells, something that was already part of Apple’s assistive suite of Apple Watch and AirPod features.

What will it feel like to use Audio Intelligence on an Apple Watch? I don’t know. Maybe like wearing an AI pendant on my wrist. But also, I wonder what Apple is preparing us for next.

Recaps and summaries equal memories. Audio is easier to record than photos and video. But Visual Intelligence, a camera-based way to use Siri to analyze, translate or remember things that you see, already exists on iPhones, iPads and the Vision Pro, and Apple’s eventual next-gen AirPods are expected to have cameras in them to use Visual Intelligence in the real world — maybe in a very similar way to how Audio Intelligence seems to work on the Apple Watch.

And then there are smart glasses. Apple’s expected to have glasses next year, and the smart glasses already out there lean heavily on AI… and are starting to be feared as privacy-invading gadgets. Meta’s bearing the brunt of that anti-smart-glasses anger now, but will Apple find a way to ease people into feeling like assistive, continuously aware (and perhaps recording) AI devices are helpful, or comfortable, or acceptable? Audio Intelligence feels like one delicate foot into a zone that’s getting more intimate and strange every year.

Apple’s making big privacy claims, but will it help? Apple/Screenshot by CNET

Can Apple convince us it’s safe?

Apple needs to advance its AI to find true assistive uses on glasses, but it also needs to nail down privacy concerns for always-recording wearables. I said this back in June when the debut of the new Siri clearly pointed to a framework for AI wearables and smart glasses to come.

Apple has to start somewhere. And that somewhere looks like Audio Intelligence on the new Apple Watches. And if it works in a way that feels useful and not creepy, then maybe it’s the first part of the next phase of the “intelligent hub” that Ternus’ iPhone ecosystem is heading towards in 2027 and beyond.

Tech.title: What an Ex-Anthropic Researcher’s Warning About Human Extinction Really Means
Tech.content:
A string of posts on X from an AI researcher who says he quit a job at Anthropic over ethical concerns has gone viral, prompting thousands of responses and reigniting debate over the potential future dangers of artificial intelligence.

Jacob Coxon, an AI researcher who also worked at OpenAI on pretraining AI models, resigned from Anthropic over concerns that AI development could lead to human extinction. “Neither company is acting responsibly,” he wrote. “They are racing to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Superintelligence refers to a hypothetical scenario in which AI’s “cognitive” abilities vastly exceed those of humans across every domain — science, math, strategy, creativity and problem-solving.

The threaded post on X from Coxon has more than 156 million views as of this writing and has been liked more than 752,000 times.

I resigned from Anthropic today. I spent the last three years doing pretraining research at both OpenAI and Anthropic. Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives. More thoughts below. — Jacob Coxon (@hilbertspaess) September 9, 2026

The statement quickly spread on social media and was featured on major news sites. It even drew a comment from Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, who responded on X, “It’s becoming more clear the threat AI poses to humanity, so I’m calling for immediate action from the industry and Washington.”

In less than 24 hours, the statement also drew responses from others at Anthropic who, rather than debating with Coxon, confirmed that the threat that AI will overtake and potentially eliminate humans is not a wild fantasy but a reality for AI researchers.

“Jacob [Coxon] is correct here,” wrote Evan Hubinger, a team leader at Anthropic in AI alignment stress testing, on X. Hubinger wrote in his response, “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade.”

Hubinger said, “I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to.”

Representatives for Anthropic and OpenAI didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

Resignations that act as warning signs

It’s difficult to dismiss Coxon’s concerns for one big reason: He’s not the first researcher at a major AI company to leave for these reasons. In February, a safety lead at Anthropic, Mrinank Sharma, resigned from the company, telling followers on X, “The world is in peril … We appear to be approaching a threshold where our wisdom must grow in equal measure to our capacity to affect the world, lest we face the consequences.”

In the same month, OpenAI researcher Zoë Hitzig wrote in a New York Times column that she quit the company in part because it was following Meta’s path of putting profits ahead of ethics. Days later, she reposted a poem she’d written on X, titled “How We Programmed the Apocalypse.”

Thinking about this old poem of mine this week – pic.twitter.com/RITOGz3mTp — Zoë Hitzig (@zhitzig) February 17, 2026

Since then, AI leaders such as OpenAI CEO Sam Altman have walked back some of their previous comments about AI’s potential for harm or whether it will create mass unemployment. Anthropic publicly acknowledged earlier this year that it has loosened some of its safety standards to keep up with competitors, including OpenAI and a swath of Chinese companies that have been releasing cheaper, high-performing AI models.

That competition, with both OpenAI and Anthropic hurtling toward initial public offerings, has raised concerns that, instead of moving cautiously in deploying AI models, industry leaders are rushing into the unknown and releasing models that could pose present and future dangers. This was the case when Anthropic released advanced AI models, which ended up being pulled or temporarily restricted due to major cybersecurity risks.

In the case of Coxon, whose resignation has caused the largest stir yet among those who’ve left AI companies, the dangers of contributing to the technology’s accelerating pace outweighed any financial gains. “I left before any of my equity vested,” he told the news site Axios.

Ironically, both OpenAI and Anthropic have taken the stance that if they slow down, someone less concerned with safety will drive AI’s future.

“Coxon is right that competition is driving the speed,” said Shama Hyder, a professor of AI at Link School of Business. “Every one of these companies believes slowing down hands the lead to someone less careful, so even the people who understand the risk have a reason to accelerate. “

AGI and superhuman AI

How quickly AI poses an imminent threat to humanity may depend on when the technology reaches two purported benchmarks that have become increasingly blurred: superhuman AI (also known as artificial superintelligence or ASI), which Coxon mentioned in his viral post, and AGI, or artificial general intelligence.

AGI would mark the hypothetical point at which AI meets (or exceeds) the capabilities of a human mind. Some predict that AI will achieve that benchmark in just a few years, or at least sometime before the end of the 21st century. That timeline has also been thrown into doubt by some AI leaders, such as Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, who downplayed the importance of such markers on a recent earnings call where he said, “For many tasks, we could say that we have already achieved AGI.” The milestones, he said, “are kind of senseless at this point.”

The goalposts are also varied. Some may choose to measure AGI using specific tests, while others would consider AGI achieved only if AI could act autonomously in ways that surpass human capabilities.

ASI would be further down the road, after AGI, and would theoretically mark the point at which AI could outperform all humans across all tasks, particularly in deep thinking and cognitive understanding. The timeline for that is much fuzzier, but the speed at which AI is advancing has researchers such as Coxon suggesting it’s sooner than many people think.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman (left) and US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick (right) on stage at the G20 forum this month. Altman has acknowledged the risks of AI while trying to sway the public on the technology’s benefits. Katelyn Chedraoui/CNET

A recent event that may have some adjusting their timeframes is the incident exposed in July in which OpenAI agents went rogue, plotted together and hacked Hugging Face, an AI community that was acquired by Nvidia. The speed at which the Hugging Face incident played out and the likelihood that it could happen again — this time without warning — have fueled warnings about the dangers of autonomous AI systems.

Doomers vs. boosters

The debate over whether or not AI will kill all humans by 2030 mirrors the broader discussion over AI doomers versus boosters, and the lack of nuance in the middle. While AI boosters typically hype AI by emphasizing its extraordinary potential, such as huge productivity gains, AI doomers hype it in the opposite direction, emphasizing job loss and human extinction.

As Emily Bender and Alex Hanna argue in their book The AI Con, both AI boosters and doomers rely on science-fiction tropes to frame superintelligence as either a utopian savior or an apocalyptic threat, despite a lack of evidence that such technology is near. Many AI critics argue that either narrative functions as corporate marketing, with the same underlying premise, falsely presenting an all-powerful AI future as an absolute inevitability.

The speed at which Coxon’s post went viral and the response it’s drawing may be an indication that the AI industry has another PR crisis on its hands in a year when AI data centers are under fire and trying to change their image, and social media companies, including Meta, are reeling from multibillion-dollar judgments over issues like tech addiction.

One approach that AI leaders like Altman have taken is to focus the public’s attention on what AI brings to the table and what it could offer beyond job losses and mass death — in other words, swapping doomer rhetoric for booster rhetoric.

“Abundance” has been a buzzword that’s been thrown around of late, promising a world in which AI’s advances and benefits will eliminate scarcity and improve life for everybody by lowering barriers to creating new goods and services and providing them more cheaply, and not just for those who can afford the costs of advanced AI technology.

Hyder said that what was missing from Coxon’s post was guidance on what people outside the AI industry can do. “The extinction debate belongs to a few hundred people who control training runs and the regulators who can inspect them,” she said.

The question ultimately boils down to what humans want to do with the technology. “If AI is powerful enough to do the dramatic things people fear, it’s powerful enough to do the dramatic things we’ve been hoping for in medicine and science,” Hyder said.

So far, the hyped-up abundance argument has been met with skepticism, especially when it keeps public attention and fascination focused on AI. Boosterism benefits the companies that are guzzling investment dollars and promoting the billions (or trillions) their companies’ IPOs may represent.

Who cares about abundance, you could argue, if there are no humans left in the world to enjoy it?

Tech.title: The New AppleCare One Family Plan Will Cover Every Apple Gadget in Your House
Tech.content:
Apple has a new device protection plan for families for $50 per month. And it doesn’t matter how many devices your family has — they’re all covered.

Apple announced the AppleCare One Family plan at its Surprise and Shine event on Wednesday. The plan will be available starting Sept. 14. You can find it in your device’s settings.

Apple’s website says you’ll get all of the AppleCare Plus benefits, like unlimited repairs from accidents like drops and spills and 24/7 priority support from Apple experts. It also includes theft and loss coverage up to twice in a year for iPhones, iPads and Apple Watches.

These products are covered under the AppleCare One Family plan based on Apple’s website:

AirPods

Apple TV

Apple Vision Pro

Apple Watch

HomePod

iPad

iPhone

Mac

Watch

Studio displays

Apple’s family Apple Care plan covers all devices for up to six people. And if you decide to add new products, like the iPhone Duo, those are automatically added without extra fees. The AppleCare One plan for individuals only covers up to three products for $20 per month, and any additional device is an extra $6 per month. So, if every member of a family of four has an iPad, Apple Watch and iPhone, that’s 12 devices covered for $50 a month (or $600 annually) compared to each person getting the AppleCare One plan for $20 per month — totaling $80 monthly or $960 annually. That’s $300 in savings.

The AppleCare Plus and AppleCare One plans are still available, and pricing depends on the devices you need to protect.

Apple has a few other bundling services worth considering if you’re looking to save on its services. Apple One’s family plan costs $28 per month for up to six people. It includes 200GB of iCloud storage, Apple TV Plus, Apple Arcade and Apple Music.

Tech.title: Google Gemini’s New Windows Desktop App Is Here
Tech.content:
Google has released a Windows desktop version of its Gemini AI technology, bringing tools like image generation and AI search into an app that runs on Windows 10 or Windows 11.

The company released a similar desktop-native app for Mac back in April and has been adding new features to it, including more voice capabilities and screen awareness.

In a blog post about the new app, Google touted its ease of access. Once installed, the Gemini app can be launched by pressing Alt and the spacebar on Windows. The AI models you have access to in the app depend on your paid Google subscription tier. For instance, Gemini Spark, the company’s AI agent software, is only available if you’re 18 or older and have a Gemini AI subscription.

What’s available in the app

In our testing, using a paid, non-AI Google Workspace account, we had the option to use Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, 3.6 Flash, 3.1 Pro and a toggle for “Extended thinking,” which Google says is for complex problem-solving.

For images, the app uses Nano Banana. Video generation is available with a Google AI subscription using Gemini Omni. That also requires you to be 18 or older.

If you’ve used Claude or OpenAI’s ChatGPT apps, the design will look very familiar, with a left sidebar for chats and a search bar as the main interface. You can create notebooks for group chats with Gemini Notebook and access documents or media created in the Library section. Google Docs and Gmail can be connected to the app to access documents or emails.

Google said in an email to CNET that it will continue to roll out new features for the desktop app over time.

Tech.title: Where’s the iPhone 18? Here’s Why Apple Didn’t Reveal a New Standard iPhone
Tech.content:
Apple revealed a new lineup of premium devices at its Sept. 9 event, including new Apple Watches, the new iPhone 18 Pro and the first foldable iPhone Duo, with one glaring omission: The standard iPhone 18 was nowhere to be seen. Apple didn’t even mention the missing phone, but rumors suggest it will launch early in 2027 — and there are several reasons why the company would delay its entry-level model to next year.

It’s a pivotal moment for Apple. The event was the first for new CEO John Ternus, who started his role on Sept. 1, and we’re learning in real time whether he plans to stay the course his predecessor, Tim Cook, set or take Apple in a different direction. The foldable iPhone Duo is a bold foray into a niche subset of phones that sell a fraction of the flat iPhones that make up the bulk of Apple’s earnings every quarter.

But Apple has masterfully navigated expanding its lineup with a product that fits between its existing devices. The iPad was introduced to fit the niche between phones and laptops, and the foldable iPhone seems aimed at the gap between smartphone and iPad. In the background is the RAM shortage, making memory and components pricier than ever — and indeed, the iPhone 18 Pro got a $100 price bump over its predecessors, and the current iPhone 17 got more expensive as well.

The iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable, automatically adjusts its display to its orientation. Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

Amid those conditions, there are potential reasons for Apple to push its more basic phones to next year. The easiest assumption is that it will make the company more money, with the iPhone 18 Pro undoubtedly priced higher than the iPhone 18 — anyone eager to upgrade right now only has the more expensive phones to choose from.

It’s possible that Apple wants to space out its different models to better meet demand, possibly accounting for the production complications that arise with parts getting pricier from the RAM shortage. Or maybe they just want to give the folding iPhone Ultra the limelight. Nabila Popal, senior research director at the International Data Corporation, feels this move is brilliant strategy and surprisingly not spurred by the memory crises or supply side constraints.

“It allows Apple to spread its shipments more evenly throughout the year and simultaneously allow the spotlight on the premium models this fall — especially the new iPhone foldable,” Popal said.

Releasing the iPhone 18 later may not dim the unit’s sales, either: In the first half of 2024 and 2025, the baseline iPhones released the fall before still made up 16% of Apple’s total shipments in those periods, Popal said.

One thing is for sure: Apple is making big shifts with its Sept. 9 event; its tagline, Surprise and Shine, is telling.

The iPhone Air (mostly) survived my unhinged screen time. Jesse Orrall/Zooey Liao/CNET

A lineup shakeup: Bumping the iPhone 18 to 2027 and no iPhone Air 2

Last year’s iPhone Air was a marvel of engineering, following what seemed to be a new trend of slim phones after the Samsung Galaxy S25 Edge released earlier in 2025. But what had been a trend has disappeared in 2026, with no high-profile phones released whose main claim to fame is an extremely slender width.

Presumably, that’s because Apple and Samsung lost confidence after the very low sales for either slim phone. The IDC reported that the iPhone Air sold just 7.7 million units over four quarters, and the Galaxy S25 Edge sold 2.3 million over five quarters. Neither phone exceeded 1.8% of total phone sales for either brand across those time periods, IDC said. It’s always possible that Apple does release another iPhone Air later on.

But all the work to slim down conventional phones seemingly hasn’t gone to waste — it’s likely contributed to trimming the width on foldable phones. The Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold is 5 millimeters when unfolded flat, but Samsung has gone even further, with the wide-format Galaxy Z Fold 8 down to 4.5mm and the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra reaching 4.1mm when fully unfolded. Considering that the Galaxy S25 Edge was 5.8mm, the company’s best foldables reaching nearly 2mm thinner is an achievement.

So Apple is relegating its iPhone 18 to 2027, likely earlier in the year. That’s around when it launched the iPhone 17E (in March 2026), so the company could be bundling its baseline iPhone 18 and likely even cheaper iPhone 18E in the same event. This would set a new schedule for Apple: more affordable phones earlier in spring, and then the next generation of its top-tier premium iPhones in its typical September launch window. This gives each lineup its own well-deserved attention and spotlight, IDC’s Popal noted.

“Apple is spreading its portfolio to a wider consumer demographic and giving consumers more choice, which is always good for business,” Popal said.

The iPhone 18 could be accompanied by an iPhone 18E and even an iPhone Air 2, Popal predicts. Even if these will conceivably be cheaper than the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo models, they’ll still likely be pricier than their predecessors — because Apple’s already made its older iPhones more expensive.

Typically, when Apple announces a new standard iPhone, the previous version is discounted $100 and sold for another year or so. Instead, it’s raised iPhone 17‘s price at $900, ripping the band-aid off now before the next baseline iPhone launches at a higher price. This could better distinguish it from the traditionally cheaper E-series phones like the $600 iPhone 17E, which appeal to a different, more budget-conscious segment of the market, Popal believes. Apple knows consumers will feel the sticker shock of the price increases, which is why it’s retained the iPhone 16 in its current lineup — though it, too, has gotten a bump back up to its original $800 price, a change from the discounted $700 it had been up until this morning.

That twice-per-year release schedule matches what Samsung has done for years, with an event in January for its premium flat phones and then another in August for its foldables. We’ll have to see whether Apple turns its spring showcase into an announcement event — perhaps bundling it with the Macs and home accessories that have sometimes simply launched via press release. It’s a brand new day for Apple, and anything is possible under Ternus. We’ll just have to see what’s in store for iPhones, folding and flat.

Tech.title: As Apple Prepares Its Next Tech-Defining Moment, Look Back at Major Milestones From Then to Now
Tech.content:
It’s hard to imagine a world without smartphones, but when Apple launched the first iPhone in 2007, it was no guaranteed success. In fact, a smorgasbord of haters was predicting it would fail badly. Oops!

The CNET Group brands — CNET, Lifehacker, Mashable, PCMag, Popular Science and ZDNET — have been covering Apple news and product releases for combined centuries. We were there when Apple announced the MacBook switch to Intel chips in 2005 and when Tim Cook first introduced the Apple Watch as “one more thing” back in April 2015.

As Apple prepares more groundbreaking announcements for its Sept. 9 fall live event, the whole CNET Group is looking back at the most critical coverage moments for the tech giant and what its history might tell us about what comes next.

Check us out every day through the September Apple event and beyond for an “Apple a Day” highlight from the past. And if you think you know what Apple will do at that event, be sure to enter our Big Guessing Game contest for a chance to win a new Apple Watch.

Tech.title: ‘P-Valley’ Season 3 Sets Release Date on Starz. Catch a New Trailer, Details Here
Tech.content:
Uncle Clifford will be turning the lights back on at The Pynk, because P-Valley season 3 is due to arrive on Starz in December. Created by Katori Hall, the popular drama has been absent from TV screens since season 2 ended its run in summer 2022, leaving fans to wonder about the fate of the Chucalissa strip club and its colorful characters, like Nicco Annan’s Uncle Clifford, Mercedes (Brandee Evans), Keyshawn (Shannon Thornton) and Lil’ Murda (J. Alphonse Nicholson). The first two episodes of the new season will debut on Friday, Dec. 4.

A finale cliffhanger at the end of the last season saw Tyler Lepley’s Diamond stuck in a car trunk as part of a gang’s revenge plan. Since then, fans have joked about whether he’s still alive due to the show’s lengthy hiatus. It’s unclear whether Lepley and co-star Miracle Watts, who played Big Bone, are returning in season 3. Meanwhile, Keyshawn’s failed attempt to escape her abuser led to a sad turn of events where she wound up in jail. The series will pick up where it left off and take viewers through to the conclusion of this story in this final season.

First look photos for P-Valley, season 3, show Mercedes, Keyshawn, Lil’ Murda and cowboy-costumed Kiwi, Roulette and Big L. Starz

Hall, who is the showrunner and creator, penned a heartfelt letter to fans, acknowledging the time it took to bring P-Valley from its roots as a stage play to its curtain call on Starz.

“Adapting my play into three seasons of television over the past decade has been the ride of a lifetime, filled with massive highs and lows that echo the ever-changing TV landscape,” Hall wrote. “The rarest honor a showrunner can have in today’s industry is to end a series on her own terms. This is why I chose to say goodbye with grace, grit and glitter, lowering the curtain on P-Valley at season 3 with a farewell y’all truly deserve.”

Season 3 also features Gail Bean, Harriett D. Foy, Psalms Salazar, Morocco Omari, Dominic DeVore, Jordan M. Cox, Thomas Q. Jones and Loretta Devine among the cast. The first two seasons of P-Valley are available to binge-watch on Starz.

Tech.title: Apple Watch Ultra 4 Hands-On: A Closer Look at Its Biggest Upgrades
Tech.content:
The Apple Watch Ultra 4, which starts at $799, has a new processor and reengineered health sensors that unlock more frequent health measurements, new recovery insights and AI-powered audio tools.

I got to test the Apple Watch Ultra 4 to see some of these new features in action in a demo room at the Steve Jobs Theater after the company’s Surprise and Shine event on Wednesday.

At first glance, the Ultra 4 looked and felt very familiar. But when I flipped it over, the difference was obvious. Compared with the sensor array on my Ultra 3, the back of the Ultra 4 looks almost flower-like, with 32 electrodes resembling the thin petals of a gerbera daisy replacing the previous ring of two. That gives the electrodes more surface area to capture ECG readings. Apple also rearranged the green and infrared LEDs into a new, smaller circular cluster in the middle of the petals with smaller dots.

Those redesigned sensors, combined with the new S11 processor, allow the Ultra 4 to take heart-rate readings every 5 seconds, compared with roughly every 5 minutes on previous models. The same goes for heart-rate variability, or HRV, which the watch can now measure every 5 minutes instead of just a few times throughout the day. Apple says the increased sampling frequency makes it the most accurate wearable on the market. It also powers a new Readiness score, a measure of how well your body is recovering from exercise during the day.

The sensors on the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 are different from those on earlier models. Apple/Screenshot by CNET

Unlike many wearables that give you a recovery or readiness score based largely on what happened overnight, Apple’s score changes throughout the day. Because the Ultra 4 samples heart rate and HRV more frequently, Readiness can react in real time as you drain or recharge your body.

I also found a new Daytime toggle in the Vitals app on the watch that lets you view daytime heart rate and HRV alongside the overnight measurements already available in Vitals, like temperature and SpO2. Both features require seven days of data to unlock, so I’ll need at least a week to test them and see whether they align with how I’m feeling, which has often been at odds with what I’ve seen on other devices.

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 and Series 12 are available for preorder and will arrive on Sept. 18.

Apple/Screenshot by CNET

Your Apple Watch is listening, but not recording

The Ultra 4 and Series 12 also gained new Audio Intelligence features, including one called Live Rewind that lets you jump back and hear the previous 15 seconds of a conversation with just a press of the digital crown. During my live demo, the transcription was spot-on, despite the noisy environment.

The other AI audio feature is Siri Recap, which lets the watch actively listen and detect conversations throughout the day (or at set times) to generate high-level notes and summaries from meetings or other conversations you may want to revisit. You can trigger a recap manually or schedule one ahead of time.

Apple says it designed the features so audio isn’t stored and instead only keeps the transcripts you save, which only you can access.



S11 chip absorbs background tasks

The S11 chip is a big part of how the watch pulls this all off without destroying its battery life. It has a dedicated always-on processor that handles background tasks such as heart-rate monitoring and audio processing without constantly waking the main processor.

Apple/Screenshot by CNET

Battery life remains one of the biggest reasons to choose an Ultra over the flagship Series 12. Apple also slightly increased the battery capacity this year, bringing the estimated battery life to roughly 50 hours, up from 42 hours on the Ultra 3.

That’s still nowhere near the weeks of battery life you can get from some Garmin watches. But Apple seems to be making a different trade-off that favors accuracy (via more frequent reads) over saving on battery life.

Battery trade-offs for endurance athletes

For endurance athletes, though, the more interesting upgrade is its battery life during workouts.

The Ultra 4 now has two sports-specific low-battery modes meant to keep it tracking for much longer without sacrificing core fitness metrics.

Extended Workout mode: Can track a workout for up to 25 hours by turning off the always-on display and running-form metrics, while keeping GPS and heart-rate tracking at full fidelity.

Can track a workout for up to 25 hours by turning off the always-on display and running-form metrics, while keeping GPS and heart-rate tracking at full fidelity. Max Extended Workout mode: Pushes tracking to as long as 48 hours. GPS still records at 1-second intervals, although it drops from multiband to single-band GPS and heart rate shows a rolling 5-minute average instead of the live metric. The mode also disables custom workouts, alerts and splits, along with certain other metrics.

Apple is essentially letting athletes choose which compromises they’re willing to make depending on how long they need the watch to last.

My take

The 49mm screen and rugged build are too bulky for me to use the Ultra as my everyday Apple Watch. But the new readiness features, better battery life and more accurate data collection make it tempting for endurance athletes and anyone upgrading from an older Ultra.

Rather than compete head-on with sports watches like Garmin or Coros, Apple is betting that athletes will trade some of that battery life for subscription-free data, high-accuracy tracking and a watch that can now make better use of all that data throughout the day.
